title: World-Model-Aware Responsibility Allocation in Heterogeneous Logistics Systems
summary: Logistics systems increasingly mix \emph{autonomous logistic equipment} (ALE) with non-autonomous machinery under a central control system (CS), where the best decision-maker depends on who holds the most current world model, yet authority is fixed at design time. When an ALE's local model and the CS global model diverge, both act on incompatible beliefs and produce deadlocks that resource-based handling neither explains nor prevents. We propose the World-Model-Aware Responsibility Framework (WMARF), which assigns authority dynamically from CS world-model quality and equipment automation level, and classifies deadlocks by the state of authority -- none, in transition, or divergent. In a discrete-event simulation of two ALE converging on a semi-automated transfer point, reproduced over the VDA~5050 interface, a divergence deadlock under static control is prevented by a proximity-triggered handoff. Because authority follows information quality rather than a shared protocol, the scheme stays valid as autonomy grows.

AI.tldr: WMARF dynamically assigns decision authority based on world-model quality and equipment autonomy level, classifying deadlocks by authority state and preventing divergence deadlocks through proximity-triggered handoffs in mixed-autonomy logistics systems.
AI.motivation: In mixed-autonomy logistics systems, static authority assignment causes deadlocks when autonomous logistic equipment (ALE) local models diverge from the central control system's global model. Existing resource-based deadlock handling cannot explain or prevent these divergence deadlocks, necessitating a dynamic authority framework tied to information quality.
AI.method: The World-Model-Aware Responsibility Framework (WMARF) dynamically assigns authority based on two factors: (1) the quality of the central system's world model and (2) the equipment's automation level. Deadlocks are classified by authority state: none, in transition, or divergent. Validation uses discrete-event simulation of two ALE converging on a semi-automated transfer point, reproduced over the VDA 5050 interface, with a proximity-triggered handoff mechanism preventing divergence deadlocks.
AI.result: Under static control, divergence deadlocks occurred. WMARF's proximity-triggered handoff successfully prevented these deadlocks by dynamically shifting authority to the entity with superior information quality at the critical moment.
AI.conclusion: Because WMARF ties authority to information quality rather than a fixed shared protocol, it remains valid as autonomy levels increase, offering a scalable solution for evolving mixed-autonomy logistics environments.

title: Multi-Scale Equilibrium under Variable Indicator Dimensionality: Faithful Reduction of Dynamic Attractors in Urban Mobility Systems
summary: Equilibrium analysis of urban mobility systems is formulated in a high-dimensional indicator space, whilst data availability varies sharply across cities and disruption contexts. This paper gives a formal treatment of that mismatch. It presents a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor for disrupted urban mobility, in which a fast performance layer relaxes towards an indicator-dependent target, a slow strategic layer supplies a joint traffic, modal and learning fixed point, and antifragility is classified through a statistical decision rule on the post-to-baseline performance ratio. It then characterises when a lower-dimensional indicator projection is faithful to this equilibrium structure, establishing four results: conditions for exact and approximate projectability of the attractor with an explicit error bound; preservation of the coupled two-layer fixed point up to a contraction boundary; the retained Fisher information and decision power of any indicator support under a measurement model on observable urban indicators; and a one-sided restoration-time bias, whereby reduced monitoring can only understate recovery duration. A simulation study on three stylised pilot-city configurations verifies each result, and shows that two observable channels suffice for the candidate classification target where the indicator catalogue permits. The framework gives city authorities a principled basis for deciding which indicators must be maintained.

AI.tldr: The paper formally addresses the mismatch between high-dimensional equilibrium models of urban mobility and the variable availability of data across cities. It develops a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor framework, derives four theoretical results on when lower-dimensional indicator projections remain faithful to the full equilibrium structure, and validates findings via simulations on three pilot-city configurations.
AI.motivation: Urban mobility equilibrium analysis requires high-dimensional indicator spaces, but data availability varies greatly across cities and disruption contexts. There is no formal treatment of when reduced indicator sets can faithfully represent the underlying equilibrium dynamics, creating a risk of biased inference for city authorities making resource-allocation and monitoring decisions.
AI.method: The authors construct a dynamic multi-layer equilibrium attractor with (1) a fast performance layer that relaxes toward an indicator-dependent target, (2) a slow strategic layer supplying a joint traffic-modal-learning fixed point, and (3) an antifragility classification via a statistical decision rule on the post-to-baseline performance ratio. They then derive four formal results: exact/approximate projectability conditions with error bounds, preservation of the two-layer fixed point up to a contraction boundary, retained Fisher information and decision power under a measurement model, and a one-sided restoration-time bias. A simulation study on three stylised pilot-city configurations is conducted.
AI.result: Four principal results are established: (1) conditions for exact and approximate projectability of the attractor with explicit error bounds; (2) the coupled two-layer fixed point is preserved up to a well-defined contraction boundary; (3) Fisher information and decision power are retained for any indicator support under the measurement model; and (4) reduced monitoring can only understate recovery duration (one-sided restoration-time bias). Simulations verify each result and demonstrate that two observable channels suffice for the candidate classification target where the indicator catalogue permits.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides city authorities with a principled, theoretically grounded basis for deciding which indicators must be maintained in disrupted urban mobility monitoring, showing that even sparse indicator sets can retain decision-relevant information if selected consistent with the equilibrium structure's projectability conditions.

title: Randomized routing strategies of fleets of CAVs may prove market efficient
comment: 13 pages, 9 Figures, accepted to 14th Symposium of the European Association for Research in Transportation (hEART 2026)
summary: In future cities every driver may own a vehicle which could be either independently driven (HDV), or autonomously routed and piloted (CAV). The autonomous operations could be handled by a few competing companies. What is the market structure which would make this market aligned with city goals? In this paper we discuss a variant of the emerging market of collectively routed fleets of CAVs, where revenue for fleet operators is proportional to market share. We provide benchmark scenarios to compare the routing algorithms. We present several routing algorithms and demonstrate that, when the attitudes of human drivers towards CAVs exhibit significant diversity, randomised CAV routing, resulting in unpredictable travel times for HDVs, is more efficient than routing proportional to system optimum/user equilibrium. Based on this, we propose to improve the design of the market by augmenting the market-share objective with mean systemwide travel time in order to limit antisocial randomised strategies of fleet operators and drive the competition towards social welfare oriented cooperation.

AI.tldr: This paper examines a future urban mobility market where competing CAV fleet operators earn revenue proportional to market share. It demonstrates that randomized CAV routing—which creates unpredictable travel times for human-driven vehicles (HDVs)—can be more efficient than standard routing when HDV drivers show diverse attitudes toward CAVs. The authors propose augmenting the market-share objective with mean systemwide travel time to curb antisocial randomized strategies and steer competition toward socially beneficial cooperation.
AI.motivation: In future smart cities, multiple private fleet operators may manage competing CAV fleets, each maximizing its own market share. The authors investigate what market structure aligns operator incentives with city-wide goals such as minimizing congestion, given that unregulated competition could lead to inefficient or antisocial routing strategies.
AI.method: The authors define a market where CAV fleet operators earn revenue proportional to market share. They develop benchmark scenarios to compare routing algorithms, including system optimum (SO), user equilibrium (UE), and randomized routing. They model heterogeneous HDV driver attitudes toward CAVs and analyze how different routing strategies affect overall system efficiency, measured by mean travel time.
AI.result: When HDV drivers exhibit significant diversity in their attitudes toward CAVs, randomized CAV routing—which introduces unpredictability in HDV travel times—proves more efficient than routing proportional to system optimum or user equilibrium. However, unregulated randomized strategies can become antisocial. Augmenting market-share objectives with a mean systemwide travel time metric helps limit such behavior.
AI.conclusion: Market design for CAV fleet competition should incorporate social welfare metrics alongside profit motives. Specifically, tying operator revenue not only to market share but also to systemwide travel time can discourage antisocial randomized routing and foster cooperation that benefits both operators and the city.

title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments whose incentives can shape their behavior. We introduce The Energy Society, a minimal survival economy for studying how competitive and cooperative incentives affect emergent behavior when inference cost is directly tied to survival: Agents spend energy based on model size when generating tokens, regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations, and deactivate if their energy reaches zero. We compare competitive and cooperative objectives against a baseline setting and several control variants. Across experiments, larger models consistently consume the most energy and spend more energy than they gain, even in those settings where token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially alter behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes at the cost of their own survival, and job allocation changes. Ablations reveal that allowing agents to recommend actions to each other supports coordination and ambitious job selection, while memory helps agents calibrate risk from past outcomes. Agents rarely choose direct sabotage, but show more subtle signs of self-serving behavior in the competitive setting. The Energy Society is a compact testbed for studying the interaction between token costs and group incentives under a survival pressure. Source code is available at https://github.com/LucasBergholdt/EnergySociety

AI.tldr: The Energy Society is a minimal multi-agent testbed where LLM-based agents face a survival economy: token generation costs energy (scaled by model size), energy is regained through jobs or donations, and zero energy means deactivation. The paper compares competitive vs. cooperative incentives and finds that larger models consistently consume more energy than they gain, cooperation leads to altruistic donations and better job allocation, and design choices like inter-agent recommendations and memory support coordination.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, their behavior is shaped by environmental incentives. However, there is limited understanding of how inference costs—directly tied to survival—interact with competitive or cooperative incentives to shape emergent agent behavior. The authors aim to fill this gap with a controlled, minimal testbed.
AI.method: The authors introduce The Energy Society, a survival economy where agents: (1) spend energy per token generated, proportional to model size; (2) regain energy by completing jobs or receiving donations; and (3) deactivate if energy reaches zero. They compare competitive vs. cooperative objective conditions against a baseline, along with ablation variants. Key ablations include removing inter-agent action recommendations and removing memory. Behavior is analyzed through energy consumption patterns, donation dynamics, job allocation strategies, and signs of self-serving or sabotage behavior.
AI.result: Larger models consistently consume the most energy and run net-negative (spend more than they gain), even when token cost is not size-dependent. Cooperative incentives substantially shift behavior: agents donate to reactivate others, sometimes sacrificing their own survival; job allocation also changes qualitatively. Inter-agent recommendations support coordination and more ambitious job selection; memory helps agents calibrate risk based on past outcomes. Agents rarely engage in direct sabotage but exhibit subtle self-serving behaviors under competitive conditions.
AI.conclusion: The Energy Society provides a compact, reproducible testbed for studying how token-based inference costs and group incentives interact under survival pressure. The findings highlight that model size, cooperation mechanisms, recommendations, and memory all significantly shape emergent multi-agent economic behavior.

title: Just Keep Prompting: Evaluating Repetitive Socratic Prompting in VLMs
summary: Deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in real-world settings requires not only strong visual reasoning but also stability under sustained conversational pressure. We introduce Just Keep Prompting (JKP), a multi-turn evaluation framework that measures VLM epistemic stability when users repeatedly challenge, question, or contradict a model's answer. JKP probes models for up to 10 follow-up turns using three strategies: Adversarial Negation (repeated rejection), Pure Socratic Interrogation (repeated calls to reassess certainty), and Context-Aware Socratic Summarization (reflecting the model's prior rationale back before asking for reconsideration). We evaluate GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen3-VL-30B on a subset of the STAR benchmark across 720 multi-turn runs. Aggregate accuracy changes modestly from Turn 0 to Turn 10, but trajectory-level analysis reveals substantial instability: correct answers regress, wrong answers recover, and many runs exhibit repeated answer flipping. Repeated prompting has bounded upside and often acts as a destabilizer rather than a reasoning aid. The effect is strongly model-dependent: Qwen3-VL-30B achieves the highest final accuracy but becomes confidently wrong under direct contradiction; Gemini 2.5 Pro is comparatively stable but token-expensive; GPT-4o is the most brittle and oscillatory. These findings reveal that multi-turn VLM evaluation captures not just additional reasoning but pressure-response profiles: how models trade off visual grounding, calibration, and conversational compliance under repeated challenge.

AI.tldr: Just Keep Prompting (JKP) is a multi-turn evaluation framework that tests VLM epistemic stability by repeatedly challenging model answers across up to 10 turns. Evaluated on GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen3-VL-30B, results show that repeated prompting often destabilizes models rather than improving reasoning, with strongly model-dependent pressure-response profiles.
AI.motivation: Real-world VLM deployment requires stability under sustained conversational pressure. Prior benchmarks evaluate static, single-turn visual reasoning but overlook how models behave when users repeatedly question, contradict, or challenge answers — a gap that obscures epistemic fragility in practical use.
AI.method: The JKP framework tests VLMs over up to 10 follow-up turns using three probing strategies: (1) Adversarial Negation — repeatedly rejecting answers; (2) Pure Socratic Interrogation — repeatedly asking the model to reassess its certainty; (3) Context-Aware Socratic Summarization — reflecting the model's prior rationale back before soliciting reconsideration. Evaluation covers 720 multi-turn runs on the STAR benchmark subset across GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Qwen3-VL-30B.
AI.result: Aggregate accuracy shifts modestly from Turn 0 to Turn 10, but trajectory-level analysis reveals substantial instability: correct answers regress, wrong answers recover, and repeated answer-flipping is common. Repeated prompting has bounded upside and often destabilizes reasoning. Effects are model-dependent: Qwen3-VL-30B achieves highest final accuracy but becomes confidently wrong under contradiction; Gemini 2.5 Pro is comparatively stable but token-expensive; GPT-4o is the most brittle and oscillatory.
AI.conclusion: Multi-turn evaluation captures not merely additional reasoning but pressure-response profiles — how models trade off visual grounding, calibration, and conversational compliance under repeated challenge. These profiles are critical for safe VLM deployment and reveal that repeated prompting is an unreliable strategy for improving reasoning.

title: "Trust Junk" Leads to Unjustified Support for Highly Discriminatory Predictive Models
summary: The persuasive power of data visualizations can go awry: for instance, in an explainable AI (XAI) context, visualizations can produce over-trust of predictive models. In this paper, we use a crowdsourced study to show that providing accurate (but superfluous or irrelevant) data in a model explanation can, in fact, result in unjustified trust and other positive beliefs about a model, even when the model is patently discriminatory and unfair. Our results suggest that XAI designers and developers need to consider the implicit or explicit rhetorics of their work, and beware of the potential of visualizations to imbue models with unearned trust.

AI.tldr: Excessive or irrelevant data in explainable AI visualizations can generate unwarranted trust in discriminatory models, revealing a persuasive rhetoric effect that designers must guard against.
AI.motivation: The authors observed that data visualizations, while intended to provide transparency in XAI, may inadvertently persuade users to over-trust predictive models. They aimed to investigate whether the mere presence of accurate but superfluous visual data in model explanations can produce unjustified positive beliefs, even when the model is clearly unfair and discriminatory.
AI.method: A crowdsourced user study was conducted in which participants were presented with explanations of a predictive model that was patently discriminatory and unfair. The explanations included accurate but superfluous or irrelevant data visualizations. Researchers then measured participants' trust and other positive beliefs about the model to determine whether the presence of such visualizations influenced perceptions despite the model's discriminatory nature.
AI.result: The study demonstrated that providing accurate but irrelevant data in model explanations led to unjustified trust and positive beliefs about the model, even when the model was clearly discriminatory. This indicates that visualizations can exert a persuasive, rhetorical effect that overrides rational assessment of model fairness.
AI.conclusion: XAI designers and developers must critically examine the implicit and explicit rhetorics embedded in their visualization choices. There is a tangible risk that visualizations can lend models an unearned aura of credibility and trustworthiness, necessitating greater caution in how explanatory data is presented.

title: Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest
comment: Accepted at KDD '26: The 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
summary: Pinterest is where people turn inspiration into action as users browse ideas, then take steps toward realization, often by discovering shoppable content. To support this journey, we must distribute commerce content when it helps, not when it distracts. We frame this as a causal decision of triggering shopping candidate generators in early retrieval and deploy a production system at Pinterest that learns personalized and contextualized triggering policies. A deep multi-task model jointly predicts outcomes and uplift of multiple events, trained with a doubly-robust pseudo-outcome alongside calibrated outcome losses for stable, single-robust uplift learning. A randomized data logging supplies counterfactual coverage, and the model is evaluated by both regular and reverse metrics for full assessment. A linear-time offline replay is designed to select thresholds and forecast policy impact with extremely high consistency with online results. For productionization, the model runs in parallel with remote retrieval calls without end-to-end latency regression. At web scale, we cut shopping triggers by up to 85% while holding key shopping sessions neutral, improving important total sessions (+0.26%) and Pin saves (+1.10%), with significant infrastructure savings. By unifying deep causal learning with reliable offline replay and demonstrating production-grade deployment, this work provides a generally practical recipe for early-retrieval optimizations in modern cascading recommenders beyond shopping, aligning exploration and cost with user intent at scale.

AI.tldr: Pinterest deploys a causal deep learning system to decide when to trigger shopping content retrieval, reducing unnecessary triggers by up to 85% while maintaining shopping engagement and improving overall user metrics, with a practical offline replay method for policy evaluation.
AI.motivation: In Pinterest's cascading recommender, shopping candidate generators should be invoked only when helpful, not distracting. The core problem is deciding causally whether to trigger commerce retrieval early in the funnel, balancing relevance, user intent, and infrastructure cost at web scale.
AI.method: A deep multi-task model jointly predicts outcomes and uplift using doubly-robust pseudo-outcomes with calibrated outcome losses for stable single-robust uplift learning. Randomized data logging provides counterfactual coverage. A linear-time offline replay selects thresholds and forecasts policy impact with high online consistency. The model runs in parallel with remote retrieval calls to avoid latency regression.
AI.result: Shopping triggers reduced by up to 85% while key shopping sessions remained neutral. Total sessions improved by +0.26%, Pin saves by +1.10%, with significant infrastructure savings. Offline replay showed extremely high consistency with online results.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a general, production-grade recipe for early-retrieval optimizations in cascading recommenders, unifying deep causal learning with reliable offline evaluation, applicable beyond shopping to align exploration and cost with user intent at scale.

title: Exploring Delay-based PUFs for Energy-Efficient Low-Overhead Security of Wearable Devices
summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) was introduced almost two decades ago. In the past two decades, technology has seen huge advancements. Many devices have become powerful and have less power consumption. Many IoT architectures and environments were introduced to help make life easier, especially in wearable devices. The market for these wearable devices has constantly increased over the years and is expected to reach its maximum in the next couple of years. They also pose a threat to users' privacy and security because they constantly store and transmit personal information such as location, heart rate, and other sensitive data. Therefore, addressing the security vulnerabilities is a crucial aspect of this research. This paper presents a hardware-assisted, energy-efficient, low-overhead security solution for wearable devices. Specifically, two Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) architectures: Arbiter PUF and Hybrid Oscillator Arbiter (HOA) PUF are analyzed for integration in IoT systems. The result shows that Arbiter PUF consumes 25 $μ$W, whereas HOA PUF consumes only 2.7 $μ$W to generate keys for cryptographic purposes. These architectures introduce minimal power overhead while providing robust security, making them well suited for resource-constrained IoT ecosystems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hardware-assisted, energy-efficient security solution for wearable IoT devices using Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs). Two PUF architectures — Arbiter PUF and Hybrid Oscillator Arbiter (HOA) PUF — are analyzed, with HOA PUF consuming only 2.7 μW compared to 25 μW for Arbiter PUF, demonstrating minimal power overhead suitable for resource-constrained IoT ecosystems.
AI.motivation: Wearable IoT devices have seen explosive market growth but pose significant privacy and security threats due to continuous collection and transmission of sensitive personal data (location, heart rate, etc.). Given the resource-constrained nature of these devices, there is a pressing need for security solutions that are both robust and energy-efficient, with minimal hardware overhead.
AI.method: The authors present a hardware-assisted security approach leveraging Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) for cryptographic key generation. Two specific PUF architectures are implemented and comparatively analyzed: (1) Arbiter PUF, and (2) Hybrid Oscillator Arbiter (HOA) PUF. Both are evaluated for their suitability in IoT wearable systems, with particular focus on power consumption and integration feasibility.
AI.result: The comparative analysis shows that Arbiter PUF consumes 25 μW for key generation, while the HOA PUF achieves the same cryptographic purpose with only 2.7 μW — approximately a 9× reduction in power consumption. Both architectures introduce minimal power overhead relative to typical wearable device budgets while providing robust hardware-rooted security.
AI.conclusion: HOA PUF is the superior choice for wearable IoT devices, offering strong security guarantees with ultra-low power consumption (2.7 μW). Both PUF architectures are well-suited for resource-constrained IoT ecosystems, demonstrating that hardware-assisted security can be achieved without compromising the stringent energy budgets of wearables.

title: Beyond Object Validation: Relational Conformance in Multi-Artifact Agent Releases
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Schema Sandbox Research Preprint
summary:
Agent systems validate inputs, tool calls, and generated objects. The final package often escapes the same scrutiny. In one DRSS release, the ledger supported 60 points and a failed certificate; the report announced a 100-point Gold Path. Every local gate was green. The package contradicted itself.
  We study that failure alongside Schema Docs, where similar faults became product contracts, and Brand Shuttle GEO, where evidence is turned into repair work. The result is a candidate Schema-SIP Relational Conformance profile (SIP-RC). It models a release as a graph: claims point to evidence, decisions carry bounded authority, derived artifacts retain their execution conditions and lineage, and published bytes must match the package that was checked. Hard failures cannot be averaged away, and a validator recomputes critical decisions on a separate path. The paper establishes the failure class and shows that several mechanisms are practical. Whether the full profile performs better than existing checks remains an open experiment.

AI.tldr: A failure class is identified where final release packages contradict internally-passed local checks. The paper proposes SIP-RC, a relational conformance profile that models releases as evidence-linked graphs with bounded authority, immutable lineage, and separate-path recomputation, showing practical mechanisms but leaving full-profile efficacy as an open experiment.
AI.motivation: Current agent system validation focuses on inputs, tool calls, and intermediate objects, but the final released package escapes equivalent scrutiny. This gap allows contradictory artifacts—such as a DRSS ledger showing 60 points and a failed certificate while the report claims 100-point Gold Path—to pass local gates while being globally inconsistent. The paper aims to establish this as a distinct failure class and propose structural defenses.
AI.method: The paper studies three case examples: (1) a DRSS release where internal checks passed but the package contradicted itself; (2) Schema Docs, where similar faults hardened into product contracts; and (3) Brand Shuttle GEO, where evidence is redirected into repair work. From these, it derives a candidate Schema-SIP Relational Conformance profile (SIP-RC) that models a release as a graph with claims linked to evidence, decisions carrying bounded authority, derived artifacts preserving execution conditions and lineage, and published bytes matching the checked package. A validator recomputes critical decisions on a separate path, and hard failures are prevented from being averaged away.
AI.result: The paper establishes the failure class of package-level contradictions passing local gate checks and demonstrates that several of the proposed SIP-RC mechanisms are practically implementable. However, whether the full profile outperforms existing checks remains an open experimental question.
AI.conclusion: Package-level relational conformance is an under-examined vulnerability in agent systems. SIP-RC offers a structured defense through graph-based modeling, evidence linkage, bounded authority, lineage preservation, and independent recomputation. The mechanisms are practical, but empirical validation of the complete profile is deferred to future experiments.

title: Position: Explainability Research Must Prioritize Foundations over Ad-hoc Methods
comment: Accepted to ICML 2026 Position Paper Track
summary: Despite the proliferation of Explainable AI (XAI) techniques -- from feature attributions to sparse autoencoders -- explanations rarely influence real-world workflows. In practice, they are often generated and discarded without guiding meaningful action. This gap reflects foundational shortcomings: research has not yet established methodologies for integrating explanations into end-to-end, human-in-the-loop systems. This position paper argues that the machine learning community must pivot from ad-hoc XAI methods toward addressing foundational & structural challenges, including unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation objectives, and the absence of pipelines for explanation-driven feedback. We support this claim through an analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers and a survey of XAI practitioners, revealing recurring issues that limit cumulative progress. We conclude by outlining a practical checklist designed to shift XAI toward a more human-centered, action-oriented paradigm. By emphasizing foundational clarity over the development of ad-hoc methods, we hope to provide a roadmap for integrating explanations into actionable, feedback-driven AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that XAI research suffers from foundational shortcomings—unclear problem formulations, vague evaluation criteria, and lack of feedback pipelines—that prevent explanations from influencing real-world workflows. Through analysis of top-tier ML papers and a practitioner survey, the authors advocate shifting from ad-hoc methods toward a human-centered, action-oriented paradigm, concluding with a practical checklist.
AI.motivation: Despite the abundance of XAI techniques, explanations are rarely integrated into real-world decision-making; they are generated and discarded without guiding action. This disconnect stems from the field's failure to address foundational issues such as ill-defined problems, underspecified evaluation objectives, and the absence of explanation-driven feedback loops.
AI.method: The authors adopt a position-paper approach combining: (1) an analysis of recent papers from ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR to identify recurring shortcomings in XAI research, and (2) a survey of XAI practitioners to capture real-world perspectives on the gap between explanation generation and actionable use.
AI.result: The analysis reveals persistent issues across top-venue publications: ambiguous problem formulations, evaluation metrics misaligned with practical utility, and a systemic lack of pipelines that close the loop from explanation to action. The practitioner survey corroborates these findings, confirming that explanations rarely influence downstream workflows.
AI.conclusion: The ML community should pivot from developing ad-hoc XAI methods toward resolving foundational and structural challenges. The authors propose a practical checklist to guide researchers toward human-centered, action-oriented XAI, emphasizing problem clarity, aligned evaluation, and explanation-driven feedback as prerequisites for cumulative progress.

title: Intelligent Three Level Learning Architecture for Autonomous UAV Swarms in Search and Rescue
summary:
This paper presents a novel three level hierarchical learning architecture for autonomous UAV swarms performing search and rescue operations. Unlike conventional approaches that apply a single learning paradigm across all hierarchy levels, the proposed architecture integrates three qualitatively different learning mechanisms corresponding to the biological hierarchy of reflexes, skills, and reasoning such as Hebbian neuroplasticity for individual agent adaptation, multi agent reinforcement learning with graph neural networks and behavior trees for tactical coordination, and model agnostic meta learning with BDI reasoning and a digital twin for strategic decision making.
  The architecture is formalized through twenty two architectural contracts organized across six components such as BDI, Behavior Trees, GNN, MARL, Neuroplasticity, Meta Learning that collectively provide six classes of formal guarantees such as safety, budget correctness, optimality, liveness, starvation freedom, and inter level consistency.
  We introduce Swarm Meta Cognition as a compositional property arising from the structured interaction of all three levels, enabling the swarm to monitor its own cognitive state and switch between cognitive strategies. Five constructive progress functions for SAR task types bridge the gap between abstract optimization theory and concrete operational scenarios.
  The main integration theorem establishes that when all contracts are satisfied, the hybrid neuro-symbolic system preserves all six guarantee classes. For the dynamic case with active learning, five new contracts extend the framework with three additional guarantees such as cognitive resilience, graceful degradation, and monotonic meta improvement. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the architecture addresses five fundamental limitations of existing hierarchical RL approaches.

AI.tldr: A three-level hierarchical learning architecture for autonomous UAV swarms in search and rescue, integrating Hebbian neuroplasticity, MARL with GNNs/behavior trees, and MAML with BDI reasoning/digital twins. The framework is formalized through 22 architectural contracts providing six classes of formal guarantees, introduces Swarm Meta-Cognition as an emergent compositional property, and proves via an integration theorem that all guarantees are preserved when contracts are satisfied.
AI.motivation: Existing hierarchical RL approaches suffer from five fundamental limitations: they typically apply a single learning paradigm uniformly across all hierarchy levels, fail to provide formal guarantees across safety/budget/optimality/liveness dimensions, lack inter-level consistency, cannot support dynamic strategy switching based on cognitive state, and do not bridge abstract optimization theory with concrete operational SAR scenarios.
AI.method: The architecture structures three levels: (1) Individual agent adaptation via Hebbian neuroplasticity; (2) Tactical coordination via MARL with graph neural networks and behavior trees; (3) Strategic decision-making via model-agnostic meta-learning with BDI reasoning and a digital twin. Formalization uses 22 architectural contracts across six components (BDI, Behavior Trees, GNN, MARL, Neuroplasticity, Meta-Learning) yielding six guarantee classes (safety, budget correctness, optimality, liveness, starvation freedom, inter-level consistency). Five constructive progress functions map SAR task types to operational scenarios. For dynamic/active learning, five additional contracts provide three further guarantees (cognitive resilience, graceful degradation, monotonic meta-improvement). A main integration theorem proves guarantee preservation under contract satisfaction.
AI.result: The integration theorem establishes that the hybrid neuro-symbolic system preserves all six guarantee classes when all contracts are satisfied. The dynamic extension adds cognitive resilience, graceful degradation, and monotonic meta-improvement guarantees. Theoretical analysis demonstrates resolution of five fundamental limitations in existing hierarchical RL approaches.
AI.conclusion: The three-level biologically-inspired architecture with formal contracts provides a principled framework for autonomous UAV swarms in SAR, offering both rigorous guarantees and adaptive cognitive capabilities through structured inter-level interaction and Swarm Meta-Cognition.

title: Stigmergic Graph Memory: An Environment-Aware Approach for Many-to-Many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery
comment: 16 pages total: 7 pages main text, 2 pages references, and 7 pages appendix
summary: Automated fulfillment warehouses must continuously assign and execute pickup-and-delivery work while avoiding congestion. In many-to-many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD), a request specifies a stock-keeping unit rather than fixed endpoints, requiring the controller to select an agent, source, and destination before path planning. Existing graph-guidance methods primarily influence routing after goals are fixed, leaving endpoint instantiation uninformed by recent traffic. We introduce Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM), a bounded, decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and directed edges to rank feasible endpoints and route preferences without altering collision constraints or planner validity. Across paired request streams on five layouts, three load levels, and 25 seeds per condition, SGM outperforms two reconstructed many-to-many allocation baselines in all 15 map-load conditions, with paired throughput gains of 20.5-36.7%. These results show that recent execution memory can improve warehouse throughput by shaping which feasible goals enter the planner, not only how agents travel to already fixed goals.

AI.tldr: SGM introduces a decaying memory layer recording recent execution signals on warehouse nodes/edges to inform endpoint selection in many-to-many MAPD, achieving 20.5–36.7% throughput gains over baselines by shaping which goals enter the planner rather than only routing to fixed goals.
AI.motivation: In many-to-many MAPD, requests specify SKUs rather than fixed endpoints, requiring the controller to simultaneously select agent, source, and destination. Existing graph-guidance methods only influence routing after goals are fixed, leaving endpoint instantiation uninformed by recent traffic and congestion patterns. This gap motivates a memory mechanism that leverages recent execution history to make smarter endpoint choices.
AI.method: Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM): a bounded, decaying memory layer that records recent execution signals on warehouse nodes and directed edges. These signals are used to rank feasible endpoints and express route preferences without altering collision constraints or planner validity. The approach is evaluated across five warehouse layouts, three load levels, and 25 seeds per condition against two reconstructed many-to-many allocation baselines.
AI.result: SGM outperforms both baselines in all 15 map-load conditions, yielding paired throughput gains of 20.5–36.7% across the full experimental matrix.
AI.conclusion: Recent execution memory significantly improves warehouse throughput by shaping which feasible goals are presented to the planner — demonstrating that endpoint selection informed by traffic history is complementary and superior to approaches that only optimize routing to already-fixed goals.

title: Quantum Compositional NLP for Arabic: Grammar, Morphology, and Word Sense in Circuit Topology
summary: We present the first application of pregroup grammar-based quantum compositional natural language processing (QNLP) to Arabic; a morphologically rich, free-word-order language whose structural complexity provides a uniquely demanding testbed for theories of meaning composition in quantum circuits. Our system converts Arabic sentences into quantum circuits whose topology mirrors grammatical structure: subjects, verbs, and objects become quantum gates, and the typed dependencies between them (the pregroup grammar) determine how those gates are wired together. We conduct three controlled experiments spanning word order, morphological tense, and verb sense disambiguation, comparing quantum circuit methods against classical baselines including AraVec (Arabic word embeddings) and AraBERT (a pre-trained Arabic transformer).

AI.tldr: First application of pregroup grammar-based QNLP to Arabic, converting sentences into quantum circuits where grammar determines gate wiring. Experiments on word order, tense, and verb disambiguation benchmark against AraVec and AraBERT.
AI.motivation: Arabic's morphological richness, free word order, and structural complexity present an unexplored, demanding testbed for quantum compositional NLP. No prior QNLP work has addressed a language with these properties, making it a strong validation case for whether quantum meaning composition generalizes beyond English-like fixed-word-order languages.
AI.method: Sentences are parsed into pregroup grammar types; subjects, verbs, and objects map to quantum gates; type reductions (grammatical dependencies) dictate circuit wiring. Three controlled experiments compare quantum circuit classifiers against AraVec embeddings and AraBERT on word-order variation, morphological tense, and verb sense disambiguation tasks.
AI.result: Not fully specified in the abstract, but the paper reports comparative performance across the three tasks, benchmarking quantum circuit methods against classical baselines (AraVec, AraBERT).
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the abstract, but the work demonstrates feasibility and provides an empirical comparison of quantum-vs-classical compositional methods for a morphologically complex language.

title: From Product-Centred Retrieval to Experience-Led Commerce:Twelve Candidate Design Principles for Fashion E-Commerce User Experience
summary: This paper proposes twelve candidate Experience-Led Commerce design principles for high-constraint, relational fashion e-commerce, surfaced through design-led induction while building VogueDrop, a multi-vendor prototype. The principles address multi-entry discovery, experience continuity, relational exploration, preference sovereignty, evidence-scoped correspondence, recommendation-time feasibility, customer-compatible commercial ranking, adaptive but stable workspaces, attributable transaction authority, outcome-linked learning, shared composition authoring, and accountable human to agent handoff. The paper uses fashion as an intentionally bounded domain in which fit, composition, material, identity-sensitive preference, seller fragmentation, visual correspondence, and delivery timing make the interaction breakdown observable; it does not claim universal applicability across e-commerce. Each candidate principle is paired with a prespecified hypothesis, primary behavioural outcome, and rejection condition. A formative critical-incident study and a preregistered matched-interface experiment are specified, with user-experience and platform-facing outcomes reported separately. No empirical superiority is claimed before those studies are completed.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes twelve candidate design principles for Experience-Led Commerce in high-constraint relational fashion e-commerce, derived from building the VogueDrop prototype. Each principle includes a prespecified hypothesis, behavioral outcome, and rejection condition, with planned formative and preregistered experimental validation.
AI.motivation: Fashion e-commerce presents high-constraint interaction challenges — fit, composition, material, identity-sensitive preferences, seller fragmentation, visual correspondence, and delivery timing — that make breakdowns in user experience readily observable. Existing e-commerce design lacks principles that address relational, experience-led interaction under such constraints, motivating a structured, falsifiable approach to surfacing candidate design principles.
AI.method: Design-led induction through building VogueDrop, a multi-vendor fashion e-commerce prototype. Twelve candidate design principles were surfaced and each paired with a prespecified hypothesis, primary behavioral outcome, and rejection condition. A formative critical-incident study and a preregistered matched-interface experiment are specified to test the principles, with user-experience and platform-facing outcomes reported separately.
AI.result: The paper delivers the twelve candidate principles themselves as the primary output — covering multi-entry discovery, experience continuity, relational exploration, preference sovereignty, evidence-scoped correspondence, recommendation-time feasibility, customer-compatible commercial ranking, adaptive but stable workspaces, attributable transaction authority, outcome-linked learning, shared composition authoring, and accountable human-to-agent handoff. No empirical results are reported, as the validation studies remain to be completed.
AI.conclusion: The twelve principles offer a structured, falsifiable framework for Experience-Led Commerce design in high-constraint relational e-commerce, with fashion serving as a bounded test domain. Empirical validation is pending; no claims of superiority are made until the planned studies are executed.

title: Long-History User Transformers for Real-Time Ad Ranking
summary: Long interaction histories are among the most informative inputs for click-through rate (CTR) prediction, yet in online advertising they collide with a hard serving constraint: ads must be scored within a few hundred milliseconds to enter the auction, which rules out running a large sequence encoder at request time. We describe how a production advertising system resolves this conflict by decoupling history encoding from real-time inference. A high-capacity offline transformer asynchronously encodes the user's full cross-surface interaction history into a compact representation cached in a feature store, while a lightweight runtime model combines this cached representation with the user's most recent events and the request context at serving time. The offline encoder is pre-trained autoregressively on large-scale interaction logs with a dual objective - feedback prediction and next-item prediction - and the two-stage architecture is then fine-tuned for CTR prediction on the target advertising surface. Offline, the split design recovers 72-80% of the quality of a full-history runtime transformer that would be too expensive to deploy, and the cached representation is robust enough to staleness to permit inexpensive refresh policies. In production A/B experiments, the system improves the primary ranking metric by +2.77% in search advertising and +2.1% on the Yandex Advertising Network, with revenue gains of +2.26% and +0.43% respectively - without increasing serving latency.

AI.tldr: A production ad system decouples user history encoding from real-time inference by using an offline transformer to pre-compute compact user representations, cached for lightweight runtime CTR prediction. This achieves 72–80% of a full-history transformer's quality, with significant ranking and revenue gains at zero latency increase.
AI.motivation: Long user interaction histories are highly informative for CTR prediction, but running large sequence encoders at request time is infeasible under the strict latency constraints (hundreds of milliseconds) of online advertising auctions. The authors seek a practical architecture that leverages full cross-surface history without violating serving latency SLOs.
AI.method: A two-stage decoupled architecture: (1) a high-capacity offline transformer pre-trained autoregressively on large-scale interaction logs with dual objectives—feedback prediction and next-item prediction—encodes the user's full cross-surface history into a compact, cacheable representation; (2) a lightweight runtime model combines this cached representation with recent events and request context for real-time CTR prediction. The full pipeline is fine-tuned end-to-end for CTR on the target ad surface. Cached representations tolerate staleness, enabling inexpensive refresh policies.
AI.result: Offline evaluation shows the split design recovers 72–80% of the quality of a full-history runtime transformer. In production A/B tests, ranking metrics improve by +2.77% (search advertising) and +2.1% (Yandex Ad Network), with revenue gains of +2.26% and +0.43% respectively, all without increasing serving latency.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling history encoding from inference via offline pre-computation and caching is a practical and effective strategy for deploying large-scale user-sequence models in latency-constrained ad serving systems, delivering substantial business gains without compromising speed.

title: Better Privacy Guarantees for Larger Groups
comment: 20 pages, 2 tables. Addresses the Pujol and Desfontaines open problem under an explicit zero-tolerant formulation. Revised exposition, added theorem-level summary and references; results unchanged
summary: Pujol and Desfontaines asked whether a private histogram can allow more error on larger counts and use that slack to protect members of larger groups more strongly. We study this question for fixed disjoint groups under add-or-remove-one adjacency. The privacy budget $v(n)$ depends on the affected count, is nonincreasing, and must bound both Rényi-divergence directions at every order. This is the count-dependent form of zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) studied here. The original strict relative-error condition is impossible at count zero. We therefore make the boundary tolerance explicit by requiring $\mathbb{E}\lvert\widehat{x}_i-x_i\rvert < r\max\{x_i,1\}$, without changing the requirement at any positive count. Our main result determines the best dependence on group size. For the upper bound, we directly specialize an existing shifted-transformation framework. The resulting shifted-log Gaussian mechanism has a certified budget $v(n)=O_r(n^{-2})$. Conversely, for every fixed $0<r<1$, any mechanism satisfying the same positive-count utility requirement and count-dependent zCDP must have $v(n)=Ω_r(n^{-2})$. Thus the inverse-square rate is optimal under the repaired formulation. A many-count information argument further places the leading coefficient in the large-count-then-small-error limit between $π/(4e^2)$ and $1/π$, a factor below three. At $r=1$, a data-independent release meets the repaired criterion with zero privacy loss.

AI.tldr: This paper studies count-dependent differential privacy for histograms with fixed disjoint groups. It establishes that the optimal privacy budget v(n) decays as Θ(n⁻²) when requiring expected relative error bounded by r·max{x_i,1}, with a boundary tolerance at count zero. The leading coefficient is pinned between π/(4e²) and 1/π.
AI.motivation: Pujol and Desfontaines asked whether private histograms can allocate more error (i.e., looser privacy) to larger counts, using the slack to better protect larger groups. Prior work imposed a strict relative-error condition that fails at count zero. This paper repairs the formulation by introducing explicit boundary tolerance, and investigates the optimal dependence of the privacy budget on group size under count-dependent zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP).
AI.method: The authors adopt count-dependent zCDP, where the privacy budget v(n) is nonincreasing in the affected count and bounds both directions of Rényi divergence at every order. They specialize an existing shifted-transformation framework to obtain the shifted-log Gaussian mechanism, which achieves v(n) = O_r(n⁻²). For the lower bound, they prove via an information-theoretic argument that any mechanism satisfying the positive-count utility requirement must have v(n) = Ω_r(n⁻²), establishing optimality of the inverse-square rate. They further refine the leading constant using a many-count information argument.
AI.result: The shifted-log Gaussian mechanism achieves certified budget v(n) = O_r(n⁻²). Conversely, for any fixed 0 < r < 1, every mechanism meeting the utility requirement has v(n) = Ω_r(n⁻²), proving the inverse-square rate is optimal. The leading coefficient in the large-count-small-error limit lies between π/(4e²) and 1/π (a factor below 3). At r = 1, a data-independent release satisfies the criterion with zero privacy loss.
AI.conclusion: The inverse-square decay of the privacy budget with group size is both achievable and optimal under the repaired relative-error formulation with boundary tolerance. The tight constant characterization leaves only a small gap (factor < 3) between upper and lower bounds. The r = 1 edge case reveals a trivial regime where no privacy cost is incurred.

title: Natural-Language to SysMLv2 Translation via Conformance-Driven Iterative Refinement
comment: Accepted for presentation and publication in the Proceedings of the ASME 2026 International Design Engineering Technical Conferences and Computers and Information in Engineering Conference (IDETC/CIE 2026)
summary: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) relies on formal system models as primary technical artifacts for representing requirements, structure, and behavior across the system lifecycle. With the standardization of SysMLv2 as a textual language, interest is increasing in translating natural-language descriptions directly into executable models. For practical deployment, generated models must be accepted by industrial modeling environments, not merely satisfy grammar constraints. We present a conformance-checker-driven framework for reliable natural-language-to-SysMLv2 translation that enforces production-level acceptance as the termination condition. The system embeds a SysMLv2 conformance checker within a generate-check-repair loop. Each model is evaluated using the checker, and deterministic diagnostics are incorporated into revisions until zero conformance errors are achieved. Using the production checker as the oracle ensures the framework targets deployability rather than grammar plausibility. We evaluate the approach on the full SysMBench prompt set of 151 prompts across four large language model backends, yielding 604 prompt-model cases. Single-shot generation achieves 51.16% production-conformance acceptance, while our approach achieves 100.00% conformance. By elevating production conformance from a post-processing check to a control mechanism within generation, the framework converts probabilistic outputs into production-accepted SysMLv2 artifacts suitable for loading, visualization, and engineering use.

AI.tldr: A conformance-checker-driven framework with a generate-check-repair loop achieves 100% production-level acceptance for LLM-generated SysMLv2 models, compared to 51.16% for single-shot generation, across 604 prompt-model cases on the SysMBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Despite growing interest in translating natural language to SysMLv2, LLM-generated models typically fail to meet industrial tooling conformance requirements beyond mere grammar correctness. Practical deployment demands that generated models be accepted by production modeling environments, not just syntactically valid. Prior work lacks mechanisms that treat production conformance as a first-class constraint during generation.
AI.method: The framework embeds a production SysMLv2 conformance checker within a generate-check-repair loop. An LLM generates an initial model, the checker evaluates it and produces deterministic diagnostics, and these diagnostics are fed back into a repair step. The loop iterates until zero conformance errors are reached, using the production checker as an oracle. This converts conformance from a post-processing filter into an active control mechanism guiding generation.
AI.result: Evaluated on the full SysMBench prompt set (151 prompts) across four LLM backends, yielding 604 prompt-model cases. Single-shot generation achieved only 51.16% production-conformance acceptance, while the proposed framework reached 100.00% conformance, producing models suitable for loading, visualization, and engineering use in industrial tools.
AI.conclusion: Elevating production conformance from a post-processing check to a control mechanism within generation reliably converts probabilistic LLM outputs into production-accepted SysMLv2 artifacts. The generate-check-repair loop with a production checker as oracle is an effective paradigm for bridging the gap between NL-to-model translation and industrial deployability.

title: CARPRT: Class-Aware Zero-Shot Prompt Reweighting for Black-Box Vision-Language Models
summary: Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) enable zero-shot image classification by computing the similarity score between an image and textual descriptions, typically formed by inserting a class label (e.g., "cat") into a prompt (e.g., "a photo of a"). Since the score for a given image-class pair is sensitive to the choice of prompt, existing studies ensemble multiple prompts using a weighting vector to aggregate scores across different prompts. Yet, in current strategies, the weighting vector assigned to each prompt is shared across all classes, implicitly assuming that prompts are conditionally independent of classes, which often does not hold in practice, as a prompt like "an aerial view of" might be apt for "airport" but ill-suited for "apple". To address this, we propose class-aware zero-shot prompt reweighting (CARPRT). This scoring scheme adjusts the weighting vector for each class label by capturing the class-specific relevance of different prompts in a training-free manner. For each class label and every available prompt, we quantify their class-specific relevance by averaging image-text relevance scores over images predicted to that class under the given prompt. These estimates are then normalized to derive class-specific weights. Evaluations on standard image classification benchmarks show that CARPRT outperforms existing class-independent reweighting methods, confirming that modeling prompt-class dependencies is crucial for effective zero-shot prediction and even broader VLM-based application settings that rely on prompt ensembling. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/CARPRT.

AI.tldr: CARPRT introduces class-aware prompt reweighting for zero-shot VLM classification, computing class-specific weights by measuring prompt-class relevance from image-text scores, outperforming class-independent ensemble methods.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt ensembling methods assign a single weighting vector shared across all classes, implicitly assuming prompts are conditionally independent of class labels. This assumption fails in practice — e.g., "an aerial view of" suits "airport" but not "apple" — degrading zero-shot classification performance.
AI.method: CARPRT is a training-free, class-aware reweighting scheme. For each (class, prompt) pair, it estimates class-specific relevance by averaging image-text similarity scores over images predicted to that class under that prompt. These relevance scores are normalized to produce class-specific weights, yielding a per-class weighting vector rather than a globally shared one.
AI.result: CARPRT outperforms existing class-independent reweighting methods on standard image classification benchmarks, validating the importance of modeling prompt-class dependencies.
AI.conclusion: Modeling class-specific prompt relevance is crucial for effective zero-shot prediction and broader VLM applications relying on prompt ensembling. CARPRT provides a simple, training-free solution with strong empirical results.

title: HG-RAG: Hierarchy-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Knowledge Graphs
summary: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has proven to be a widely successful process at improving the quality of outputs from a Large Language Model (LLM) for wider context. However, RAG systems typically retrieve context from flat document stores, which struggles when queries require hierarchical or relational reasoning across structured knowledge. I present HG-RAG (Hierarchy-Guided RAG), a framework that performs graph-traversal over a hierarchical knowledge graph to deliver structured context to a language model. My retrieval pipeline resolves a named entity anchor from the query, then expands context upward through parent nodes, laterally through relational neighbors, and downward through child nodes when needed. I evaluate HG-RAG against a dense retrieval baseline across three world scales (18-800 nodes) with four query types: local fact, hierarchical, neighborhood, and multi-hop. Results show HG-RAG consistently outperforms the flat baseline on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop reasoning tasks, while reducing hallucination and maintaining locality coherence.

AI.tldr: HG-RAG introduces a hierarchy-guided retrieval framework that traverses a hierarchical knowledge graph (up/down/lateral) to provide structured context to LLMs, outperforming flat dense retrieval on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop queries while reducing hallucination.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems retrieve context from flat document stores, which fails when queries demand hierarchical or relational reasoning across structured knowledge. There is a need for a retrieval paradigm that can leverage graph structure to support complex, multi-hop, and structured queries.
AI.method: HG-RAG uses a hierarchical knowledge graph and a graph-traversal retrieval pipeline: (1) resolve a named entity anchor from the query, (2) expand context upward through parent nodes, laterally through relational neighbors, and downward through child nodes as needed. The framework is evaluated across three world scales (18–800 nodes) with four query types: local fact, hierarchical, neighborhood, and multi-hop.
AI.result: HG-RAG consistently outperforms the flat dense retrieval baseline on hierarchical, relational, and multi-hop reasoning tasks, while reducing hallucination and maintaining locality coherence.
AI.conclusion: A hierarchy-guided, graph-traversal approach to context retrieval significantly improves LLM performance on structured reasoning tasks compared to flat document retrieval, particularly for queries requiring hierarchical, relational, or multi-hop inference.

title: Latent Communication Between Language Model Agents: Channels, Alignment, and the Limits of Text
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) are utilized in many contexts and many professions. Those MAS rely on inter-agent communication, usually implemented by clear-text message passing. We hypothesize that Large Language Models may have a world model at their disposal that exceeds expressibility in text when complex concepts need to be communicated. Our aim is to approach a proof of this hypothesis with structured experiments. In this work, we show that LLM agents communicating via text lose information, which we quantify via Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis. We construct three communication channels and measure concept-discriminating information in each. We first show that the SAE-sparse channel retains a 99.4% probe accuracy at 28-fold compression over the dense-latent channel vs 80.4% for the text channel. We then proceed to examine the same for cross-architecture communication by using sparse latent space alignment. We find for Procrustes alignment a 92% top-1 retrieval between Llama and Mistral. Using a text round-trip, we perform feature survival analysis to find that text serialization destroys 88% of SAE features, replacing them with a different feature set. We attribute the loss to identity replacement, not attenuation. By our analysis, we were able to attribute a 3-10pp performance penalty to the linear Procrustes alignment, improving with nonlinear alignment methods. In a task-level evaluation we find that the latent channel matches the text channel on cross-lingual concept tasks but never exceeds it. Text augmentation with latent features provides no benefit, leading us to negative conclusions for the initial hypothesis: lost features mostly or completely encode surface form, not task-relevant semantics. To pinpoint the practical advantage of latent communication over a text channel, deeper tasks eliciting complex concepts and an corresponding analysis framework are needed.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLM agents lose information when communicating via text compared to latent representations. Using SAE feature analysis, the authors find that text serialization destroys 88% of SAE features, but conclude the lost features encode surface form rather than task-relevant semantics, failing to support the hypothesis that latent communication conveys richer conceptual content.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems typically communicate via clear-text messaging, but the authors hypothesize that LLMs may possess world models exceeding what can be expressed in text, particularly for complex concepts. The work aims to test whether latent-space communication preserves more concept-discriminating information than text.
AI.method: The authors construct three communication channels (text, dense-latent, SAE-sparse) and measure concept-discriminating information in each using Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) feature analysis. They perform cross-architecture communication via sparse latent space alignment (Procrustes alignment between Llama and Mistral), conduct feature survival analysis on text round-trips, and evaluate task-level performance including cross-lingual concept tasks and text augmentation with latent features.
AI.result: The SAE-sparse channel retains 99.4% probe accuracy at 28× compression vs 80.4% for text. Procrustes alignment achieves 92% top-1 retrieval between Llama and Mistral. Text serialization destroys 88% of SAE features via identity replacement (not attenuation). Nonlinear alignment improves over linear Procrustes by 3–10pp. Latent channels match but never exceed text on cross-lingual concept tasks; text augmentation with latent features provides no benefit.
AI.conclusion: The initial hypothesis is rejected: lost features predominantly encode surface form, not task-relevant semantics. Latent communication offers no practical advantage over text on the tasks tested. Deeper tasks eliciting complex concepts and a corresponding analysis framework are needed to identify any practical benefit of latent over text communication.

title: LBA: Textual Hard-Label Adversarial Attack under Low Query Budgets
summary: Generating high-quality adversarial texts with low query budgets remains a challenging problem in the hard-label scenario. Most existing approaches rely on greedy algorithms, where one position in the text is selected for substitution, followed by the substitutions of other positions. This local search approach may fail to discover high-quality adversarial examples and often leads to excessive query costs. Ideally, an optimal adversarial sample would consider all possible position combinations in the text, but exhaustive search is computationally impractical. To address this challenge, we propose a sampling-based method called LBA, which constructs an approximate distribution of high-quality adversarial examples by integrating both prior and posterior knowledge, and utilizes this distribution for sampling. As sampling progresses, posterior knowledge updates the approximate distribution, which in turn guides more effective sampling. Extensive experiments on six language models, ranging from small-scale to large-scale architectures across four datasets, demonstrate that LBA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on all evaluation metrics. Additionally, LLM-based assessment indicates that LBA generates more semantically preserved and comprehensible adversarial texts.

AI.tldr: LBA proposes a sampling-based method for hard-label adversarial text generation that constructs an approximate distribution of high-quality adversarial examples by integrating prior and posterior knowledge, outperforming greedy-based baselines across multiple models and datasets while maintaining semantic preservation.
AI.motivation: Existing hard-label adversarial text generation methods rely on greedy local search (sequential position substitution), which often misses optimal combinations and incurs high query costs. Ideally, all position combinations should be considered, but exhaustive search is computationally infeasible.
AI.method: LBA uses a sampling-based approach that constructs an approximate distribution over high-quality adversarial examples. This distribution integrates prior knowledge with posterior knowledge, where posterior knowledge is iteratively updated as sampling progresses, guiding more effective subsequent sampling toward better adversarial candidates.
AI.result: Experiments across six language models (small to large-scale) on four datasets show LBA significantly outperforms SOTA baselines on all evaluation metrics. LLM-based assessment further confirms LBA produces more semantically preserved and comprehensible adversarial texts.
AI.conclusion: LBA effectively addresses the hard-label adversarial text generation problem by replacing greedy local search with a prior-posterior knowledge-guided sampling strategy, achieving superior attack performance with lower query budgets while maintaining text quality.

title: Not Just Pockets: Understanding Phone-Carrying Behaviors of Wheelchair Users for Mobile Context-Awareness
summary: Smartphone-based context-awareness holds significant promise for wheelchair users -- from detecting everyday accessibility barriers to enabling ability-based adaptations. Such capabilities often build on passive context inference through mobile sensing, yet their accuracy hinges on how and where phones are carried and the resulting signal quality. While prior work documents phone-carrying behaviors in the general population, patterns specific to wheelchair users remain underexplored. Through a mixed-methods approach combining a survey of 91 and interviews with 15 wheelchair users, we systematically investigate their phone-carrying locations and influencing factors. Our findings reveal distinct patterns extending beyond pocket storage to diverse wheelchair-mounted accessories and around-body placements, shaped by the interplay of physical ability, wheelchair design, and everyday contexts, including social, activity, and device factors. Grounded in these findings, we articulate how carrying location can serve as a proxy for user context to enable novel context-aware experiences, and discuss design implications for developing inclusive and effective mobile context-aware applications.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods study (survey + interviews) reveals that wheelchair users employ distinct phone-carrying strategies — including wheelchair-mounted accessories and around-body placements — shaped by physical ability, wheelchair design, and social/activity contexts. These carrying locations can serve as proxies for user context to inform inclusive context-aware applications.
AI.motivation: Smartphone-based context-awareness holds promise for wheelchair users (e.g., detecting accessibility barriers, enabling ability-based adaptations), but inference accuracy depends on phone-carrying location and signal quality. Existing research on phone-carrying behaviors focuses on the general population, leaving wheelchair users' patterns underexplored.
AI.method: Mixed-methods approach: a survey of 91 wheelchair users combined with in-depth interviews of 15 wheelchair users, systematically investigating phone-carrying locations and their influencing factors.
AI.result: Wheelchair users exhibit distinct phone-carrying patterns that go beyond traditional pocket storage, including diverse wheelchair-mounted accessories and around-body placements. These patterns are shaped by the interplay of physical ability, wheelchair design, and everyday contextual factors (social, activity, and device-related).
AI.conclusion: Phone-carrying location can serve as a proxy for inferring user context, enabling novel context-aware experiences. The paper discusses design implications for building mobile context-aware applications that are both inclusive and effective for wheelchair users.

title: Impact of Expert-Following Strategies in Financial Asset Recommendation
summary: Financial institutions hold rich transaction histories, yet delivering recommendations that simultaneously maximize investment returns and ensure preference alignment remains a significant challenge. Existing approaches, namely return-based and preference-based strategies, each optimize a single objective, resulting in a fundamental trade-off between profitability (ROI) and relevance (nDCG). In this paper, we propose the Expert-Following Strategies: a framework that identifies top-performing investors based on their historical ROI and recommends the assets they purchased, scored by ROI-weighted purchase frequency. Our experiments using real-world transaction histories show that our strategy achieves statistically significant improvement over the market-average baseline in both ROI and nDCG simultaneously across all four thresholds.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Expert-Following Strategies, a framework that identifies top-performing investors by historical ROI and recommends assets they purchase, weighted by ROI-weighted purchase frequency. Experiments on real transaction data show statistically significant simultaneous improvements in both ROI and nDCG over market-average baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing recommendation strategies in finance optimize either returns (ROI) or preference relevance (nDCG), creating an inherent trade-off. No current approach simultaneously maximizes both objectives, leaving a gap for a unified framework that balances profitability with preference alignment.
AI.method: The Expert-Following Strategies framework operates by: (1) identifying top-performing investors based on historical ROI, (2) aggregating the assets purchased by these expert investors, and (3) scoring and ranking recommendations using ROI-weighted purchase frequency. The method essentially leverages the wisdom of high-performing investors as a collaborative filtering signal.
AI.result: Experiments using real-world transaction histories demonstrate that the proposed strategy achieves statistically significant improvements over the market-average baseline in both ROI and nDCG simultaneously, across all four evaluated thresholds.
AI.conclusion: The Expert-Following Strategies framework successfully bridges the gap between return-maximizing and preference-aligning recommendation approaches, demonstrating that following top-performing investors' purchase patterns can jointly optimize both objectives without compromise.

title: A Measurement Study of AI-Environment Realism Gaps in Malware-Analysis Sandboxes
summary:
Sandboxing remains a core technique for observing suspicious program behavior, yet environment-aware malware increasingly suppresses execution when analysis is suspected. Prior generations of sandbox evasion focused on virtualization artifacts, timing discrepancies, and wear-and-tear realism. In this paper, we present the first systematic measurement study of AI-environment artifacts as a new sandbox-evasion surface. We operationalize this realism gap through AIprint, a probe framework that captures persistent artifacts left behind by AI-capable software ecosystems, including AI-assistant configuration directories, model caches, environment variables, local inference services, and package dependencies.
  We systematically extract 450 unique artifacts from 284 open-source AI projects on GitHub, compile them into unprivileged Windows probes, and evaluate them across seven commercial and open-source sandbox backends together with three AI-capable reference hosts. Our results show that traditional VM-detection baselines fail to reliably distinguish real AI-capable systems from modern sandboxes, whereas twelve AI-environment artifacts appear on the reference hosts and on none of the evaluated backends. A controlled 214-step installation experiment establishes a causal relationship between AI tool and package installation and measurable AI-environment artifact accumulation, while adaptive spoofing experiments reveal a fundamental operational asymmetry: reproducing convincing AI software environments is substantially more expensive than detecting shallow spoofing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AIprint, a framework that systematically identifies AI-environment artifacts (configuration directories, model caches, environment variables, etc.) as a novel sandbox-evasion surface. Evaluating 450 artifacts across seven sandbox backends, the authors find that 12 AI-specific artifacts reliably distinguish real AI-capable hosts from sandboxes, demonstrating that modern malware can leverage the absence of AI tooling as an evasion signal. The paper further shows that spoofing convincing AI environments is significantly more expensive than detecting shallow spoofing.
AI.motivation: Traditional sandbox evasion focuses on virtualization artifacts and timing discrepancies, but the widespread deployment of AI development tools creates a new realism gap: malware can detect whether it runs in an AI-capable environment. The authors aim to systematically measure and characterize this under-explored evasion surface.
AI.method: The authors built AIprint, a probe framework that captures persistent artifacts from AI software ecosystems (AI assistants, model caches, inference services, package dependencies). They extracted 450 unique artifacts from 284 open-source GitHub AI projects and compiled them into unprivileged Windows probes. These probes were evaluated against seven commercial/open-source sandbox backends and three AI-capable reference hosts.
