A controlled 214-step installation experiment established causality between AI tool installation and artifact accumulation, and adaptive spoofing experiments assessed the cost asymmetry between creating convincing environments and detecting shallow spoofing.
AI.result: Traditional VM-detection baselines fail to reliably distinguish real AI-capable systems from modern sandboxes. However, 12 AI-environment artifacts appear exclusively on reference hosts and never on evaluated sandbox backends, providing a reliable evasion signal. The installation experiment confirms that AI tool and package installation causally produces these artifacts. Spoofing experiments reveal a fundamental operational asymmetry: convincingly reproducing AI software environments is substantially more expensive than detecting shallow spoofing attempts.
AI.conclusion: AI-environment artifacts constitute a viable and previously unmeasured sandbox-evasion surface. The cost asymmetry between spoofing and detection suggests that defenders face a structural disadvantage, highlighting the need for sandbox operators to incorporate realistic AI-ecosystem footprints into their environments.

title: Towards Reliable AI-Assisted Analog Design: Template-Constrained LLM Agents for SAR ADC Generation
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant capability in software code generation, their application to analog Electronic Design Automation (EDA) is bottlenecked. Owing to limited circuit topology understanding and data, directly prompting LLMs and multimodal models leads to hallucinations and failure to produce schematics capable of passing rigorous SPICE simulations, as we show in our work. Instead, we propose an end-to-end, multi-step LLM agentic framework ATLAS, capable of generating a functional Successive Approximation Register (SAR) Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) that successfully passes simulation validation. To adhere to the rigid constraints of analog design, we utilize expert knowledge to ground the LLM in its planning, selection, parameterization, and iterative modification. As part of ATLAS, we introduce Template-Constrained Generation - which unlike other template-based works - builds towards a more generalized SAR ADC generation flow. We demonstrate a strong proof-of-concept of our framework by developing SAR ADCs across technology nodes and input specs. Overall, our expert-knowledge grounded multi-step agentic ATLAS establishes a pragmatic foundation for integrating LLMs into reliable analog design methodologies.

AI.tldr: ATLAS is an LLM-based agentic framework for analog EDA that uses expert knowledge grounding, multi-step planning, and template-constrained generation to produce functional SAR ADC schematics that pass SPICE simulation, overcoming the hallucination problems of direct LLM prompting.
AI.motivation: LLMs show strong code generation capabilities but fail in analog EDA due to limited circuit topology understanding and data scarcity. Direct prompting leads to hallucinations and schematics that cannot pass SPICE simulation, creating a bottleneck for LLM application in analog design.
AI.method: ATLAS is an end-to-end multi-step LLM agentic framework employing: (1) expert knowledge grounding for planning, component selection, parameterization, and iterative modification; (2) Template-Constrained Generation for generalized SAR ADC flow; (3) SPICE simulation-based validation. The system constrains the LLM within rigid analog design rules rather than allowing unconstrained generation.
AI.result: The framework successfully generates functional SAR ADC designs across multiple technology nodes and input specifications, with all outputs passing SPICE simulation validation, demonstrating a viable proof-of-concept.
AI.conclusion: Expert-knowledge grounded, multi-step agentic frameworks like ATLAS provide a pragmatic path toward integrating LLMs into reliable analog design methodologies, bridging the gap between general-purpose LLM capabilities and the stringent requirements of analog EDA.

title: Explainable Geospatial AI for Satellite Ground Station Siting Using LiDAR-Derived Terrain Intelligence
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 22nd International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (IEEE CASE 2026)
summary: Representative clutter height (RCH) is a key parameter in radio propagation and interference analysis because it captures the dominant height of local obstructions that drive terminal clutter loss. Current practice often relies on fixed clutter heights assigned to land use classes in Recommendation ITU-R P.452-18, but this misses within class variation and can lead to conservative exclusion zones and poor site ranking for low Earth orbit ground station siting and spectrum coordination. We present an interpretable, globally deployable machine learning framework for predicting RCH from open geospatial data. The model is trained using LiDAR derived labels from the U.S. Geological Survey 3D Elevation Program and inference time features from global land-cover, terrain, demographic, thermal, and optical remote sensing products. We define RCH using a robust 75th percentile clutter height statistic, evaluate multiple regressors, and select LightGBM for its accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility with feature attribution analysis. The final model achieves a mean absolute error of 1.79m and an R^2=0.765, reducing absolute error by more than 60% relative to the ITU baseline. Beyond aggregate fit, we evaluate domain facing criteria relevant to RF planning, including meter scale error, tolerance band accuracy, over and under estimation tails, agreement with ITU clutter height regimes, and SHAP-based physical plausibility. SHAP identifies tree canopy cover, land-cover semantics, and spectral reflectance as the most influential predictors. Studies on segmentation derived features, non-forest ablations, and land-cover matched international validation show that open geospatial data can improve clutter modeling at scale without sacrificing interpretability or deployability.

AI.tldr: A global machine learning framework using LightGBM predicts representative clutter height (RCH) from open geospatial data, achieving MAE of 1.79m (R²=0.765) and reducing error by 60% versus ITU-R P.452-18 fixed land-use class assignments, with SHAP analysis confirming physical plausibility.
AI.motivation: Current practice using fixed clutter heights per land-use class (ITU-R P.452-18) ignores within-class variation, leading to conservative exclusion zones and poor site ranking for LEO ground station siting. A globally deployable, interpretable ML solution using open geospatial data is needed.
AI.method: RCH is defined as the 75th percentile clutter height statistic. LiDAR-derived labels from USGS 3DEP are used as training targets. Inference features come from global land-cover, terrain, demographic, thermal, and optical remote sensing products. Multiple regressors are evaluated; LightGBM is selected for accuracy, efficiency, and feature attribution compatibility. SHAP values are used for interpretability and physical plausibility checks. Validation includes segmentation-derived features, non-forest ablations, and land-cover-matched international data.
AI.result: MAE = 1.79m, R² = 0.765, >60% absolute error reduction vs. ITU baseline. Evaluated on meter-scale error, tolerance band accuracy, over/under-estimation tails, agreement with ITU regimes, and SHAP-based plausibility. Tree canopy cover, land-cover semantics, and spectral reflectance are the most influential predictors. International validation confirms scalability.
AI.conclusion: Open geospatial data combined with interpretable ML (LightGBM + SHAP) can substantially improve clutter height modeling at global scale, outperforming static ITU land-use class assignments without sacrificing interpretability or deployability — directly benefiting RF planning, interference analysis, and LEO ground station siting.

title: IMEX Interaction-Based Model Explanation
summary: In predictive modeling, the ability to explain why a model produces a given target prediction has become increasingly important [5, 10]. Black-box models do not provide a transparent description of the internal mechanisms that generate the prediction, making even accurate predictions difficult to interpret and validate. In critical contexts, predictive accuracy alone is not a sufficient validation metric if the reasons underlying model decisions remain unexplained. The IMEX (Interaction-Based Model Explanation) approach represents a methodological direction within explainable predictive modeling. IMEX is designed to identify which variables contribute most to the target prediction and which interactions among variables are significant in determining the target. The method does not impose limitations on higher-order interaction analysis, allowing the investigation of feature subsets with cardinality greater than two. Beyond the identification of feature importance, IMEX enables the exploration of interaction patterns that may be consistent with latent mechanisms influencing the outcome. Through the application of the IMEX algorithm, it is possible to construct an interpretability map of the predictions. The IMEX framework is built on two complementary metrics: Static Correlation Power (PCS), which quantifies the contribution of individual features, and Interaction Correlation Power (PCI), which captures non-additive effects among features. In the present work, the PCS component is experimentally validated through a comparison with INVASE [18] on three synthetic datasets with known structures. The results indicate that IMEX can recover relevant feature-level structures in the presence of non-linear, conditional, and multicollinear relationships between input features and prediction targets.

AI.tldr: IMEX is an explainable predictive modeling framework that identifies important features and their interactions using two metrics (PCS and PCI). This paper experimentally validates its PCS metric against INVASE on synthetic datasets, showing IMEX can recover feature-level structures under non-linear, conditional, and multicollinear conditions.
AI.motivation: Black-box models lack transparency, making accurate predictions difficult to interpret and validate, especially in critical contexts where understanding the reasons behind model decisions is essential. There is a need for methods that not only identify important features but also capture higher-order interactions among variables without cardinality limitations.
AI.method: The IMEX (Interaction-Based Model Explanation) framework employs two complementary metrics: Static Correlation Power (PCS) for quantifying individual feature contributions, and Interaction Correlation Power (PCI) for capturing non-additive interaction effects among features. The method supports higher-order interaction analysis (feature subsets with cardinality >2). Validation is performed experimentally by comparing PCS against the INVASE method on three synthetic datasets with known ground-truth structures.
AI.result: Experimental results on three synthetic datasets demonstrate that IMEX successfully recovers relevant feature-level structures even in the presence of non-linear relationships, conditional dependencies, and multicollinearity between input features and prediction targets.
AI.conclusion: The PCS component of IMEX is experimentally validated as effective for identifying important features under challenging data conditions. This supports IMEX's broader goal of constructing interpretability maps of predictions through combined feature importance and interaction analysis.

title: Orchestrating Power Grid Studies with Multi-Agent AI and MCP Servers
summary: This position paper explores how Agentic AI and Model Context Protocol (MCP) can support power-grid studies in a Transmission System Operator (TSO) context. We focus on integrating Large Language Models with numerical simulation tools, structured workflows, and human supervision. We identify key industrial requirements for agent assisted grid studies and introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface exposing selected capabilities of our simulation tool, pypowsybl to AI agents. This first step provides a testbed to study how agents can setup simulations, execute analyses, retrieve results, and interact with power-system simulators through standardized tool calls. We also discuss principles for human-in-the-loop, multi-agent workflows and outline an evaluation strategy combining technical metrics and practitioner feedback. The paper positions MCP-based tool integration as a step toward more interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments.

AI.tldr: This position paper proposes using Agentic AI with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enhance power-grid simulation workflows in Transmission System Operator environments, introducing pypowsybl-mcp as a testbed interface that enables AI agents to interact with numerical simulation tools through standardized tool calls.
AI.motivation: TSO grid studies are complex, involving numerous numerical simulations, structured workflows, and expert judgment. Current workflows lack the interactivity, auditability, and scalability that AI-assisted automation could provide. The authors see an opportunity to integrate Large Language Models with existing simulation tools to support (not replace) human operators, while addressing industrial requirements for reliability and oversight.
AI.method: The authors introduce pypowsybl-mcp, an MCP-based interface that wraps selected capabilities of the pypowsybl power-system simulation tool. This exposes simulation functions as standardized tool calls consumable by AI agents. The paper defines industrial requirements for agent-assisted grid studies, proposes human-in-the-loop principles, outlines multi-agent workflow designs, and establishes an evaluation strategy based on technical metrics and practitioner feedback.
AI.result: As a position paper, it presents no empirical results. It contributes a conceptual framework, the pypowsybl-mcp interface as a concrete testbed, and a roadmap for evaluating AI-assisted grid-study environments.
AI.conclusion: MCP-based tool integration represents a promising direction for building interactive, auditable, and scalable grid-study environments that augment rather than replace human expertise in TSO operations.

title: UniSAGE: Unifying Static and Dynamic Attributes with Hyper-Structure
summary: With the rapid growth of digital data, real-world applications increasingly involve hierarchical information that combines static attributes with dynamic records. Modeling such heterogeneous data in a unified and generalizable manner remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on extensive manual design, are tightly coupled to specific data schemas, and typically process static and dynamic attributes in isolation, thereby overlooking their implicit interactions. We propose UniSAGE, a unified framework for modeling data with both static and dynamic attributes. UniSAGE constructs a global attribute graph that represents hierarchical and temporal relationships in a unified structure. To ensure representational consistency, it introduces two orthogonal parameter subspaces that jointly support static aggregation and dynamic reasoning within a shared semantic space. Building on these unified representations, UniSAGE further enables task-specific interaction between static and dynamic attributes via a lightweight hyper-structure mechanism. UniSAGE is fully automated, robust to evolving data schemas, and capable of capturing complex cross-attribute dependencies. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks and a real-world financial behavior dataset demonstrate that UniSAGE consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving performance improvements of over 10% on several tasks.

AI.tldr: UniSAGE is a unified framework that models hierarchical data with both static and dynamic attributes by constructing a global attribute graph, using dual parameter subspaces for consistent representation, and enabling cross-attribute interaction via a lightweight hyper-structure mechanism — outperforming existing methods by over 10% on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Real-world applications increasingly involve heterogeneous, hierarchical data combining static attributes and dynamic temporal records. Existing methods are heavily hand-crafted, schema-dependent, and process static and dynamic attributes separately, failing to capture their implicit interactions. A unified, automated, and generalizable modeling framework is needed.
AI.method: UniSAGE constructs a global attribute graph to unify hierarchical and temporal relationships. It introduces two orthogonal parameter subspaces for static aggregation and dynamic reasoning within a shared semantic space, ensuring representational consistency. A lightweight hyper-structure mechanism then enables task-specific interaction between static and dynamic attributes. The framework is fully automated and robust to evolving data schemas.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmarks and a real-world financial behavior dataset show UniSAGE consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving performance improvements of over 10% on several tasks.
AI.conclusion: UniSAGE provides an effective, unified solution for modeling heterogeneous data with static and dynamic attributes, demonstrating strong empirical gains and robustness to schema evolution without relying on manual feature engineering.

title: Skeleton: Visual Authoring of Non-visual Data Experiences
comment: 9 pages core, 2 pages acknowledgements + references, 4 pages appendices. Accepted at IEEE VIS 2026, to appear in November 2026
summary: When sighted practitioners author accessible data visualizations, they build navigation structures (the nodes, edges, and input bindings that govern how assistive technologies traverse an interface) entirely in code, with no visual representation. Without a representation to react to, practitioners cannot develop judgment about what makes navigation good or bad, and the quality ceiling of non-visual experiences is set by the absence of a feedback loop. We address this problem through longitudinal co-design with practitioners across cartography, design systems, and open-source visualization, and make three contributions. First, we introduce an Inspector that renders navigation graphs as interactive node-link diagrams, and a Dimensions API that expresses navigation in terms of data dimensions rather than explicit graph construction. Second we present Skeleton, a direct-manipulation authoring environment in which the properties of an accessible navigation structure are translated into visual representations authors can observe and manipulate. Key techniques include a dual-view editor that simultaneously shows the system's navigation model and the end user's spatial experience, a scaffolding engine that automates spatial node placement by repurposing a visualization rendering pipeline, a live label-template editor with real-time screen-reader-output preview, and a testing mode that makes traversal sequence visually trackable. Third, we evaluate Skeleton through an in-situ study with 8 practitioners across visualization design, engineering, and research. Making navigation structure visible changed how practitioners engaged with accessible design: they reconsidered the architecture of their own visualizations, attended to a broader range of input modalities, and shifted from treating accessibility as a compliance task to treating it as a design problem. (abstract shortened for arxiv)

AI.tldr: Skeleton is a direct-manipulation authoring environment that makes accessible navigation structures visually representable and editable, transforming how visualization practitioners engage with accessibility from compliance to design.
AI.motivation: Practitioners building accessible data visualizations construct navigation structures (nodes, edges, input bindings for assistive technologies) entirely in code with no visual feedback. This absence of representation prevents practitioners from developing judgment about navigation quality, capping the quality of non-visual experiences.
AI.method: Longitudinal co-design with practitioners across cartography, design systems, and open-source visualization. Three contributions: (1) an Inspector rendering navigation graphs as interactive node-link diagrams with a Dimensions API expressing navigation via data dimensions; (2) Skeleton, featuring a dual-view editor (navigation model + spatial experience), a scaffolding engine for automated spatial node placement, a live label-template editor with screen-reader preview, and a visually trackable testing mode; (3) in-situ evaluation with 8 practitioners.
AI.result: Making navigation structure visible changed practitioner behavior: they reconsidered visualization architecture, attended to broader input modalities, and shifted from treating accessibility as compliance to treating it as a design problem.
AI.conclusion: Visual representation of navigation structures via direct-manipulation environments like Skeleton can fundamentally shift practitioner engagement with accessible design, elevating the quality ceiling of non-visual experiences.

title: LLM-Based Re-Ranking for Real Estate Search
summary: QuintoAndar Group operates the leading housing marketplace in Latin America for both rentals and sales. The platform replaces traditionally paper-heavy workflows with a fully digital experience, making housing transactions faster and more accessible to tenants, buyers, and landlords in the region. Finding the ideal home in such a vast catalog is inherently difficult. At the same time, the widespread adoption of conversational assistants is reshaping user expectations: people increasingly want to express their needs through open, multi-turn dialog rather than rigid filter menus and faceted search. This shift is particularly pronounced in housing, where intent is multi-dimensional, context-dependent, and rarely reducible to a small set of structured constraints. To meet these expectations, we propose a Large Language Model (LLM) based re-ranker that augments a conversational recommendation system by reordering retrieved candidates according to the nuanced, context-rich intent expressed across the user's conversation. We additionally construct a large-scale offline evaluation dataset for conversational real-estate search, containing 960,000 query-item pairs constructed from both synthetic and production queries and annotated using an LLM-as-a-Judge framework with human validation. We validate our approach both offline, on this proprietary dataset, and online, through a production A/B test. Both evaluations show consistent improvements in ranking quality, including a statistically significant increase in production of +5.3% in click-through rate and +4.8% in scheduled visits, demonstrating the value of integrating conversational context into housing recommendations.

AI.tldr: QuintoAndar developed an LLM-based re-ranker for conversational housing search that reorders listings based on multi-turn dialog context, validated through a 960K-pair offline dataset and a production A/B test showing +5.3% CTR and +4.8% scheduled visits.
AI.motivation: Traditional faceted search with rigid filters cannot capture the multi-dimensional, context-dependent intent users express when searching for housing. With the rise of conversational assistants, users increasingly expect to articulate their needs through open, multi-turn dialog rather than structured menus. This gap is especially acute in real-estate, where preferences are nuanced and hard to reduce to simple constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-stage retrieval pipeline: a standard retriever first fetches candidate listings, then an LLM-based re-ranker reorders them using the full conversational context. They also construct a large-scale offline evaluation dataset of 960,000 query-item pairs from both synthetic and production queries, annotated via an LLM-as-a-Judge framework with human validation. The approach is evaluated both offline on this proprietary dataset and online via a production A/B test.
AI.result: The LLM-based re-ranker yielded consistent ranking quality improvements in both offline and online evaluations. The production A/B test demonstrated statistically significant gains: +5.3% in click-through rate and +4.8% in scheduled visits.
AI.conclusion: Integrating conversational context into housing recommendations via an LLM-based re-ranker produces measurable, significant improvements in user engagement and conversion. The work validates that conversational recommendation is not merely a UX preference but a driver of tangible business outcomes in real-estate marketplaces.

title: Disclosure Divergence: Measuring Privacy Policy and Data Safety Misalignment at Scale
summary: With the rapid growth of mobile applications, user data privacy has become an increasing concern. While privacy policies describe how apps collect and share data, platforms such as Google Play provide Data Safety labels intended to summarize these practices. Because these disclosure channels are declared separately, they may present inconsistent representations of app data practices, creating uncertainty for users and regulators. In this work, we conducted a large-scale empirical study of disclosure consistency across 6,051 Android apps. Using an LLM-based extraction framework and a unified schema over 14 Google Play data categories and two operations (collection and sharing), we measure per-app and per-category consistency and introduce a sensitivity-weighted risk score that emphasizes high-risk data types. We find that misalignment disproportionately affects sensitive categories such as personal information and device identifiers, with sharing disclosures exhibiting lower consistency than collection disclosures. Elevated privac risk is concentrated in app categories associated with persistent monitoring and communication. Overall, our findings highlight structural gaps in current disclosure mechanisms and underscore the need for stronger verification and greater transparency in platform-level privacy reporting.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study of 6,051 Android apps reveals significant inconsistencies between privacy policies and Google Play Data Safety labels, particularly for sensitive data types like personal information and device identifiers, with sharing disclosures showing lower consistency than collection disclosures.
AI.motivation: Privacy policies and platform-level Data Safety labels (e.g., Google Play) are declared separately, potentially creating inconsistent representations of app data practices. This inconsistency undermines user trust and regulatory oversight, yet no large-scale empirical study had systematically measured the alignment between these two disclosure channels.
AI.method: The authors developed an LLM-based extraction framework applied to a unified schema covering 14 Google Play data categories and two operations (collection and sharing). They analyzed 6,051 Android apps, measuring per-app and per-category consistency, and introduced a sensitivity-weighted risk score that prioritizes high-risk data types to quantify privacy risk from misalignment.
AI.result: Misalignment disproportionately affects sensitive categories such as personal information and device identifiers. Sharing disclosures exhibit lower consistency than collection disclosures. Elevated privacy risk is concentrated in app categories associated with persistent monitoring and communication (e.g., social media, tracking apps).
AI.conclusion: Structural gaps exist in current disclosure mechanisms. The findings underscore the need for stronger verification and greater transparency in platform-level privacy reporting to ensure consistency between privacy policies and safety labels.

title: Stop Means Stop: Measuring and Repairing the Enforcement Gap in Agent-Framework Control Primitives
summary: Production LLM-agent frameworks expose control primitives -- human-in-the-loop approval gates, run cancellation, and execution timeouts -- whose names and documentation imply barrier semantics: while a run is paused, cancelled, or timed out, no gated side effect executes. We show this implied contract holds on none of the six widely used open-source frameworks we test. Model-free differential probes isolate a recurring sibling leak -- an approval gate suspends its own branch while a sibling branch's effect executes during the pause, so a later rejection cannot prevent it -- in every framework shipping a pre-execution gate (five of six), plus three further gaps: replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, and timeout zombies. The hazard is reachable, not merely constructible: under an a-priori-fixed protocol, frontier models emit the leak-triggering plan shape at pooled rates up to 14%, and when live models drive the unmodified frameworks under an approval pause, 215 of 1,200 runs execute their effect during the pause, across three schedulers and two language runtimes. To repair the measured gaps we present SOUNDGATE, an environment-external effect gate in Rust through which every side effect must be admitted, enforcing hold-until-decided, reject-cancels, dedup-on-replay, and fence-on-cancel -- one property per violation class -- under a stated complete-mediation contract discharged for network egress by kernel-enforced routes. We verify the properties over a model of the admission core (Verus; TLA+/TLC, exhaustive to 7.5e7 states; TLAPS), model-check the deployed Rust with Loom, and bridge model to code by differential conformance over 1.2e7 operations -- refinement evidence, not a mechanized proof. SOUNDGATE blocks every measured violation end-to-end on all six frameworks while releasing legitimate effects, at about 1 ms admission per write and 12k-26k durable admissions per second.

AI.tldr: LLM-agent frameworks fail to enforce barrier semantics for approval gates, cancellations, and timeouts. The authors systematically uncover four violation classes (sibling leaks, replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, timeout zombies) across six frameworks, demonstrate real-world exploitability with frontier models, and present SOUNDGATE — a formally-modeled, kernel-enforced external effect gate that blocks all measured violations with ~1ms latency.
AI.motivation: Production LLM-agent frameworks expose control primitives (approval gates, cancellation, timeouts) whose documentation implies that no gated side effect executes while a run is paused or terminated. The authors hypothesize this contract is systematically violated and set out to measure, categorize, and repair these safety-critical gaps.
AI.method: (1) Model-free differential probes to detect violations across six open-source frameworks. (2) Taxonomy of four violation classes: sibling leaks, replay double-execution, cancellation orphans, timeout zombies. (3) Empirical exploitability study using frontier models under a fixed protocol, measuring leak rates up to 14% and 215/1200 runs executing effects during pause. (4) SOUNDGATE: a Rust-based external effect gate enforcing hold-until-decided, reject-cancels, dedup-on-replay, and fence-on-cancel. Verified via Verus, TLA+/TLC (exhaustive to 7.5e7 states), TLAPS, and Loom model-checking, with differential conformance over 1.2e7 operations bridging model to code.
AI.result: All six frameworks exhibited at least one violation class; five of six had sibling leaks in pre-execution gates. Frontier models triggered the leak shape at pooled rates up to 14%. In live testing across three schedulers and two language runtimes, 215 of 1,200 runs executed effects during an approval pause. SOUNDGATE blocked every measured violation end-to-end while admitting legitimate effects at ~1ms per write and 12k–26k durable admissions/second.
AI.conclusion: The implied barrier contract of LLM-agent control primitives is universally broken in current frameworks, and the gaps are practically exploitable by frontier models. SOUNDGATE demonstrates that a formally-modeled, kernel-enforced external gate can close these gaps with acceptable performance overhead, providing a principled defense-in-depth mechanism for LLM-agent safety.

title: Certified Domain Consistency for Multi-Domain Retrieval: Label-Free Per-Domain Contamination Control with Conformal Risk Guarantees
summary: Retrieval over corpora that mix several domains often returns relevant but wrong-domain evidence that ranking metrics miss and that conformal risk control bounds only marginally, under-covering the worst domains. This work introduces C3R, a drop-in control layer that, from an inferred domain posterior and no query-time label, certifies a per-domain contamination budget where feasible and otherwise abstains rather than silently violating; on the hardest domains it guarantees a reduction, not a tight bound. The core is a two-split scheme built on risk-controlling prediction sets, whose finite-sample transfer bound crosses from the inferred to the true domain with fully estimable slack, supports heterogeneous budgets, and inverts for deployment. Population validity rests on this bound and a controlled simulation; across a thousand resampled calibrations the certificate never violates (a stability result) while marginal control violates the most-contaminated domain in every draw, and soft demotion retains more recall than the strongest calibrated cascade at equal certified contamination. The method replicates across open testbeds including an independent one from public federal regulations, and an LLM-judged downstream probe indicates wrong-authority grounding rises with contamination and falls under control. The layer is frozen-stack and reranker-agnostic.

AI.tldr: C3R is a drop-in control layer for multi-domain retrieval that uses inferred domain posteriors and risk-controlling prediction sets to certify per-domain contamination budgets, abstaining when infeasible. It guarantees contamination reduction on hard domains via a two-split scheme with finite-sample transfer bounds, and empirically never violates its certificate while marginal control consistently fails on the worst domain.
AI.motivation: Multi-domain retrieval systems often return wrong-domain evidence that ranking metrics fail to detect and conformal risk control bounds only marginally, systematically under-covering the worst domains. There is a need for domain-aware control that provides per-domain contamination guarantees rather than aggregate bounds that mask domain-specific failures.
AI.method: C3R employs a two-split scheme built on risk-controlling prediction sets (RCPS). It infers a domain posterior without query-time labels, then uses a finite-sample transfer bound that crosses from the inferred domain to the true domain with fully estimable slack. This supports heterogeneous per-domain contamination budgets and inverts for deployment. The method certifies a contamination budget where feasible and abstains otherwise. Population validity is established via the transfer bound and controlled simulation.
AI.result: Across a thousand resampled calibrations, C3R's certificate never violates (a stability result), while marginal control violates the most-contaminated domain in every draw. Soft demotion retains more recall than the strongest calibrated cascade at equal certified contamination. The method replicates across open testbeds, including an independent corpus of public federal regulations. An LLM-judged downstream probe shows wrong-authority grounding rises with contamination and falls under control.
AI.conclusion: C3R provides a frozen-stack, reranker-agnostic control layer that delivers per-domain contamination guarantees where marginal methods fail. By abstaining rather than silently violating on hard domains and offering a reduction guarantee rather than merely a tight bound, it enables safer deployment of retrieval systems over mixed-domain corpora.

title: RegNetAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Cross-Network Regulatory Driver Identification in Cancer Genomics
summary: We introduce RegNetAgents, an AI-oriented multi-agent framework for structured, query-driven regulatory candidate identification across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks. The system enables unified analysis of bulk tumor and single-cell-derived ARACNe networks by integrating TCGA-derived cancer networks with large-scale single-cell regulatory networks from the GREmLN project. For a given focal gene, the framework performs dual-network classification, cancer gene filtering using OncoKB annotations, and mode-of-action (MoA) assignment for tumor-derived regulatory relationships. Candidates are ranked by evidence consistency across networks (Both, TCGA-only, GREmLN-only). The system is implemented as a multi-agent LangGraph DAG workflow, accessible through a unified Python API and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client, operating as a downstream analytical layer over precomputed regulatory networks rather than a network inference method. Across eleven breast cancer (BRCA) and twelve colorectal cancer (COAD) focal genes, RegNetAgents identifies candidate regulators significantly enriched for OncoKB-annotated cancer genes. TCGA-derived candidates show strong enrichment (Stouffer Z = 6.69 for BRCA and 6.95 for COAD), while GREmLN-derived candidates also demonstrate significant enrichment (Z = 5.51 for BRCA and 7.06 for COAD; all p < 0.0001). No enrichment is observed in housekeeping or non-driver control gene sets, supporting signal specificity. An extended module enables structured evaluation of oncogenic potential, druggability, clinical relevance, and network vulnerability, supporting end-to-end interpretation from candidate identification to biological hypothesis generation. RegNetAgents establishes an interpretable AI framework for cross-network regulatory candidate identification in cancer genomics.

AI.tldr: RegNetAgents is a multi-agent AI framework that identifies and ranks candidate regulatory genes across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks (TCGA bulk tumor and single-cell GREmLN) using OncoKB filtering and mode-of-action assignment, demonstrating significant cancer gene enrichment in BRCA and COAD cohorts.
AI.motivation: There is a need for structured, query-driven approaches to identify candidate regulatory genes across heterogeneous gene regulatory networks (bulk tumor vs. single-cell) in cancer, moving beyond network inference to downstream analytical interpretation.
AI.method: A multi-agent LangGraph DAG workflow performs dual-network classification, OncoKB cancer gene filtering, and mode-of-action (MoA) assignment for tumor-derived regulatory relationships. Candidates are ranked by evidence consistency (Both, TCGA-only, GREmLN-only) and evaluated for oncogenic potential, druggability, clinical relevance, and network vulnerability.
AI.result: TCGA-derived candidates showed strong cancer gene enrichment (Stouffer Z = 6.69 BRCA, 6.95 COAD); GREmLN-derived candidates were also significantly enriched (Z = 5.51 BRCA, 7.06 COAD; all p < 0.0001). No enrichment was seen in housekeeping or non-driver controls, confirming signal specificity.
AI.conclusion: RegNetAgents provides an interpretable, AI-driven framework for cross-network regulatory candidate identification in cancer genomics, supporting end-to-end biological hypothesis generation from candidate discovery to clinical interpretation.

title: ReasFlow: Assisting Reasoning-Centric Scientific Discovery in Applied Mathematics via a Knowledge-Based Multi-Agent System
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models have fueled autonomous AI agents capable of tackling complex scientific tasks, yet existing automated research systems remain predominantly focused on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, leaving theory-driven discovery, particularly in mathematically grounded disciplines requiring rigorous proofs and synthesis of domain knowledge, largely underexplored. Key challenges include the difficulty of verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning ability for autonomous frontier exploration, and a scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature. We introduce ReasFlow, an end-to-end autonomous agent system for reasoning-centric scientific discovery that operationalizes a collaborative paradigm where the human expert acts as Principal Investigator while the agent executes rigorous derivations as a capable graduate student. ReasFlow incorporates (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors prior to human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that proactively surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics, substantially reducing expert intervention. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation in a single system. Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieves the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric. ReasFlow is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform, providing a collaborative workspace for AI-assisted theoretical research. Github repo: https://github.com/ReasLab/ReasFlow.git.

AI.tldr: ReasFlow is an end-to-end autonomous agent system for theory-driven scientific discovery that frames human-AI collaboration as Principal Investigator–graduate student, featuring an internal verification loop and automated knowledge retrieval. It autonomously generated five complete research papers from minimal prompts, achieving top scores among open-access baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing automated research systems focus on empirically driven domains with quantitative benchmarks, neglecting theory-driven discovery—particularly in mathematically grounded fields requiring rigorous proofs. Key gaps include the difficulty of verifying theoretical reasoning at scale, insufficient reasoning ability for frontier exploration, and a scarcity of procedural heuristics in the literature.
AI.method: ReasFlow operationalizes a human-expert-as-PI, agent-as-graduate-student collaborative paradigm. It features (i) a robust internal verification loop that audits logical coherence and corrects fundamental errors before human inspection, and (ii) an automated knowledge retrieval and self-improvement mechanism that surfaces both declarative facts and overlooked procedural heuristics. The system unifies literature synthesis, algorithm design, theorem proving, experimentation, and manuscript preparation.
AI.result: Deployed to autonomously generate five complete research papers with rigorous theoretical and empirical content from minimal prompts, ReasFlow consistently achieved the highest evaluation scores among state-of-the-art open-access baselines under a curated LLM-based review rubric.
AI.conclusion: ReasFlow demonstrates that autonomous agents can effectively conduct theory-driven scientific discovery when equipped with robust internal verification and knowledge retrieval. The system is publicly accessible via the ReasLab platform and its code is open-sourced on GitHub.

title: Conversational Tactile Data Interfaces: Co-Designing Accessible Data Experiences with Blind Users Using Refreshable Tactile Displays and Conversational AI
comment: Accepted to be presented at IEEE VIS 2026 and published in IEEE TVCG
summary: Combining refreshable tactile displays (RTDs) with conversational AI offers a promising approach to accessible data visualization for people who are blind or have low vision (BLV). However, it remains an open question how these modalities should be integrated to support accessible data experiences. We address this through a co-design process with three BLV co-designers. Building on our prior Wizard-of-Oz study, we created a conversational tactile data interface (CTDI) that combines an RTD with an LLM-powered conversational agent, refined through four workshops over eight months. In addition to the resulting system, Graphy, we contribute design knowledge and recommendations for CTDIs. Co-designers used touch as the primary sensemaking channel for spatial understanding of the data's shape, trends, and relationships, reserved the agent for what touch could not resolve (e.g., calculation and analysis), and used the chart on the RTD to verify the agent's responses. Key findings include: a layered presentation that scaffolds chart exploration through progressive, interactive layers; a feedback grammar that distinguishes user- and agent-initiated tactile feedback; and a sequential interaction pattern -- select, confirm, ask, verify -- where each step grounds the last.

AI.tldr: A co-design study with three BLV co-designers over eight months produced Graphy, a conversational tactile data interface (CTDI) combining a refreshable tactile display with an LLM-powered agent. The paper contributes design knowledge including layered chart presentation, a feedback grammar distinguishing user- vs. agent-initiated tactile feedback, and a select-confirm-ask-verify interaction pattern.
AI.motivation: While refreshable tactile displays combined with conversational AI hold promise for accessible data visualization for BLV users, there is a lack of design knowledge on how to effectively integrate these two modalities. The paper seeks to close this gap through co-design.
AI.method: A co-design process involving three BLV co-designers across four workshops spanning eight months, building on a prior Wizard-of-Oz study. The process iteratively refined a conversational tactile data interface (CTDI) combining an RTD with an LLM-powered conversational agent, culminating in the system Graphy.
AI.result: Three key design findings: (1) layered presentation that scaffolds chart exploration through progressive, interactive layers; (2) a feedback grammar distinguishing user-initiated from agent-initiated tactile feedback; and (3) a sequential interaction pattern (select → confirm → ask → verify) where each step grounds the previous one. Co-designers primarily used touch for spatial sensemaking (shape, trends, relationships) and the conversational agent for calculation and analysis, using the tactile chart to verify agent responses.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes both the Graphy system and actionable design knowledge for building CTDIs, demonstrating that touch and conversation serve complementary roles — touch for spatial understanding and the agent for analytical tasks — with verification as a critical grounding mechanism between modalities.

title: Does generative AI supersede supervised XMLC? A Benchmark Study on Automated Subject Indexing with German Scientific Literature
summary: With a large controlled vocabulary as the label set, the task of automated subject indexing in a library can be understood as a multi-label classification task. If the set of subject terms is large, the problem fits the Extreme Multi-Label Classification (XMLC) objective. In this study, we apply a selection of specialised supervised XMLC methods to the test case of subject indexing contemporary German scientific literature, collected at the German National Library (DNB). We contrast these results by including a classical lexical matching baseline and three of our own recently developed LLM-based methods into the benchmark. Algorithms are evaluated and compared in several metrics. This includes binary relevance comparisons with previously indexed material, as well as graded relevance ratings by professional subject librarians. A challenge for all methods is to reliably make suggestions from the long tail of the subject vocabulary. We find that supervised XMLC algorithms relying on transformer-based dense features give best results in terms of overall binary relevance metrics. However, focusing on graded relevance and performance in the long tail of our subject vocabulary, the LLM-based generative methods give better results, making them a promising alternative for future productive use.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks supervised Extreme Multi-Label Classification (XMLC) methods against lexical matching baselines and LLM-based generative approaches for automated subject indexing at the German National Library. While transformer-based XMLC methods excel in overall binary relevance, LLM-based generative methods perform better on graded relevance and long-tail subject terms.
AI.motivation: Automated subject indexing in libraries with large controlled vocabularies is a challenging XMLC problem, particularly for reliably suggesting terms from the long tail. The authors aim to determine whether modern supervised XMLC or LLM-based generative methods offer viable alternatives to existing approaches for the German National Library's indexing workflow.
AI.method: The study benchmarks multiple approaches on contemporary German scientific literature from the DNB: (1) a classical lexical matching baseline, (2) a selection of specialised supervised XMLC methods using transformer-based dense features, and (3) three custom LLM-based generative methods developed by the authors. Evaluation uses both binary relevance comparisons against previously indexed material and graded relevance ratings from professional subject librarians.
AI.result: Supervised XMLC algorithms with transformer-based dense features achieve the best overall binary relevance metrics. However, LLM-based generative methods outperform on graded relevance assessments and in handling the long tail of the subject vocabulary, where reliable suggestion generation is most challenging for all methods.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based generative methods are a promising alternative for future productive use in automated subject indexing, particularly due to their superior performance on long-tail terms and higher graded relevance, despite XMLC methods leading on aggregate binary metrics.

title: Context Contamination in LLM Analysis of Network Security Logs: Poison with Passive Prompt Injection and Mitigation Evaluation
summary: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in Security Operations Centers for log analysis tasks including summarization, alert triage, and threat investigation. These systems ingest logs from external-facing services and process network logs as natural language contexts to generate security insights. We demonstrate that this architectural pattern introduces a critical vulnerability: adversaries can embed prompt injection payloads in log-generating fields that persist in storage and are executed when analysts query the LLM, achieving what we term passive prompt injection. We present LogInject, a systematic framework for evaluating these threats. Using LogInject-1.0, a benchmark of 12,847 log entries including 2,569 adversarial samples, we evaluate three production LLMs across four attack objectives: activity concealment, false positive generation, information exfiltration, and output hijacking. Our findings reveal an up to 88.2% attack success rate (83.4% average across models) under the baseline conditions. We introduce Context Stitching, a novel technique that fragments payloads across multiple log entries to evade stateless filters while exploiting LLM long-context reasoning, achieving a 76.4% success rate. As mitigation, we evaluate layered defenses by combining input filtering, prompt hardening, and output validation, demonstrating a 90.4% attack reduction, although 8.4% residual vulnerability persists. Our results establish that LLM-based log analysis creates an inherent confused deputy vulnerability where untrusted data and trusted instructions compete indistinguishably for model attention, requiring defense in-depth architectures and continued human oversight for security-critical decisions.

AI.tldr: LLM-based log analysis systems are vulnerable to passive prompt injection, where adversaries embed malicious payloads in log entries that persist in storage and execute when analysts query the LLM. The authors present LogInject, a benchmark of 12,847 log entries, demonstrating up to 88.2% attack success rate across production LLMs, introduce the Context Stitching evasion technique (76.4% success), and show layered defenses reduce attacks by 90.4% but leave 8.4% residual vulnerability.
AI.motivation: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) increasingly deploy LLMs for log analysis tasks (summarization, alert triage, threat investigation), ingesting logs from external-facing services as natural language contexts. This architectural pattern creates a novel attack surface where untrusted log data can contain prompt injection payloads that persist in storage and activate upon analyst querying — a vulnerability the authors term "passive prompt injection." The work is motivated by the need to systematically evaluate and characterize this emerging threat vector before widespread operational deployment.
AI.method: The authors develop LogInject, a systematic evaluation framework with LogInject-1.0, a benchmark containing 12,847 log entries (2,569 adversarial samples). They evaluate three production LLMs across four attack objectives: activity concealment, false positive generation, information exfiltration, and output hijacking. They introduce "Context Stitching," a novel technique that fragments malicious payloads across multiple log entries to evade stateless input filters while exploiting LLMs' long-context reasoning capabilities. For mitigation, they evaluate layered defenses combining input filtering, prompt hardening, and output validation.
AI.result: Under baseline conditions, they achieve up to 88.2% attack success rate (83.4% average across models). The Context Stitching technique achieves 76.4% success rate despite stateless filtering. Layered defenses combining input filtering, prompt hardening, and output validation demonstrate 90.4% attack reduction, but an 8.4% residual vulnerability remains, indicating that complete mitigation is currently infeasible without architectural changes.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based log analysis creates an inherent "confused deputy" vulnerability where untrusted data and trusted instructions compete indistinguishably for model attention. Complete mitigation requires defense-in-depth architectures and continued human oversight for security-critical decisions, as purely technical defenses leave residual risk.

title: Structured Feedback Improves Repair in an LLM Agent Loop
summary: LLM agents often retry after external validation rejects a candidate, but the interface between validation and the next model call remains underspecified. We introduce VeriHarness, a code-controlled agent loop in which models generate candidates while external validators control acceptance, budgets, and traces. We use it to compare raw diagnostics with feedback that identifies the failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives. Across 50 paired TextWorld games under a four-call cap, feedback containing all three fields raises terminal success from 14/50 to 36/50 for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (+44 percentage points) and from 8/50 to 29/50 for Llama-3.1-8B (+42 points). Ablations locate most of the gain in the admissible alternatives: feedback containing only the location and observed value remains near the raw diagnostic baseline. Presenting the complete repair information in prose instead of a keyed JSON record yields nearly the same success, providing no evidence that JSON syntax itself improves repair. The ordering persists across the tested call budgets and one sampled-decoding setting.

AI.tldr: VeriHarness introduces a code-controlled agent loop where external validators manage acceptance, budgets, and traces. Experiments across 50 TextWorld games show that failure feedback containing admissible alternatives dramatically boosts LLM agent success rates, with JSON vs. prose format showing no significant difference.
AI.motivation: The interface between external validation and the next model call in LLM agent retry loops is underspecified. Prior work lacks systematic study of what information validators should return to maximize repair success, and whether structured formats (e.g., JSON) offer advantages over natural language.
AI.method: The authors built VeriHarness, a code-controlled agent loop separating generation from validation. They compared raw diagnostics against structured feedback containing three fields: failure location, observed value, and admissible alternatives. Experiments ran across 50 paired TextWorld games with a four-call budget, testing Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and Llama-3.1-8B. Ablations isolated each feedback field, and format was varied between keyed JSON and prose.
AI.result: Feedback with all three fields raised terminal success from 14/50 to 36/50 for Qwen2.5-Coder-14B (+44pp) and from 8/50 to 29/50 for Llama-3.1-8B (+42pp). Ablations revealed admissible alternatives drove most gains; location-plus-observed-value alone performed near baseline. JSON vs. prose presentation yielded nearly identical success, and this ordering held across different call budgets and a sampled-decoding setting.
AI.conclusion: Admissible alternatives are the critical component of validator feedback for LLM repair. Structured JSON offers no inherent advantage over prose for conveying repair information. The VeriHarness framework provides a principled interface for studying and deploying validator-guided retry loops.

title: QFireNet: A Quantum-Enhanced U-Net for Wildfire Segmentation from Sentinel-2 Imagery
summary: Wildfire detection from satellite imagery is a semantic image segmentation problem that has proven to be difficult due to challenges such as class imbalance, feature complexity, and atmospheric interference. In this paper, we build on the foundational U-Net image segmentation model to develop a quantum-hybrid solution in hopes of more effectively modeling the high-dimensional spectral feature space of the Sen2Fire dataset. We inject a variational quantum circuit in the bottleneck portion of U-Net, specifically the QuFeX and QB-Net ansatzes. We test a classical Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) for further comparative analysis of the model, and we also explore classical improvements to the U-Net model and its training process, including a compression of parameters, alternative loss functions, and uniform mixing of input data. Our primary finding is that under matched conditions, both QB-Net (with an $F_1$ score of 31.18) and QuFeX ($F_1 = 30.79$) outperformed the classical U-Net baseline results ($F_1 = 28.71$). Additionally, the classical FPN achieved a comparable score of 31.13. A crucial finding was that data mixing removed a significant domain shift between the geographically-separated train and test sets, which boosted the classical FPN $F_1$ score to 39.76. We validate the architecture's robustness and generalizability to the wildfire detection problem via cross-dataset transfer on the California Burned Areas (CaBuAr) dataset. Overall, we find that quantum machine learning has potential to provide an advantage in the problem of wildfire image segmentation, and further experiments will continue to validate and expand upon this finding.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes quantum-hybrid U-Net variants (QuFeX, QB-Net) with variational quantum circuits injected at the bottleneck for wildfire detection from satellite imagery. Both quantum models modestly outperformed the classical U-Net baseline (F1: ~31 vs 28.71), but a classical FPN with data mixing achieved the best result (F1: 39.76), highlighting the critical role of addressing domain shift.
AI.motivation: Wildfire detection from satellite imagery is challenging due to class imbalance, high-dimensional spectral features, and atmospheric interference. The authors hypothesize that quantum machine learning may better model the complex high-dimensional spectral feature space of the Sen2Fire dataset than purely classical approaches.
AI.method: The authors extend U-Net by injecting variational quantum circuits (QuFeX and QB-Net ansatzes) at the bottleneck. They compare against a classical Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and explore classical improvements: parameter compression, alternative loss functions, and uniform data mixing across geographically-separated train/test splits. Cross-dataset transfer validation is performed on the CaBuAr dataset.
AI.result: Under matched conditions, QB-Net (F1=31.18) and QuFeX (F1=30.79) outperformed the classical U-Net baseline (F1=28.71). The classical FPN scored similarly (31.13). Data mixing removed a significant domain shift, boosting the classical FPN to F1=39.76. Cross-dataset transfer on CaBuAr validated generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Quantum machine learning shows potential for advantage in wildfire image segmentation, with quantum-hybrid models modestly surpassing classical U-Net. However, addressing domain shift via data mixing yielded far greater improvements, suggesting practical gains currently stem more from data engineering than from quantum components.

title: DialogueVPR: Towards Conversational Visual Place Recognition
summary: Inspired by how humans communicate spatial information, language-guided geo-localization has gained significant traction for its intuitive and practical value. Despite this progress, most methods still rely on a static, one-shot retrieval paradigm, which fails to handle the ambiguity and incompleteness inherent in real-world natural language descriptions. We propose a paradigm shift to reasoning retrieval and introduce Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), which casts localization as an interactive, dialogue-driven reasoning process. To support this new task, we present DlgQuest-Cities, the first large-scale dialogue-based benchmark for place recognition, and a unified reasoning framework that couples a cross-modal multi-level retriever with an intelligent questioner, DQ-pilot. DQ-pilot is trained in a curriculum: supervised fine-tuning on a curated DQ-cities-20k subset followed by reinforcement refinement on a harder DQ-cities-10k split via GRPO. Two task-aligned metrics guide learning: a Discriminative Difficulty Index (DDI) for curriculum sampling and a Positional Retrieval Gain (PRG) reward that directly measures retrieval improvement induced by a question. Experiments show this reasoning-based approach significantly outperforms baselines. The code and model are available at https://github.com/Graysonggg/DlgPR.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dialogue Place Recognition (DlgPR), shifting geo-localization from static one-shot retrieval to interactive, dialogue-driven reasoning. It contributes DlgQuest-Cities (a large-scale benchmark), a unified reasoning framework with a cross-modal retriever and an intelligent questioner (DQ-pilot) trained via supervised fine-tuning and GRPO-based reinforcement, using DDI for curriculum sampling and PRG as a retrieval-improvement reward. The approach significantly outperforms baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing language-guided geo-localization methods rely on static one-shot retrieval, which cannot handle the ambiguity and incompleteness of real-world natural language descriptions. This motivates a paradigm shift toward interactive, reasoning-based retrieval.
AI.method: The authors propose DlgPR with a unified framework coupling a cross-modal multi-level retriever and an intelligent questioner (DQ-pilot). DQ-pilot undergoes curriculum training: supervised fine-tuning on DQ-cities-20k, then GRPO-based reinforcement on DQ-cities-10k. A Discriminative Difficulty Index (DDI) drives curriculum sampling, and a Positional Retrieval Gain (PRG) reward measures retrieval improvement from each question.
AI.result: The reasoning-based DlgPR approach significantly outperforms baseline methods on the newly introduced DlgQuest-Cities benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Dialogue-driven reasoning retrieval represents a superior paradigm for language-guided geo-localization, effectively addressing ambiguity and incompleteness in natural language queries through interactive question-asking.

title: Automatic Hard Example Synthesis with Multi-Level Agentic Data Curation
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed for nuanced content safety and moderation tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks and out-of-distribution edge cases. Traditional active learning and manual annotation fail to scale against the complexity and volume of novel multimodal threats. In this paper, we propose an automated, agentic red-teaming framework that systematically synthesizes difficult examples using an iterative strategy that proposes novel hypotheses as well as mutating on past attempts. Leveraging a multi-agent architecture that consists of a high-reasoning Architect agent, an advanced image generator, and a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters, our system autonomously uncovers boundary-pushing violations and ambiguous policy edge cases without any human intervention. By employing these carefully synthesized adversarial examples as in-context demonstrations via test-time Retrieval, we substantially improve the target model's robustness, reducing the False Negative Rate (FNR) from 41.2% to 24.5% in a public image safety benchmark without relying on any human labeling.

AI.tldr: An automated multi-agent red-teaming framework iteratively synthesizes adversarial multimodal examples to uncover safety policy violations, then uses these as in-context retrieval demonstrations to improve MLLM robustness, reducing FNR from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image safety benchmark without human annotation.
AI.motivation: MLLMs deployed for content safety/moderation are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and OOD edge cases. Traditional active learning and manual annotation cannot scale to handle the complexity and volume of novel multimodal threats, creating a need for automated, scalable red-teaming methods.
AI.method: An agentic red-teaming framework with three components: (1) a high-reasoning Architect agent that proposes novel hypotheses and mutates past attempts iteratively; (2) an advanced image generator; and (3) a multi-level verification committee of LLM raters. The system autonomously generates boundary-pushing adversarial examples, which are then used as in-context demonstrations via test-time retrieval to improve the target model's robustness.
AI.result: The approach reduced the False Negative Rate from 41.2% to 24.5% on a public image safety benchmark, achieved without any human labeling.
AI.conclusion: Automated agentic red-teaming with iterative hypothesis-driven synthesis and test-time retrieval augmentation can effectively harden MLLMs against adversarial safety violations, offering a scalable alternative to human annotation-dependent methods.

title: UzWordnet and Generative AI for Learning Uzbek by Game Playing
summary: This paper presents an educational system architecture that enables learners to practice the Uzbek language through game-playing. The architecture integrates UzWordnet and the largest currently available orthographic dictionary for Uzbek as core lexical resources, together with generative AI as a fundamental component for learning support. We design four educational games to facilitate Uzbek language learning and propose a game-based methodology for improving UzWordnet as a direct by-product of game dynamics. Our approach combines game design and lexical resources to address objectives that are at the same time educational (language learning) and lexical (improvement and enrichment of a lexical resource).

AI.tldr: An educational system using games for Uzbek language learning that integrates UzWordnet, an orthographic dictionary, and generative AI, while simultaneously improving the lexical resource through gameplay.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of digital educational tools for Uzbek language learning while simultaneously enriching the UzWordnet lexical resource — a dual-purpose approach combining pedagogy and lexicography.
AI.method: Design of an educational architecture integrating UzWordnet, the largest Uzbek orthographic dictionary, and generative AI as core components. Four educational games are designed with a game-based methodology that allows improvement of UzWordnet as a by-product of player interactions.
AI.result: An architecture and methodology that achieves dual objectives: facilitating Uzbek language acquisition through game-based learning and enabling continuous lexical resource enrichment through gameplay dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Integrating game design with lexical resources creates a symbiotic system where language learners benefit from rich lexical data, and the lexical resource is simultaneously improved through learner interactions.

title: Memory-Driven Self-Disclosure and Relational Turning Points: A Longitudinal Multimodal Study of Human-AI Interaction
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to ICMI 2026 (International Conference on Multimodal Interaction), October 5-9, 2026, Napoli, Italy
summary: As conversational AI systems are designed for repeated use, a central question is how a series of interactions becomes a relationship. We present a longitudinal multimodal study of a memory-augmented conversational agent (24 participants x 10 sessions), in which participants rated five relational constructs -- familiarity, self-disclosure, perceived memory, conversational quality, and enjoyment -- after each session. Two complementary dynamics emerge. First, conversational quality strongly shapes how enjoyable a session feels in the moment but does not carry forward across sessions, whereas perceived memory is relationally conditioned -- predicted by prior relational state rather than reflecting system capability alone -- and it shapes later enjoyment indirectly, via subsequent self-disclosure. Second, relationships are punctuated by discrete turning points -- crashes and surges -- that are partially traceable in multimodal behavior and open different intervention windows: surges are more behaviorally detectable in the moment, enjoyment surges persist more reliably than enjoyment crashes recover, and some crashes are better forecast from person-specific behavioral drift than detected after they have already occurred. Together, the findings suggest that longitudinal human-AI relationships are built through both slow accumulation and abrupt turning points.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal study (24 participants, 10 sessions each) examining how human-AI relationships form over time with a memory-augmented conversational agent. Two dynamics emerge: (1) conversational quality drives momentary enjoyment but doesn't carry forward, while perceived memory is relationally conditioned and shapes future enjoyment indirectly through self-disclosure; (2) relationships feature discrete turning points (crashes and surges) traceable in multimodal behavior, with different intervention windows for each.
AI.motivation: As conversational AI moves toward repeated, long-term deployment, understanding how individual interactions accumulate into a sustained human-AI relationship becomes critical. Existing work focuses largely on single-session evaluations, leaving a gap in understanding the longitudinal dynamics, relational constructs, and behavioral signals that characterize evolving human-AI relationships.
AI.method: A longitudinal, multimodal study with 24 participants engaging in 10 sessions each with a memory-augmented conversational agent. After each session, participants rated five relational constructs: familiarity, self-disclosure, perceived memory, conversational quality, and enjoyment. The authors analyzed temporal dynamics between these constructs (carry-forward vs. momentary effects) and identified discrete turning points (crashes and surges) using multimodal behavioral signals, examining detectability, persistence, and forecastability.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) Conversational quality exerts only a momentary effect on enjoyment and does not carry forward across sessions, whereas perceived memory is predicted by prior relational state and indirectly shapes later enjoyment through promoting subsequent self-disclosure. (2) Relational trajectories are punctuated by discrete turning points — enjoyment surges are more behaviorally detectable in the moment than crashes; surges persist more reliably than crashes recover; and some crashes are better forecast from person-specific behavioral drift than detected post hoc.
AI.conclusion: Longitudinal human-AI relationships are built through dual mechanisms: slow accumulation of relational constructs (particularly via perceived memory and self-disclosure) and abrupt turning points (crashes and surges). These distinct dynamics suggest different intervention strategies — some turning points can be anticipated from behavioral drift, while others must be detected and addressed in real time.

title: CoSimRec: Measuring Coordinated-Content Penetration in Recommender Feedback Loops
summary: Recommender systems increasingly shape which content reaches users, making it important to understand whether coordinated activity is amplified beyond the accounts that initiate it. Existing robustness evaluations largely focus on static target-rank changes and do not capture how coordinated interactions, recommendation, and user response evolve within a feedback loop. To address this gap, we propose CoSimRec, an offline agent-based evaluation framework that models coordinated accounts, dynamic ranking, non-bot responses, and ranking interventions in a shared closed-loop process. CoSimRec introduces the Algorithmic Penetration Rate (APR) metric family to measure target content's share of non-bot exposure and engagement, lift against matched no-attack baselines, and exposure gained per coordinated interaction. We evaluate CoSimRec on MIND, MovieLens, and LastFM using random, popularity-based, feedback-sensitive, MF, and BPR-MF recommenders, with ten-seed inference for the primary APR analysis and population-scale experiments of up to 1000 users. Random controls show no statistically supported positive penetration, whereas popularity-based and feedback-sensitive ranking produce significant positive APR-Lift in all six master-worker dataset--recommender settings, reaching 0.4505 on LastFM; synchronization-aware ranking reduces APR in every corresponding defense setting.

AI.tldr: CoSimRec is an offline agent-based framework that models coordinated attacks, dynamic ranking, non-bot responses, and interventions in a closed feedback loop to evaluate recommender system vulnerability. It introduces Algorithmic Penetration Rate (APR) metrics and shows that popularity-based and feedback-sensitive recommenders amplify coordinated activity, while synchronization-aware ranking mitigates it.
AI.motivation: Existing robustness evaluations focus on static target-rank changes and fail to capture how coordinated interactions, recommendation algorithms, and user responses co-evolve within a feedback loop. The authors aim to assess whether coordinated activity is amplified beyond the initiating accounts in dynamic, closed-loop settings.
AI.method: Proposes CoSimRec, an offline agent-based evaluation framework simulating coordinated accounts, dynamic ranking, non-bot user responses, and ranking interventions in a shared closed-loop process. Introduces APR metrics: target content share of non-bot exposure/engagement, lift over matched no-attack baselines, and exposure per coordinated interaction. Evaluated on MIND, MovieLens, and LastFM using five recommenders (random, popularity-based, feedback-sensitive, MF, BPR-MF) with ten-seed inference and population-scale experiments up to 1000 users.
AI.result: Random recommenders show no statistically supported positive penetration. Popularity-based and feedback-sensitive ranking yield significant positive APR-Lift across all six dataset–recommender settings, reaching 0.4505 on LastFM. Synchronization-aware ranking reduces APR in every corresponding defense setting.
AI.conclusion: Recommendation algorithms that incorporate popularity or feedback signals amplify coordinated manipulation in closed-loop settings, while synchronization-aware ranking serves as an effective defense. The APR metric family provides a systematic way to quantify algorithmic penetration beyond static rank-based measures.

title: Fully Automated End-to-End Adversary Emulation from MITRE ATT\&CK Based Cyber Threat Intelligence Using LLMs
summary: This paper presents a fully automated end-to-end framework for adversary emulation from MITRE ATT&CK-aligned CTI reports using LLMs. Unlike prior work, which either executes prewritten playbooks or partially automates playbook generation, our framework unifies playbook generation, execution, and failure recovery in a single workflow. In particular, although AURORA, the most recent prior study, generates playbooks from CTI reports, it still requires partial manual intervention and does not revise playbooks based on execution failures. Our framework generates Caldera playbooks from CTI reports, executes them automatically, and revises failed Abilities through a failure-type-aware recovery mechanism. Evaluated on 11 CTI reports with Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok 4 Fast, the framework achieved its best results with Claude Sonnet 4.5: 27.3 Abilities per playbook, 84.22% execution success after revision, and CTI Precision, Recall, and F1 of 73.95%, 52.48%, and 60.50%, respectively. The failure recovery mechanism consistently improved execution success across all evaluated LLM models by 14.59%p to 17.23%p. On the 10 CTI reports selected from AURORA's dataset, this mechanism further increased the final execution success rate, surpassing that of AURORA, which represents the state-of-the-art adversary emulation system.

AI.tldr: A fully automated end-to-end framework that uses LLMs to generate, execute, and self-correct adversary emulation playbooks from CTI reports using a failure-type-aware recovery mechanism, outperforming prior state-of-the-art (AURORA) in execution success rates.
AI.motivation: Existing adversary emulation systems either rely on prewritten playbooks, require partial manual intervention, or lack mechanisms to revise playbooks based on execution failures. AURORA, the most recent approach, partially automates playbook generation but still needs human input and does not handle failure recovery. A fully automated, closed-loop system from CTI report to verified execution is needed.
AI.method: The framework consists of three unified stages: (1) LLM-based playbook generation from MITRE ATT&CK-aligned CTI reports, producing Caldera-compatible playbooks; (2) fully automated execution of generated playbooks; and (3) a failure-type-aware recovery mechanism that analyzes execution failures and revises failed Abilities accordingly. The system was evaluated using four LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok 4 Fast across 11 CTI reports, with a subset of 10 reports compared against AURORA's dataset.
AI.result: Best performance was achieved with Claude Sonnet 4.5: 27.3 Abilities per playbook, 84.22% post-revision execution success, and CTI Precision/Recall/F1 of 73.95%, 52.48%, and 60.50%. The failure recovery mechanism improved execution success by 14.59–17.23 percentage points across all LLMs. On the AURORA subset, the framework surpassed AURORA's final execution success rate.
