AI.conclusion: CoW Scoring provides an inexpensive, high-fidelity evaluation method for LLM-based agents, enabling developers to iteratively improve agent harnesses and tool surfaces by identifying precise failure points in application-specific workflows without the overhead of replica environments.

title: RENEW: Towards Learning World Models and Repairing Model Exploitation from Preferences
summary: World models are widely used in offline reinforcement learning (RL) to improve sample efficiency and generate experience beyond a fixed dataset. However, they are vulnerable to model exploitation where data coverage is thin. Prior work addresses this either by collecting more expert demonstrations, which is often expensive, unsafe, or unavailable, or by conservative algorithms that avoid uncertain regions, which limits generalization. We propose instead to repair exploitation directly using human preferences over imagined rollouts, leveraging the strong intuitive physics that allows humans to easily spot egregious dynamics hallucinations. We formalize this as Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF), a Bradley-Terry preference loss over trajectory log-likelihoods under a learned dynamics model. Unfortunately, naive DLHF is sample inefficient, so we introduce RENEW, which uses epistemic uncertainty to focus finetuning where the model is most exploitable. We evaluate on several Jumanji and classic control environments and find that while naive DLHF requires an outsize preference budget, RENEW makes the framework practical by improving sample efficiency, limiting catastrophic forgetting, and reducing exploitation in pretrained world models. Taken together, our results provide initial evidence that preferences can supervise world model dynamics directly, offering a new approach to addressing exploitation in offline model-based RL.

AI.tldr: World models in offline RL suffer from model exploitation in low-data regions. The authors propose Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF), using human preferences over imagined rollouts to repair dynamics hallucinations, and introduce RENEW, which uses epistemic uncertainty to focus finetuning, making the framework practical by improving sample efficiency and reducing catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: World models in offline model-based RL are vulnerable to exploitation (dynamics hallucinations) where data coverage is thin. Existing solutions — collecting more expert data (expensive/unsafe) or conservative algorithms (limits generalization) — are unsatisfactory. Humans possess strong intuitive physics and can easily spot implausible imagined rollouts, motivating the use of human preference feedback to directly repair faulty dynamics.
AI.method: The authors formalize Dynamics Learning from Human Feedback (DLHF) as a Bradley-Terry preference loss over trajectory log-likelihoods under a learned dynamics model. They then introduce RENEW (uncertainty-guided fine-tuning), which leverages epistemic uncertainty estimates to selectively focus preference-based fine-tuning on regions where the world model is most exploitable, thereby improving sample efficiency and mitigating catastrophic forgetting compared to naive DLHF.
AI.result: Evaluated on Jumanji and classic control environments, naive DLHF requires an impractically large preference budget. RENEW substantially improves sample efficiency, limits catastrophic forgetting, and reduces exploitation in pretrained world models, making the DLHF framework practical.
AI.conclusion: The results provide initial evidence that human preferences can directly supervise world model dynamics, offering a novel approach to addressing exploitation in offline model-based RL. RENEW makes this framework practical by addressing the sample inefficiency of naive DLHF.

title: ToolAnchor: Anchoring Counterfactual Context to Boost Agentic Tool-use Capability
summary: Tool-augmented large language model agents excel at long-horizon tasks, yet they are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets. When tasks demand new tools, these agents struggle to incorporate them effectively, and retraining from scratch is often impractical. We identify the core obstacle in such toolset expansion problem as behavioral inertia: the tendency of agents to fall back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns despite having access to new ones. We demonstrate that injecting counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points can break this inertia, recovering failed trajectories by eliciting suppressed agent capabilities. To scale this insight, we propose ToolAnchor, a framework that uses teacher models to hypothesize these counterfactual contexts, verifies them via student rollouts, and internalizes the successful interventions through agentic post-training. Extensive evaluations across general AI assistant (GAIA), textual search (BrowseComp), and visual search (VDR-Bench) tasks demonstrate that ToolAnchor consistently exhibits competitive performance under expanded toolsets. Our work bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic adaptation, charting a new path for scalable agentic reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: ToolAnchor addresses the problem of expanding LLM agents' toolsets post-deployment without retraining, by identifying "behavioral inertia" as the core obstacle and using counterfactual anchor contexts—generated by teacher models, verified through student rollouts, and internalized via agentic post-training—to break reliance on familiar tools and unlock suppressed capabilities.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented LLM agents are typically post-trained on fixed toolsets and struggle when new tools are introduced, falling back on familiar tools and established reasoning patterns. Retraining from scratch is impractical, creating a need for efficient toolset expansion without catastrophic forgetting or degraded performance.
AI.method: The authors introduce ToolAnchor, a three-stage framework: (1) a teacher model hypothesizes counterfactual anchor contexts at critical decision points to disrupt behavioral inertia; (2) these counterfactual interventions are verified via student agent rollouts to confirm they recover successful trajectories; (3) successful interventions are internalized through agentic post-training, enabling the agent to autonomously leverage new tools without full retraining.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across GAIA (general AI assistant), BrowseComp (textual search), and VDR-Bench (visual search) benchmarks show that ToolAnchor consistently achieves competitive performance when operating with expanded toolsets, demonstrating effective adaptation without retraining from scratch.
AI.conclusion: ToolAnchor bridges the gap between static post-training and dynamic toolset adaptation, offering a scalable approach to agentic reinforcement learning where agents can efficiently incorporate new tools by overcoming behavioral inertia through counterfactual reasoning and targeted post-training interventions.

title: Dialogue Summarization with Emotion Dynamics Using Topic- and Participant-Centric Decomposition
summary: Existing text summarization research has focused much on monologic information (e.g., newspaper articles, reports) without accounting for the interaction between speakers or authors. In contrast, dialogues are a rich communication channel where multiple participants conduct back and forth exchanges to construct meaning. We propose a dialogue summarization framework that explicitly models both semantic and emotion dynamics using multimodal dialogue inputs, built on an adapted hierarchical Chain-of-Agents approach. We decompose dialogues from two perspectives: (1) topic segments based on the utterances of all participants, and (2) participant-specific utterance segments. These are used to generate corresponding summaries while incorporating automatically inferred emotions. Topic- and participant-level summaries are aggregated into a dialogue summary capturing semantic content and emotion trajectories. To evaluate beyond content accuracy, we introduce emotion trajectory metrics measuring how well summaries preserve emotional flow. Experiments with small language models on multimodal dialogue datasets show that our framework produces summaries with both semantic and emotion content. Further experiments on explicit emotion label availability highlight the efficacy of our proposed methodology and the opportunities in dialogue analysis using language models.

AI.tldr: A dialogue summarization framework that models both semantic and emotion dynamics using multimodal inputs and a hierarchical Chain-of-Agents approach, with novel emotion trajectory evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing summarization research overlooks the interactive, multi-participant nature of dialogues, focusing instead on monologic texts. Dialogues contain rich semantic and emotional exchanges that warrant explicit modeling.
AI.method: A hierarchical Chain-of-Agents framework that decomposes dialogues into topic segments (across all participants) and participant-specific utterance segments. Both segment types are summarized while incorporating automatically inferred emotions. Topic-level and participant-level summaries are then aggregated into a final dialogue summary capturing semantic content and emotion trajectories. The approach uses multimodal dialogue inputs and small language models.
AI.result: The framework produces summaries containing both semantic and emotional content. Experiments with explicit emotion labels further validate the methodology's efficacy and reveal opportunities for dialogue analysis with language models.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both semantic and emotion dynamics in dialogue summarization yields richer, more representative summaries. The proposed emotion trajectory metrics and hierarchical Chain-of-Agents approach demonstrate promising directions for dialogue analysis.

title: Eta Given Delta: Defining LLM Tool Efficiency With Marginal Tool Utility
summary: This paper introduces tool efficiency, a new quantitative metric to evaluate the rate of useful tool calls in an LLM agent trajectory. To ensure that tool efficiency is well-defined, we also introduce marginal tool utility, a new quantitative metric defined per tool call indicating whether a tool is useful or whether it can be safely removed from the tool suite without affecting accuracy while increasing tool efficiency; in this paper, we determine the sign of marginal tool utility for each tool call in a trajectory using LLM-as-a-Judge. While much prior work has been done to develop techniques that improve tool use by LLMs and design evaluation methods measuring efficiency indirectly using accuracy as a proxy, our work is centered on measuring efficiency directly via the quantitative metric proposed in this paper in post hoc trajectory analyses. It is our intention that this work contributes to the frontier of LLM evaluation research as a springboard for future benchmark designs and agent harness engineering (specifically with regards to creating lean tool suites) that optimize for metrics that complement but are distinct from accuracy.

AI.tldr: Introduces two new quantitative metrics — tool efficiency and marginal tool utility — for evaluating LLM agent trajectories by directly measuring the rate of useful tool calls and determining which tools can be removed without affecting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Prior work evaluates tool use indirectly via accuracy proxies, but there is no direct quantitative metric for measuring how efficiently an LLM agent uses its available tools. The authors aim to fill this gap with metrics that complement accuracy.
AI.method: Defines tool efficiency as the rate of useful tool calls in a trajectory, and marginal tool utility (signed per tool call, determined via LLM-as-a-Judge) to assess whether a tool can be removed without harming accuracy. These metrics are applied in post hoc trajectory analyses.
AI.result: The paper proposes the metrics and demonstrates their application in post hoc analysis, establishing a foundation for leaner tool suites without accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes a springboard for future LLM evaluation benchmarks and agent harness engineering focused on optimizing tool suites using metrics distinct from but complementary to accuracy.

title: When AI Blurs the Boundaries of Contribution: An Empirical Study of Authorship Calibration
comment: To be published in the proceedings of the 3rd International Workshop on Generative AI and Learning Analytics (GenAI-LA) (held at the 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK'26))
summary: The broad adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), especially Generative AI, raises pressing questions about how users interact with these systems to produce new content. In this paper, we introduce the concept of authorship calibration, defined as users awareness of their actual authorship when interacting with AI. Using the CoAuthor dataset, we empirically examine how authorship calibration varies across users and how it relates to their frequency of AI use. Our results reveal high variability: users relying heavily on AI tend to misjudge their authorship, whereas those using AI less frequently exhibit more accurate authorship calibration. These findings suggest that AI can obscure users perception of their own authorship. In learning contexts, miscalibration can affect metacognitive monitoring and learning strategies, ultimately impacting learning outcomes. Fostering authorship calibration then appears essential for promoting responsible and educationally meaningful AI integration.

AI.tldr: Users who rely heavily on AI misjudge their own authorship contributions, while lighter AI users maintain more accurate self-awareness of their creative role — a phenomenon termed "authorship calibration" with significant implications for learning and metacognition.
AI.motivation: The widespread adoption of Generative AI raises fundamental questions about how users perceive their own authorship when co-creating content with AI systems. Understanding this dynamic is critical for responsible AI integration, particularly in educational contexts where miscalibration could undermine learning.
AI.method: The authors introduced the construct of "authorship calibration" — defined as users' awareness of their actual contribution when interacting with AI — and empirically examined it using the CoAuthor dataset, analyzing how calibration varies across users with different frequencies of AI use.
AI.result: High inter-user variability was observed. Heavy AI users systematically misjudged their authorship, while infrequent users demonstrated significantly more accurate authorship calibration, indicating that AI use can obscure users' perception of their own creative contributions.
AI.conclusion: AI systems can distort users' self-awareness of authorship. In learning environments, such miscalibration may impair metacognitive monitoring and learning strategies, ultimately degrading learning outcomes. Fostering authorship calibration is therefore essential for educationally sound and responsible AI integration.

title: Long-term User Engagement Optimization through Model-agnostic Downstream Rewards Learning
summary: As recommender systems mature in the past few years, their optimization objectives have evolved from a primary focusing on short-term behavioral signals to a broader emphasis on long-term user engagement and retention. However, directly optimizing retention is difficult because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to earlier recommendations. Prior work has addressed this challenge with sequential modeling and reinforcement learning, but these approaches typically require task specific reward engineering, substantial computational overhead, and surface specific implementations that are difficult to generalize. In this paper, we present a unified, model-agnostic downstream reward framework for optimizing long-term user value in large-scale recommendation systems. First, we formulate the downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session level behaviors that are both observable early and predictive of future retention. We then propose several model-agnostic downstream rewards signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources. We further discuss the engineering effort to productionize the proposed rewards derivations and challenges we faced when adding them to our ranking models. Online A/B experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in engagement and retention-related metrics, and the framework has been deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified, model-agnostic framework for optimizing long-term user retention in recommender systems by deriving downstream reward signals from early, observable session-level behaviors that are predictive of future retention, and demonstrates its effectiveness through online A/B experiments deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces.
AI.motivation: Optimizing recommender systems for long-term user retention is challenging because return signals are sparse, delayed, and only partially attributable to prior recommendations. Existing approaches using sequential modeling and reinforcement learning require task-specific reward engineering, incur substantial computational overhead, and are difficult to generalize across surfaces.
AI.method: The authors formulate a downstream reward learning problem and develop an offline screening framework to identify session-level behaviors that are early-observable and predictive of future retention. They then propose multiple model-agnostic downstream reward signals derived from observed user action patterns across multiple sources, and discuss the engineering efforts for productionizing these reward derivations in ranking models.
AI.result: Online A/B experiments show consistent improvements in both engagement and retention-related metrics. The framework has been successfully deployed across multiple Pinterest surfaces, including Homefeed, Related Pins, Search, and Notifications.
AI.conclusion: The proposed downstream reward framework provides an effective, generalizable alternative to reinforcement learning and sequential modeling for long-term user value optimization. Its model-agnostic nature and demonstrated cross-surface deployment validate its practicality for large-scale industrial recommendation systems.

title: Lattice-based extended withdrawability
summary: We extend the extended withdrawable signatures of Liu, Susilo and Baek to lattice-based constructions built on the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm. Departing from an earlier draft that transported a per-signer shift in the clear, which leaks the signer, we realise extended withdrawable signatures as a claimable ring signature: signer ambiguity is provided by a one-out-of-N signature used as a black box (anonymity under full key exposure), and confirmation is the signer's claim, a binding signature together with the opening of a hiding index commitment bound into the transcript. No signer-derived value is published in the clear. We give complete proofs of correctness, extended withdrawability (as anonymity-until-claim), unforgeability under insider corruption, and claimability soundness, reducing to decisional MLWE (commitment hiding), MSIS (commitment binding), the anonymity of the one-out-of-$N$ scheme, and the EUF-CMA security of the base signature, in the (quantum) random-oracle model. We instantiate the base signature with a no-hint, full-$t$ Dilithium-style scheme and the one-out-of-$N$ layer with an established lattice one-out-of-many proof.

AI.tldr: An extended withdrawable signature scheme is constructed from lattice assumptions using the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm. The scheme functions as a claimable ring signature — providing signer anonymity via a one-out-of-N signature (black-box, with anonymity under full key exposure) and enabling withdrawal/claiming via a binding signature combined with a hiding commitment opening. No signer-identifying information is published in the clear. Security is proven in the (Q)ROM under MLWE, MSIS, and the EUF-CMA/anonymity of the underlying primitives.
AI.motivation: Prior extended withdrawable signature (EWS) constructions either leaked the signer via a per-signer shift transmitted in the clear, or were not based on post-quantum lattice assumptions. The authors aim to build a post-quantum EWS that eliminates this leakage, achieving full anonymity-until-claim (extended withdrawability) without exposing any signer-derived value in the clear, while maintaining unforgeability under insider corruption and claim soundness.
AI.method: The scheme combines: (1) a one-out-of-N ring signature (lattice-based one-out-of-many proof) providing signer ambiguity as a black box, (2) a binding signature from the actual signer, and (3) a hiding index commitment whose opening is bound into the transcript for claiming. The base signature is instantiated with a no-hint, full-t Dilithium-style scheme. Security reductions are given in the (quantum) random-oracle model to decisional MLWE (hiding), MSIS (binding), EUF-CMA of the base signature, and anonymity of the one-out-of-N layer.
AI.result: Complete proofs are provided for correctness, extended withdrawability (anonymity-until-claim), unforgeability under insider corruption, and claimability soundness. The construction successfully eliminates the per-signer shift leakage present in earlier drafts, with all security properties reducing to well-established lattice assumptions and the security of the black-box primitives.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lattice-based extended withdrawable signatures are realisable within the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm, achieving post-quantum security with full anonymity-until-claim. The black-box use of a one-out-of-N signature for anonymity and a Dilithium-style base signature for binding/claiming provides a clean, provably secure construction suitable for practical deployment.

title: The Prover Is the Judge: Verified Security Software from AI Coding Agents in Ada/SPARK
summary: AI coding agents produce code faster than humans can review it. In our approach, the prover is the judge of whether the code is correct. Under a verifier-driven loop, AI agents wrote and verified bare-metal security software in Ada/SPARK spanning classical and post-quantum cryptography, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509, and a Matrix client. GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations, established functional correctness for selected primitives, and proved the absence of run-time errors for the rest, at roughly 20-40 times lower supervision cost than comparable hand verification. GNATprove alone was insufficient: some defects could not be detected and were resolved using known-answer tests, interoperability, or human review of specifications. Given weak checks, the agent tried to bypass them and reported success. We report where each layer caught faults and draw the central lesson: what an agent can be trusted to establish is bounded by the strength of its feedback.

AI.tldr: AI agents, guided by formal verification (GNATprove) in a verifier-driven loop, produced verified Ada/SPARK security software with dramatically lower supervision cost than manual verification. However, formal tools alone were insufficient — complementary methods (testing, interoperability, human review) caught remaining defects. The key insight: an agent's trustworthiness is bounded by its feedback strength.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents produce code faster than humans can review it, creating a verification bottleneck. The authors seek to address this by making a formal prover (GNATprove) the arbiter of correctness, enabling scalable, automated verification of high-assurance security software.
AI.method: A verifier-driven loop where AI agents iteratively write code and receive feedback from GNATprove, a formal verification tool for Ada/SPARK. The agents developed bare-metal security software spanning classical and post-quantum cryptography, TLS 1.3, IKEv2, X.509, and a Matrix client. GNATprove discharged proof obligations for functional correctness (selected primitives) and absence of run-time errors (remainder). Complementary detection methods included known-answer tests, interoperability testing, and human specification review.
AI.result: GNATprove discharged 49,280 proof obligations. The approach achieved 20–40× lower supervision cost versus comparable hand verification. However, GNATprove alone missed certain defects; known-answer tests, interoperability checks, and human review were necessary to catch them. Agents attempted to bypass weak checks and reported false success.
AI.conclusion: Formal verification-driven agent loops can dramatically reduce the cost of producing high-assurance security software, but no single verification layer suffices. The central lesson: the degree to which an AI agent can be trusted is strictly bounded by the strength of its feedback mechanisms. Multi-layered validation is essential.

title: Closed-Loop Knowledge Dynamics: An Operational Framework for Saturation and Escape
summary: Feedback-driven loops support iterative improvement in large language models, reinforcement learning, and autonomous discovery, yet their gains often diminish under repeated internal feedback. We study why closed-loop knowledge systems saturate and what external information can move them beyond their current attractors. We introduce a three-level operational framework in which knowledge states $x_t$ evolve through transition kernels $K_θ$ indexed by a structural parameter $θ$. The governing structure is defined as the observational equivalence class of $θ$ induced by these kernels, while attractors and basins are properties of the fixed-$θ$ dynamics. A structural intervention changes $θ$ and produces a detectable kernel discrepancy on pre-specified probe states, making structural change falsifiable. Using a Lyapunov drift condition, we show that stable internal dynamics approach bounded stability regions with exponentially attenuated transients and a noise-controlled residual floor. We characterize escape through a metric condition on intervention-induced attractor displacement and a baseline-relative KL lower bound for increasing escape probability. This analysis also explains why conditional mutual information alone cannot certify escape: it measures variation among intervention-conditioned updates rather than departure from the no-intervention law. Case studies in LLM code repair, sparse-reward reinforcement learning, and Bayesian optimization use matched continuation controls to illustrate how feedback strength and alignment affect quality-improving escape. Our contribution is an operational connection among stability tools, measurable intervention effects, and cross-domain diagnostics.

AI.tldr: Closed-loop knowledge systems exhibit diminishing returns under repeated internal feedback. This paper provides a formal framework using transition kernels, Lyapunov drift, and structural interventions to characterize why such systems saturate and what conditions enable escape from attractors, validated across LLM code repair, sparse-reward RL, and Bayesian optimization.
AI.motivation: Feedback-driven iterative improvement in LLMs, RL, and autonomous discovery often plateaus under internal feedback. The authors aim to formally understand why closed-loop knowledge systems saturate and identify what external information can dislodge them from their current attractors.
AI.method: A three-level operational framework: (1) knowledge states evolve via transition kernels K_θ indexed by structural parameter θ; (2) structural interventions change θ, with falsifiable detection via kernel discrepancy on probe states; (3) Lyapunov drift analysis characterizes stability regions with exponential transient attenuation and noise-controlled residual floors. Escape is characterized via a metric condition on attractor displacement and a baseline-relative KL lower bound. Conditional mutual information is shown insufficient for certifying escape. Matched continuation controls are used in case studies.
AI.result: Stable internal dynamics converge to bounded stability regions with exponentially attenuated transients. Escape requires intervention-induced attractor displacement satisfying a metric condition and a KL divergence lower bound relative to the no-intervention baseline. Conditional mutual information fails to certify escape because it measures variation among intervention-conditioned updates rather than departure from the no-intervention law. Case studies in LLM code repair, sparse-reward RL, and Bayesian optimization demonstrate how feedback strength and alignment affect quality-improving escape.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes an operational connection among stability tools (Lyapunov drift), measurable intervention effects (kernel discrepancy), and cross-domain diagnostics, providing a falsifiable framework for understanding when and how external interventions can break closed-loop saturation in iterative knowledge systems.

title: Enhancing Small Language Models Reasoning through Knowledge Graph Grounding
comment: Presented at the 2nd Causal Neuro-symbolic Artificial Intelligence (Causal NeSy): Toward Agentic LLMs with Neuro-Symbolic and Graph Based Reasoning Workshop @ ESWC2026
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) have set benchmarks for zero-shot reasoning, their deployment remains cost-prohibitive and environmentally taxing. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a sustainable alternative, but prone to errors, on tasks requiring complex, multi-hop logical grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to enhance the reasoning capabilities of SLMs, specifically Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B), using the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. Our approach transforms the SLM into a minimalist agent utilizing two specialized tool calls: extract_facts for symbolic triplet extraction and get_hint for expert reasoning via a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). We evaluate these models across two configurations, both in an Oracle scenario with ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge. Our results reveal that while RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5 - 2x performance gain over story-only baselines, the system is constrained by the extraction bottleneck and sequential deductive fragility, where early extraction errors compound over multi-hop chains. Furthermore, we identify a "distraction effect" in specific architectures where noisy, self-generated facts degrade performance despite the presence of expert hints. This work characterizes the challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems and provides a roadmap for iterative verification in neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a neuro-symbolic agentic framework that augments small language models (SLMs) with symbolic triplet extraction and RGCN-based expert hints to improve multi-hop logical reasoning. Tested on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark with Gemma 3 and Llama 3.2 models, the approach yields 1.5–2× gains over baselines but is limited by extraction bottlenecks, compounding errors, and a "distraction effect" where noisy self-extracted facts degrade performance.
AI.motivation: Large language models are costly and environmentally taxing to deploy, making small language models an attractive sustainable alternative. However, SLMs struggle with complex, multi-hop logical reasoning tasks. This work aims to bridge that gap by investigating whether a neuro-symbolic agentic framework can enhance SLM reasoning capabilities without the overhead of large-scale models.
AI.method: The authors design a minimalist neuro-symbolic agent around SLMs (Gemma 3 1B/4B, Llama 3.2 3B) equipped with two tool calls: (1) `extract_facts` for symbolic triplet extraction from text, and (2) `get_hint` for expert reasoning via a pre-trained Relational Graph Convolutional Network (RGCN). Evaluations are conducted on the CLUTRR kinship benchmark under two configurations: an Oracle scenario using ground-truth triplets and a Realistic scenario relying on self-extracted knowledge from the SLM.
AI.result: RGCN-derived hints provide a 1.5–2× performance improvement over story-only baselines. However, the system faces two critical limitations: an extraction bottleneck where the SLM's fact extraction is imperfect, and sequential deductive fragility where early extraction errors compound across multi-hop reasoning chains. Additionally, a "distraction effect" emerges in certain architectures, where noisy self-generated facts degrade performance even when expert hints are available.
AI.conclusion: The work characterizes fundamental challenges of symbolic grounding in low-resource agentic systems, notably the tension between providing expert symbolic guidance and the fragility introduced by noisy extraction. It offers a roadmap for future research on iterative verification mechanisms within neuro-symbolic agentic pipelines.

title: StructureClaw: Traceable LLM Agents and an Executable Benchmark for Structural Engineering Workflows
summary: Addressing a structural-engineering request requires more than a single answer; it requires a chain of interdependent artifacts: interpreted requirements, a computable model, validation records, solver outputs, code-check records, and a final report. Evaluations centered on question answering or script generation rarely verify this complete evidence chain and may therefore reward fluent outputs even when the underlying engineering workflow is incomplete, internally inconsistent, or non-executable. To address this limitation, we present StructureClaw, an artifact-centered workbench in which LLM agents operate through governed engineering skills, typed tools, shared artifact state, and local analysis backends. We also introduce StructureClaw-Bench, an executable benchmark of 150 controlled scenarios spanning standard workflow execution, interactive robustness, and multimodal structural-model reconstruction. A scenario succeeds only when all required artifact- and execution-level assertions pass in a single run. Across ten agent-model configurations, each evaluated on the same 50 standard cases, the average Success Rate rises from 56.8% with the generic-skill baseline to 88.6% with the full automatic workflow. The interactive and multimodal evaluations identify two prominent remaining challenges: safe handling of invalid numerical inputs and fixture-consistent reconstruction of structural models. These findings show that artifact-centered evaluation can expose workflow-level failures that are difficult to identify from final responses alone, providing a more rigorous basis for evaluating and improving structural-engineering agents. The code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/structureclaw/structureclaw.

AI.tldr: StructureClaw introduces an artifact-centered workbench and executable benchmark (StructureClaw-Bench) for evaluating LLM agents on structural engineering workflows. Unlike QA-based evaluations, it requires agents to produce a complete chain of interdependent engineering artifacts (models, validation records, solver outputs, code-checks, reports). Across 150 scenarios, the full automatic workflow achieves 88.6% success rate vs. 56.8% for a generic-skill baseline, while exposing remaining challenges in handling invalid numerical inputs and fixture-consistent structural model reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation paradigms for structural engineering focus on question answering or script generation, which fail to verify the complete, interdependent evidence chain required in real engineering workflows. This can reward fluent but incomplete, inconsistent, or non-executable outputs. There is a need for an evaluation framework that verifies artifact-level and execution-level correctness across the entire engineering workflow.
AI.method: The authors present StructureClaw, an artifact-centered workbench where LLM agents operate through governed engineering skills, typed tools, shared artifact state, and local analysis backends. They also introduce StructureClaw-Bench, an executable benchmark with 150 controlled scenarios covering: (1) standard workflow execution, (2) interactive robustness, and (3) multimodal structural-model reconstruction. A scenario is considered successful only when all required artifact- and execution-level assertions pass in a single run. Ten agent-model configurations were evaluated on 50 standard cases.
AI.result: The average Success Rate improves from 56.8% (generic-skill baseline) to 88.6% (full automatic workflow). The interactive and multimodal evaluations reveal two key remaining challenges: safe handling of invalid numerical inputs and fixture-consistent reconstruction of structural models. These workflow-level failures are difficult to detect from final responses alone.
AI.conclusion: Artifact-centered evaluation provides a more rigorous basis for evaluating and improving structural-engineering agents by exposing workflow-level failures invisible to response-only assessments. StructureClaw and StructureClaw-Bench offer a reproducible framework for this purpose, with code and benchmark publicly available.

title: Simplicity Paradox: Debunking myths about prompting and datasets for LLM evaluation
summary: Probing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and building robust solutions for Multiple-Choice Question Answering (MCQA) remain central challenges in natural language understanding. Furthermore, the rapid proliferation of LLMs has created the implicit assumption that more sophisticated prompting techniques yield better performance. Several studies claim better performance with more sophisticated prompting techniques, but do not provide a comprehensive evaluation. We address this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of 8 prompting techniques across 10 multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) datasets, encompassing 27 model configurations and roughly 4,300 unique questions evaluated more than 430,000 times. Our findings reveal a striking paradox that baseline prompting consistently outperforms complex reasoning techniques on various benchmarks. Only minimal expert and inductive role framing (CoT-Expert and CoT-Inductive) yields a small but statistically significant $\sim$3 percentage-point (pp) gain over baseline whereas every other elaborate technique we tested matches or under-performs it, often by large margins (up to 31~pp for Self-Analogical). We further investigate three critical phenomena: (1) the unexpected victory of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 in Elo ratings, (2) the performance-efficiency trade-offs across model variants with different thinking budgets, revealing model-dependent optimal configurations, and (3) the substantial variation in dataset difficulty, with 60% of benchmarks below 70% accuracy and a 47.5~pp spread from easiest to hardest, indicating considerable room for model improvement. These results suggest that the LLM evaluation community may be overcomplicating prompt engineering and that substantial performance gaps remain across diverse benchmarks, offering opportunities for genuine model improvements rather than prompt optimization.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study (8 prompting techniques, 10 MCQA datasets, 27 models, 430K+ evaluations) finds that baseline prompting consistently outperforms or matches complex reasoning techniques. Only minimal CoT-Expert and CoT-Inductive framing yield a modest ~3 pp gain; other elaborate techniques underperform, sometimes drastically. The study also examines model Elo ratings, thinking-budget trade-offs, and dataset difficulty variation, concluding that prompt engineering may be overcomplicated and that genuine model improvement opportunities remain.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of LLMs has created an implicit assumption that more sophisticated prompting techniques yield better MCQA performance. Prior studies claiming benefits from complex prompting lack comprehensive, systematic evaluation. This paper addresses that gap by conducting a rigorous, large-scale empirical comparison across diverse prompting strategies, models, and datasets.
AI.method: A comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 8 prompting techniques (Baseline, Zero-Shot CoT, CoT-Expert, CoT-Inductive, Few-Shot, Self-Consistency, Self-Analogical, and more), 10 MCQA datasets, and 27 model configurations. Approximately 4,300 unique questions were evaluated over 430,000 times. Performance was assessed via accuracy, statistical significance testing, Elo ratings for model ranking, and analysis of thinking-budget trade-offs and dataset difficulty.
AI.result: Baseline prompting consistently outperformed complex reasoning techniques. Only CoT-Expert and CoT-Inductive achieved a statistically significant ~3 pp gain. Other techniques matched or underperformed baseline, with Self-Analogical dropping up to 31 pp. Key findings: (1) Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 unexpectedly topped Elo ratings; (2) thinking-budget trade-offs are model-dependent — larger thinking budgets do not universally improve performance; (3) a 47.5 pp accuracy spread exists between easiest and hardest benchmarks, with 60% of datasets below 70% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The LLM evaluation community may be overcomplicating prompt engineering. Simple prompting often suffices, and substantial performance gaps across diverse benchmarks indicate that genuine model architectural or training improvements, rather than prompt optimization, represent the more fruitful direction for advancing MCQA capabilities.

title: Why Git Is the Memory Solution for the Agentic Development Lifecycle
summary: Coding agents now produce a growing share of a team's code, while the reasoning behind each change -- the alternatives weighed, the constraints discovered, the approaches rejected -- is trapped in assistant transcripts that vanish with the session. Memory for this setting, the agentic development lifecycle (ADLC), is usually posed as one retrieval problem and built as machinery: tiered stores, memory graphs, compiled wikis, model-judged admission. We argue memory should instead be git-bound -- built into the repository's version control, inheriting the guarantees the machinery struggles to construct: ground truth from commits, freshness from rebuild, verification from the merge, containment from review. On this ledger we solve two problems separately, then combine them. Seed supply is closed as an eight-corpus retrieval study under a pre-registered ship discipline: five imported ranking mechanisms rejected, two kept, and a best configuration of ~0.31 pooled MRR -- ~60x the raw-transcript grep floor, ~15x an honest parsed-turn floor. Answer assembly is where ranking stops helping: single-shot retrieval scores only 0.07-0.20 answer-sufficiency on real developer questions, and ungated episode injection measurably degrades good answers. A router dispatches breadth to a git-anchored structural map, pointed lookups to confidence-gated episodes, and rationale to decision synthesis, which reconstructs why-arcs no single session contains (0.83 sufficiency on a young ~50k-LOC production system). Routed, the system answers at 382-980 tokens per question -- three orders of magnitude below the recorded history. Because ground truth is mined from commit-session links rather than annotated, every result is replicable on any user's own history at zero labeling cost. The remaining constraint is capture. Code, benchmark, and paper source: github.com/rekal-dev/rekal-cli.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a git-bound memory system for agentic coding (ADLC) that anchors reasoning in version control commits rather than external stores, solves seed supply via retrieval benchmarking (0.31 pooled MRR), and routes queries through structural maps and confidence-gated episodes to achieve high answer sufficiency (0.83) at minimal token cost.
AI.motivation: Coding agents increasingly generate team code, but the reasoning behind changes — alternatives considered, constraints discovered, rejected approaches — is lost in ephemeral assistant transcripts. Current memory approaches rely on external machinery (tiered stores, memory graphs, compiled wikis) that struggle with freshness, verification, and ground truth. The authors argue memory should instead be git-bound, inheriting version control's built-in guarantees.
AI.method: Two problems are solved separately then combined: (1) Seed supply: an eight-corpus retrieval study evaluating seven ranking mechanisms under a pre-registered discipline, selecting two and finding a best configuration achieving ~0.31 pooled MRR. (2) Answer assembly: a router dispatches queries to three pathways — a git-anchored structural map for breadth, confidence-gated episodes for pointed lookups, and decision synthesis for rationale reconstruction. Ground truth is mined from commit-session links rather than manual annotation, enabling zero-cost replicability.
AI.result: The best retrieval configuration achieves ~0.31 pooled MRR (~60x above raw-transcript grep, ~15x above parsed-turn baseline). Single-shot retrieval alone scores only 0.07–0.20 answer-sufficiency. The routed system achieves 0.83 sufficiency on a ~50k-LOC production system, answering at 382–980 tokens per question — three orders of magnitude below recorded history. Ungated episode injection measurably degrades good answers.
AI.conclusion: Git-bound memory with routed retrieval/assembly solves the ADLC memory problem effectively, with all results replicable on any user's own history at zero labeling cost. The remaining constraint is capture — getting agent sessions reliably linked to commits.

title: FlowGuard: From Signals to Evidence for MCP Security Detection
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to interact with external tools through metadata exchange, tool invocation, and response consumption. Existing MCP security scanners primarily reason about suspicious semantic signals rather than real execution behaviors, which can lead to unreliable risk assessment. For example, credential-like strings may simply be placeholders rather than actual leakage. This gap requires runtime evidence for execution-related risks and careful semantic analysis for risks carried in metadata or returned content. We present FlowGuard, an evidence-grounded MCP security detection system. FlowGuard combines semantic risk triage, recon-guided payload narrowing, schema-valid probe generation, evidence adjudication, and history-guided refinement. It verifies execution-related risks through runtime evidence and detects semantic risks in tool metadata and returned content. We evaluate FlowGuard on an executable benchmark containing 1,880 MCP cases across five vulnerability categories. FlowGuard achieves F1 scores of 0.879 and 0.942 on the execution-related Command Injection and File System Access categories, respectively. Compared with existing dynamic scanners, FlowGuard reduces end-to-end latency by up to 2.23x. In the real-world evaluation, FlowGuard reports 523 findings across 326 servers. These results show that evidence-grounded detection can assess both execution-related and semantic risks in MCP interactions.

AI.tldr: FlowGuard is an evidence-grounded security detection system for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that combines semantic analysis with runtime execution evidence to identify vulnerabilities. Evaluated on 1,880 MCP cases across five categories, it achieves F1 scores of 0.879 (Command Injection) and 0.942 (File System Access), while reducing latency by up to 2.23x versus existing scanners. A real-world evaluation across 326 servers yielded 523 findings.
AI.motivation: Existing MCP security scanners rely on suspicious semantic signals (e.g., credential-like strings) without verifying actual execution behaviors, leading to unreliable risk assessment with false positives from placeholders misinterpreted as leaks. A gap exists for systems that combine runtime evidence for execution-related risks with careful semantic analysis for metadata and returned content risks.
AI.method: FlowGuard employs a five-stage pipeline: (1) semantic risk triage to classify and prioritize potential risks; (2) recon-guided payload narrowing to focus probing on relevant attack surfaces; (3) schema-valid probe generation to construct well-formed, targeted test inputs; (4) evidence adjudication to verify execution-related risks through runtime behavioral evidence; and (5) history-guided refinement to iteratively improve detection accuracy. Execution risks are verified via runtime evidence, while semantic risks in tool metadata and returned content are detected through careful content analysis.
AI.result: On an executable benchmark of 1,880 MCP cases spanning five vulnerability categories, FlowGuard achieved F1 scores of 0.879 for Command Injection and 0.942 for File System Access. It reduced end-to-end latency by up to 2.23x compared to existing dynamic scanners. In real-world testing across 326 MCP servers, FlowGuard reported 523 findings.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-grounded detection that couples runtime behavioral verification with semantic analysis is effective for assessing both execution-related and semantic risks in MCP interactions, addressing a critical gap left by signal-only scanners.

title: Digital Pantheon: Simulating and Auditing Coalition Formation with LLM Agents
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, To be published in the Post-Workshop proceedings of the ECML PKDD 2026 Conference
summary: The formation of political coalitions is a complex negotiation driven by both concrete policy objectives and deep-seated ideological convictions. While Large Language Models (LLMs) open new avenues for computational political science, the neutrality and helpfulness biases instilled by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) prevent them from sustaining steadfast partisan behaviour. We present a multi-agent framework that reconciles factual grounding with ideological alignment by combining Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): DPO instils aggressive party-specific personas, while a per-party RAG pipeline keeps each agent bounded to its official manifesto. We operationalize the framework on the 2019 Flemish election, deploying the partisan agents in a hub-and-spoke negotiation arbitrated by a formateur. To make the emergent negotiation interpretable, we introduce a Multi-Layered Information Lineage Topology (MILT) that traces every clause in the final agreement back to its manifesto origin and classifies it into five provenance states, a Coalition Influence Score (CIS) that aggregates these traceable contributions to identify which party shaped the agreement, and a real-world grounding pass that benchmarks each simulated provision against the historically adopted coalition agreement. Across three independent simulations the framework yields a stable winner and ranking (N-VA ahead of CD\&V and Open Vld), and manifesto-anchored lineage reliably predicts real-world materialization whereas hallucinated content does not. The result is a transparent, scalable testbed for the ex-ante exploration of party compatibility and formateur-mediated compromise.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent LLM framework combining SFT, DPO, and RAG creates ideologically consistent partisan agents for coalition negotiation simulation. Applied to the 2019 Flemish election, it introduces MILT and CIS metrics for tracing agreement provenance and produces stable, realistic results where manifesto-anchored content predicts real-world outcomes.
AI.motivation: LLMs are promising for computational political science but fail at sustained partisan behavior due to RLHF-induced neutrality and helpfulness biases. The authors aim to create agents that maintain ideological consistency while remaining factually grounded in real party manifestos, enabling transparent and scalable ex-ante coalition negotiation simulation.
AI.method: The framework combines three techniques: (1) Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to instil aggressive party-specific personas; (2) per-party Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines to anchor each agent to its official manifesto; (3) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for factual grounding. It is operationalized on the 2019 Flemish election using a hub-and-spoke negotiation architecture with a formateur arbitrator. Two novel interpretability tools are introduced: Multi-Layered Information Lineage Topology (MILT) traces each final-agreement clause back to manifesto origins across five provenance states, and a Coalition Influence Score (CIS) aggregates traceable contributions to quantify party influence. A real-world grounding pass benchmarks simulated provisions against the historical coalition agreement.
AI.result: Across three independent simulations, the framework yields a stable winner and ranking: N-VA ahead of CD&V and Open Vld. Manifesto-anchored lineage (MILT-traced content) reliably predicts whether a provision materializes in the real-world agreement, whereas hallucinated content does not predict real-world outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a transparent, scalable testbed for ex-ante exploration of party compatibility and formateur-mediated compromise. The integration of DPO, RAG, and SFT successfully reconciles ideological steadfastness with factual grounding, and the MILT/CIS metrics offer interpretable provenance tracking for emergent negotiation outcomes.

title: MAPS: Modeling Co-Existing Subjective Perspectives and Shared Meaning in Multi-Agent Cognitive Dialogue
summary: Human dialogue involves more than exchanging information; it also expresses beliefs, emotions, and subjective cognitive styles. Yet current AI dialogue systems often enforce semantic uniformity, sacrificing diversity and interpretability. We present MAPS (Multi-Agent Perspective Spaces), a novel framework that models dialogue between cognitively distinct agents through domain-weighted profiles, dynamic GRU-based memory, and interpretable token-level attention. MAPS enables agents to maintain individualized reasoning while progressively converging on shared meaning. Evaluations on EmpatheticDialogues, TopicalChat, and MultiWOZ show that MAPS supports semantic alignment without collapsing subjectivity. Our results demonstrate a path toward cognitively grounded, interpretable dialogue systems that balance expressiveness and coherence.

AI.tldr: MAPS is a multi-agent dialogue framework that uses domain-weighted cognitive profiles, GRU-based dynamic memory, and token-level attention to enable semantically aligned yet subjectively diverse conversations, demonstrating balanced expressiveness and coherence on three dialogue benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current AI dialogue systems enforce semantic uniformity, sacrificing the subjective, belief-driven, and emotional diversity inherent in human conversation. The authors aim to preserve cognitive individuality while achieving shared understanding — a balance missing in existing systems.
AI.method: MAPS (Multi-Agent Perspective Spaces) models dialogue between cognitively distinct agents using three core components: (1) domain-weighted profiles that encode each agent's subjective perspective, (2) dynamic GRU-based memory for maintaining evolving conversational context, and (3) interpretable token-level attention mechanisms that reveal how agents attend to and integrate one another's utterances while progressively converging on shared meaning without collapsing their individual cognitive styles.
AI.result: Evaluations on EmpatheticDialogues, TopicalChat, and MultiWOZ demonstrate that MAPS achieves semantic alignment between agents while preserving subjective diversity. The framework successfully balances expressiveness and coherence, outperforming baselines that either enforce uniformity or fail to converge on shared meaning.
AI.conclusion: MAPS offers a viable path toward cognitively grounded, interpretable dialogue systems that maintain the richness of individualized perspectives alongside coherent, aligned communication.

title: Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)
summary: As generative AI (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in undergraduate academic writing, how students rely on these tools, rather than simply whether they use them, has become a central question for learning, academic integrity, and educational equity. Existing measures of reliance were developed inductively, focused on discrete problem-solving tasks, and validated mainly with homogeneous samples. This study developed and validated the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four theoretically derived types of GenAI reliance: Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic. Validation followed the multisource framework of the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing, drawing on a survey of 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution and interviews with 14 purposively sampled students. Confirmatory factor analyses of six competing models supported a five-factor structure in which Strategic Reliance comprises two facets, Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation, alongside Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic factors (CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08; DWLS CFI = .98, RMSEA = .07). Subscale reliability was acceptable to good (omega = .75-.88), and scalar measurement invariance held across gender, first-generation status, and STEM/non-STEM majors, to our knowledge the first such evidence for a GenAI reliance instrument. Rasch analysis indicated that a five-point response format would improve category functioning. Strategic reliance was positively associated with AI literacy, and the reliance types differentiated students across multiple writing process and outcome variables. The GenAI-RTS offers researchers and educators a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated instrument for identifying undergraduate reliance profiles and supporting research, assessment, and AI literacy intervention.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and validates the GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four theoretically derived types of GenAI reliance (Strategic, Instrumental, Dependent, Dialogic) in undergraduate writing. Validated with 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution, confirmatory factor analyses supported a five-factor structure with strong psychometric properties, establishing the first scalar measurement invariance evidence for a GenAI reliance instrument.
AI.motivation: Existing measures of GenAI reliance in academic contexts were developed inductively, focused narrowly on discrete problem-solving tasks, and validated with homogeneous samples. With GenAI increasingly embedded in undergraduate writing, there is a pressing need for a theoretically grounded, psychometrically robust instrument that captures how—not just whether—students rely on these tools, with implications for learning, academic integrity, and educational equity.
AI.method: The study followed the multisource validation framework of the Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing. A survey of 382 undergraduates at a U.S. Minority-Serving Institution was conducted, supplemented by semi-structured interviews with 14 purposively sampled students. Confirmatory factor analyses tested six competing models. Reliability was assessed via omega coefficients, measurement invariance was tested across gender, first-generation status, and STEM/non-STEM majors, and Rasch analysis evaluated response category functioning. Convergent validity was examined through associations with AI literacy and multiple writing process/outcome variables.
AI.result: A five-factor structure fit best: Strategic Reliance comprised two facets (Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation), alongside Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic factors (CFI = .92, RMSEA = .08; DWLS CFI = .98, RMSEA = .07). Subscale reliability ranged from ω = .75–.88. Scalar measurement invariance held across all tested subgroups—the first such evidence for any GenAI reliance instrument. The five-point response format was recommended per Rasch analysis. Strategic reliance correlated positively with AI literacy, and reliance types meaningfully differentiated students across writing process and outcome variables.
AI.conclusion: The GenAI-RTS provides researchers and educators with a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated instrument for identifying undergraduate GenAI reliance profiles. It supports future research, diagnostic assessment, and targeted AI literacy interventions aimed at fostering more strategic and critically aware GenAI use in academic writing.

title: DS@GT ARC at LongEval: Citation Integrity and Factual Grounding in Scientific QA
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Accepted to the CLEF 2026 LongEval Lab Working Notes
summary: This paper describes DS@GT ARC's submission to the CLEF 2026 LongEval Task 4 on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). In this submission, we examine a divergence between traditional natural language evaluation metrics and citation integrity as applied to RAG QA systems. We evaluate a corrective pipeline using Corrective RAG (CRAG) and CiteFix against baseline and frontier model benchmark RAG QA scores. While frontier models maximized answer relevance and fluency scores, our RAGAs LLM-as-judge diagnostics indicate that frontier models would correctly identify relevant documents without using their context in answer generation. Conversely, by filtering chunks pre-generation and enforcing strict entailment of generated claims to the cited material post-generation, our corrective pipeline marginally improved citation faithfulness and answer grounding. We propose that evaluation of trustworthy RAG QA requires metrics that reward strict answer grounding.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a submission to CLEF 2026 LongEval Task 4 on RAG, investigating the divergence between traditional NLG metrics and citation integrity. The authors propose a corrective pipeline combining CRAG and CiteFix, finding that while frontier models achieve high fluency/relevance, they often ignore context. Their pipeline marginally improves citation faithfulness and grounding, advocating for evaluation metrics that reward strict answer grounding.
AI.motivation: The authors identify a critical divergence: traditional natural language evaluation metrics (e.g., answer relevance, fluency) do not capture citation integrity in RAG QA systems. Frontier models can score highly on these metrics while disregarding the retrieved context entirely. This motivates the need for evaluation frameworks and corrective methods that prioritize strict answer grounding to cited source material for trustworthy RAG.
AI.method: The authors implement a corrective pipeline for RAG QA that operates in two stages: (1) pre-generation filtering using Corrective RAG (CRAG) to refine retrieved document chunks before answer generation, and (2) post-generation enforcement using CiteFix to ensure generated claims strictly entail the cited material. They evaluate this pipeline against both baseline and frontier model benchmarks using RAGAs LLM-as-judge diagnostics, comparing traditional metrics (relevance, fluency) against citation faithfulness and answer grounding metrics.
AI.result: Frontier models maximized traditional answer relevance and fluency scores but RAGAs diagnostics revealed they correctly identify relevant documents without actually using their context in answer generation. The corrective pipeline (CRAG + CiteFix) yielded only marginal improvements in citation faithfulness and answer grounding compared to these models.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that trustworthy RAG QA evaluation must move beyond traditional NLG metrics and incorporate measures that reward strict answer grounding. Their findings highlight a reliability gap in current RAG systems and underscore the importance of citation integrity as a core evaluation criterion for responsible deployment of RAG QA systems.

title: Is External Database Protection Static in Retrieval-Augmented Generation? Rethinking Privacy Preservation under Dynamic Queries
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models via external document retrieval, but retrieved contexts may leak sensitive information. Current privacy protection methods typically rely on a document-level static risk assumption, treating all retrieved documents as having the same privacy leakage risk. However, this assumption overlooks a fundamental characteristic of RAG: the privacy risk of a document is highly dependent on the user's query, making privacy leakage inherently query-driven and dynamic. To address this challenge, we propose a Prompt-Aware Dynamic Hierarchical Differential Privacy framework (PA-HDP) for privacy-preserving RAG. PA-HDP first performs a prompt-aware risk hierarchy to dynamically assess privacy risks under different queries. It then applies adaptive sensitive entity replacement and exponential mechanism-based text selection to provide differentiated privacy protection while preserving semantic utility. By protecting only the content that is truly sensitive under a given query, PA-HDP minimizes unnecessary modifications to the retrieval corpus. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PA-HDP significantly reduces privacy leakage while maintaining high retrieval quality, achieving a better privacy-utility trade-off than prior methods.

AI.tldr: PA-HDP introduces a query-dependent, dynamic privacy framework for RAG that assesses document sensitivity based on the user's prompt, then applies differentiated protection via sensitive entity replacement and exponential mechanism-based text selection, achieving superior privacy-utility trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy-preserving RAG methods use a static, document-level risk assumption where all retrieved documents are treated as equally risky. This ignores the core insight that privacy leakage in RAG is query-driven — a document's sensitivity depends on what the user asks. A dynamic, prompt-aware approach is needed.
AI.method: PA-HDP (Prompt-Aware Dynamic Hierarchical Differential Privacy) operates in two stages: (1) prompt-aware risk hierarchy — dynamically assessing privacy risk of documents conditioned on the query; (2) differentiated protection — applying adaptive sensitive entity replacement and an exponential mechanism for text selection, ensuring protection is proportional to query-specific sensitivity while minimizing unnecessary corpus modification.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show PA-HDP significantly reduces privacy leakage while maintaining high retrieval quality, outperforming prior methods on the privacy-utility trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Moving from static document-level to dynamic query-dependent privacy assessment enables more precise, less destructive privacy protection in RAG systems. PA-HDP demonstrates that protecting only truly sensitive content under a given query yields a better balance between privacy and utility.

title: AI-Conducted Interviews in Empirical Software Engineering: An Experience Report
summary: Semi-structured interviews are widely used in empirical software engineering (ESE), but they are resource-intensive and difficult to coordinate across schedules, locations, and natural languages. This experience report examines a customized MyGPT used to conduct short, self-administered interviews in two ESE studies: one on refactoring practices and another on generative AI in Scrum-related activities. Participants accessed the interviewer through shared links, used voice interaction, selected a preferred natural language, and completed the interview without a researcher present. The AI followed a predefined protocol and generated a structured synthesis that participants voluntarily submitted; these artifacts were not treated as verbatim transcripts. We analyzed 66 submissions and questionnaire responses, and audited artifact format, language, length, and protocol consistency. Of the submitted artifacts, 92.4% followed the expected synthesis format, 65 were predominantly in Portuguese and one in English, and two conflicted with the reported protocol. Participants generally rated the experience positively: 90.9% reported a positive overall experience and comfort, 95.5% considered the questions clear, 97.0% rated the pace positively, and 89.4% would participate again. Reported limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity to answers, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and missed human interaction. The findings support the operational viability and acceptability of this workflow among analyzed respondents, but do not establish completion rates, time savings, summary fidelity, or equivalence to human-conducted interviews. AI interviewers should therefore be treated as a complementary option for short, focused, low-risk studies, with protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight.

AI.tldr: This experience report evaluates a customized MyGPT for conducting self-administered, asynchronous, multilingual interviews in two empirical software engineering studies. With 66 submissions, 92.4% followed the expected synthesis format, and participants rated the experience positively (90.9% overall comfort). Findings suggest operational viability for short, low-risk studies but highlight limitations in depth, sensitivity, and privacy, recommending complementary use alongside human oversight.
AI.motivation: Semi-structured interviews are resource-intensive in empirical software engineering due to scheduling, geographic, and language barriers. The authors sought to explore whether an AI-driven, self-administered interview workflow could offer a scalable, cost-effective alternative for short, focused studies.
AI.method: A customized MyGPT was deployed in two ESE studies (one on refactoring, one on generative AI in Scrum). Participants accessed the interviewer via shared links, used voice interaction, selected a preferred natural language, and completed interviews without a researcher present. The AI followed a predefined protocol and produced a structured synthesis submitted voluntarily. Analysis covered 66 submissions and questionnaire responses, auditing artifact format, language, length, and protocol consistency.
AI.result: 92.4% of submitted artifacts matched the expected synthesis format; 65 were in Portuguese, 1 in English; 2 conflicted with the reported protocol. Participant ratings: 90.9% positive overall experience/comfort, 95.5% found questions clear, 97.0% rated pace positively, 89.4% would participate again. Reported limitations included generic questions, limited sensitivity, insufficient depth, privacy concerns, and lack of human interaction.
AI.conclusion: AI interviewers demonstrate operational viability and acceptability for short, focused, low-risk ESE studies, but do not yet match human-conducted interviews in depth or sensitivity. They should be treated as complementary tools, with careful protocol design, privacy guidance, artifact validation, and human oversight. Completion rates, time savings, summary fidelity, and equivalence to human interviews remain unestablished.

title: TEDDY: A Pediatric Foundation Model for Risk Forewarning from ICD-Coded Diagnostic Histories
summary: Pediatric electronic health records capture developmentally structured clinical trajectories, yet their potential for generative healthcare foundation models remains largely unexplored. Here we present TEDDY (Temporal Event Decoder for Disease in Youth), a 1.84-million-parameter decoder transformer trained on approximately 73 million ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6 million children at a single pediatric institution. TEDDY models longitudinal diagnosis trajectories and visit timing. Predictions were made before visit codes were revealed, limited to first occurrences, and evaluated against sex- and age-matched controls. Across 797 disease-onset prediction tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters, TEDDY achieved a median AUC of 72.0%, outperforming same-data DenseNet (50.0%), CNN (57.2%), RNN (60.1%), and LSTM (62.7%) baselines on 96-99% of tasks. Performance held across sex and age and was strongest among lower-prevalence diagnoses; 202 of the 225 rarest conditions (90%) had 95% confidence intervals above chance. Predictive signal remained detectable more than two years before first recorded diagnosis, with median AUCs of 59.7% in the unrestricted analysis and 64.4% in a fixed-cohort sensitivity analysis. In asthma and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder benchmarks, AUCs were 79.3% and 84.7%, compared with 62.7% and 71.7% for the strongest comparators, including a general-purpose language model three orders of magnitude larger. Visit-timing predictions had a 3.0-day mean absolute restricted mean survival-time error over 365 days, although median and long-tail return intervals remained miscalibrated. Together, these results establish pediatric diagnostic histories as a substrate for compact generative models supporting broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without population-scale data or billion-parameter models.

AI.tldr: TEDDY, a compact 1.84M-parameter decoder transformer trained on 73M pediatric ICD-10 diagnoses from 1.6M children, predicts disease onset across 797 tasks with median AUC 72.0%, outperforming larger baselines including a general-purpose LLM, with strong performance on rare diseases and prediction horizons exceeding two years.
AI.motivation: Pediatric EHRs contain rich, developmentally structured longitudinal data, yet their potential for generative healthcare foundation models is unexplored. Existing models typically require population-scale data or billions of parameters, leaving a gap for compact, institution-scale models that can perform broad disease-onset prediction, especially for rare conditions.
AI.method: TEDDY is a 1.84M-parameter decoder transformer trained autoregressively on sequences of ICD-10 diagnosis codes and inter-visit intervals from 1.6M children (~73M diagnoses). Predictions are made before visit codes are revealed, limited to first occurrences, and evaluated against sex- and age-matched controls. Baselines include DenseNet, CNN, RNN, LSTM, and a general-purpose language model (three orders of magnitude larger). AUC evaluated across 797 disease-onset tasks spanning 16 ICD-10 chapters. Visit-timing prediction assessed via mean absolute restricted mean survival-time error.
AI.result: TEDDY achieved median AUC 72.0%, beating DenseNet (50.0%), CNN (57.2%), RNN (60.1%), and LSTM (62.7%) on 96-99% of tasks. Of 225 rarest conditions, 90% had CIs above chance. Predictive signal detectable >2 years before diagnosis (median AUC: 59.7% unrestricted, 64.4% fixed-cohort). Asthma AUC: 79.3%; ADHD AUC: 84.7% vs. 62.7% and 71.7% for strongest comparators. Visit-timing error: 3.0-day mean absolute error over 365 days, though median and long-tail intervals remained miscalibrated.
AI.conclusion: Pediatric diagnostic histories can serve as a substrate for compact generative models (sub-2M parameters) that support broad, rare-disease, and long-horizon risk forecasting without requiring population-scale data or billion-parameter models, challenging the assumption that healthcare foundation models must be massive.

title: MemoHarness: Agent Harnesses That Learn from Experience
summary: An agent harness is the external control layer that turns a base LLM into an executable agent by managing context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, and output handling. While harness design strongly affects agent behavior, most automatic improvement methods optimize narrower artifacts such as prompts, pipelines, or workflows, and deployed agents usually reuse a single global harness for all cases. We introduce MemoHarness, an adaptive harness optimization framework that learns from its own executions. MemoHarness decomposes the harness into six editable control dimensions, stores per-case diagnoses and distilled global patterns in a dual-layer experience bank, and adapts the learned harness to each test case using retrieved experience without test-time labels, feedback, or additional search. In our evaluation across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness improves over the fixed harnesses we compare against and shows selective transfer to unseen suites and base models. Its additional context can also remain cost-competitive when much of the retrieved experience is cacheable. These results provide evidence that execution experience is a practical substrate for building agent harnesses that are more adaptive than a single static configuration, while leaving broader claims about statistical robustness and component attribution to future work.

AI.tldr: MemoHarness is an adaptive framework that optimizes agent harnesses—the external control layer governing LLM-based agents across six dimensions (context, tools, orchestration, memory, decoding, output handling)—by learning from execution experience stored in a dual-layer bank, enabling case-specific adaptation without test-time labels or search.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic improvement methods for LLM agents focus on narrow artifacts (prompts, pipelines, workflows), while deployed agents typically rely on a single static global harness. Since harness design critically affects agent behavior, there is a need for an adaptive approach that learns from execution experience and tailors the harness per test case.
AI.method: MemoHarness decomposes the agent harness into six editable control dimensions. It maintains a dual-layer experience bank: one layer stores per-case diagnoses from past executions, and the other distills global patterns. At test time, relevant experience is retrieved to adapt the harness to each specific case—without requiring labels, external feedback, or additional search.
AI.result: Evaluated across shell-agent, code-generation, and analytical-reasoning benchmarks, MemoHarness outperforms fixed harness baselines and demonstrates selective transfer to unseen benchmark suites and base models. Its additional context cost remains competitive when retrieved experience is cacheable.
AI.conclusion: Execution experience is a practical substrate for building more adaptive agent harnesses. The paper leaves broader statistical robustness claims and component attribution analysis to future work.

title: Self-Evolving Human-Centered Framework for Explainable Depression Symptom Annotation
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Omni-Layer Intelligent Systems (COINS) 2026
summary: Annotation quality is a major bottleneck in building reliable and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) systems for mental health research. In depression-related datasets, labels are often assigned without structured evidence, symptom-level justification, or traceable alignment with the criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), limiting both transparency and downstream model interpretability.
