We propose a self-evolving, expert-in-the-loop annotation framework for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) that combines large language model (LLM)-assisted labeling with expert verification. The framework is intended to support the construction of explainable, DSM-5-TR-aligned datasets rather than to perform clinical diagnosis. It operates in three stages: candidate evidence selection from textual records, criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and case-level synthesis that produces label-level diagnostic and severity annotations. A dual-memory architecture, composed of Example Memory and Reflection Memory, is designed to internalize expert feedback and iteratively improve future annotations without retraining. We describe this mechanism and leave its evaluation across multiple feedback cycles to future work. In addition to final labels, the framework exports clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories, enabling comprehensive auditability. In a pilot study using expert-reviewed samples, the proposed approach improves annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a self-evolving annotation framework for Major Depressive Disorder datasets that combines LLM-assisted labeling with expert verification, structured around DSM-5-TR criteria. It employs a dual-memory architecture (Example Memory and Reflection Memory) to internalize expert feedback iteratively, and exports evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories for auditability. A pilot study demonstrates improved annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort.
AI.motivation: Annotation quality is a major bottleneck in mental health XAI systems. Depression-related datasets often lack structured evidence, symptom-level justification, and traceable alignment with DSM-5-TR criteria, limiting transparency and model interpretability. The authors aim to address this gap by designing a framework that produces explainable, criterion-aligned annotations rather than performing clinical diagnosis.
AI.method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) candidate evidence selection from textual records, (2) criterion-level DSM-5-TR analysis, and (3) case-level synthesis producing diagnostic and severity label annotations. A dual-memory architecture is introduced: Example Memory stores annotated exemplars, while Reflection Memory captures expert corrections and feedback patterns. This design internalizes expert input to iteratively refine future annotations without model retraining. The framework also exports clinical evidence, reasoning traces, and edit histories for full auditability.
AI.result: In a pilot study using expert-reviewed samples, the framework improved annotation consistency and explainability while reducing manual revision effort compared to conventional approaches. The dual-memory mechanism and its longitudinal evaluation across multiple feedback cycles are described but deferred to future work.
AI.conclusion: The proposed expert-in-the-loop, self-evolving framework offers a promising direction for constructing reliable, DSM-5-TR-aligned, and explainable mental health datasets. By integrating LLM assistance with structured expert oversight and memory-based iterative refinement, it addresses key annotation quality challenges in depression research. Future work will focus on evaluating the dual-memory mechanism over extended feedback cycles.

title: Introspection Fine-Tuning (IFT): Training Small LLMs to Introspect
summary: Can small language models detect and report on perturbations their own internal activations? We investigate this question through the lens of activation steering: injecting concept vectors into a model's residual stream and measuring whether the model can accurately report on the perturbation. We first show that the binary detection paradigm used in prior work -- prompting the model to answer Yes'' or No'' to whether it detects an injected thought -- is confounded in small models, as steering biases the model toward affirmative responses regardless of the question content. We therefore propose two confound-free evaluation paradigms: sentence localization (identifying which of $N$ sentences was perturbed, chance $= 1/N$) and strength comparison (identifying which of two sentences received a stronger injection, chance $= 50\%$). Evaluating across six models from two families (Llama-3.2 and Gemma-4), we find that models as small as 2B parameters introspect reliably well above chance, and that introspective ability generally increases with scale. Llama-1B, however, performs at or below chance. We then introduce \emph{Introspection Fine-Tuning} (IFT): supervised fine-tuning on sentence-localization examples constructed from the model's own perturbed forward passes. IFT raises Llama-1B sentence-localization accuracy from $9.6\%$ to $60.6\%$ (a $6\times$ improvement), with gains generalizing zero-shot to the held-out strength-comparison task ($30.2\% \to 52.2\%$). IFT also improves introspection for 3B and 8B models, while inducing negligible degradation on standard capability benchmarks. Our results suggest that introspective ability is not fixed by scale alone: it can be directly trained, and doing so unlocks latent self-monitoring capacity with implications for AI transparency and alignment. Our code is \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/IFT-introspection-2092/README.md}{here}.

AI.tldr: Small language models can be trained to detect perturbations in their own internal activations via a method called Introspection Fine-Tuning (IFT), which improves self-monitoring from near-chance to well above chance, with gains generalizing across tasks and scaling with model size.
AI.motivation: Prior work on activation steering used a binary Yes/No detection paradigm that is confounded in small models — steering biases them toward affirmative responses regardless of content. The authors aim to develop confound-free evaluation methods and investigate whether introspective ability can be directly trained rather than being solely determined by model scale.
AI.method: Two confound-free paradigms are proposed: (1) sentence localization — identifying which of N sentences was perturbed; (2) strength comparison — identifying which of two sentences received a stronger injection. Six models (Llama-3.2 and Gemma-4, 1B–8B) are evaluated. Introspection Fine-Tuning (IFT) is then introduced: supervised fine-tuning on sentence-localization examples from the model's own perturbed forward passes, with zero-shot generalization tested on strength comparison.
AI.result: Models ≥2B parameters introspect above chance, with ability increasing with scale; Llama-1B performs at or below chance. IFT raises Llama-1B localization accuracy from 9.6% to 60.6% (6× improvement) and strength comparison from 30.2% to 52.2%. Gains also observed for 3B and 8B models, with negligible degradation on standard benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Introspective ability is not fixed by scale alone — it can be directly trained via IFT, unlocking latent self-monitoring capacity. This has significant implications for AI transparency and alignment.

title: Project Kaleidoscope: Contextual, Human-Aligned Evaluation for Real-World AI Applications
summary: Evaluations (Evals) are a deployment bottleneck for real-world AI applications: public benchmarks rarely match a team's users, context, or policies, and human review is often tedious to scale. Motivated by our work with AI applications in the public sector, this project addresses recurring evaluation challenges encountered when applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. We present Kaleidoscope, an integrated workflow for contextual functional evaluation that links persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review for reliability-gated automated scoring. Generated test cases are scored against application-specific rubrics; human annotations provide reviewable labels; and LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with those labels meets a configured threshold. Kaleidoscope is therefore a practical, inspectable, iterative workflow for product teams. We report early evidence from a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q\&A pairs spanning four domains and 14 evaluation dimensions. The results highlight useful features for end-to-end reliable, automated scoring.

AI.tldr: Kaleidoscope is an integrated evaluation workflow that combines persona-based test generation, contextualized rubrics, and human review with reliability-gated automated scoring, addressing deployment bottlenecks in real-world AI applications where public benchmarks fail to match specific user contexts and policies.
AI.motivation: Public benchmarks rarely align with the specific users, contexts, or policies of real-world AI application teams. Human review for evaluation is tedious and difficult to scale. This is especially acute in the public sector, where applications must satisfy local policy and governance requirements. A practical, scalable, and inspectable evaluation workflow is needed.
AI.method: Kaleidoscope integrates three components: (1) persona-based test case generation for contextual relevance; (2) application-specific contextualized rubrics for scoring; and (3) a reliability-gated mechanism where LLM judges automate scoring only when their agreement with human annotations meets a pre-configured threshold. The workflow is iterative and inspectable. Validation involved a three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and custom-rubric judge experiments on 108 annotated Q&A pairs spanning 4 domains and 14 evaluation dimensions.
AI.result: The three-week pilot across four organizational use cases and experiments on 108 annotated Q&A pairs (4 domains, 14 evaluation dimensions) provided early evidence highlighting useful features for end-to-end reliable automated scoring, demonstrating the feasibility of the reliability-gated judging approach.
AI.conclusion: Kaleidoscope offers a practical, inspectable, and iterative evaluation workflow for product teams operating in real-world, policy-constrained environments. The reliability-gated LLM judging approach shows promise for scaling evaluations while maintaining accountability through human review.

title: SAGA: Schema-Aware Grounding for Agentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation
summary: Complex knowledge base question answering (KBQA) is commonly approached through either information retrieval over a question-specific subgraph or semantic parsing into an executable logical form. We study the latter paradigm. Recent large language model agents make semantic parsing interactive: they alternate between reasoning, querying the knowledge base, and extending a partial SPARQL query. This interleaving reduces reliance on one-shot generation, but makes the quality of \emph{KB grounding} depend on what the interaction tools expose. Existing agents retrieve or prune candidate properties mainly through lexical relevance and instance-level observations, without systematically conditioning on entity types, property domains and ranges, or the expected answer type. We call this failure mode \emph{type-blind grounding}. It enlarges the grounding search space and often produces plausible-looking but semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results. We propose SAGA (\underline{S}chema-\underline{A}ware \underline{G}rounding for \underline{A}gentic Text-to-SPARQL Generation), a training-free framework that turns property exploration into a schema-constrained grounding operation. SAGA maintains a persistent bidirectional type state, filters known-incompatible property candidates at construction time, presents the remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and handles missing schema information permissively through empirical and trace-local evidence. Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings and the highest exact-match accuracy on eight, while reducing empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.

AI.tldr: SAGA proposes a training-free framework for agentic text-to-SPARQL generation that addresses "type-blind grounding" by enforcing schema-aware constraints (entity types, property domains/ranges, answer types) during interactive KB query construction, achieving state-of-the-art results across nine benchmark settings.
AI.motivation: Existing interactive LLM agents for KBQA ground properties using only lexical relevance and instance-level observations, ignoring schema constraints like entity types, property domains/ranges, and expected answer types. This "type-blind grounding" expands the search space and produces semantically incompatible triple patterns that execute to empty results.
AI.method: SAGA replaces property exploration with schema-constrained grounding via: (1) a persistent bidirectional type state that tracks candidate entity types and answer types throughout query construction, (2) filtering property candidates at construction time based on domain/range compatibility, (3) presenting remaining graph patterns in a compact schema-annotated format, and (4) permissively handling missing schema information using empirical and trace-local evidence.
AI.result: Across nine benchmark settings over Wikidata and Freebase, SAGA achieves the highest F1 on all nine settings, highest exact-match accuracy on eight of nine, and reduces empty-result queries across all reported Wikidata settings.
AI.conclusion: Schema-constrained grounding via type-state tracking significantly improves agentic semantic parsing for KBQA by reducing grounding errors, narrowing the search space, and preventing semantically invalid queries that yield empty results.

title: The Distributed Open-Source Vulnerability Ecosystem
summary: Identifying known software vulnerabilities is a central task in software supply chain security management. Although publicly available vulnerability information is based on shared standards, different vulnerability scanners often report divergent results for identical software inventories. These differences do not arise solely from individual data sources or scanner implementations. They can emerge at several stages of the open-source vulnerability ecosystem. This paper presents a conceptual framework that describes vulnerability management as a distributed process of information exchange and transformation. It traces vulnerability information from its creation and standardization through enrichment to context-dependent interpretation. The analysis identifies heterogeneous information sources, divergent identity and version models, temporal change, and context-dependent assessment as major causes of inconsistent scanner findings. It then discusses the implications for interpreting analysis results, designing reproducible evaluation methods, and handling dynamic vulnerability knowledge in practice.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a conceptual framework describing vulnerability management as a distributed information exchange process, identifying four key causes of inconsistent scanner results: heterogeneous information sources, divergent identity/version models, temporal change, and context-dependent assessment.
AI.motivation: Different vulnerability scanners frequently produce divergent results for identical software inventories, and these discrepancies cannot be explained solely by differences in data sources or scanner implementations. The paper seeks to systematically understand where and why such inconsistencies emerge across the open-source vulnerability ecosystem.
AI.method: The authors develop a conceptual framework that models vulnerability management as a distributed process of information exchange and transformation, tracing vulnerability information through its entire lifecycle — from creation and standardization, through enrichment, to context-dependent interpretation — and analyze the stages where divergence can occur.
AI.result: The analysis identifies four major causes of inconsistent scanner findings: (1) heterogeneous information sources, (2) divergent identity and version models, (3) temporal change in vulnerability knowledge, and (4) context-dependent assessment of vulnerability applicability and severity.
AI.conclusion: The findings have significant implications for interpreting scanner analysis results, designing reproducible evaluation methodologies, and managing dynamic vulnerability knowledge in practice. The framework helps practitioners and researchers better understand the inherent limitations and sources of divergence in automated vulnerability identification.

title: Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have accelerated the adoption of software development agents, now widely available as Integrated Development Environment (IDE) extensions and standalone applications. While these agents are typically general-purpose, it remains unclear whether specialist agents justify their additional development effort. We investigate this question in the context of business process automation, focusing on the transformation of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) diagrams into executable agentic workflows. Since BPMN specifies explicit control-flow semantics, we focus on deterministic workflows in which a fixed process model and inputs uniquely determine the executed path. We introduce a specialist workflow for this task and compare it against generalist agents such as Roo and Cline. Our results show that the specialist solution produces agents that outperform generalist baselines by approximately 9-20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, 2-4x in penalty-adjusted latency, and 3x fewer tool-call errors, while reducing generation token cost by over 95% and eliminating repair iterations. We also find that generalist agents generate code inconsistently in both functionality and quality, limiting their suitability for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are essential.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether specialist software development agents justify their extra development effort compared to generalist agents. Focusing on BPMN-to-executable-workflow transformation, the authors introduce a specialist workflow that outperforms generalist agents (Roo, Cline) by 9-20 pp in tool-use exactness, 2-4x better latency, 3x fewer tool errors, and >95% lower token cost, while eliminating repair iterations entirely.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLM-based software agents are widely available, but it is unclear whether building specialist agents for specific domains provides enough benefit to justify the additional development effort. This is particularly relevant in industrial business process automation, where reliability, maintainability, and deterministic execution are critical.
AI.method: The authors focus on the task of transforming BPMN diagrams into executable agentic workflows. They design a specialist workflow that exploits BPMN's explicit control-flow semantics to produce deterministic workflows. This specialist solution is evaluated against two generalist agents (Roo and Cline) using metrics including tool-use exactness, penalty-adjusted latency, tool-call error rates, token costs, and the number of repair iterations required.
AI.result: The specialist workflow outperforms generalist agents by approximately 9-20 percentage points in tool-use exactness, achieves 2-4x improvements in penalty-adjusted latency, makes 3x fewer tool-call errors, reduces generation token cost by over 95%, and requires zero repair iterations. Generalist agents also exhibit inconsistent code generation in both functionality and quality.
AI.conclusion: Specialist agents offer substantial and measurable advantages over generalist agents for deterministic, control-flow-explicit tasks like BPMN-to-workflow transformation. The inconsistency of generalist-generated code further limits their suitability for industrial settings where reliability and maintainability are paramount, justifying the investment in specialist solutions.

title: When a Verified World Model Still Loses: Play-Adequacy vs Prediction-Accuracy in LLM-Synthesized Code World Models
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. Code and reproduction log: https://github.com/JaviMaligno/code-world-models
summary:
Large language models can synthesize a game's rules as executable code - a Code World Model (CWM) - which a classical planner then searches over. Such models are typically accepted when they reach high transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. We argue this is the wrong notion of adequacy for planning.
  We show four things. (1) An LLM-synthesized CWM can pass a sampling gate at 100% transition accuracy and be $\geq 98\%$ state-accurate on the planner's own search distribution, yet lose systematically at play, because the $<1\%$ it gets wrong is exactly the pivotal dynamics; the play cost of the omitted rule is $0.091$ (seed-clustered 95% CI $[0.065,0.117]$, $n=4800$). We call this the verified-vs-correct gap, and confirm it end-to-end through the synthesis pipeline. (2) The harm follows a quantitative law, $\mathrm{danger}=\mathrm{play\_cost}\times(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$, whose $(1-\mathrm{rarity})^N$ gate-miss factor is proven exact and whose play cost is empirically bounded. (3) The failure is not repaired by more data: LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not rule inference, and did not infer the omitted rule across models (GPT-5.x) and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples). (4) The same mechanism recurs on the belief-inference function of imperfect-information CWMs: we prove a coverage bound (a size-$N$ gate is identifying when $N\gtrsim b^{d_{\max}}$), explaining why shallow games such as Kuhn poker show no gap, and hand-construct Beacon, a verified-but-wrong inference function that passes the gate yet loses every game.
  These results suggest adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the search distribution or by play directly, not by prediction accuracy on sampled transitions.

AI.tldr: LLM-synthesized Code World Models can achieve near-perfect transition accuracy yet fail catastrophically in planning because the tiny fraction of errors concentrates on pivotal dynamics. The authors formalize this "verified-vs-correct gap," derive a quantitative danger law, and show the failure persists across models, data regimes, and extends to imperfect-information settings — arguing that sampling-based accuracy is the wrong evaluation metric for planning-oriented world models.
AI.motivation: The standard practice for validating LLM-synthesized Code World Models (CWMs) is to test transition accuracy on sampled trajectories. The authors challenge this, arguing that high sampling-gate accuracy can mask critical failures that emerge only during planning or play, where errors on rare but pivotal transitions disproportionately affect outcomes.
AI.method: The paper combines empirical and theoretical approaches across four contributions: (1) End-to-end demonstration of the verified-vs-correct gap using an LLM synthesis pipeline, measuring state accuracy on planner search distributions vs. actual play outcomes with confidence intervals. (2) Derivation of a quantitative danger law: danger = play_cost × (1 − rarity)^N, with a proven exact gate-miss factor and empirically bounded play cost. (3) Controlled experiments across GPT-5.x models and data regimes (including DAgger and targeted examples) to test whether more data repairs the gap. (4) Extension to imperfect-information CWMs via a coverage bound (N ≳ b^{d_max}) and construction of Beacon, a hand-crafted verified-but-wrong inference function.
AI.result: (1) A CWM with 100% sampling-gate accuracy and ≥98% state accuracy on the planner's search distribution loses systematically; the omitted rule has play cost 0.091 [95% CI: 0.065, 0.117, n=4800]. (2) The danger law quantitatively predicts failure from rarity and play cost. (3) LLM synthesis behaves as rule translation, not inference — it fails to infer omitted rules regardless of model scale or data regime. (4) For imperfect-information CWMs, the coverage bound shows a size-N gate is identifying only when N ≳ b^{d_max}; shallow games like Kuhn poker show no gap, but the constructed Beacon function passes the gate yet loses every game.
AI.conclusion: Adequacy for planning-oriented world models should be measured on the planner's search distribution or by direct play performance, not by prediction accuracy on randomly sampled transitions. The verified-vs-correct gap is a systematic failure mode arising from the interaction between rare pivotal dynamics and sampling-based evaluation.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Reliability and Scaling in Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are evaluated as though perfect reliability is achievable for any task given sufficient scale. We show this assumption is information-theoretically unjustified. Every generative task has a reliability ceiling that no model can exceed, determined by how much output uncertainty is resolvable from observable context. The gap decomposes into a resolvable component closable with additional context and a subjective component inherent to task ambiguity. Autoregressive generation further degrades this ceiling at a rate governed by the task's dependency kernel, which quantifies inter-token correlations in the output. From these two primitives, we derive a first-principles scaling law where LLM performance is bottlenecked by the scarcer resource: training data or model capacity. This law recovers the Chinchilla scaling law as a special case and provides a structural account of when scaling improves reliability. Beyond scaling, our framework unifies diverse practical phenomena, such as the benefits of retrieval-augmentation and the spectral mechanics of catastrophic forgetting. Our work formalizes the resource-complexity tradeoffs that govern model performance across domains, offering a unified theory of performance limits in generative language models.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that LLMs have an information-theoretic reliability ceiling determined by context-resolvable uncertainty and task ambiguity. It derives a first-principles scaling law where performance is constrained by the scarcer of training data or model capacity, unifies phenomena like retrieval-augmentation and catastrophic forgetting, and recovers the Chinchilla scaling law as a special case.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation implicitly assumes perfect reliability is achievable with sufficient scale. The authors challenge this, arguing it is information-theoretically unjustified. They seek to formalize the fundamental limits on generative model performance and explain when and why scaling helps — or does not.
AI.method: The authors decompose the reliability gap into a resolvable component (addressable with additional context) and a subjective component (inherent to task ambiguity). They introduce a dependency kernel to quantify inter-token correlations and derive a first-principles scaling law showing that LLM performance is bottlenecked by the scarcer resource between training data and model capacity.
AI.result: The derived scaling law recovers the Chinchilla scaling law as a special case. The framework also structurally explains when scaling improves reliability and unifies diverse phenomena including retrieval-augmentation benefits and the spectral mechanics of catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a unified theory of performance limits in generative language models, formalizing the resource-complexity tradeoffs governing model performance across domains.

title: The Misclassification of Autistic Writing as AI-Generated
comment: Author Accepted Manuscript, Artificial Intelligence in Education 2025
summary: Recent findings suggest that detection models for artificial intelligence (AI) cannot accurately identify AI-generated text and may exhibit bias against certain minority groups. In the present study, anecdotal claims that autistic writers more often have their work flagged as AI-generated are examined empirically. A corpus of approximately 60,000 Reddit posts split into "likely-autistic" and "general-Reddit" subcorpora is used to compare the distribution of probabilities output by the OpenAI GPT-2 detection model. Differences in textual features between subcorpora are observed and compared to reported features of AI-generated text. Results showed that while less than two-percent of either subcorpus was flagged as AI-generated by the model, significantly more texts from the likely-autistic subcorpus were flagged. Connections between features of text with likely-autistic authors and AI-generated text were not straightforward. The widespread use of AI-detection models with a potential bias against autistic writers in their output prompts ethical scrutiny, and the authors recommend further critical examination of the models themselves as well as their use in academic contexts.

AI.tldr: This study empirically tests claims that autistic writers are disproportionately flagged by AI-detection models, finding that while overall flagging rates are low (<2%), texts from likely-autistic Reddit users are significantly more likely to be flagged as AI-generated, though the textual feature overlap is not straightforward.
AI.motivation: Addressing anecdotal claims and broader concerns that AI-detection models exhibit bias against minority groups—specifically, that autistic writers are disproportionately misclassified as AI-generated, raising ethical and fairness issues in academic and professional contexts where such detectors are deployed.
AI.method: A corpus of ~60,000 Reddit posts was split into "likely-autistic" and "general-Reddit" subcorpora. The OpenAI GPT-2 detection model was applied to compute probability scores, and the distributions were compared between subcorpora. Textual features (e.g., stylistic, lexical, syntactic) were also analyzed and contrasted with known characteristics of AI-generated text.
AI.result: Less than 2% of either subcorpus was flagged as AI-generated. However, the likely-autistic subcorpus had a significantly higher proportion of flagged texts. The overlap in textual features between autistic-authored and AI-generated text was not straightforward, suggesting the bias may stem from more complex model behaviors rather than simple feature mimicry.
AI.conclusion: AI-detection models exhibit measurable bias against autistic writers. The authors call for ethical scrutiny of both the models and their deployment in academic settings, recommending further critical examination of detection tools given their potential for disproportionate harm to neurodivergent populations.

title: Accelerating A/B-Tests with Counterfactual Estimation: Reducing Variance through Policy Overlap
summary:
Online controlled experiments are the gold standard for hypothesis testing in online platforms. Notwithstanding their ubiquity, they are notoriously expensive to run, and issues of variance hamper statistical power in assessing treatment effects. While standard variance reduction techniques leverage model-based control variates to reduce outcome noise, they remain agnostic to potential structural relationships between competing policies.
  In this work, we identify a critical inefficiency in the standard A/B-testing protocol: when a treatment and control policy agree on an action, the resulting outcome contributes noise but no signal regarding the treatment effect -- unnecessarily inflating confidence intervals. We propose a novel experimental protocol that exploits this policy overlap to accelerate experimentation. The key insight is to frame the randomised treatment assignment mechanism as a meta-policy, and leverage $Δ$-Off-Policy Estimation methods to obtain unbiased estimates for average treatment effects. We prove analytically that our approach recovers standard A/B-testing practices in the general case, but that its variance scales with the divergence between policies rather than raw outcome variance. Hence, we dominate the standard Difference-in-Means estimator whenever policies have common support, and the improvement is strict whenever the overlap region contributes non-zero residual variance. Empirical results corroborate these theoretical insights -- holding promise for significant impact on the real-world evaluation of recommender systems, information retrieval pipelines, and large language model interfaces.

AI.tldr: Standard A/B tests treat all observations equally, even when treatment and control policies agree on an action — contributing noise but no signal. The authors propose exploiting this "policy overlap" by framing randomization as a meta-policy and using Δ-Off-Policy Estimation to obtain unbiased treatment effect estimates with variance that scales with policy divergence rather than raw outcome variance, strictly improving on Difference-in-Means when policies share support.
AI.motivation: Online controlled experiments (A/B tests) are expensive and suffer from variance issues that limit statistical power. Existing variance reduction techniques (control variates) ignore structural relationships between competing policies. The key insight is that when treatment and control policies take the same action, the resulting outcome adds only noise — inflating confidence intervals without contributing signal about the treatment effect.
AI.method: The authors reframe the randomized treatment assignment mechanism as a meta-policy and apply Δ-Off-Policy Estimation methods to obtain unbiased estimates of average treatment effects (ATE). The approach conditions estimation on instances where the policies diverge, effectively down-weighting or excluding observations from the overlap region. They prove analytically that the estimator recovers standard A/B-testing in the general case, but with variance proportional to policy divergence rather than raw outcome variance.
AI.result: The proposed estimator dominates the standard Difference-in-Means estimator whenever treatment and control policies share common support, with strict improvement when the overlap region contributes non-zero residual variance. Empirical results corroborate the theoretical variance reduction claims.
AI.conclusion: The method holds significant promise for accelerating real-world evaluation across recommender systems, information retrieval pipelines, and LLM interfaces — potentially reducing the cost and duration of online experiments.

title: A Queueing-Stability Criterion for Causal IPD-QIM Network Flow Watermarking
summary: On multi-hop encrypted links such as Tor and cascaded VPNs, tunneling flattens packet lengths and protocol fields, leaving inter-packet delay (IPD) as the main carrier for active flow attribution. Causality lets the embedder delay packets but never advance them, so each quantization-index-modulation (QIM) alignment injects nonnegative dwell into a delay buffer; unbounded dwell breaks lattice alignment and delays the host connection unacceptably. Whether a causal QIM watermark embeds stably on bursty traffic has largely been left to empirical configuration rather than analysis. We model the embedder as a reflected dwell queue under the fixed dual-lattice, equiprobable-bit rule, where injection is state-dependent -- set by the current interval and bit -- rather than exogenous. The substitution $Y_i=δ_i-r_i$ gives only an algebraic Lindley-form identity; stability is governed by the busy-state drift at large dwell, where the effective interval collapses to zero and the mean injection becomes $Δ/4$. Away from the critical boundary, the buffer is stable iff $μ_d>Δ/4$ (i.e. $Δ<4μ_d$) for i.i.d. backgrounds, and, under stationary-ergodic and finite-state Markov-modulated traffic with instantaneous overload, iff the time-average intensity $\barρ<1$. With the exogenous decoding floor $Δ\ge cσ_ξ$ ($c=4Q^{-1}(ε/2)$), this yields the operating window $Δ\in[cσ_ξ,4\barμ_d)$. Simulations confirm a sharp transition at $ρ=1$ set only by the mean; on four real IPD traces, with each simulated chain confined to a single flow, the criterion gives the correct stability direction under flow-local correlation and burstiness, while pooled cross-flow means overestimate the margin. These results give a testable stable-embeddability criterion and a quantization-step configuration baseline for causal QIM network flow watermarking.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first rigorous stability analysis of causal QIM (Quantization Index Modulation) watermarking on encrypted tunnels. It models the embedder as a reflected dwell queue and derives the stability condition μ_d > Δ/4 for i.i.d. traffic, extending to stationary-ergodic and Markov-modulated backgrounds where stability holds iff time-average intensity ρ̄ < 1. This yields an operating window Δ ∈ [cσ_ξ, 4μ̄_d), validated by simulations and real IPD traces.
AI.motivation: On multi-hop encrypted links like Tor, active flow attribution relies on inter-packet delay (IPD) watermarking since packet lengths and protocol fields are flattened by tunneling. Causal embedders can only delay (never advance) packets, so each QIM alignment injects nonnegative dwell. Unbounded dwell breaks lattice alignment and causes unacceptable connection delay. Prior work has left whether causal QIM watermarks embed stably on bursty traffic to empirical trial-and-error, lacking formal analysis of stability conditions.
AI.method: The authors model the causal QIM embedder as a reflected dwell queue under a fixed dual-lattice, equiprobable-bit rule, where injection is state-dependent on the current interval and bit. Through the substitution Y_i = δ_i - r_i, they obtain an algebraic Lindley-form identity. Stability is analyzed via busy-state drift at large dwell, where the effective interval collapses to zero and mean injection becomes Δ/4. The analysis covers three traffic models: i.i.d. backgrounds, stationary-ergodic processes, and finite-state Markov-modulated traffic with instantaneous overload. The stability criterion yields an operating window bounded below by the decoding floor (Δ ≥ cσ_ξ, where c = 4Q^{-1}(ε/2)) and above by 4 times the mean inter-packet delay.
AI.result: Simulations confirm a sharp phase transition at ρ = 1 governed solely by the mean. Tests on four real IPD traces, with each simulated chain confined to a single flow, show the criterion correctly predicts stability direction under flow-local correlation and burstiness. Notably, pooled cross-flow means overestimate the stability margin. The derived operating window Δ ∈ [cσ_ξ, 4μ̄_d) provides a principled baseline for quantization step configuration.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a testable stable-embeddability criterion and a quantization-step configuration baseline for causal QIM network flow watermarking, replacing empirical guesswork with formal analysis. The sharp ρ = 1 transition and the flow-local (rather than cross-flow pooled) stability boundary are the key practical takeaways for watermark designers.

title: Predicting Human Visual Attention on Words in Source Code
summary: This paper presents a computational model to predict human visual attention over words in software source code. The visual attention of software engineers when reading source code has long been studied as a means to understand human cognitive processes during software engineering tasks. Predicting this visual attention is important for perfecting user interface design and understanding what information human programmers need. We propose a model of programmer visual attention in which we design a novel loss function that computes similarity between human attention measured during eye tracking experiments and the internal attention of the artificial neural network. We evaluate our model by comparing its outputs to actual eye tracking data from three separate datasets. Two are in the Java programming language and one is in the C programming language. Our model outperforms the baseline in software engineering by 64%, 16%, and 467% in each of these studies according to Pearson correlation. We used scanpath prediction as an example to demonstrate that our model is more capable of the task that requires the understanding of human thought process. Our model achieves a statistically significant improvement over the close baseline in the reading task according to normalized Levenshtein distance and outperforms both Claude and GPT-5 on both reading and writing tasks.

AI.tldr: A computational model using a novel loss function (comparing human eye-tracking attention with neural network internal attention) predicts programmer visual attention over source code, outperforming baselines by 16–467% across three datasets and surpassing Claude and GPT-5 on reading/writing tasks.
AI.motivation: Understanding where programmers look when reading source code is critical for improving UI design and identifying what information developers need. Existing models inadequately capture human visual attention patterns, motivating a better predictive model grounded in cognitive processes.
AI.method: The authors propose a neural network model that learns to predict visual attention over source code tokens. The key innovation is a custom loss function that directly measures similarity between ground-truth human attention (from eye-tracking) and the model's internal attention weights. Evaluation uses three eye-tracking datasets (two Java, one C), with performance measured via Pearson correlation. Scanpath prediction is used as a downstream task, evaluated with normalized Levenshtein distance.
AI.result: The model outperforms the software engineering baseline by 64%, 16%, and 467% (Pearson correlation) on the three datasets respectively. It achieves statistically significant improvement over the closest baseline on reading tasks (normalized Levenshtein distance) and outperforms both Claude and GPT-5 on reading and writing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Aligning neural network internal attention with human visual attention via a dedicated similarity loss yields substantial gains in predicting programmer gaze. The model generalizes across programming languages (Java, C) and surpasses state-of-the-art LLMs, demonstrating its utility for tasks requiring understanding of human cognitive processes in software engineering.

title: Augmentations for Robust and Efficient Imitation Learning in Streamed Video Games
comment: To be published in proceedings of IEEE Conference on Games (CoG), 2026
summary: Imitation learning is an appealing way to scale game-playing agents to complex 3D environments by training policies to map visual observations to actions from human demonstrations. However, these demonstrations are expensive to collect and modern game-playing is often done through streaming in which network delay and compression introduce spatiotemporally correlated visual artifacts that can cause a covariance shift at test time. To address these challenges, we propose streaming augmentations that mimic four types of artifacts commonly encountered during streaming with low-bandwidth network connection: pixelated blocks and scrubs, global blur, and ghosting. We instantiate our approach on top of predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDM), which combine future-state conditioning with an inverse dynamics policy in a learned latent space, and evaluate the impact of our augmentations across three tasks in modern 3D video games. Under stable streaming conditions, agents trained with spatiotemporal augmentations achieve up to 41% higher evaluation performance compared to agents trained without augmentations under an identical data budget. When network lag is introduced, agents trained with augmentations degrade by only 7.45% vs 49.82% of the original performance for agents trained only with the original data. These results clearly indicate that spatiotemporal augmentations tailored for the streaming setting are a simple yet powerful tool to train robust and efficient game-playing agents.

AI.tldr: To train robust game-playing agents from human demonstrations under streaming conditions, the authors propose spatiotemporal augmentations that mimic common streaming artifacts (pixelation, blur, ghosting, scrubs). When combined with Predictive Inverse Dynamics Models (PIDM), these augmentations yield up to 41% higher performance under stable streaming and significantly mitigate degradation under network lag (7.45% vs 49.82% performance drop).
AI.motivation: Human demonstrations for imitation learning in 3D games are expensive to collect, and modern gameplay often occurs via streaming where network delay and compression introduce correlated visual artifacts. These artifacts cause a covariance shift between training and test distributions, degrading agent performance at deployment time.
AI.method: The authors propose four spatiotemporal streaming augmentations — pixelated blocks, scrubs, global blur, and ghosting — that simulate low-bandwidth streaming artifacts. These are applied on top of Predictive Inverse Dynamics Models (PIDM), which learn a latent space combining future-state conditioning with an inverse dynamics policy. The augmentations are injected during training to bridge the domain gap.
AI.result: Under stable streaming, agents trained with augmentations achieved up to 41% higher evaluation performance versus unaugmented agents with equal data. Under network lag, augmented agents degraded by only 7.45% compared to a 49.82% drop for unaugmented agents.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporal augmentations tailored for streaming artifacts are a simple yet effective method for training robust, efficient game-playing agents, substantially improving both nominal performance and resilience to network-induced visual degradation.

title: T5-CSBoost: Adversarial Perturbation Resistant LLM Fingerprinting
comment: 14 pages, 3 datasets, code and data will be provided
summary:
While many AI-generated text (AIGT) detectors achieve strong performance on clean inputs, their accuracy degrades significantly under light paraphrasing, word substitutions, character edits, and distribution shifts. We present T5 Contrastive Style Boosted Classifier (T5-CSBoost), an extension to the T5-Sentinel framework that keeps the original next-token prediction objective for source attribution while introducing an auxiliary margin-based triplet loss over decoder embeddings.
  This contrastive style regularization encourages the learning of compact, perturbation-resistant stylistic representations, offering a lightweight yet effective alternative to prior approaches that rely on architectural modifications, adversarial training, or complex multi-task objectives without altering the underlying T5-small backbone. T5-CSBoost achieves state-of-the-art multiclass source attribution and binary human-vs-LLM detection on OpenLLMText and HC3 AIGT benchmarks. More importantly, T5-CSBoost demonstrates enhanced robustness to word and character level adversarial perturbations of up to 90% intensity, achieving state-of-the-art on the challenging MAGE/Deepfake stress-test suite, including unseen models, unseen domains, and extreme paraphrasing scenarios. Our results highlight that explicitly regularizing stylistic embeddings via contrastive learning is a practical and effective strategy for building more robust LLM fingerprinting systems in real-world adversarial settings.

AI.tldr: T5-CSBoost extends the T5-Sentinel AIGT detector with a contrastive triplet loss over decoder embeddings to learn perturbation-resistant stylistic representations. It achieves SOTA on source attribution and human-vs-LLM detection benchmarks while demonstrating strong robustness against adversarial perturbations up to 90% intensity.
AI.motivation: Current AI-generated text detectors degrade significantly under light paraphrasing, word substitutions, character edits, and distribution shifts, necessitating more robust detection methods that do not require heavy architectural modifications.
AI.method: The authors propose T5-CSBoost, which extends T5-Sentinel by adding an auxiliary margin-based triplet loss over decoder embeddings alongside the original next-token prediction objective. This contrastive style regularization encourages compact, perturbation-resistant stylistic representations without modifying the T5-small backbone.
AI.result: T5-CSBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiclass source attribution and binary human-vs-LLM detection on OpenLLMText and HC3 benchmarks, and demonstrates SOTA robustness on the MAGE/Deepfake stress-test suite under word/character-level adversarial perturbations up to 90% intensity, including unseen models, domains, and extreme paraphrasing.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly regularizing stylistic embeddings via contrastive learning is a practical and effective strategy for building robust LLM fingerprinting systems in real-world adversarial settings.

title: Setup Complete, Now You Are Compromised: Weaponizing Setup Instructions Against AI Coding Agents
summary: AI coding agents set up projects by reading documentation and installing the dependencies it lists, without verifying their names, sources, or known vulnerabilities. By editing only a README, requirements file, or Makefile, an attacker can redirect the agent to an untrusted registry, a known-vulnerable version, or a wrong-but-plausible name: documentation becomes a vector for code execution. We present the first systematic evaluation of package-install-time supply-chain attacks delivered through ordinary project-setup documentation across production coding-agent harnesses, probing frontier models on twelve scenarios in five attack classes, grounded in documented incidents. The same model catches an attack through one harness and installs it through another: install-time security rests on the harness-model combination, not the model alone. Agents catch blatant typosquats reliably, but plausible separator-confusion names (azurecore for azure-core) slip through, and how often depends on the harness-model pairing. Source-based attacks like registry redirection are missed almost everywhere. The source blind spot recurs on npm and Cargo, where nearly every model installs the untrusted dependency; name detection carries over less consistently across ecosystems. Security-oriented prompts recover part of the gap but only for the dimension they name; a deterministic pre-install check that verifies names, sources, and versions before any code runs closes most of it.

AI.tldr: AI coding agents blindly install dependencies from project documentation, making READMEs and requirements files a viable attack vector. The paper systematically evaluates package-install-time supply-chain attacks across production coding-agent harnesses, finding that security depends on the harness-model combination, that source-based attacks (registry redirection) are missed almost universally, and that pre-install verification checks can close most of the gap.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are increasingly used to autonomously set up software projects by reading documentation and installing dependencies. However, these agents lack verification of package names, sources, or known vulnerabilities. An attacker who compromises only documentation files (README, requirements.txt, Makefile) can redirect agents to untrusted registries or malicious packages. Despite documented real-world incidents of such attacks, no systematic evaluation of this threat across coding-agent platforms existed prior to this work.
AI.method: The authors conduct the first systematic evaluation of package-install-time supply-chain attacks via project documentation. They design twelve attack scenarios spanning five attack classes: typosquatting, separator confusion, registry redirection, dependency confusion, and known-vulnerable version pinning. These are tested across multiple production coding-agent harnesses (e.g., different agent frameworks and execution environments) using frontier language models. The methodology probes both cross-harness and cross-ecosystem (npm, Cargo) behavior, and evaluates mitigations including security-oriented prompting and deterministic pre-install verification checks.
AI.result: Security is a function of the harness-model pairing, not the model alone: the same model may catch an attack through one harness but install it through another. Agents reliably detect blatant typosquats but frequently miss plausible separator-confusion names (e.g., azurecore vs. azure-core). Source-based attacks, particularly registry redirection, are missed almost universally across all harnesses and models. This source blind spot persists across npm and Cargo ecosystems. Security-oriented prompts partially recover detection gaps but only for the explicitly named attack dimension. A deterministic pre-install check verifying names, sources, and versions before code execution closes most vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Project documentation constitutes a practical and underappreciated vector for supply-chain attacks against AI coding agents. The harness-model combination, not model capability alone, determines install-time security posture. Source verification is a critical, nearly universal blind spot. The authors recommend mandating deterministic, pre-install verification of package names, sources, and versions as a baseline defense, and caution against relying solely on model-level mitigations.

title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in Tool-Integrated Large Language Models have made web search a core capability of information-seeking agents. However, as interaction histories grow, agents increasingly struggle to track task progress. When search attempts fail to yield useful evidence, current single- and multi-agent systems can become trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and ultimately compromising the quality and completeness of the final output. We introduce SearchOS, a system-level multi-agent framework that turns fragile, implicit search progress into explicit, persistent, and shared state. First, we formulate open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations, where agents discover entities, populate attributes across linked tables, and anchor each value to source evidence. Then we design Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM), which externalizes the evolving state into Frontier Task, an Evidence Graph, a Coverage Map, and Failure Memory. Built on SOCM, SearchOS applies a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps the execution of sub-agents and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps to improve utilization and throughput. To schedule and control the execution of search agents, SearchOS introduces a Search Tool Middleware Harness that intercepts model and tool interactions to record grounded evidence and react to stalls or budget exhaustion, and provides a reusable hierarchical skill system comprising strategy and access skills to augment the agents' search process and avoid repeating failed search patterns across runs. On WideSearch and GISA, SearchOS leads all metrics among the evaluated single- and multi-agent baselines, paving the way toward robust information-seeking collaboration.

AI.tldr: SearchOS is a multi-agent framework that externalizes implicit search progress into explicit, persistent shared state using Search-Oriented Context Management (SOCM). It employs a pipeline-parallel scheduler, a search tool middleware harness, and hierarchical skills to prevent repetitive loops, improve throughput, and achieve state-of-the-art performance on WideSearch and GISA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based search agents suffer from tracking task progress over long interaction histories. When searches fail repeatedly, both single-agent and existing multi-agent systems get trapped in repetitive loops, wasting search budgets and degrading output quality. There is a need for explicit, persistent, and shared state to manage search progress systematically.
AI.method: The paper first formulates open-domain information seeking as relational schema completion with grounded citations. Then it introduces SearchOS with two core components: (1) SOCM (Search-Oriented Context Management), which externalizes evolving state into four structures — Frontier Task, Evidence Graph, Coverage Map, and Failure Memory; (2) a pipeline-parallel scheduling mechanism that overlaps sub-agent execution and continuously refills freed slots with tasks targeting unresolved coverage gaps. Additionally, a Search Tool Middleware Harness intercepts model–tool interactions to record evidence and react to stalls/budget exhaustion, while a hierarchical skill system (strategy and access skills) augments agents to avoid repeating failed search patterns.
AI.result: SearchOS achieves leading performance across all metrics on the WideSearch and GISA benchmarks compared to all evaluated single-agent and multi-agent baselines.
AI.conclusion: By making search progress explicit, persistent, and shared across agents, SearchOS overcomes the fragility of implicit progress tracking and sets a new state-of-the-art for robust, collaborative information-seeking agents.

title: NFSA: Non-Forward Secure Aggregation with One Server via Two Layer Secret Sharing
comment: Accepted by ACM CCS 2026. This is a full version including appendices
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training while preserving privacy by keeping data local. However, the risk of sensitive data leakage through model updates necessitates the use of secure aggregation protocols. Existing server-based secure aggregation protocols typically require the server to forward sensitive data shared between users, which increases communication overhead and introduces potential security risks. In this work, we propose a novel secure aggregation protocol based on two-layer secret sharing to address these issues. By combining Shamir's Secret Sharing with 2-out-of-2 additive secret sharing using a Pseudo-Random Function (PRF), our protocol eliminates direct communication between users, thereby removing the need for the server to forward data. We further extend the protocol with Key-homomorphic PRF (KhPRF) to support high-dimensional data aggregation and apply it to FL, enabling one-shot secure aggregation with a single server and no intermediary data forwarding. To reduce user overhead, we design a new encoding method based on the Chinese Remainder Theorem for the almost KhPRF-based mask, reducing the number of KhPRF calls and mitigating the model update expansion issue after masking. Experimental results show that our scheme significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of auxiliary node overhead. For instance, when the number of users is 100, our scheme improves communication efficiency by nearly 100 times and reduces computational overhead by approximately 17\%. Moreover, user computation time can be reduced by 51\% to 75\% when the input length is $2^{18}$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel two-layer secret sharing protocol for Federated Learning that combines Shamir's Secret Sharing with 2-out-of-2 additive secret sharing via PRF, eliminating direct user-to-user communication and server-forwarded data. It extends to Key-homomorphic PRF for high-dimensional aggregation, and uses Chinese Remainder Theorem-based encoding to reduce user overhead. Results show ~100x communication improvement and 51-75% user computation reduction.
AI.motivation: Existing server-based secure aggregation protocols require the server to forward sensitive data between users, causing increased communication overhead and potential security risks. The authors aim to eliminate this intermediary forwarding while maintaining secure aggregation for FL.
AI.method: The protocol uses a two-layer secret sharing approach: (1) combining Shamir's Secret Sharing with 2-out-of-2 additive secret sharing using a Pseudo-Random Function (PRF) to remove direct user-to-user communication; (2) extending with Key-homomorphic PRF (KhPRF) for high-dimensional data aggregation, enabling one-shot secure aggregation with a single server; (3) designing a Chinese Remainder Theorem-based encoding method for almost KhPRF-based masks to reduce KhPRF calls and mitigate model update expansion after masking.
AI.result: For 100 users, the scheme improves communication efficiency by nearly 100x and reduces computational overhead by ~17%. User computation time is reduced by 51-75% when the input length is 2^18. Overall, the scheme significantly outperforms existing methods in auxiliary node overhead.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol effectively eliminates intermediary data forwarding by the server, reduces both communication and computational overhead, and is well-suited for practical FL deployments requiring secure aggregation with a single untrusted server.

title: A Deterministic Binary Fingerprinting Framework with Zero-Trained Feature Extraction for Sparse Count Matrices
summary: Sparse count matrices from single-cell transcriptomes to k-mer profiles and document-term frequencies are conventionally analyzed via PCA-reduced graph clustering or iterative optimization in continuous embedding spaces. We introduce MMTB, a deterministic non-learned binary representation framework that requires no label supervision, model fitting, or gradient-based optimization. Column-wise Min-Max normalization followed by fixed cutoffs maps each sample to a thermometer fingerprint whose Hamming distances show empirical correspondence with normalized L1 distances, with Pearson correlation approximately 0.92 on single-cell RNA-seq pairs. In a favorable three-cell-line mixture, the 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell. Under a fair Hamming nearest-neighbor graph plus Leiden readout, MMTB approaches PCA plus Leiden on this coarse task. On challenging tissue-like annotations, continuous pipelines often lead; PBMC Seurat NMI is 0.39 for MMTB versus 0.49 for Scanpy, underscoring that MMTB is suited for coarse-grained separation and resource-constrained deployments rather than fine-grained subtype discovery or as a general replacement for continuous embeddings. Relative to dense float32 representations, MMTB fingerprints reduce memory by approximately 10-fold while providing fixed-width Hamming-indexable codes. PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR may be smaller; we do not claim universal compression. A label-free suitability score is provided as a deployment guideline, not a performance predictor.

AI.tldr: MMTB introduces a deterministic, non-learned binary representation framework that converts sparse count matrices into thermometer fingerprints via Min-Max normalization and fixed cutoffs, achieving ~0.92 Pearson correlation between Hamming and L1 distances, with ~10× memory reduction over float32, suited for coarse-grained clustering in resource-constrained settings.
AI.motivation: Traditional analysis of sparse count matrices (scRNA-seq, k-mer profiles, document-term frequencies) relies on PCA-based graph clustering or iterative continuous embedding optimization, which requires model fitting and gradient-based learning. The authors seek a lightweight, deterministic alternative that requires no label supervision, model fitting, or optimization, targeting resource-constrained deployments where coarse-grained separation suffices.
AI.method: The MMTB framework applies column-wise Min-Max normalization to sparse count matrices, then uses fixed cutoff thresholds to map each sample to a binary "thermometer fingerprint." Hamming distances between these fingerprints empirically approximate normalized L1 distances. Clustering proceeds via a Hamming nearest-neighbor graph with Leiden community detection. A label-free suitability score is provided for deployment guidance.
AI.result: On a three-cell-line mixture, the 3-threshold fingerprint achieves NMI of 0.99 at 188 bytes per cell, approaching PCA+Leiden performance. On PBMC data, MMTB achieves NMI of 0.39 versus Scanpy's 0.49, demonstrating suitability for coarse-grained separation but not fine-grained subtype discovery. Fingerprints reduce memory ~10× versus dense float32 and provide fixed-width Hamming-indexable codes, though PCA30 embeddings and sparse CSR may be smaller.
AI.conclusion: MMTB is a viable lightweight alternative for coarse-grained clustering tasks in resource-constrained environments, but it is not a general replacement for continuous embeddings and underperforms on fine-grained, tissue-like annotations. The label-free suitability score aids practitioners in determining when MMTB is appropriate for deployment.

title: Privacy Leakage in Federated Learning in Radiology Reports: A Comparative Evaluation of Tokenizer-Driven Privacy Risks
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multi-institutional training on clinical text without sharing raw data, but gradient inversion can reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates. The extent of this leakage for radiology reports, and the role of tokenizer design, remains unclear. We quantify gradient-based text reconstruction in FL and compare privacy risk across three tokenizers with the model architecture held fixed. Six FL clients trained a GPT-2-style transformer (sequence length 32) on public radiology corpora (368,751 diagnostic reports, 98,206 discharge summaries, 1,500 MIMIC-CXR free-text reports) using the GPT-2, RadBERT, and LLaMA-2 tokenizers at batch sizes of 64, 128, and 256. Assuming an active malicious server that modifies the shared architecture before distribution, we applied analytic gradient inversion and measured reconstruction fidelity over five runs. Exact sentence reconstruction ranged from 31% to 44% across tokenizers (30.6-43.5% across the 27 tokenizer x dataset x batch-size cells). At batch size 64 on the Discharge dataset, accuracy was 42.1% (GPT-2), 42.3% (RadBERT), and 39.4% (LLaMA-2), decreasing to 37.3%, 37.2%, and 34.3% at batch size 256. S-BLEU declined as batch size grew (GPT-2: 0.44 to 0.33; RadBERT: 0.48 to 0.35). RadBERT yielded the highest reconstruction fidelity and recovered the most clinical terms (18.1% of a 1,440-term reference vocabulary, vs 12.5% for GPT-2 and 9.4% for LLaMA-2), yet no tokenizer prevented leakage. Substantial portions of report text are therefore recoverable from FL gradients even at larger batch sizes and with domain-specific tokenizers. Tokenizer design influences leakage severity and is a privacy-relevant decision, not only a utility one; safeguards such as secure aggregation and differential privacy are likely necessary to meet HIPAA and GDPR requirements for FL in radiology NLP.

AI.tldr: Federated learning on radiology reports is vulnerable to gradient inversion attacks, with 31–44% of sentences exactly reconstructed. Tokenizer choice affects leakage severity—RadBERT leaked the most clinical terms—but no tokenizer prevents it. Safeguards like secure aggregation and differential privacy are necessary for compliance.
AI.motivation: Federated learning promises privacy-preserving multi-institutional training on clinical text, but gradient inversion attacks can reconstruct sensitive data from shared model updates. The extent of this leakage for radiology reports and the impact of tokenizer design on privacy risk have not been previously quantified.
AI.method: Six FL clients trained a GPT-2-style transformer (sequence length 32) on three public radiology corpora (368,751 diagnostic reports, 98,206 discharge summaries, 1,500 MIMIC-CXR reports) using three tokenizers (GPT-2, RadBERT, LLaMA-2) at batch sizes 64, 128, and 256. An active malicious server scenario was simulated by modifying the shared architecture before distribution. Analytic gradient inversion was applied, and reconstruction fidelity was measured over five runs using exact sentence match accuracy, S-BLEU, and clinical term recovery rates.
AI.result: Exact sentence reconstruction ranged from 30.6% to 43.5% across all 27 tokenizer × dataset × batch-size conditions. At batch size 64 on the Discharge dataset, accuracy reached 42.1% (GPT-2), 42.3% (RadBERT), and 39.4% (LLaMA-2), declining at batch size 256 to 37.3%, 37.2%, and 34.3%. S-BLEU decreased with larger batches (GPT-2: 0.44→0.33; RadBERT: 0.48→0.35). RadBERT yielded the highest reconstruction fidelity and recovered 18.1% of a 1,440-term clinical vocabulary, vs. 12.5% (GPT-2) and 9.4% (LLaMA-2). No tokenizer prevented leakage.
AI.conclusion: Substantial portions of radiology report text are recoverable from FL gradients even at larger batch sizes and with domain-specific tokenizers. Tokenizer design is a privacy-relevant decision affecting leakage severity, not merely a utility consideration. Secure aggregation and differential privacy are likely necessary to meet HIPAA and GDPR requirements for FL in radiology NLP.

title: RxBrain: Embodied Cognition Foundation Model with Joint Language-Visual Reasoning and Imagination
summary: Embodied cognition requires agents to connect high-level task reasoning with the physical states to be achieved. We introduce Hy-Embodied-RxBrain, an embodied cognition foundation model with joint language-visual reasoning and imagination. Unlike vision-language models that emphasize scene understanding and textual decision making, or generative world models that mainly predict future visual states, RxBrain represents embodied plans in a single planning sequence where language and visual imagination play complementary roles. Language provides the abstract structure of a plan, including task decomposition, planning primitives, constraints, temporal order, and decision logic, while visual imagination grounds this structure through world state prediction and joint subgoal planning, associating each planning step with intermediate and final physical states. RxBrain adopts a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports language, image, and video understanding and generation within one model. To train this capability, we build an automatic pipeline that converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps and aligning them with visual state transitions. We further introduce RxBrain-Bench to evaluate whether models can represent embodied plans through joint textual and visual components rather than separate understanding or generation. Experiments show that RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, and produces plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. We also extend RxBrain to continuous robot action generation, where it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining. These results provide an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RxBrain, an embodied cognition foundation model that jointly performs language-visual reasoning and imagination by representing plans as a single sequence where language provides abstract task structure and visual imagination grounds it in physical state predictions. Built on a unified multimodal MoE architecture, trained via automatic video-to-plan supervision, it demonstrates coupled reasoning and promising real-robot action generation.
AI.motivation: Embodied cognition demands agents that bridge high-level task reasoning with concrete physical states. Existing VLMs focus on scene understanding/textual decisions, while world models only predict future visuals. Neither tightly couples abstract planning structure with grounded physical state imagination in a unified framework.
AI.method: RxBrain uses a unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers architecture supporting joint language, image, and video understanding/generation. Plans are represented as a single sequence where language handles task decomposition, primitives, constraints, and logic, while visual imagination provides world state prediction and joint subgoal planning. Training uses an automatic pipeline that converts embodied videos into joint text-visual planning supervision by decomposing videos into planning steps aligned with visual state transitions. RxBrain-Bench is introduced to evaluate joint textual-visual plan representation.
AI.result: RxBrain maintains embodied understanding and generation abilities, producing plans with coupled textual reasoning, world state prediction, and joint subgoal planning. Extended to continuous robot action generation, it shows promising real-robot performance without large-scale action-data pretraining.
AI.conclusion: RxBrain represents an initial step toward foundation models for embodied cognition by tightly integrating language-based planning with visual state imagination in a single unified framework, validated on both planning benchmarks and real-robot tasks.

title: CoEvoT: Co-Evolving Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Graph-LLM Reasoning
summary: Graph learning under distribution shift presents a persistent challenge, where models adapt to new graphs with limited or even no supervision. Recent graph--LLM approaches move toward label-efficient prediction by linearizing graphs into prompts and using large language models (LLMs) as predictors, and can adopt Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to exploit LLM's multi-step reasoning capability. However, existing CoT-based graph--LLM methods generate intermediate thoughts while conditioning on fixed graph tokens, limiting step-wise refinement of structural cues. In this paper, we propose CoEvoT, a simple yet effective co-evolving CoT prompting framework for graph--LLM reasoning. CoEvoT couples text-to-graph token rewriting and graph-to-text reasoning guidance in a closed loop: each intermediate textual thought is used to update the graph token evidence state via a lightweight condition network, and the updated tokens are fed back into the next-step instruction to guide subsequent LLM reasoning. This enables step-wise, state-aware evidence refinement, rather than reasoning over a fixed graph snapshot. Extensive experiments on eight datasets demonstrate that CoEvoT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: CoEvoT introduces a co-evolving Chain-of-Thought prompting framework for graph-LLM reasoning, where textual thoughts and graph tokens are mutually refined in a closed loop, enabling step-wise structural evidence updates rather than reasoning over fixed graph snapshots.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT-based graph-LLM methods generate intermediate reasoning steps while conditioning on fixed graph tokens, which prevents step-wise refinement of structural cues. This limits the model's ability to adaptively incorporate graph evidence during multi-step reasoning.
AI.method: CoEvoT couples text-to-graph token rewriting and graph-to-text reasoning guidance in a closed loop. Each intermediate textual thought updates the graph token evidence state via a lightweight condition network, and the updated tokens are fed back into the next-step instruction to guide subsequent LLM reasoning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on eight datasets show that CoEvoT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving textual reasoning and graph token states enables more effective step-wise evidence refinement, leading to superior performance in graph learning under distribution shift with limited supervision.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret visualizations, yet current evaluations remain largely chart-centric and provide limited evidence of understanding of scientific visualization (SciVis). We benchmark six MLLMs on the scientific visualization literacy assessment test, a standardized SciVis literacy assessment comprising 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, spanning 8 techniques and 11 task types. We evaluate three closed-source and three open-source models under a closed-world protocol and compare their performance using data from 485 human participants. Results show that current MLLMs do not exhibit uniform SciVis literacy. Gemini is the strongest model overall, exceeding the human mean across the evaluated subsets, whereas the open-source models remain below the human baseline. Performance is highly uneven across techniques and tasks: models perform best on scientific illustration, search, and spatial understanding, but struggle on texture-based and integration-based visualizations and on quantitative estimation. Error analysis reveals recurring failures in fine-grained quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation, and grounded encoding interpretation. These findings position SciVis literacy as a necessary benchmark dimension for evaluating multimodal AI systems. Our code and model outputs are publicly available at https://github.com/patdmp/mllm-scivis-lit-benchmark.

AI.tldr: Six MLLMs were benchmarked on a standardized scientific visualization literacy test (49 items, 18 visualizations, 8 techniques, 11 task types). Gemini outperformed the human mean, but open-source models fell below it. Performance was uneven: strong on illustration, search, and spatial tasks; weak on texture/integration-based visualizations and quantitative estimation. The paper argues SciVis literacy is a critical MLLM evaluation dimension.
AI.motivation: Current MLLM evaluations are chart-centric and fail to assess understanding of scientific visualizations (SciVis). There is limited evidence on whether MLLMs possess scientific visualization literacy — the ability to interpret domain-specific visualizations like vector fields, volume renderings, and tensor glyphs — which is essential for scientific communication and reasoning.
AI.method: The authors benchmarked six MLLMs — three closed-source (Gemini, GPT-4V, Claude) and three open-source (LLaVA, CogVLM, Fuyu) — using the Scientific Visualization Literacy Assessment Test (SVLAT), a validated instrument with 49 multiple-choice items covering 18 SciVis types across 8 techniques (e.g., isocontouring, volume rendering, streamlines, tensor glyphs) and 11 task types (e.g., search, spatial understanding, quantitative estimation, flow-direction interpretation). Model responses were collected under a closed-world protocol (no external tools, no chain-of-thought unless default). Results were compared against a human baseline of 485 participants, and error analyses were conducted across technique-task combinations.
AI.result: Gemini was the top model, exceeding the pooled human mean; all open-source models scored below the human baseline. Models excelled on scientific illustration, search tasks, and spatial understanding but performed poorly on texture-based visualizations, integration-based representations (e.g., tensor glyphs), and quantitative estimation. Recurring failure modes included fine-grained quantitative misestimation, incorrect flow-direction interpretation, and flawed grounded encoding interpretation (mapping visual features to physical quantities). Performance variance across techniques was far greater for models than for humans, indicating non-uniform SciVis literacy.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs lack uniform scientific visualization literacy, with stark disparities across visualization techniques and task types.
