SciVis literacy should be adopted as a standard evaluation dimension alongside chart understanding in multimodal AI benchmarks. The public release of code and outputs supports reproducibility and future research.

title: DataShield: Uncovering Risky Fine-Tuning Data Across LLMs Through Consensus Subspace Alignment
summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on domain-specific datasets has become a standard paradigm for adapting LLMs to specialized applications. However, recent work has shown that even fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can substantially weaken the safety capabilities of LLMs. While existing efforts have made progress in identifying data responsible for safety degradation, they usually rely on a single mean vector computed over a specific model with its tokenizer to represent the safety direction, which limits both the effectiveness and transferability of their risk assessment measures. To address these limitations, we propose DataShield, a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments through consensus subspace alignment over joint safety-critical semantic spaces derived from multiple safety-aligned LLMs. Within these spaces, DataShield extracts consensus safe and unsafe subspaces using semantic spectral decomposition over safe and unsafe data representations. The risk of a data sample or segment is then estimated by measuring its relative alignment with the unsafe and safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking. Compared with state-of-the-art filtering and masking baselines, DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6\% with sample filtering and 32.3\% with segment masking, while preserving downstream utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.

AI.tldr: DataShield is a data assessment framework that identifies risky fine-tuning samples and response segments by aligning them with consensus safe/unsafe subspaces extracted from multiple safety-aligned LLMs, achieving significant Attack Success Rate (ASR) reductions of 14.6% (sample filtering) and 32.3% (segment masking) without compromising downstream utility.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning on benign task-specific data can degrade LLM safety, but existing risk detection methods rely on a single mean vector from one model/tokenizer to represent the safety direction, limiting both effectiveness and cross-model transferability.
AI.method: DataShield constructs joint safety-critical semantic spaces from multiple safety-aligned LLMs and applies semantic spectral decomposition to extract consensus safe and unsafe subspaces. Risk is quantified by measuring a sample's or segment's relative alignment with these unsafe vs. safe subspaces, enabling both sample-level filtering and fine-grained segment-level masking.
AI.result: DataShield reduces ASR by 14.6% with sample filtering and 32.3% with segment masking compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while preserving downstream task utility and avoiding target-model-specific risk computation.
AI.conclusion: Consensus subspace alignment across multiple safety-aligned LLMs provides a more effective and transferable approach to identifying safety-degrading fine-tuning data than single-model, single-vector methods.

title: SYNAPSE: A Multi-LLM Orchestrated AI Tutor for Secure Software Development Education with Neurodivergent-First Design
comment: Accepted at the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026), Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track. Source code archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20480483
summary: Developers who maintain real systems must continually recognise and remediate vulnerabilities in existing code, yet this skill is rarely trained directly: secure software development is commonly taught only after programming fluency is acquired, and accessibility support is treated as a secondary concern, disadvantaging learners with ADHD and related executive-function differences. This paper presents SYNAPSE, a publicly deployed adaptive tutoring platform for Java, Python for cybersecurity, and secure software development. SYNAPSE coordinates Claude, GPT-4o, and Gemini through the Model Context Protocol, routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. It exposes eighteen always-visible accessibility features and anchors practice in ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, on which learners practise the detect-understand-remediate loop characteristic of software maintenance. A feasibility pilot with nineteen participants across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts returned a System Usability Scale score of 76.4 and engagement of 4.2/5, with comparable cognitive-load levels across cohorts. SYNAPSE is available at https://synapse-course.com; a screencast is available at https://youtu.be/9R17KC47qQI.

AI.tldr: SYNAPSE is an adaptive tutoring platform that integrates multiple LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) via the Model Context Protocol to teach secure software development through a Socratic hint policy, featuring comprehensive accessibility support and a deliberately vulnerable practice application, with a pilot study showing strong usability (SUS 76.4) across neurodivergent and neurotypical learners.
AI.motivation: Secure software development skills (detecting and remediating vulnerabilities in existing code) are rarely trained directly in CS education. Security is typically taught only after programming fluency, and accessibility features are treated as secondary, disadvantaging learners with ADHD and related executive-function differences. There is a need for an inclusive, accessible platform that teaches the detect-understand-remediate loop characteristic of real software maintenance.
AI.method: SYNAPSE coordinates three LLMs (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), routing interactions by pedagogical intent under a three-stage Socratic hint policy. The platform exposes 18 always-visible accessibility features. Practice is anchored in ShopSecure, a deliberately vulnerable web application mapped to six OWASP Top 10 (2021) categories, where learners practice the detect-understand-remediate loop. A feasibility pilot was conducted with 19 participants across neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts, measuring System Usability Scale (SUS), engagement, and cognitive load.
AI.result: The feasibility pilot (n=19) yielded a System Usability Scale score of 76.4, an engagement rating of 4.2 out of 5, and comparable cognitive-load levels between neurodivergent and neurotypical cohorts, indicating that the platform is both usable and inclusive across learner populations.
AI.conclusion: SYNAPSE demonstrates the feasibility of an adaptive, multi-LLM tutoring platform for cybersecurity education that provides equitable learning experiences across neurodivergent and neurotypical learners through built-in accessibility features and pedagogically structured AI interactions.

title: LIGO-PINN: Learned Initialization via Gated Optimization to Alleviate Convergence Failures in Physics Informed Neural Networks
comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 13 tables. Code available at https://github.com/scailab/ligo-pinn
summary:
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have had a broad research impact in modeling domains governed by partial differential equations (PDE). However, PINNs have been shown to perform poorly, sometimes even converging to trivial solutions, in challenging PDE domains, or when generalizing to unseen but related PDE domains. Previously proposed solutions detail hyperparameter tuning to reduce loss imbalance between data-driven and physics guided losses, curriculum learning based training strategies, or dynamic re-sampling of hard collocation points. These methods face certain pitfalls: hyperparameter tuning is expensive, designing a training curriculum is ambiguous in multi-parameter PDE settings, and dynamic resampling still fails in complex PDE settings. Complementary to this line of thinking, we believe the initial PINN network weights also play a crucial role in the emergence of catastrophic failures during training, yet the effect of PINN weight initialization has been surprisingly under-investigated. To this end, we propose a framework for Learned Initialization via Gated Layerwise Optimization (LIGO-PINN) to overcome PINN convergence failures. Through rigorous evaluation on 1D and 2D PDE domains, including a challenging 2D fluid dynamics setting, we demonstrate that our methodology outperforms state-of-the-art methods designed to alleviate PINN failures, achieving a 91.5% average performance improvement across six baselines and 81% over the strongest baseline. We also verify that LIGO-PINN generalizes to 3D unstructured domains. Finally, we analyze training dynamics across all three PDE domains to explain both LIGO-PINN's improvement and the convergence failure of traditional PINNs. Code: https://github.com/scailab/ligo-pinn
  Keywords: Machine Learning, Physics-Informed Neural Networks, Deep Learning, PDE Modeling

AI.tldr: PINNs often fail due to poor weight initialization, an underexplored factor. The authors propose LIGO-PINN, a learned initialization framework using gated layerwise optimization, achieving 91.5% average improvement over six baselines and outperforming the strongest by 81%, while also generalizing to 3D unstructured domains.
AI.motivation: Existing solutions to PINN convergence failures (hyperparameter tuning, curriculum learning, dynamic resampling) are expensive, ambiguous, or still fail in complex PDE settings. The effect of weight initialization on PINN failures has been surprisingly under-investigated, motivating a complementary approach focused on learned initialization.
AI.method: LIGO-PINN (Learned Initialization via Gated Layerwise Optimization) — a framework that learns optimal initial network weights through a gated, layerwise optimization strategy to prevent convergence failures in PINNs.
AI.result: LIGO-PINN outperforms state-of-the-art methods across 1D and 2D PDE domains (including challenging fluid dynamics), with 91.5% average improvement over six baselines and 81% over the strongest. It also generalizes to 3D unstructured domains. Training dynamics analysis explains both the improvement and traditional PINN failure modes.
AI.conclusion: Weight initialization is a critical yet overlooked factor in PINN training failures. LIGO-PINN provides an effective learned initialization framework that significantly outperforms existing mitigation strategies and generalizes across diverse PDE domains.

title: How Artificial Intelligence LLM Engines Shape the Global Conflict Information Environment
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) answer engines now field a growing share of the questions that analysts, scholars, and the public ask about issues of peace and conflict. Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to hallucinate under certain conditions, but do these errors have discernible patterns when they are asked about conflicts, and if so what can that teach us about the changing global conflict information environment? To answer, we first asked a battery of questions about 28 conflicts to five leading answer engines and scored their 5,460 answers against documented evidence. We found that the thinner the retrievable record around a given conflict, the more the engines invent, misattribute, and miscount. Thin records don't just encourage hallucination, but create structural exposure to mis- and disinformation, because they are the easiest records to warp through Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) to bias engine responses. Through an analysis of 1,048 websites that the AI LLMs pulled conflict facts from, we found that GEO source optimization is already happening, and while state-partisan digital capture remains incipient it is rapidly growing. We explain what these findings mean for scholarship with the rise of GEO information warfare, and for policy argue for a return to the deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI tools cannot replicate, closing with a discussion of future research opportunities and challenges in this fast-moving space.

AI.tldr: AI answer engines hallucinate more about conflicts with thinner retrievable records, creating structural vulnerability to Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)-based information warfare — a phenomenon already underway and growing.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLM hallucinations about peace and conflict follow discernible patterns, and what those patterns reveal about the evolving global conflict information environment, given the rising use of AI answer engines for conflict-related queries.
AI.method: A battery of questions about 28 conflicts was posed to five leading AI answer engines, producing 5,460 answers scored against documented evidence. Additionally, 1,048 websites used as sources by the LLMs were analyzed for signs of GEO-based manipulation.
AI.result: Thinner retrievable records correlate with more hallucination (invention, misattribution, miscounting). Thin records also create structural exposure to mis/disinformation via GEO. Analysis confirmed GEO source optimization is already occurring, with state-partisan digital capture incipient but rapidly growing.
AI.conclusion: The rise of GEO information warfare demands a return to deep local monitoring and translation-based research that AI cannot replicate. The paper calls for policy responses and outlines future research challenges in this domain.

title: ReportMedSAM: Guiding Segmentation Through Radiology Reports
summary: Free-form radiology reports contain rich clinical descriptions, yet converting them for reliable segmentation remains challenging due to the inherent variability of natural language. Existing pipelines often rely on predefined organ phrases or brittle rule-based inference-time extraction, which limits their scalability to novel anatomical structures and makes them sensitive to linguistic variations. To address this, we propose ReportMedSAM, a report-driven framework that replaces discrete extraction with a learnable concept bank. By leveraging a frozen medical vision-language encoder (BiomedCLIP), we align organ-level concept embeddings with large-scale clinical corpora through contrastive learning, establishing mutually orthogonal semantic anchors. Our approach explicitly mitigates organ-level semantic collapse and ensures high robustness against diverse clinical synonyms (e.g., "renal" vs. "kidney" ). During inference, a clinical report is embedded and matched against this concept bank to dynamically activate task-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules. This decoupled design allows new concepts and experts to be added without retraining existing components, providing a parameter-isolated extension mechanism while keeping previously learned experts unchanged. Evaluated on the AbdomenAtlas 3.0 dataset, ReportMedSAM effectively interprets free-form reports, achieves competitive segmentation accuracy, and demonstrates seamless, non-interfering extension to novel clinical tasks.

AI.tldr: ReportMedSAM replaces rule-based report parsing with a learnable concept bank aligned via BiomedCLIP contrastive learning, using MoE modules activated by concept matching to enable scalable, synonym-robust segmentation from free-form radiology reports.
AI.motivation: Free-form radiology reports are rich but difficult to use for segmentation due to natural language variability. Existing methods depend on brittle, predefined organ phrases and rule-based extraction, limiting scalability to new anatomical structures and sensitivity to linguistic variation (e.g., synonyms).
AI.method: ReportMedSAM introduces a learnable concept bank aligned with BiomedCLIP embeddings via contrastive learning, producing mutually orthogonal organ-level semantic anchors to prevent semantic collapse. At inference, the report is embedded and matched against the bank to dynamically activate task-specific Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) modules. The decoupled architecture allows adding new concepts/experts without retraining existing ones.
AI.result: Evaluated on AbdomenAtlas 3.0, ReportMedSAM achieves competitive segmentation accuracy, robustly handles diverse clinical synonyms (e.g., "renal" vs. "kidney"), and demonstrates seamless, non-interfering extension to novel clinical tasks.
AI.conclusion: The concept-bank + MoE design provides a scalable, parameter-isolated framework for report-driven segmentation that overcomes the brittleness of prior rule-based approaches and supports open-world extension to new anatomical concepts.

title: Automated Template-free Synthesis of Instruction-Centric Leakage Contracts for Black-Box CPUs
comment: 16 pages (12 pages main body, 4 pages bibliography and appendix), 4 figures, 6 tables
summary:
Side-channel attacks pose a significant security threat for modern computing platforms, because they exploit subtle discrepancies in CPU behaviors to leak sensitive information. To model the information leaked by a CPU via microarchitectural side-channels, recent work proposed leakage contracts: an ISA-level security abstraction that provides the foundations for secure CPU programming. Unfortunately, due to the complexity of current microarchitectures, devising a leakage contract for a CPU requires extensive manual effort and thus modern CPUs lack dedicated leakage contracts.
  We present a methodology to extract instruction-centric leakage contracts for major CPU architectures with minimal manual intervention. We implemented this technique in malcos, the first template-free tool that automates the synthesis of leakage contracts for black-box CPUs. We evaluate malcos on x86 and ARM CPUs, and show that the contracts it synthesizes are precise and sound with respect to all leaks observed during synthesis. Our results demonstrate that learning leakage contracts from black-box CPUs is feasible.

AI.tldr: malcos is a tool that automatically synthesizes instruction-centric leakage contracts for black-box CPUs (x86 and ARM) with minimal manual intervention, demonstrating that learning precise and sound leakage contracts from CPUs is feasible.
AI.motivation: Side-channel attacks exploit microarchitectural CPU behaviors to leak sensitive information. Leakage contracts — ISA-level security abstractions — have been proposed to model this leakage, but creating them requires extensive manual effort due to microarchitectural complexity. Consequently, modern CPUs lack dedicated leakage contracts, motivating the need for automated extraction.
AI.method: The authors present a template-free methodology that extracts instruction-centric leakage contracts with minimal manual intervention. They implement this technique in malcos, which treats the CPU as a black box and automatically synthesizes leakage contracts by observing CPU behaviors during synthesis, without relying on pre-defined templates or detailed knowledge of the microarchitecture.
AI.result: malcos was evaluated on both x86 and ARM CPUs. The synthesized contracts were shown to be precise and sound with respect to all leaks observed during the synthesis process, validating the feasibility of learning leakage contracts from black-box CPUs.
AI.conclusion: Automated synthesis of leakage contracts from black-box CPUs is practical and effective. malcos demonstrates that it is possible to derive precise, sound ISA-level security abstractions without extensive manual reverse-engineering, paving the way for broader adoption of leakage contracts in modern CPUs.

title: Rethinking Issue Resolution for AI/ML Systems
comment: In proceedings at the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution, ICSME 2026
summary: We advocate for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks tailored to maintenance workflows and the nature of modern AI/ML systems. Existing issue resolution frameworks largely emerged for traditional software maintenance practices and do not explicitly account for characteristics common in AI/ML systems, such as stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts beyond source code. To identify the unique characteristics of issue resolution in AI/ML systems and motivate the need for tailored frameworks, we conducted a qualitative study of issue resolution workflows documented in 100 issue reports and pull requests across four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. Our findings suggest that issue resolution in AI/ML systems involves: recurring AI/ML-related activities that span multiple resolution stages; iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; and coordinated changes across artifacts such as datasets, prompts, and model configurations. We also observed challenges related to reproducibility, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination. Building on these findings, we present a vision for AI/ML issue resolution frameworks and discuss research directions and tooling support needed to realize this vision.

AI.tldr: A qualitative study of 100 issue reports/PRs from TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT reveals that AI/ML issue resolution involves unique characteristics — stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, multi-artifact coordination — not addressed by traditional software maintenance frameworks. The paper presents a vision and research directions for tailored AI/ML issue resolution frameworks.
AI.motivation: Existing issue resolution frameworks are designed for traditional software and fail to account for AI/ML-specific characteristics: stochastic/nondeterministic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and heterogeneous artifacts (datasets, prompts, model configurations) beyond source code. No framework explicitly addresses these, motivating a need for tailored approaches.
AI.method: The authors conducted a qualitative study analyzing 100 issue reports and pull requests from four widely used AI/ML systems: TensorFlow, scikit-learn, MLflow, and AutoGPT. They examined documented issue resolution workflows to identify recurring patterns, activities, and challenges unique to AI/ML systems.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) AI/ML issue resolution involves recurring AI/ML-specific activities spanning multiple resolution stages; (2) it requires iterative experimentation and adaptive verification; (3) coordinated changes are needed across heterogeneous artifacts (datasets, prompts, model configurations). Challenges include reproducibility, nondeterministic behavior, and artifact coordination.
AI.conclusion: The authors present a vision for AI/ML-specific issue resolution frameworks and outline research directions and tooling support needed, emphasizing that future frameworks must accommodate stochastic behavior, experimentation-driven workflows, and multi-artifact coordination inherent to modern AI/ML systems.

title: MIDiff: Tackling Sparsity and Imbalance in Mobile Usage Generation via Multivariate-Imaging Diffusion
summary: Mobile usage traces are critical for tasks such as user behavior prediction and app recommendation, yet their use is constrained by privacy restrictions and costly large-scale data collection. Although generative models perform well on general time series, their application to mobile usage data remains challenging because (i) limited user activity causes severe sparsity, (ii) heterogeneous variable types complicate joint modeling, and (iii) functional differences across apps create pronounced usage imbalance. To address these challenges, we propose Multivariate-Imaging Diffusion (MIDiff), a diffusion-based framework operating in an imaging space defined by Cross-Gramian Angular Sum Field (C-GASF). C-GASF transforms sparse multivariate sequences into correlation images, while MIDiff employs Triple Attention in a U-Net to preserve temporal consistency and variable dependencies. Experiments show that MIDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance across fidelity metrics. In particular, it obtains a Discriminative Accuracy (DA) of 0.1526, compared with 0.3476 for the strongest baseline, ZITS-VAE, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating realistic and diverse mobile usage traces. Our code is available at https://github.com/YilaiLiu-HKU/MIDiff.

AI.tldr: MIDiff is a diffusion-based framework that transforms sparse multivariate mobile usage traces into correlation images via C-GASF, then uses a U-Net with Triple Attention to generate realistic synthetic traces, achieving state-of-the-art fidelity with a Discriminative Accuracy of 0.1526.
AI.motivation: Mobile usage traces are essential for user behavior prediction and app recommendation but are hard to collect at scale due to privacy constraints. Existing generative models struggle with three key challenges: (i) severe sparsity from limited user activity, (ii) heterogeneous variable types complicating joint modeling, and (iii) pronounced usage imbalance due to functional differences across apps.
AI.method: The authors propose MIDiff, a diffusion framework that first maps sparse multivariate mobile usage sequences into an imaging space using Cross-Gramian Angular Sum Field (C-GASF), which encodes temporal correlations across variables. A diffusion model with a U-Net backbone augmented with Triple Attention (jointly capturing temporal consistency and inter-variable dependencies) then learns to generate these correlation images, which are subsequently inverted back to realistic multivariate traces.
AI.result: MIDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance across fidelity metrics. Notably, it attains a Discriminative Accuracy (DA) of 0.1526 versus 0.3476 for the strongest baseline (ZITS-VAE), where lower DA indicates generated samples are harder to distinguish from real data.
AI.conclusion: MIDiff effectively addresses the unique challenges of mobile usage trace generation — sparsity, heterogeneity, and imbalance — by operating in a learned correlation imaging space with a tailored diffusion process, enabling realistic and diverse synthetic data generation for downstream applications.

title: Align AI to Dynamic Human-AI Workflows
summary: Current alignment approaches typically focus on emulating human behavior using static representations of human preferences, failing to capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of real-world human-AI interactions. In this paper, we argue for a shift from static and emulative to interactive and complementary alignment, where preferences emerge through interaction and alignment is defined not by satisfying preferences alone. We first formalize this gap by contrasting existing alignment with a trajectory-level view in which human and model behavior co-evolve over time. Because these interaction dynamics have not been adequately captured within existing ML formulations, we ground this perspective in insights from an interdisciplinary workshop. We draw on lessons from social-science accounts of human-human collaboration and then argue that human-AI systems amplify these dynamics, introducing new asymmetries that make reasoning about uncertainty harder and introduce new coordination challenges. Based on these lessons and new challenges, we conclude by outlining a research agenda for developing AI systems that align with humans in interaction, requiring an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning and the social and decision sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current alignment methods using static human preferences are insufficient for real-world human-AI interaction. It advocates shifting to interactive, complementary alignment where preferences emerge dynamically. Drawing on interdisciplinary social-science insights, the authors identify novel asymmetries and coordination challenges in human-AI systems, concluding with a research agenda integrating ML with social and decision sciences.
AI.motivation: Current alignment approaches rely on static representations of human preferences and merely emulate human behavior. This fails to capture the dynamic, context-dependent, co-evolving nature of real-world human-AI interactions, where preferences are not pre-existing but emerge through interaction.
AI.method: The paper adopts a conceptual and interdisciplinary approach. It first formalizes the gap by contrasting existing static alignment with a "trajectory-level view" where human and model behavior co-evolve. It then grounds this perspective using insights from an interdisciplinary workshop and draws on social-science accounts of human-human collaboration to analyze how human-AI systems amplify interaction dynamics, introduce new asymmetries, and create novel coordination and uncertainty-reasoning challenges.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that human-AI interaction dynamics amplify asymmetries present in human-human collaboration, making reasoning about uncertainty more difficult and introducing new coordination challenges not adequately captured by existing ML formulations.
AI.conclusion: A shift from static, emulative alignment to interactive, complementary alignment is necessary. The authors outline a research agenda for developing AI systems that align dynamically in interaction, requiring an interdisciplinary synthesis of machine learning with social and decision sciences.

title: Heterogeneous Element-Aware Cross-Version Differencing of Scientific Documents via Layout-Aware Alignment and Structure-Aware Reasoning
summary: Cross-version differencing of scientific documents is essential in scholarly publishing and technical documentation, but remains challenging because scientific documents are page-structured artifacts containing heterogeneous elements such as text, tables, formulas, figures, and layout cues. Existing text-sequence-based methods often lose layout and structural information, while image-based methods lack semantic interpretability and are sensitive to rendering variation. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a layout-aware heterogeneous element-aware framework for scientific document differencing. The framework decomposes document versions into semantically typed elements, establishes cross-version correspondence through an alignment-first mechanism that jointly models spatial, content, and structural compatibility, and performs type-aware difference reasoning over aligned element pairs. It supports unified change detection, localization, structure-awareness analysis, and alignment/matching evaluation across text, tables, formulas, and figures. Experiments on real-world scientific PDF data from journal production proofreading workflows show that the proposed framework consistently outperforms element-specific baselines. It achieves detection F1 scores of 0.903, 0.855, 0.862, and 0.845 for text, tables, formulas, and figures, respectively, with further improvements in localization, structure awareness, and matching quality. Ablation and sensitivity analyses confirm the effectiveness of cross-version alignment, type-specific representations, structure-aware reasoning, and compatibility-weight design. These results demonstrate that heterogeneous element-aware differencing provides a robust and interpretable solution for scientific document comparison in realistic editorial production scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a layout-aware, heterogeneous element-aware framework for cross-version scientific document differencing that decomposes documents into semantically typed elements (text, tables, formulas, figures), aligns them across versions, and performs type-aware difference reasoning, achieving F1 scores of 0.845–0.903 across element types on real-world journal proofreading data.
AI.motivation: Scientific document differencing is challenging because these documents are page-structured artifacts with heterogeneous elements (text, tables, formulas, figures, and layout cues). Existing text-sequence-based methods lose layout and structural information, while image-based methods lack semantic interpretability and are sensitive to rendering variations. A unified framework is needed that handles all element types while preserving structural and spatial context.
AI.method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) decomposition of document versions into semantically typed elements; (2) cross-version correspondence via an alignment-first mechanism that jointly models spatial, content, and structural compatibility; (3) type-aware difference reasoning over aligned element pairs. It supports unified change detection, localization, structure-awareness analysis, and alignment/matching evaluation across heterogeneous element types.
AI.result: On real-world scientific PDF data from journal production proofreading workflows, the framework outperforms element-specific baselines, achieving detection F1 scores of 0.903 (text), 0.855 (tables), 0.862 (formulas), and 0.845 (figures), with further improvements in localization, structure awareness, and matching quality. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of cross-version alignment, type-specific representations, structure-aware reasoning, and compatibility-weight design.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous element-aware differencing provides a robust and interpretable solution for scientific document comparison in realistic editorial production scenarios, demonstrating that jointly modeling spatial, content, and structural compatibility across diverse element types yields superior performance over element-specific or modality-limited approaches.

title: teLLMe Why (Ain't Nothing but a Jam): Exploratory Causal Analysis of Urban Driving Data
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on UrbanAI. 6 pages
summary: Traffic agencies now have access to large volumes of video-derived data for studying safety and congestion. Most of these data are observational and collected without interventions, which makes causal questions such as "How would rain change traffic density?" difficult to answer. We present teLLMe, a system for exploratory causal analysis of urban driving datasets. The system starts from a structured event table built from dashcam annotations and combines causal structure learning with the PC algorithm, bootstrap-based stability checks, and query-specific effect estimation using linear regression and DoWhy. Natural-language questions are mapped to structured causal queries through a schema-aware LLM, enabling users to specify treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations. teLLMe returns a "Causal Card" that summarizes effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, and assumptions, followed by a short natural-language explanation. Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events show that the system can surface plausible relationships involving weather, peak hours, and traffic density, while making uncertainty and modeling choices explicit. The system is designed as a tool for hypothesis generation and expert reasoning rather than a source of definitive causal claims.

AI.tldr: teLLMe is an exploratory causal analysis system that combines causal structure learning (PC algorithm), bootstrap stability checks, and DoWhy-based effect estimation with an LLM interface to answer natural-language causal queries about urban driving from dashcam-derived traffic event tables.
AI.motivation: Traffic agencies possess large volumes of observational video-derived data for studying safety and congestion, but these data lack experimental interventions, making it challenging to answer causal questions (e.g., "How would rain change traffic density?"). Existing tools do not adequately bridge natural-language querying with principled causal inference on such datasets.
AI.method: The system constructs a structured event table from dashcam annotations. It employs the PC algorithm for causal structure learning, bootstrap-based stability checks for DAG robustness, and linear regression with DoWhy for query-specific effect estimation. A schema-aware LLM maps natural-language questions to structured causal queries (specifying treatments, outcomes, and subpopulations). Results are presented as a "Causal Card" with effect estimates, adjustment sets, DAG support, assumptions, and a natural-language explanation.
AI.result: Case studies on BDD-derived traffic events demonstrate that teLLMe can surface plausible relationships among weather, peak hours, and traffic density while explicitly communicating uncertainty and modeling assumptions.
AI.conclusion: teLLMe is positioned as a hypothesis-generation and expert reasoning tool rather than a source of definitive causal claims, emphasizing transparency in assumptions and uncertainty.

title: LLM-Driven Approach to Modeling Tool Interoperability in Automotive Domain
summary: Interoperability between heterogeneous modeling tools remains a significant challenge in Model-Driven Engineering (MDE), particularly in the automotive domain where multiple modeling languages, as well as defacto standard proprietary and open-source tools coexist. This paper presents an LLM-driven approach for automated model interoperability by considering two relevant aspects: 1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel 2) merging of metamodels. The proposed methodology is demonstrated through transformations involving Ecore and SysML v2 based metamodels and incorporates structural validation of generated model instances against user-defined target models. Automotive case studies illustrate the feasibility of the approach and show that large language models can significantly reduce manual transformation effort while generating structurally valid target models for cross-tool interoperability.

AI.tldr: An LLM-driven approach automates model interoperability in MDE by mapping model instances to target metamodels and merging metamodels, demonstrated via Ecore/SysML v2 transformations in automotive case studies, reducing manual effort while ensuring structural validity.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous modeling tools in MDE, especially in the automotive domain, lack seamless interoperability due to multiple coexisting modeling languages and proprietary/open-source tools. Manual transformation between metamodels is labor-intensive and error-prone.
AI.method: An LLM-driven methodology addressing two aspects: (1) mapping model instances to a target metamodel, and (2) merging metamodels. Transformations involve Ecore and SysML v2 based metamodels, with structural validation of generated instances against user-defined target models.
AI.result: Automotive case studies demonstrate feasibility, showing that LLMs significantly reduce manual transformation effort and produce structurally valid target models suitable for cross-tool interoperability.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer a promising, automation-driven path toward reducing the manual overhead of model interoperability, generating valid models that bridge heterogeneous MDE tools in the automotive sector.

title: Local Additive Feature Attribution: A Mathematical Taxonomy and Reporting Checklist
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, and 19 tables. Ancillary files include the axiom matrix, reporting checklist, related-survey scoring, and review-corpus summary
summary: Feature-attribution methods are central to explainable artificial intelligence. Their assumptions are expressed in several mathematical languages: cooperative-game values, path integrals, gradient operators, perturbation distributions, and backpropagation rules. This survey proposes a common framework for local additive feature attribution. It organizes Shapley, path-based, gradient/backpropagation, perturbation, and CAM-style methods around five specification choices: value function, reference, path, perturbation distribution, and conservation rule. It then compares these methods through an axiom-by-method matrix and links common failure modes, including baseline sensitivity, off-manifold perturbations, sanity-check failures, adversarial manipulation, and method disagreement, to the assumptions that produce them. Finally, the survey proposes a ten-item reporting checklist for studies that use local additive attributions. The central message is that attribution results are meaningful only relative to the mathematical assumptions under which they are defined, and that those assumptions should be reported.

AI.tldr: A unified framework for local additive feature attribution methods, organizing Shapley, path-based, gradient, perturbation, and CAM-style approaches around five specification choices, linking failure modes to assumptions, and proposing a reporting checklist.
AI.motivation: Feature attribution methods in XAI are expressed in disparate mathematical languages (game theory, path integrals, gradients, perturbations, backpropagation), making it difficult to compare them, understand their assumptions, and diagnose failure modes. The paper aims to unify these diverse approaches under a common framework.
AI.method: The survey proposes a unified framework organizing local additive feature attribution methods around five specification choices: (1) value function, (2) reference/baseline, (3) path, (4) perturbation distribution, and (5) conservation rule. It then constructs an axiom-by-method matrix to systematically compare methods and maps common failure modes (baseline sensitivity, off-manifold perturbations, sanity-check failures, adversarial manipulation, method disagreement) to the specific assumptions that cause them. Finally, it proposes a ten-item reporting checklist.
AI.result: The framework reveals that seemingly disparate methods (Shapley values, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, LRP, CAM, etc.) differ primarily in their choices across the five specification dimensions. The axiom-by-method matrix shows which methods satisfy which axioms. Failure modes are directly attributable to specific assumption violations — e.g., off-manifold perturbations arise from unrealistic value functions, sanity-check failures from architectures breaking conservation rules.
AI.conclusion: Attribution results are meaningful only relative to the mathematical assumptions under which they are defined. Researchers and practitioners should explicitly report these assumptions using the proposed checklist to ensure reproducibility and proper interpretation of feature attribution results.

title: The Steering Budget: Examples beat Knobs
summary:
Generative models are steered with knobs -- prompts, guidance scales, property tags. Turn one as hard as you like and, past a point, it stops moving the property you care about. We find that ceiling is not a shortcoming of the model but a budget, set by the training data before the model is trained: a property's movable range splits in two -- the part a knob can reach, and a second, significant part that only examples -- concrete instances of what you want more of -- can reach. That second part is usually much larger, but not always, and the same budget says so in advance.
  Reaching that second part takes a different move: instead of turning a knob, you show the model examples, composed from what it already learned rather than added to its training. A cheap audit of the training data measures the budget; we give a recipe for building the example set that reaches all of it.
  This buys two things a knob can't. Reach: it moves a property across the whole budget, not just the part a knob reaches. Expressiveness: it steers toward targets you can only specify by example -- including ones you can't put into words. We turn these into a handful of falsifiable claims and verify them in two unrelated domains, image and crystal-structure generation -- marking where a knob is enough, and where only examples will do.

AI.tldr: Generative models have a fundamental budget — set by training data — that limits how far "knobs" (prompts, guidance scales) can steer a property. The remaining range can only be accessed through examples. The paper provides a method to audit training data to measure this budget and construct example sets that unlock full reach and expressiveness, validated on image and crystal-structure generation.
AI.motivation: Knobs in generative models (prompts, guidance scales, property tags) exhibit a ceiling effect: beyond a certain point, turning them further fails to move the target property. The authors investigate whether this ceiling reflects a model limitation or a deeper structural constraint, hypothesizing that the training data imposes a fundamental budget on how far a property can be steered, with a significant portion only reachable through examples rather than knobs.
AI.method: The authors propose that a property's movable range is split into two segments: a "knob-reachable" part and a larger "example-reachable" part, both predetermined by the training data budget. They develop: (1) a cheap audit method on the training data to measure this budget in advance, and (2) a recipe for constructing example sets (composed from what the model already learned, not via additional training) that can reach the full budget. Falsifiable claims are derived and tested across two distinct domains — image generation and crystal-structure generation — to demarcate where knobs suffice and where examples are necessary.
AI.result: The training data indeed imposes a budget that splits each property's movable range. The example-reachable portion is typically much larger than the knob-reachable portion. The proposed audit reliably predicts this split in advance. Example-based steering successfully accesses the full budget, achieving both greater reach (the entire movable range) and greater expressiveness (targets specifiable only by example, including ineffable ones). These findings hold across both image and crystal-structure generation domains.
AI.conclusion: The ceiling encountered when steering generative models with knobs is not a model flaw but a training-data budget. To access the full movable range of a property, one must use examples rather than knobs. The audit method allows practitioners to determine in advance whether a knob will suffice or examples are needed. Example-based steering offers superior reach and expressiveness, enabling control over targets that resist verbal specification.

title: Budgeted Subset Refinement for Execution-Aware LLM Research Ideation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate research ideas that appear novel to expert reviewers, but recent work also shows that such ideas often lack diversity, are difficult for LLMs to evaluate reliably, and may fail to translate into strong executed projects. This paper evaluates a controlled proxy benchmark for a pre-execution scaffolding problem: given a noisy pool of LLM-generated research ideas, how should a system allocate limited refinement effort to construct a stronger, more diverse, more execution-aware portfolio for human researchers under a fixed rubric? We introduce Budgeted Subset Refinement, a family of strategies that refine only a selected subset of candidates rather than refining all candidates uniformly. In a unified shared-candidate-pool evaluation across 10 random seeds and 10 research-ideation environments, raw generation and reranking alone produce no research-strong nonduplicate ideas under the benchmark rubric, while refinement is necessary for strong proxy-rated portfolios. Uniform refinement produces strong individual ideas but is not the best portfolio-level allocation of compute. Random-k refinement is a strong low-cost baseline, while diversity-aware MMR-k refinement gives the best overall proxy tradeoff: the highest research-strong nonduplicate yield, the lowest duplicate rate among successful methods, and the best cost per research-strong nonduplicate idea. A blinded external-judge robustness check on a balanced 72-item sample supports the broad refinement effect across independent model families, while showing that per-item rankings among refined strategies vary by judge. These results suggest that LLM research ideation systems should be evaluated not only as idea generators, but as budgeted support-allocation systems. The claims are scoped to proxy-rated portfolio quality and do not substitute for expert review or execution-grounded validation.

AI.tldr: Evaluates strategies for allocating limited refinement effort across a pool of LLM-generated research ideas, finding that diversity-aware subset refinement (MMR-k) yields the best portfolio-level tradeoff: highest yield of research-strong nonduplicate ideas, lowest duplicate rate, and best cost efficiency compared to uniform or random-k refinement.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated research ideas often lack diversity, are hard to evaluate reliably, and may not translate into strong executed projects. Existing work focuses on generation quality, but the practical problem of how to allocate limited refinement compute across a noisy candidate pool to maximize portfolio-level quality under a fixed rubric remains unaddressed.
AI.method: Introduces Budgeted Subset Refinement, a family of strategies that selectively refine only a subset of candidates rather than all uniformly. Evaluated in a unified shared-candidate-pool benchmark across 10 random seeds and 10 research-ideation environments, comparing raw generation, reranking, uniform refinement, random-k refinement, and diversity-aware MMR-k refinement. Includes a blinded external-judge robustness check on a balanced 72-item sample.
AI.result: Raw generation and reranking alone produce no research-strong nonduplicate ideas. Uniform refinement produces strong individual ideas but suboptimal portfolio allocation. Random-k refinement is a strong low-cost baseline. MMR-k gives the best overall proxy tradeoff: highest research-strong nonduplicate yield, lowest duplicate rate, and best cost per research-strong nonduplicate idea. External-judge robustness check supports the broad refinement effect across model families, though per-item rankings among refined strategies vary by judge.
AI.conclusion: LLM research ideation systems should be evaluated not only as idea generators but as budgeted support-allocation systems. Claims are scoped to proxy-rated portfolio quality and do not substitute for expert review or execution-grounded validation.

title: Beyond Success Rate: Cost-Aware Evaluation of Offensive and Defensive Security Agents
summary: Security-agent evaluations commonly measure peak offensive capability under generous inference budgets, emphasizing vulnerability discovery, exploit development, penetration testing, and CTF completion. Such measurements are useful but incomplete: in operational security, every reasoning step, tool call, telemetry query, and enrichment request consumes budget. We evaluate language-model security agents through this cost-success lens on offensive Cybench challenges and defensive Splunk BOTS v1 investigation challenges. Instead of reporting only best-case success, we compare models at fixed cost levels and decompose performance by inference spend and tool spend. Our results show distinct scalingregimes for red- and blue-team tasks. Offensive CTF performance improves with additional test-time compute, and scaled open-weight models can approach frontier proprietary systems while remaining cost-competitive. Defensive SOC investigation does not scale in the same way: success depends more heavily on disciplined tool use, telemetry navigation, and selective enrichment than on raw reasoning budget alone. We argue that security-agent benchmarks should measure economic efficiency and operational fit alongside task success. Cost-aware, SOC-native evaluations provide a clearer picture of which models are practically useful today and where defensive agents still need to improve. We present an interactive website with our results https://evals.frontier.security.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that security-agent evaluations should measure cost-efficiency alongside task success. Through experiments on offensive Cybench CTF challenges and defensive Splunk BOTS v1 investigations, the authors show that offensive performance scales with test-time compute (open-weight models can approach proprietary systems cost-competitively), while defensive SOC investigations depend more on disciplined tool use and telemetry navigation than raw reasoning budget. They advocate for cost-aware, SOC-native benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional security-agent evaluations focus on peak offensive capability under generous inference budgets, ignoring the operational reality that every reasoning step, tool call, and telemetry query incurs cost. This incomplete picture fails to reveal which models are practically deployable under real-world budget constraints, particularly for defensive SOC workflows.
AI.method: The authors evaluate language-model security agents through a cost-success lens, comparing models at fixed cost levels rather than only reporting best-case success. They decompose performance into inference spend and tool spend across two domains: offensive Cybench challenges and defensive Splunk BOTS v1 investigation challenges, examining scaling behavior for both red-team and blue-team tasks.
AI.result: Offensive CTF performance improves with additional test-time compute; scaled open-weight models approach frontier proprietary systems while remaining cost-competitive. Defensive SOC investigation does not scale similarly — success depends more on disciplined tool use, telemetry navigation, and selective enrichment than on raw reasoning budget alone.
AI.conclusion: Security-agent benchmarks should incorporate economic efficiency and operational fit alongside task success. Cost-aware, SOC-native evaluations provide a clearer picture of practical utility and reveal where defensive agents still need improvement. Results are publicly available on an interactive website.

title: Large Language Models for Code Generation from Multilingual Prompts: A Curated Benchmark and a Study on Code Quality
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform differently on identical programming tasks when prompted in different natural languages, a phenomenon known as language bias. While this behavior has been widely studied for general text generation, its impact on code generation quality and programming conventions remains largely unexplored. We investigate how the language used to describe programming tasks affects the source code generated by GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, and Claude. Our study comprises 460 coding tasks spanning Python (230) and Java (230). We translate and manually curate the original English prompts into Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian while preserving their technical meaning. We evaluate the generated code using multiple dimensions, including functional correctness through test pass rates, structural quality using established code metrics, issues detected by static analysis tools, and lexical characteristics such as the language used in identifiers and comments. Our results show that (i) English prompts do not consistently produce the best functional correctness or code quality, (ii) the impact of prompt language depends on both the programming language and the LLM, and (iii) generated code frequently mixes English with the prompt language in comments and string literals. These findings provide the first curated multilingual benchmark for studying language bias in code generation and offer insights for developing more robust multilingual code generation systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the natural language of prompts (English, Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, Italian) affects code generation quality across GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, and Claude for Python and Java tasks. Key findings: English does not consistently yield the best results; prompt language impact varies by both programming language and LLM; and generated code often mixes English with prompt language in comments/strings.
AI.motivation: While language bias in LLMs has been widely studied for general text generation, its specific impact on code generation quality and adherence to programming conventions remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by systematically examining how prompt language influences multiple dimensions of generated code.
AI.method: The study uses 460 coding tasks (230 Python, 230 Java) with original English prompts manually translated into Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian while preserving technical meaning. Three LLMs are evaluated (GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek, Claude). Generated code is assessed across multiple dimensions: functional correctness (test pass rates), structural quality (established code metrics), static analysis issues, and lexical characteristics (identifier/comment language).
AI.result: Three main findings: (i) English prompts do not consistently produce the best functional correctness or code quality across all scenarios; (ii) the effect of prompt language is contingent on both the target programming language and the specific LLM used; (iii) generated code frequently exhibits language mixing, where comments and string literals blend English with the prompt language.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first curated multilingual benchmark for studying language bias in code generation and offers insights to guide the development of more robust, language-agnostic code generation systems.

title: Lyapunov Guidance: A Unified Framework for Stabilizing Generative Flows
summary: Flow matching has emerged as an effective framework for learning complex data distributions, but adapting pretrained flow models to new tasks often requires computationally expensive retraining. Post-training guidance provides a more efficient alternative, but existing methods are largely heuristic and offer no explicit stability guarantees. We address this limitation by proposing LyaGuide, a unified Lyapunov-guided framework that formulates flow guidance as a Lyapunov control problem. Our main theoretical result establishes an equivalence between guided flow matching and Lyapunov control, thereby unifying common guidance strategies, such as classifier guidance, reward guidance, and energy-based guidance, within a single control-theoretic framework. To enforce the Lyapunov condition, we introduce a pseudo-projection operator with a closed-form expression that endows learned or heuristic guidance terms with explicit stability guarantees. LyaGuide supports two practical settings: a model-driven setting, where the target guidance distribution is specified through a known Lyapunov function, and a data-driven setting, where the guidance is adapted from task-specific downstream data. LyaGuide is compatible with existing guidance methods, introduces minimal additional computational overhead, and is straightforward to integrate in practice. Extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks, image inverse problems, reinforcement learning planning, and energy-based modeling demonstrate consistent improvements in sample quality, guidance fidelity, and robustness, while maintaining computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: LyaGuide reformulates flow matching guidance as a Lyapunov control problem, establishing a theoretical equivalence that unifies existing guidance methods and provides explicit stability guarantees via a closed-form pseudo-projection operator, with both model-driven and data-driven variants.
AI.motivation: Adapting pretrained flow models to new tasks is computationally expensive if retraining is required. While post-training guidance offers a cheaper alternative, existing guidance methods (classifier, reward, energy-based) are heuristic and lack explicit stability guarantees, potentially leading to unreliable sample quality.
AI.method: The authors propose LyaGuide, which casts flow guidance as a Lyapunov control problem. The key theoretical result establishes equivalence between guided flow matching and Lyapunov control, unifying common guidance strategies under one framework. A pseudo-projection operator with a closed-form expression is introduced to enforce the Lyapunov stability condition on learned or heuristic guidance terms. The framework supports two settings: model-driven (guidance via a known Lyapunov function) and data-driven (guidance adapted from downstream data).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks, image inverse problems, reinforcement learning planning, and energy-based modeling show consistent improvements in sample quality, guidance fidelity, and robustness, with minimal additional computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: LyaGuide provides a principled, control-theoretic foundation for flow matching guidance, unifying existing heuristic methods while guaranteeing stability. It is computationally efficient, easy to integrate, and broadly applicable across diverse generative modeling tasks.

title: Semantic Register Compression in Multi-Agent LLM Cascades
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems commonly decompose complex tasks into specialized roles. However, this modularity introduces a representational risk: when intermediate agents transform text across linguistic registers, they can systematically compress the semantic distinctions needed for accurate downstream decisions. We term this phenomenon semantic register compression and characterize it as an observable failure mode in multi-agent cascades. Using a three-agent pipeline (Collector-Evaluator-Decider), we quantify compression via inter-label separation in sentence-transformer embedding space. Across political fact-checking (LIAR), sentiment analysis (SST-5), and medical triage (Triagegeist), critical evaluation consistently reduces label separability by 41.7% at the Evaluator stage, while identity passthrough preserves it nearly fully. Five architectural variants causally isolate oriented semantic transformation as the primary driver. A credibility-seeking variant produces minimal geometric compression yet shifts outputs toward mostly-true, demonstrating that transformation valence controls the direction of distributional collapse independently of compression magnitude. Compression generalizes across the three domains with varying intensity: 41.7% in fact-checking, 27.2% in sentiment, and 20.0% in triage. Prompt-level regression explains 78% of the variance, with operational constraints associated with lower compression. These results demonstrate that semantic register compression is a measurable and generalizable phenomenon in multi-agent LLM systems, with implications for safety evaluation in high-stakes domains.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems exhibit "semantic register compression" — a failure mode where intermediate agents systematically reduce semantic separability of labels, with a 41.7% drop observed across fact-checking, sentiment analysis, and medical triage tasks. Oriented semantic transformation, not mere information loss, drives this distributional collapse.
AI.motivation: Modular multi-agent LLM pipelines decompose tasks by role, but the representational risk introduced when intermediate agents transform text across linguistic registers is underexplored. The authors aim to identify and quantify a systematic failure mode — termed semantic register compression — that degrades downstream decision fidelity.
AI.method: A three-agent pipeline (Collector → Evaluator → Decider) is tested across three domains: LIAR (political fact-checking), SST-5 (sentiment analysis), and Triagegeist (medical triage). Compression is quantified via inter-label separation in sentence-transformer embedding space. Five architectural variants are used for causal isolation, including identity passthrough and a credibility-seeking variant. Prompt-level regression is employed to explain variance in compression magnitude.
AI.result: Critical evaluation at the Evaluator stage reduces label separability by 41.7% (fact-checking), 27.2% (sentiment), and 20.0% (triage). Identity passthrough nearly fully preserves separability. Oriented semantic transformation is causally isolated as the primary driver. The credibility-seeking variant produces minimal geometric compression but shifts outputs toward "mostly-true," showing transformation valence controls distributional collapse direction independently of compression magnitude. Prompt-level regression explains 78% of the variance; operational constraints correlate with lower compression.
AI.conclusion: Semantic register compression is a measurable, generalizable phenomenon in multi-agent LLM systems with significant implications for safety evaluation in high-stakes domains like medical triage and fact-checking. The findings highlight that compression is driven by oriented semantic transformation rather than simple information loss.

title: Breaking Refusal in the First Half: A Mechanistic Study of the Prefill Jailbreak
comment: 31 pages, 3 figures. Code and derived artifacts: https://github.com/collapseindex/breaking-refusal
summary: Aligned language models refuse harmful requests, but a one-line prefill ("Sure, here is") strips the refusal. We ask where and how it fails. The harm representation stays intact: on the prompts the attack flips to compliance, a linear probe reads harm as high as on the refused ones (0.91-0.98), while behavioral refusal drops to chance. This holds across four models and three families (1.5-3.8B, and at 14B). Refusal is therefore a shallow, response-site computation. We localize it to an early window: a dose-matched position control shows the first half of the response suffices to break refusal, while the second half is nearly inert. Three causal probes converge on that window. Restoring the harm direction there partially re-engages refusal. Injecting the model's own refuse-state reverses the jailbreak (74%, held-out). And knocking out the early response's attention to the prefill, but not an equal attention mass elsewhere, selectively collapses the harmful continuation. A base-model control identifies the mechanism: the same knockout collapses the continuation prefill-specifically even in a non-safety-tuned base model (64% to 25% harmful content vs a matched control's 64%, replicated at 7B). So the prefill's grip is generic autoregressive conditioning, not safety-specific suppression, and "refusal restoration" is a model-dependent fallback. The dominant mechanism is passive. A small safety-specific attractor remains on top (logit-trace concentration 0.24 vs 0.03), whose active-vs-passive character we size but do not fully separate. No single direction or component is a clean handle either: the decision is decodable but distributed, and refusal tracks harm rather than scary surface. The consequence is structural: a monitor reading the untouched prompt-side representation is immune by construction, but only to response-site attacks. The mechanism is diffuse; the failure surface is local.

AI.tldr: Aligned language models' refusal to answer harmful requests can be bypassed by a simple prefill ("Sure, here is"). The paper shows that refusal is a shallow, response-site computation localized to the first half of the response, driven primarily by generic autoregressive conditioning rather than safety-specific mechanisms. The harm representation remains intact on the prompt side, making prompt-side monitors immune to such attacks by construction.
AI.motivation: To understand where and how the "prefill attack" (adding "Sure, here is") breaks refusal in aligned language models, and to characterize whether refusal is a deep, safety-specific mechanism or a shallow, generic autoregressive phenomenon.
AI.method: The authors use linear probes to measure harm representations across prompts, causal interventions (knockouts, direction restoration, state injection) to localize refusal to the early response window, dose-matched position controls to test which response portions matter, and base-model comparisons to disentangle safety-specific vs. generic autoregressive effects. Experiments span four models across three families (1.5B–14B parameters).
AI.result: Harm representations on prompts remain high (0.91–0.98 probe accuracy) even when behavioral refusal drops to chance. Refusal is localized to the first half of the response; the second half is nearly inert. Knocking out early-response attention to the prefill collapses harmful continuations. This effect replicates in non-safety-tuned base models (64% to 25% harmful content), indicating the prefill's grip is generic autoregressive conditioning. A small safety-specific attractor exists (logit-trace concentration 0.24 vs 0.03) but is modest. Refusal is decodable but distributed — no single direction is a clean handle.
AI.conclusion: Refusal is structurally shallow: a response-site computation driven primarily by passive, generic autoregressive conditioning, with only a modest safety-specific component layered on top. Prompt-side harm representations are untouched, so prompt-side monitors are immune by construction to response-site attacks. The mechanism is diffuse; the failure surface is local.

title: AI Prototyper: A Figma Plugin for Decomposition-Based GUI Prototyping with LLMs
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) prototyping remains a time-consuming activity that demands both design expertise and considerable manual effort. As GUI prototypes are non-code artifacts that evolve alongside requirements throughout the development cycle, automating their generation is directly relevant to software maintenance and evolution. We present AI Prototyper, an open-source Figma plugin that automates GUI prototyping through a decomposition and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. Given a natural-language description of a desired screen, such as a login page or a product detail card, the plugin decomposes the request into discrete GUI features, retrieves matching components from a custom 32-primitive library, and renders each component as a fully editable Figma layer with auto-layout. The pipeline uses Gemini 2.5 Flash as its LLM back-end and a Node.js/Express service. Unlike existing decomposition-based tools, AI Prototyper introduces a human-in-the-loop editing step that lets users review, modify, or extend the generated feature list before rendering, uses a different technology stack and LLM family, and supports multilingual input, producing correctly labelled interfaces in Thai, English, and Mandarin Chinese. In a preliminary evaluation, participants using AI Prototyper completed more prototypes in a fixed time window than those working manually, and expert practitioners rated the AI-generated prototypes higher across nine quality dimensions. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/pRoFAH7MQaE. The source code and component library are available at https://github.com/tongsalangsingha/AI-prototyper-tool

AI.tldr: AI Prototyper is an open-source Figma plugin that automates GUI prototyping by decomposing natural-language descriptions into discrete features, retrieving matching components from a custom primitive library via RAG, and rendering fully editable Figma layers — with a human-in-the-loop editing step and multilingual support.
AI.motivation: GUI prototyping is time-consuming, requiring both design expertise and manual effort. Since prototypes are non-code artifacts that co-evolve with requirements, automating their generation is relevant to software maintenance and evolution.
AI.method: A decomposition and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline: natural-language screen descriptions are decomposed into discrete GUI features; matching components are retrieved from a custom 32-primitive library; components are rendered as editable Figma layers with auto-layout. Uses Gemini 2.5 Flash as the LLM backend with a Node.js/Express service. Includes a human-in-the-loop editing step for reviewing/modifying feature lists before rendering. Supports Thai, English, and Mandarin Chinese.
AI.result: In preliminary evaluation, participants using AI Prototyper completed more prototypes in a fixed time window than those working manually. Expert practitioners rated AI-generated prototypes higher across nine quality dimensions.
AI.conclusion: AI Prototyper demonstrates that a decomposition-plus-RAG approach with human-in-the-loop editing can effectively accelerate GUI prototyping, produce high-quality outputs across multiple languages, and outperform manual prototyping in both speed and expert-assessed quality.

title: NeuroGRIP: Retrieval-Augmented Graph Refinement for Knowledge-Grounded EEG Seizure Diagnosis
summary: Seizure diagnosis from EEG signals is a critical yet persistently challenging task, due to the complicated neural dynamics and the spurious connections in inter-channel modeling. While spatial-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs) have advanced EEG brain network representation learning, the resulting graph structures suffer from low clinical plausibility and limited interpretability due to their purely data-driven nature. To this end, we introduce NeuroGRIP, a retrieval-augmented graph refinement framework that incorporates external medical knowledge to calibrate noisy EEG graphs. We first construct a large-scale, domain-specific knowledge base derived from authoritative clinical guidelines. Leveraging large language models, we extract structured biomedical entities and relations to form a textual knowledge graph (KG), which serves as external knowledge source of clinical priors. Our framework performs alignment-aware query construction by projecting STGNN-generated EEG node embeddings into the semantic space of KG. Semantic queries are then executed via FAISS-based similarity search over knowledge triplets to retrieve relation evidence. Each predicted edge is assigned a confidence score based on retrieved similarity, relation type, and source reliability, enabling us to prune medically implausible edges from the originally predicted graph. Extensive experiments on TUSZ and CHB-MIT demonstrate that NeuroGRIP not only improves seizure detection accuracy but also enhances interpretability by grounding each prediction in clinically validated knowledge. This work provides the first unified framework that tightly couples brain dynamics with external medical expertise via retrieval-augmented reasoning, paving the way for knowledge-enhanced, explainable clinical diagnosis. The code is available at: https://github.com/LincanLi-X/NeuroGRIP.

AI.tldr: NeuroGRIP is a retrieval-augmented graph refinement framework that calibrates noisy EEG brain networks by incorporating external clinical knowledge from a textual knowledge graph, pruning medically implausible edges to improve both seizure detection accuracy and interpretability.
AI.motivation: STGNN-based EEG brain network models produce graph structures with low clinical plausibility and limited interpretability due to purely data-driven learning that generates spurious inter-channel connections. There is a need to ground these graphs in validated medical knowledge.
AI.method: NeuroGRIP constructs a domain-specific textual knowledge graph from clinical guidelines using LLMs for entity/relation extraction. It projects STGNN-generated EEG node embeddings into the KG's semantic space for alignment-aware querying. FAISS-based similarity search retrieves relation evidence over knowledge triplets, and each predicted edge is assigned a confidence score based on similarity, relation type, and source reliability, enabling pruning of implausible edges.
AI.result: Experiments on TUSZ and CHB-MIT benchmarks show improved seizure detection accuracy over baselines, with enhanced interpretability through clinically grounded predictions.
AI.conclusion: NeuroGRIP is the first unified framework coupling brain dynamics with external medical expertise via retrieval-augmented reasoning, advancing knowledge-enhanced and explainable clinical EEG diagnosis.

title: Cross-Dataset Generalization in Urdu Fake News Detection: An Empirical Study with XLM-RoBERTa and a Length Confound Analysis
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables, submitted to arXiv
summary: Urdu fake news detection remains under-resourced despite Urdu being spoken by over 231 million people worldwide. While prior work has demonstrated strong in-domain performance on individual Urdu datasets, cross-dataset generalisation has received little systematic attention. This paper presents the first cross-dataset generalisation study for Urdu fake news detection, using two publicly available balanced datasets: the Ax-to-Grind Urdu corpus (10,083 articles, 15 domains) and the Notri-Fact Urdu dataset (13,388 articles). We fine-tune xlm-roberta-base under four experimental conditions, in-domain on each dataset and two zero-shot cross-domain transfer directions, comparing against TF-IDF baselines using Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines. Our experiments reveal a striking asymmetry: Notri-Fact to Ax-to-Grind transfer achieves a macro F1 of 0.771, while the reverse collapses to F1 of 0.005, with the model predicting fake for 99.7% of test articles. We demonstrate that this collapse stems from a systematic length confound in Ax-to-Grind, where fake articles average 117 words versus 35 for real articles, a 3.4x asymmetry inducing shortcut learning. A length ablation capping articles at 50 words yields only a 0.0067 F1 drop, confirming the confound inflates but does not solely drive in-domain performance. We provide a reusable diagnostic methodology that combines bidirectional transfer analysis and prediction-collapse inspection to identify confound-driven behavior in multilingual fake news detection settings.

AI.tldr: First cross-dataset generalization study for Urdu fake news detection reveals severe brittleness: a 3.4× length confound in one dataset causes near-total prediction collapse (F1=0.005) in zero-shot transfer, despite strong in-domain performance. Authors provide diagnostic methodology combining bidirectional transfer and prediction-collapse analysis.
AI.motivation: Urdu NLP is under-resourced despite 231M+ speakers. Prior fake news detection work reports strong in-domain results but cross-dataset generalization remains unexamined. The authors aim to systematically investigate whether models learn robust features or dataset-specific shortcuts when transferred across Urdu fake news corpora.
AI.method: Fine-tune xlm-roberta-base under four conditions: in-domain on Ax-to-Grind, in-domain on Notri-Fact, and two zero-shot cross-domain transfer directions. Compare against TF-IDF + Logistic Regression/SVM baselines. Perform length ablation (capping articles at 50 words) to isolate confound effects. Employ bidirectional transfer analysis and prediction-collapse inspection as diagnostic tools.
AI.result: Striking asymmetry in cross-dataset transfer: Notri-Fact → Ax-to-Grind achieves macro F1=0.771, while Ax-to-Grind → Notri-Fact collapses to F1=0.005 (99.7% predicted fake). Root cause: Ax-to-Grind has a 3.4× length confound (fake articles avg. 117 words vs. real 35 words). Length ablation shows only 0.0067 F1 drop, confirming the confound inflates but does not solely explain in-domain performance.
AI.conclusion: Strong in-domain results can mask severe shortcut learning. The proposed diagnostic methodology — bidirectional transfer combined with prediction-collapse inspection — effectively identifies confound-driven behavior and should be adopted in multilingual fake news detection research to ensure genuine generalization.

title: Towards a Unified Multidimensional Explainability Metric: Evaluating Trustworthiness in AI Models
summary: In this paper, we present a comprehensive framework for assessing the explainability of various XAI methods, such as LIME and SHAP, across multiple datasets and machine learning models, with the ultimate goal of creating a unified multidimensional explainability score.
