AI.tldr: PIE-PINN proposes a probabilistic inverse elasticity framework that uses Laplace distributions and hierarchical half-Cauchy priors within a B-spline-guided PINN to robustly estimate heterogeneous Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio from noisy, low-resolution displacement data, with adaptive loss weighting via alternating maximum-likelihood training.
AI.motivation: Estimating spatially heterogeneous elastic properties from low-resolution, noisy displacement measurements is a severely ill-posed inverse problem. Existing methods rely on high-fidelity data and manually tuned loss weights, making them brittle to noise and resolution degradation. There is a need for a robust, adaptive framework that can handle these practical challenges.
AI.method: PIE-PINN integrates three key components: (1) Laplace likelihoods for displacement observation, strain-discrepancy, and equilibrium residuals in a unified probabilistic model; (2) a B-spline-guided displacement network that provides a smooth global representation with neural network corrections for local variations; (3) a hierarchical half-Cauchy prior on displacement residual scales that adaptively downweights severe fitting errors. Training uses alternating maximum-likelihood: updating the mean displacement via weighted residual minimization, then updating scale parameters to adapt loss weights.
AI.result: Systematic case studies across varying noise levels and observation resolutions demonstrate that PIE-PINN achieves robust recovery of both Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, significantly outperforming conventional PINN-based inverse methods under low-resolution and high-noise conditions.
AI.conclusion: The probabilistic formulation with adaptive scale modeling and B-spline guidance provides a principled and effective approach for robust inverse elasticity under realistic, degraded measurement conditions.

title: Seeing the End at Step Zero: Accelerating Diffusion MLLMs via MLP Sparsity-Aware Truncation
summary: Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (DMLLMs) are highly effective for multimodal reasoning, yet their inference efficiency is significantly hindered by fixed-length generation constraints. Since the actual output length is unknown, output sequences are padded to a predefined maximum length, resulting in substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. In this work, we discover that DMLLMs implicitly reveal their valid semantic boundary at the very first denoising step through a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity. Leveraging this observation, we propose Seer, a training-free framework that detects this boundary using a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-based criterion and performs one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix for all subsequent computations. To preserve these theoretical gains during batched serving, Seer incorporates a hybrid execution strategy that maximizes throughput while seamlessly accommodating dynamic sequence lengths. Experimental results demonstrate that Seer effectively eliminates padding waste, accelerating throughput by up to $\sim$31$\times$. Across 9 benchmarks, Seer robustly maintains overall performance and even improves accuracy on complex visual tasks by mitigating noise leakage (e.g., DocVQA score increases from 63.52 to 63.66), offering a highly efficient, plug-and-play solution for DMLLM acceleration.

AI.tldr: DMLLMs waste computation on padded [EOS] tokens. The authors discover that a shift in MLP activation sparsity at the first denoising step reveals the true semantic boundary. They propose Seer, a training-free framework using SNR-based detection for one-shot truncation, achieving up to ~31× throughput acceleration without performance loss.
AI.motivation: Diffusion Multimodal LLMs are constrained by fixed-length generation, where output sequences are padded to a predefined maximum length, causing substantial redundant computation over unnecessary [EOS] tokens. The actual output length is unknown a priori, motivating a method to dynamically detect the true semantic boundary early in the denoising process.
AI.method: Seer is a training-free framework with three key components: (1) Discovery that DMLLMs exhibit a distinct shift in MLP activation sparsity at the first denoising step, signaling the valid semantic boundary. (2) An SNR-based criterion that automatically detects this boundary for one-shot truncation of the redundant suffix in all subsequent denoising steps. (3) A hybrid execution strategy for batched serving that maximizes throughput while accommodating dynamic sequence lengths produced by the truncation.
AI.result: Seer achieves up to ~31× throughput acceleration by eliminating padding waste. Across 9 benchmarks, it robustly maintains overall performance and even slightly improves accuracy on complex visual tasks (e.g., DocVQA score: 63.52 → 63.66), attributed to mitigation of noise leakage from padding tokens.
AI.conclusion: Seer offers a highly efficient, plug-and-play, training-free solution for accelerating DMLLM inference. It demonstrates that early denoising-step activation sparsity reliably reveals semantic boundaries, enabling substantial speedups without sacrificing—and occasionally improving—downstream task performance.

title: Gate-Zero Growth: A Geometric Framework for Function-Preserving Continual Learning
summary: We introduce \emph{gate-zero growth}, a function-preserving (FP) operator for continual learning that adds new residual blocks through a zero-initialised gate. Under a transversality condition, gate-zero growth induces \emph{rank separation} in the functional Jacobian: old directions are unchanged, new-weight directions are exactly flat at the growth point, and new gate directions are the only first-order source of new functional variation. As gates open during continual learning, function drift is $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|^2)$ and Jacobian leakage $O(\|\boldsymbolα\|_\infty)$, giving a controlled departure from the FP locus. On a $300\mathrm{M}\to857\mathrm{M}$ Transformer adapted from WikiText-103 to BookCorpus, gate-zero growth reaches near-zero old-domain forgetting ($Δ_A < 0.1$) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) operating points, while a non-FP control ($G_{\text{stack}}$) suffers an order-of-magnitude larger forgetting under the same recipe. The same geometric analysis covers LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapter constructions, establishing gate-zero growth as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in CL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "gate-zero growth," a function-preserving operator for continual learning that adds residual blocks via zero-initialized gates. This induces rank separation in the functional Jacobian, yielding controlled function drift of O(||α||²) and Jacobian leakage of O(||α||∞) as gates open. On a 300M→857M Transformer, it achieves near-zero forgetting (<0.1), outperforming non-FP baselines by an order of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Continual learning requires safely expanding network capacity without disrupting previously learned functions. Existing function-preserving (FP) operators exist but lack rigorous geometric understanding of how new parameters affect the functional landscape. The authors seek a principled, analyzable expansion operator that provides controlled departure from the FP locus.
AI.method: The authors propose "gate-zero growth": adding new residual blocks where the block output is multiplied by a zero-initialized gate vector α. Under a transversality condition, they analyze the functional Jacobian spectrum, proving that at the growth point, old directions are preserved, new-weight directions are exactly flat (zero functional gradient), and new gate directions are the sole first-order source of functional variation. This "rank separation" property is formalized mathematically, and the framework is shown to encompass LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters as instances of a shared local geometry.
AI.result: On a Transformer scaled from 300M to 857M parameters (WikiText-103 → BookCorpus), gate-zero growth achieves near-zero old-domain forgetting (ΔA < 0.1) under both exact-preservation (Isolation) and joint-frontier (Freeze-Nothing) regimes. A non-FP control (G_stack) suffers an order-of-magnitude greater forgetting. The geometric analysis also reveals that LoRA, ReZero, and zero-init adapters share the same local geometry governing safe capacity activation.
AI.conclusion: Gate-zero growth is identified as the canonical instance of a shared local geometry that governs safe capacity activation in continual learning. Its rank-separation property provides mathematically controlled function drift and Jacobian leakage, making it a theoretically grounded and empirically effective FP operator for scaling networks during continual learning.

title: CoTu at EXACT 2026: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Transparent Educational QA
comment: The 2nd International XAI Challenge for Transparent Educational Question-Answering @ IEEE IJCNN 2026 Competition
summary: Transparent educational question answering asks for answers that are not only correct but explainable, and doing so with small models rules out the reasoning power of the largest proprietary systems. The EXACT 2026 competition poses this problem concretely: open-weight language models of at most 8B parameters, self-hosted, with a natural-language explanation for every answer. It pairs two tasks: logical reasoning over university regulations, and multi-step physics problem solving. We describe the system that team \cotu{} developed to address both, a neuro-symbolic Program-of-Thought pipeline in which a 4B backbone writes a program rather than stating an answer directly: for regulation queries it emits a Z3 encoding whose entailment verdict grounds the deduction, and for physics it emits numerical Python, both wrapped in a shared self-correction loop and a unified explained-JSON output. Answer-type routing, distillation-based task fine-tuning, and a latency-aware serving stack -- SGLang with speculative decoding -- keep the system within the 60-second per-query limit. The system achieved a \textbf{perfect score} on the physics task in both automated selection rounds and obtained the \textbf{highest final-round technical score} of any team -- $13.44/15$, combining automated answer evaluation with expert-judged reasoning depth -- with the equally weighted presentation score included, \cotu{} placed 3rd overall. Grounding answers in a symbolic solver yields correct, verifiable deductions at the 4B scale, and the residual difficulty lies in premise selection rather than the deduction itself.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic Program-of-Thought pipeline using a 4B-parameter model that writes Z3 encodings for regulation reasoning and Python for physics, wrapped in self-correction loops, achieved a perfect physics score and the highest final-round technical score (13.44/15) in the EXACT 2026 competition, demonstrating that symbolic solvers enable verifiable reasoning at small scale.
AI.motivation: Transparent educational QA demands correct, explainable answers, but small open-weight models (≤8B parameters) lack the raw reasoning power of large proprietary systems. The EXACT 2026 competition formalizes this challenge, requiring self-hosted models to produce natural-language explanations for logical reasoning over university regulations and multi-step physics problem solving.
AI.method: The system employs a neuro-symbolic Program-of-Thought pipeline where a 4B backbone model generates executable programs instead of direct answers: Z3 theorem-prover encodings for regulation entailment queries and numerical Python for physics problems. This is augmented by answer-type routing, distillation-based task fine-tuning, a shared self-correction loop, unified explained-JSON output, and a latency-aware serving stack using SGLang with speculative decoding to meet the 60-second per-query limit.
AI.result: The system achieved a perfect score on the physics task across both automated selection rounds and the highest final-round technical score of any team (13.44/15), combining automated answer evaluation with expert-judged reasoning depth. With the equally weighted presentation score included, the team placed 3rd overall.
AI.conclusion: Grounding answers in symbolic solvers yields correct, verifiable deductions at the 4B scale. The residual difficulty lies in premise selection rather than the deduction itself, suggesting that the neuro-symbolic approach effectively offloads formal reasoning to specialized engines while the language model focuses on interpreting and structuring the problem.

title: Sharp Stability Threshold and Certification for Designing Stable Residual Architectures
summary: We propose \emph{the sublinear-growth principle} for deep residual architectures -- a sharp stability threshold on the input-magnitude exponent of every residual block's velocity field: $$\|v(x, t)\| \leq c\,\|x\|^q + b, \qquad q \in [0, 1].$$ The threshold $q = 1$ is established via two independent arguments. Classical ODE theory gives a global forward flow on $[0, T]$ at $q \le 1$ and exhibits divergent velocity fields at any $q > 1$. The optimal-control analysis, via the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, sharpens this to a selection statement: the training optimum is bang-bang on the boundary of the admissible class, so the optimum at $q > 1$ blows up while the optimum at $q \le 1$ is safe by construction. The exponent criterion $q \le 1$ is thereby a necessary and sufficient condition for stable training. It clarifies architectural placements that ensure the stability of training and inference, explaining, for instance, the stabilizing role of layer normalization. The sublinear-growth velocity fields form \emph{the right function space} on which forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition are all well-controlled. An arithmetic of input-magnitude exponents under the five operations that build residual blocks enables efficient certification of $q_k \le 1$ at the level of architectural primitives, in place of ad hoc trial and error in the search for stable neural architectural designs. A parameter-free modification reduces the supercritical Mamba block from $q = 5$ to $q = 1$ without layer normalization, demonstrating this point. Experiments on Mamba and PatchTST confirm that the $q \le 1$ variants train stably: the criterion is the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of a normalization layer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "sublinear-growth principle" for deep residual architectures, establishing that the velocity field's input-magnitude exponent q must satisfy q ≤ 1 for stable training. This threshold is proven via classical ODE theory (global forward flow) and optimal-control analysis (bang-bang optimality). The criterion provides a principled framework for certifying architectural stability, explaining why layer normalization works, and enabling parameter-free stabilization of architectures like Mamba.
AI.motivation: Training instability in deep residual networks is poorly understood theoretically. Current practice relies on ad hoc trial-and-error with normalization layers, without a crisp mathematical criterion for when and why architectures are stable. The authors seek to establish a rigorous, principled stability condition grounded in dynamical systems theory that can guide architectural design and eliminate guesswork.
AI.method: The authors propose that residual blocks be viewed as velocity fields v(x,t) in a continuous-depth ODE. They analyze the input-magnitude growth exponent q in ‖v(x,t)‖ ≤ c‖x‖^q + b through two complementary frameworks: (1) classical ODE theory — showing global forward flow exists iff q ≤ 1, with blow-up at q > 1; (2) optimal-control/Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman analysis — proving the training optimum is "bang-bang" on the admissible-class boundary, so q > 1 optimal solutions blow up while q ≤ 1 is inherently safe. They develop an arithmetic of exponent propagation under five architectural operations (addition, composition, etc.) for composable certification. A parameter-free modification of Mamba (q=5 → q=1) and experiments on Mamba and PatchTST validate the theory.
AI.result: The exponent criterion q ≤ 1 is both necessary and sufficient for stable training. The bang-bang optimal-control analysis shows optimal solutions at q > 1 inevitably blow up. The arithmetic of exponents enables efficient, modular certification at the primitive level. Empirically, q ≤ 1 variants of Mamba and PatchTST train stably without layer normalization, demonstrating that stability depends on the input-magnitude exponent, not the presence of normalization layers per se.
AI.conclusion: The sublinear-growth principle (q ≤ 1) defines the right function space for well-controlled forward dynamics, adjoint sensitivity, and architectural composition in residual networks. It provides a rigorous, computable alternative to trial-and-error architecture search, explaining the stabilizing role of layer normalization as one mechanism to satisfy the criterion, while enabling normalization-free stable designs through direct exponent control.

title: Collaborative Spatial Learning with Multi-LLM Agents in Networked Social Experiments
comment: Accepted at ASONAM 2026; to appear in the Springer proceedings
summary: Collective problem solving often requires that group members consider the tradeoff between exploitation of known solutions and exploration for new ones, where information of known solutions can be disseminated among individual members through communication networks. The Mason--Watts experiment (PNAS 2012) showed that human groups in shorter-path networks outperform those in longer-path networks on a two-dimensional search task. In this work, we focus on the investigation of such network-efficiency effects in the setting of a group of large language model (LLM) agents. Specifically, we consider groups of sixteen LLM agents playing the Mason--Watts experiment on the eight Mason--Watts network topologies. Moreover, we develop mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents such that the performance of LLM agents can be compared with both the mechanistic agents and the human experimental data. Our computational experiments indicate that the LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect when instructed to randomize their first-round choices, but not under the default initialization. In this experiment, adding a one-sentence first-round randomization instruction improves collective payoff by more than three times the estimated payoff difference across the eight network topologies. Also, the Bayesian optimization agents obtain higher payoffs than the evaluated LLM agents on this spatial search task. We further compare the agents' exploration--exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.

AI.tldr: LLM agents playing the Mason–Watts experiment exhibit network-efficiency effects only when explicitly instructed to randomize first-round choices; a simple randomization prompt improves collective payoff dramatically. Bayesian optimization agents outperform the LLM agents on this spatial search task.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether groups of LLM agents exhibit the same network-efficiency effects observed in human groups (Mason & Watts, 2012), and to benchmark LLM agent performance against mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents and human data.
AI.method: Sixteen LLM agents play the Mason–Watts two-dimensional search task across all eight Mason–Watts network topologies. Two conditions are tested: default initialization and a first-round randomization instruction. Mechanistic Bayesian optimization agents are developed as a comparative baseline. Agents are evaluated on collective payoff, exploration–exploitation behavior, copying, and spatial diversity.
AI.result: LLM agents show a significant network-efficiency effect only under the randomization instruction, not under default initialization. The randomization prompt alone increases collective payoff by more than three times the estimated payoff difference across all eight topologies. Bayesian optimization agents achieve higher payoffs than the LLM agents overall.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents can replicate human-like network-efficiency effects but are highly sensitive to prompting strategy. Simple instructions dramatically alter collective search behavior, suggesting careful prompt design is critical for multi-agent LLM systems. Mechanistic Bayesian agents remain superior on this task.

title: SEED: Self-Evolving On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large language models are increasingly trained as interactive agents for long-horizon tasks involving multi-turn interaction, tool use, and environment feedback. Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides a practical optimization paradigm, but its sparse trajectory-level rewards offer limited guidance on intermediate decisions, leaving a supervision gap between episode-level outcomes and token-level policy learning. We propose SEED (SElf-Evolving On-Policy Distillation), a self-evolving framework that converts completed on-policy trajectories into training-time hindsight skills and distills their behavioral effect back into the policy model. SEED first fine-tunes the policy to analyze completed trajectories and generate natural-language skills that capture reusable workflows, decisive observations, or failure-avoidance rules. During RL, the current policy both collects trajectories and serves as the analyzer that extracts hindsight skills from them. Policy updates therefore improve subsequent decision making and skill analysis together, allowing hindsight supervision to evolve with the policy. SEED then re-scores the sampled actions under ordinary and skill-augmented contexts, converting the skill-induced probability shift into a dense token-level on-policy distillation signal. This signal is jointly optimized with outcome-based RL, keeping the auxiliary supervision aligned with the current trajectory distribution. Extensive experiments on text-based and vision-based agentic tasks show that SEED consistently improves performance and sample efficiency, exhibiting robust generalization to unseen scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinyangwu/SEED.

AI.tldr: SEED is a self-evolving framework that extracts hindsight skills from completed on-policy trajectories and distills them back into the policy as a dense token-level signal, jointly optimized with outcome-based RL to improve agent performance and sample efficiency on long-horizon interactive tasks.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based RL for interactive agents suffers from a supervision gap: sparse trajectory-level rewards provide insufficient guidance for intermediate token-level decisions. There is a need for dense, informative supervision that remains aligned with the evolving on-policy distribution.
AI.method: SEED operates in two stages: (1) the policy is fine-tuned to analyze its own completed trajectories and generate natural-language hindsight skills (reusable workflows, decisive observations, failure-avoidance rules); (2) during RL, these skills augment the context, and the resulting probability shift on sampled actions is converted into a dense token-level distillation signal, jointly optimized with the standard outcome-based RL objective. Both trajectory collection and skill analysis are performed by the current policy, enabling co-evolution.
AI.result: SEED consistently improves performance and sample efficiency across text-based and vision-based agentic tasks, with robust generalization to unseen scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Self-evolving hindsight distillation bridges the supervision gap in outcome-based RL by providing evolving, dense, on-policy auxiliary signals, yielding stronger interactive agents without requiring external supervision or reward shaping.

title: Auditing Fairness-Privacy Trade-offs: Subpopulation-Level Effects of Fairness-Enhancing Algorithms
summary: Machine learning (ML) models deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, law enforcement, and finance must satisfy not only utility requirements but also fairness and privacy guarantees. While prior work has largely examined how privacy-preserving techniques affect fairness, the inverse question-how fairness-enhancing algorithms influence privacy leakage-remains underexplored. We present the first comprehensive study of how fairness interventions affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. By adapting the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, we uncover privacy disparities that aggregate evaluations obscure. We further analyze how Differential Privacy (DP) interacts with fairness-enhancing methods across different categories, showing that DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations. Our results demonstrate that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. These findings reveal that fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level, and we introduce the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first comprehensive study of how fairness-enhancing algorithms affect membership inference privacy risks at the subpopulation level. Using an adapted Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) for subgroup auditing, the authors reveal that fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk; their impact varies by model architecture, subgroup size, and mitigation strategy. They also show that Differential Privacy's benefits and costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations, and introduce a unified empirical framework for jointly evaluating fairness, privacy, and utility at the subpopulation level.
AI.motivation: While prior work has extensively studied how privacy-preserving techniques (like DP) affect fairness, the inverse direction — how fairness-enhancing algorithms impact privacy leakage — remains underexplored. Moreover, existing evaluations typically assess fairness and privacy at an aggregate level, which may obscure disparities across subpopulations. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating subpopulation-level privacy risks introduced by fairness interventions.
AI.method: The authors adapt the Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) — a state-of-the-art membership inference attack — for subgroup auditing, enabling fine-grained measurement of privacy leakage per subpopulation. They systematically evaluate how different fairness-enhancing methods (across multiple categories) interact with Differential Privacy, examining the resulting privacy-utility-fairness trade-offs across subgroups defined by size and sensitive attributes.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) fairness interventions do not uniformly increase privacy risk — the effect depends on model architecture, subgroup size, and the specific mitigation strategy employed; (2) DP's privacy benefits and utility costs are unevenly distributed across subpopulations, with smaller or marginalized subgroups often bearing disproportionate costs; (3) aggregate evaluations mask significant privacy disparities that only emerge at the subgroup level.
AI.conclusion: Fairness, privacy, and utility must be jointly evaluated at the subpopulation level rather than in aggregate. The paper introduces the first unified empirical framework to support such auditing in practice, enabling practitioners to identify and mitigate disproportionate privacy harms that fairness interventions may inadvertently introduce for specific subgroups.

title: Multi-LLM Collaborative MRI Report Generation for Visual Instruction Tuning in Brain Oncology
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and their extension to vision-language models (VLMs) have made it easier to combine text and images for tasks such as report generation. Existing VLMs in medicine typically focus on 2D images (chest X-rays), and their extension to 3D imaging has been difficult because of the lack of paired 3D imaging-text data. Thus, we introduce a new method for creating a 3D image-text dataset for brain oncology using 3D MRI scans of glioma and meningioma cases. We use a cooperative system in which several LLMs work together to generate and check reports, ensuring that they are accurate and clear. By leveraging the new 3D MRI-text dataset, we further build a VLM that converts MRI scans into tokens and aligns them with text instructions. Our VLM performed better in report generation and visual question answering tasks than other 2D and 3D methods. Our method not only improves the quality of reports but also helps with better diagnosis and treatment in brain oncology.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a cooperative LLM-based method to generate a paired 3D MRI-text dataset for brain oncology and builds a vision-language model (VLM) that outperforms existing 2D and 3D methods on report generation and visual question answering tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs in medicine are predominantly limited to 2D images (e.g., chest X-rays) due to the scarcity of paired 3D imaging-text data. Extending VLMs to 3D volumetric imaging like MRI is critical for brain oncology but has been hindered by this data bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors propose a cooperative multi-LLM framework where several LLMs collaborate to generate and cross-check radiology reports, producing a high-quality paired 3D MRI-text dataset using glioma and meningioma MRI scans. They then build a VLM that tokenizes 3D MRI volumes and aligns them with text instructions for report generation and VQA.
AI.result: The proposed VLM trained on the synthetically generated 3D MRI-text dataset outperformed both 2D and 3D baseline methods on report generation and visual question answering tasks in brain oncology.
AI.conclusion: The cooperative LLM approach effectively addresses the 3D image-text data scarcity problem. The resulting VLM not only improves report quality but also has potential clinical utility for enhanced diagnosis and treatment planning in brain oncology.

title: Show Me How You Reason and I'll Tell You Who You Are: Reasoning Graphs for Robust LLM Authorship Attribution
summary: Given the current trend to employ large language models (LLMs) in almost any imaginable context, LLM-generated text detection and authorship attribution have become a pressing issue. Prior work has primarily focused on surface-level linguistic features, an approach shown to be susceptible to paraphrasing and other obfuscation techniques. In this paper, we go beyond the linguistic surface, extracting and analysing reasoning structures in LLM-generated texts with the goal of capturing more complex signals of LLM authorship. We propose a graph neural network approach that leverages reasoning graphs extracted by an argument mining pipeline, demonstrating improved robustness and generalisation over a traditional Longformer baseline. Our approach outperforms the baseline by up to 27 percentage points under the obfuscation attacks such as paraphrasing and backtranslation, and 19 percentage points when evaluated on the texts generated by the unseen model versions, simulating real-world conditions in which new LLM versions are continuously released.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a graph neural network method that extracts reasoning structures from texts via argument mining to detect LLM authorship, achieving significantly improved robustness over surface-level baselines against paraphrasing, backtranslation, and unseen model versions.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-generated text detection methods rely on surface-level linguistic features, which are easily defeated by paraphrasing and obfuscation techniques. There is a need for more robust, deeper signals of LLM authorship that persist under such attacks and generalize to unseen model versions.
AI.method: The authors propose a graph neural network (GNN) approach operating on reasoning graphs extracted through an argument mining pipeline. Instead of analyzing surface-level text features, the method captures the underlying reasoning structure of LLM-generated texts, which is hypothesized to be a more stable and distinctive signal of machine authorship.
AI.result: The GNN approach outperforms a Longformer baseline by up to 27 percentage points under obfuscation attacks (paraphrasing, backtranslation) and by 19 percentage points when evaluated on texts from unseen model versions.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning structure analysis via argument mining and graph neural networks provides a more robust and generalizable approach to LLM-generated text detection compared to surface-level methods, better handling obfuscation attacks and adapting to newly released, unseen models.

title: Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning for Long-Tailed Electrocardiogram Arrhythmia Diagnosis
summary: Long-tailed label distributions reduce the reliability of deep learning for electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia diagnosis, particularly for clinically important but rare abnormalities. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods mainly address class frequency while overlooking direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes. This study proposes Angular Gaussian Supervised Contrastive Learning (AG-SCL) for long-tailed multi-label ECG diagnosis. AG-SCL integrates three components into a unified framework: an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings, Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins, and tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7-25 Hz QRS-dominant band. The method was evaluated on the public PTB-XL benchmark and a nocturnal ECG dataset comprising 1317 hours of recordings from 141 subjects. AG-SCL achieved the best macro-level performance on both datasets. On PTB-XL, it obtained a balanced accuracy of 0.838, sensitivity of 0.709, specificity of 0.968, mean average precision of 0.495, and TPR at 5% FPR of 0.778. On Noc-ECG, the corresponding values were 0.918, 0.889, 0.947, 0.488, and 0.900. The largest gains occurred in rare or morphologically unstable rhythm classes, while ablation studies confirmed the contributions of full-covariance modelling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Open-EXG/AG-SCL-for-Long-Tailed-ECG.

AI.tldr: AG-SCL is a framework for long-tailed multi-label ECG arrhythmia diagnosis that combines Angular Gaussian contrastive learning with full-covariance uncertainty modeling, Adaptive Logit Adjustment, and tail-aware augmentation. It achieved state-of-the-art macro-level performance on PTB-XL and a nocturnal ECG dataset, with the largest gains in rare rhythm classes.
AI.motivation: Long-tailed class distributions in ECG data undermine deep learning reliability for rare but clinically important arrhythmias. Existing rebalancing and logit adjustment methods address class frequency but ignore direction-dependent morphological variability across ECG classes, which is critical for distinguishing rare abnormalities.
AI.method: AG-SCL integrates three components: (1) an Angular Gaussian contrastive branch that models full-covariance class uncertainty on unit-normalized embeddings; (2) Adaptive Logit Adjustment that learns bounded label-state-specific prior corrections instead of fixed frequency-based margins; (3) tail-aware augmentation that generates morphology-preserving views while protecting the 7–25 Hz QRS-dominant band.
AI.result: On PTB-XL: balanced accuracy 0.838, sensitivity 0.709, specificity 0.968, mAP 0.495, TPR@5%FPR 0.778. On Noc-ECG: balanced accuracy 0.918, sensitivity 0.889, specificity 0.947, mAP 0.488, TPR@5%FPR 0.900. Largest gains occurred in rare/morphologically unstable rhythm classes. Ablations confirmed contributions of all three components.
AI.conclusion: AG-SCL improves long-tailed ECG diagnosis by combining prior calibration with anisotropic representation learning, enhancing sensitivity to rare arrhythmias while maintaining clinically relevant specificity.

title: MathCoPilot: An Interactive System for Human-AI Symbiotic Paradigm of Mathematical Research
summary: Existing LLM-based theorem provers have achieved impressive results on formal mathematics benchmarks, yet they remain confined to acting as autonomous agents that prove a stated proposition. In this paper, we propose MathCoPilot, a human-in-the-loop system that embodies a new human--AI symbiotic paradigm for mathematical research, in which the mathematician steers the high-level mathematical direction while AI agents carry out the detailed formalization and proof work under continuous human guidance. MathCoPilot unifies three core capabilities: (1) an interactive workbench where the mathematician and AI agents collaborate through a living proof blueprint that decomposes a proof into navigable steps the human can directly inspect, direct, and refine; (2) automated proving skill orchestration with adaptive knowledge base search and Lean-integrated iterative verification; and (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Using MathCoPilot, we systematically compare four state-of-the-art LLMs, including Gemini~3.1~Pro, GPT-5.4, and Claude~Opus~4.7, on a FormalMATH subset and on two real PDE theorems requiring deep domain expertise, evaluating their ability to produce verified Lean~4 proofs and to identify errors in deliberately incorrect proofs. Our results show that while current models can handle undergraduate-level problems with high success rates under favorable autoformalization conditions, substantial challenges remain for domain-specific theorems requiring genuine mathematical understanding.

AI.tldr: MathCoPilot is a human-in-the-loop theorem-proving system where mathematicians direct high-level strategy while LLM agents handle formalization and verification in Lean 4. The system features an interactive proof blueprint, automated proving with knowledge base search, and paper-to-Lean formalization. Evaluation across four SOTA LLMs on FormalMATH and PDE theorems reveals strong undergraduate-level performance but significant gaps on domain-specific theorems requiring deep mathematical insight.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based theorem provers act as autonomous agents tackling stated propositions, but this misses the collaborative nature of real mathematical research. The authors argue for a symbiotic human-AI paradigm where the mathematician retains strategic control while AI handles the labor-intensive formalization and verification details.
AI.method: MathCoPilot integrates: (1) an interactive workbench with a "living proof blueprint" allowing step-by-step human inspection and refinement; (2) automated proving orchestration combining adaptive knowledge base search with iterative Lean 4 verification; (3) topic-driven paper retrieval and automated formalization into a verified Lean knowledge base. Four LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and one unnamed) are benchmarked on a FormalMATH subset and two real PDE theorems, testing both proof generation and error detection.
AI.result: Current SOTA models achieve high success rates on undergraduate-level FormalMATH problems under favorable autoformalization conditions. However, substantial challenges persist for domain-specific PDE theorems, where genuine mathematical understanding — not just formal manipulation — is required. The error-detection task further exposes limitations in models' deep comprehension.
AI.conclusion: The human-AI symbiotic approach is promising for formal mathematics, but LLMs still lack the deep domain expertise needed for research-level theorems. MathCoPilot demonstrates that keeping the human in the loop is essential for non-trivial proofs, and highlights where current models fall short.

title: Latent Trajectory Discrimination for AI-Generated Text Detection
summary: Most existing approaches to AI-Generated Text Detection (AIGTD) treat documents as static objects and base their decisions on aggregate statistics or globally compressed embeddings. However, this perspective overlooks the inherently dynamic nature of autoregressive generation, where content evolves progressively through the latent space. In this paper, we reformulate AIGTD as the problem of distinguishing between latent generation trajectories. Instead of relying on static representations, we model how textual representations evolve across the sequence. To this end, we propose Geometric Trajectory and Contrastive Learning (GTCL), a framework that segments the document into ordered local units, encodes each unit in an embedding space, and constructs a structured and sequence-level representation. GTCL then applies contrastive learning to these trajectories to learn geometric regularities associated with the autoregressive generation. Evaluations performed on three different benchmarks and several approaches show that GTCL outperforms detection baselines consistently, which implies that explicitly modeling sequential dynamics provides robust discriminative signals across models and domains. These results suggest that modeling trajectory differences could improve detection and open up a dynamic direction that has been underexplored in previous AIGTD literature.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates AI-generated text detection as distinguishing between latent generation trajectories rather than analyzing static documents. The proposed GTCL framework segments documents into ordered units, constructs sequence-level representations via embeddings, and applies contrastive learning to capture geometric regularities of autoregressive generation, outperforming baselines across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing AIGTD methods treat documents as static objects using aggregate statistics or globally compressed embeddings, ignoring the dynamic, autoregressive nature of text generation where content evolves progressively through latent space. This static perspective misses discriminative signals present in sequential generation dynamics.
AI.method: GTCL (Geometric Trajectory and Contrastive Learning) operates by: (1) segmenting documents into ordered local units, (2) encoding each unit into an embedding space, (3) constructing a structured sequence-level trajectory representation that captures how textual representations evolve, and (4) applying contrastive learning on these trajectories to learn geometric regularities characteristic of autoregressive generation.
AI.result: GTCL consistently outperforms detection baselines across three different benchmarks and multiple detection approaches, demonstrating that explicitly modeling sequential dynamics yields robust discriminative signals that generalize across models and domains.
AI.conclusion: Modeling trajectory differences provides a promising direction for AI-generated text detection. The dynamic, sequence-aware perspective has been underexplored in prior AIGTD literature and offers improved detection performance while opening new research avenues.

title: Beyond Entropy: Correctness-Aware Advantage Shaping via Contrastive Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) commonly uses entropy for advantage shaping. However, entropy cannot distinguish useful uncertainty from detrimental confusion, limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. We propose Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO), which uses token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla generation distributions for correctness-aware advantage shaping. Both theoretical and empirical results show that this disagreement reliably indicates token-level correctness. We further show that On-policy Distillation is a special case of CPO, where the posterior distribution is instantiated by an external teacher model. CPO also resolves the zero-advantage problem. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods while maintaining strong generalization. Further analysis shows that correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploration and exploitation respectively, and balancing both leads to the best performance.

AI.tldr: Contrastive Policy Optimization (CPO) replaces entropy-based advantage shaping in RLVR with token-level contrastive disagreement between reference-guided and vanilla distributions, providing a correctness-aware signal that outperforms entropy methods, resolves the zero-advantage problem, and naturally balances exploration (incorrect responses) with exploitation (correct responses).
AI.motivation: Entropy, commonly used for advantage shaping in RLVR, cannot differentiate between useful uncertainty (exploration) and detrimental confusion (incorrectness), limiting its effectiveness as a correctness signal. A more discriminative, correctness-aware signal is needed.
AI.method: CPO computes token-level contrastive disagreement between a reference-guided generation distribution and a vanilla generation distribution. This disagreement serves as a correctness-aware advantage shaping signal. On-policy Distillation emerges as a special case where the posterior is instantiated by an external teacher model. The method also addresses the zero-advantage problem.
AI.result: CPO substantially outperforms entropy-based RLVR methods on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks while maintaining strong generalization. Correct and incorrect responses naturally support exploitation and exploration respectively; balancing both yields optimal performance.
AI.conclusion: Token-level contrastive disagreement is a reliable indicator of token-level correctness, making CPO a superior alternative to entropy-based advantage shaping in RLVR, with the added benefit of naturally balancing exploration and exploitation.

title: SportD: Can VLMs Physically Strategize?
summary: Vision--language models have become increasingly capable of interpreting visual scenes, but it remains unclear whether they can use information to make strategically effective decisions. We investigate this question in soccer, where models observe the seconds preceding an on-ball decision and must choose whether to shoot or pass to a specific teammate. Unlike conventional visual-understanding tasks, soccer enables decisions to be evaluated quantitatively by estimating the value of every available action. We introduce SportD, a benchmark comprising 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each model choice is evaluated against a possession-value model that estimates the action that most increases the attacking team's probability of scoring, allowing us to measure both optimal-action accuracy and the value forfeited by suboptimal decisions. Across three frontier VLMs, the best selects the highest-valued action on 31.4% of events, compared with 38.9% for the professional players, and all models incur significantly greater regret. Further analysis reveals a systematic preference for lower-variance and lower-reward actions: VLMs shoot less often and select substantially less progressive passes than either the optimal policy or the real players. The models also reproduce the player's specific action above chance even when that action is suboptimal, suggesting partial imitation of familiar play patterns rather than consistent evaluation of counterfactual alternatives. SportD provides a value-grounded testbed for measuring physical strategic reasoning in VLMs.

AI.tldr: Introduces SportD, a soccer decision benchmark using 2022 FIFA World Cup data to evaluate whether VLMs can make strategically optimal on-ball decisions (shoot vs. pass). Frontier VLMs select the highest-value action only 31.4% of the time (vs. 38.9% for pros), exhibit systematic bias toward low-variance/low-reward actions, and tend to imitate suboptimal player choices rather than evaluating counterfactuals.
AI.motivation: VLMs excel at visual understanding but their capacity for strategically effective decision-making under quantifiable, value-grounded conditions remains unclear. Soccer provides an ideal testbed because every action (shoot/pass to specific teammate) can be assigned an expected possession value, enabling objective evaluation of decision quality.
AI.method: The authors constructed SportD, a benchmark of 478 on-ball decisions from the 2022 FIFA World Cup. Each decision is evaluated using a possession-value (PV) model that estimates the probability of scoring given each available action. Metrics include: (1) optimal-action accuracy — whether the model selects the highest-PV action, and (2) regret — the value forfeited by choosing suboptimally. Three frontier VLMs are tested against professional players' actual decisions and the PV-optimal policy.
AI.result: The best VLM achieves 31.4% optimal-action accuracy vs. 38.9% for professional players, with all models incurring significantly greater regret. VLMs systematically prefer lower-variance, lower-reward actions — shooting less and making less progressive passes than both the optimal policy and real players. Models also reproduce players' specific suboptimal actions above chance, indicating pattern imitation rather than genuine counterfactual evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs lack robust physical strategic reasoning, defaulting to conservative, imitative behavior rather than value-maximizing decisions. SportD offers a rigorous, value-grounded framework for benchmarking and improving strategic decision-making in vision-language models.

title: OmniaBench: Benchmarking General AI Agents Across Diverse Scenarios
summary: Large language models are increasingly evolving from text generators into general agents capable of understanding user requests, invoking external tools, and completing complex tasks through interaction. However, existing agent benchmarks often focus on limited scenarios, tool ecosystems, or interaction formats, making it difficult to systematically characterize model capabilities across heterogeneous application settings. We introduce OmniaBench, a benchmark for evaluating general agents across diverse scenarios with explicit state spaces. We derive application-oriented scenario knowledge from app stores, product documents, industry resources, Web retrieval, and human refinement, forming a hierarchical taxonomy that spans ToC, ToB and ToE with 90 level-1 and 354 level-2 domains. Based on this taxonomy, we construct executable environments and synthesize single-turn and multi-turn tasks through four complementary routes: DAG, DAG-S, Solver, and Program. OmniaBench further introduces a ten-dimensional capability taxonomy and eight compositional atomic difficulty factors to support fine-grained evaluation and analysis. The resulting dataset contains 1,431 tasks, together with a challenging subset of 644 tasks designed to reduce evaluation cost and mitigate potential contamination of the full set after public release. The bench presents substantial challenges to current frontier models, with even Claude-Sonnet-5 and GPT-5.6-Sol achieving Overall Pass@1 scores of only 58.54 and 57.14, respectively. Further analyses reveal clear differences across domains and capabilities, as well as persistent limitations in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction. OmniaBench provides a broad and diagnostic benchmark for characterizing the capability boundaries of general agents.

AI.tldr: OmniaBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-based general agents, featuring a hierarchical domain taxonomy (90 level-1, 354 level-2 domains spanning ToC, ToB, ToE), 1,431 tasks with executable environments, a ten-dimensional capability taxonomy, and eight atomic difficulty factors. Even top frontier models (Claude-Sonnet-5, GPT-5.6-Sol) achieve only ~57-58% Overall Pass@1.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks are limited in scope — they focus on narrow scenarios, restricted tool ecosystems, or single interaction formats — making it impossible to systematically characterize model capabilities across heterogeneous real-world application settings. There is a need for a broad, diagnostic, and fine-grained benchmark that spans diverse domains and enables detailed capability analysis.
AI.method: The authors derive scenario knowledge from app stores, product documents, industry resources, Web retrieval, and human refinement to build a hierarchical taxonomy (ToC/ToB/ToE, 90 level-1 and 354 level-2 domains). Executable environments are constructed, and tasks are synthesized via four complementary routes: DAG, DAG-S, Solver, and Program, yielding both single-turn and multi-turn tasks. A ten-dimensional capability taxonomy and eight compositional atomic difficulty factors are introduced to support fine-grained evaluation. A challenging 644-task subset is also curated to reduce evaluation cost and mitigate contamination risk.
AI.result: The full dataset comprises 1,431 tasks (plus the 644-task subset). Frontier models struggle significantly: Claude-Sonnet-5 scores 58.54 and GPT-5.6-Sol scores 57.14 Overall Pass@1. Analyses reveal clear performance disparities across domains and capabilities, with persistent weaknesses in planning, constraint maintenance, and adaptive correction.
AI.conclusion: OmniaBench provides a broad and diagnostic benchmark that effectively characterizes the capability boundaries of general agents, revealing that even the strongest current models face substantial challenges in robust planning, constraint handling, and error correction across diverse real-world scenarios.

title: PolyQ: Codesigning End-to-End Quantization Framework for Scalable Edge CPU LLM Inference
summary: CPUs are the most universal target for on-device LLM inference, but existing low-bit quantization methods offer either coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently on CPUs. We present PolyQ, a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design for activation-aware channel-wise bit allocation under a user-specified average-bit budget. PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from $\{2,3,4,8,16\}$, then uses a compile-time model compiler to permute and cluster channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, generate SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels, and merge compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path. This turns fine-grained budget fitting into a practical fractional-bit deployment method for CPU-only inference. Across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B on WikiText-2, PolyQ provides stable quality scaling from 3--6\,b and improves perplexity by 2.4--32.1\% over prior methods at a 3\,b target. End-to-end measurements on three representative CPUs -- workstation, laptop, and mobile -- show that compiler layout regularization reduces activation reorder traffic by up to 70.8\%, prefill latency and decode throughput scale nearly proportionally with the configured bit budget, and energy/token overhead stays below 2\% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end. These results show that fractional-bit CPU deployment is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets.

AI.tldr: PolyQ is a CPU-oriented compiler/quantization co-design that enables fine-grained, per-channel bit allocation (2–16 bits) under a user-specified average-bit budget for LLM inference. It uses compile-time channel permutation and clustering into bit-homogeneous blocks, SIMD/LUT-compatible kernel generation, and cross-operator layout regularization to achieve practical fractional-bit deployment with predictable performance and energy efficiency across diverse CPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing low-bit quantization methods for on-device LLM inference on CPUs either offer only coarse operating points or fine-grained mixed precision that is difficult to execute efficiently. There is a need for practical fractional-bit deployment that combines fine-grained bit allocation with CPU-efficient execution.
AI.method: PolyQ assigns per-channel bit-widths from {2,3,4,8,16} under an average-bit budget. A compile-time model compiler then: (1) permutes and clusters channels into bit-homogeneous blocks, (2) generates SIMD- and LUT-compatible kernels for these blocks, and (3) merges compatible permutations across operators to keep layout regularization off the runtime path. This transforms fine-grained budget fitting into a practical fractional-bit deployment pipeline for CPU-only inference.
AI.result: On WikiText-2 across Falcon-H1-3B, Llama2-13B, and Qwen3-32B, PolyQ achieves stable quality scaling from 3–6 bits and improves perplexity by 2.4–32.1% over prior methods at a 3-bit target. End-to-end measurements on workstation, laptop, and mobile CPUs show activation reorder traffic reduced by up to 70.8%, prefill latency and decode throughput scaling nearly proportionally with bit budget, and energy/token overhead below 2% relative to an optimized LUT-based back-end.
AI.conclusion: Fractional-bit CPU deployment of LLMs is practical, predictable, and energy-efficient across diverse edge targets. PolyQ's co-design approach successfully bridges the gap between fine-grained quantization quality and CPU runtime efficiency.

title: Action QFormer: Structured Representation Shaping under Action Supervision in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Action supervision in vision-language-action (VLA) models is often treated as a downstream objective for learning action prediction. In this paper, we study it instead as a force that shapes inherited multimodal representations. We show that this shaping has a dual effect: it is necessary for forming action-compatible representations, but when action supervision is applied too directly to the inherited multimodal pathway, it can also destabilize representations that support language-side processing and object grounding. To address this tension, we introduce Action QFormer, a query-based action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation. In zero-shot sim-to-real navigation, Action QFormer improves average closed-loop task success from 18.8% to 56.3%, raises fixed-instruction action-generation correctness from 22.5% to 75.5%, and nearly eliminates out-of-distribution instruction generations. Further analyses show that Action QFormer changes how action supervision shapes inherited multimodal representations, reducing broad upstream rewriting while preserving targeted and sometimes constructive action-supervised adaptation. These results suggest that improving VLA performance requires not only stronger pretrained backbones, but also better ways of selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how it is shaped under action supervision.

AI.tldr: Introduces Action QFormer, a query-based interface that reorganizes multimodal representations for action prediction without destabilizing language and object grounding, achieving major gains in zero-shot sim-to-real navigation.
AI.motivation: Action supervision in VLA models is typically treated as a downstream objective, but the authors argue it fundamentally reshapes inherited multimodal representations. Direct application of action supervision destabilizes language-side processing and object grounding, creating a tension between action compatibility and representation stability.
AI.method: Proposes Action QFormer — a query-based, action-facing interface that uses instruction-conditioned queries to reorganize inherited multimodal information into action-facing representations before downstream action generation, decoupling the action supervision pathway from the primary multimodal pathway.
AI.result: Zero-shot sim-to-real navigation: closed-loop task success improved from 18.8% to 56.3%; fixed-instruction action-generation correctness rose from 22.5% to 75.5%; near-elimination of out-of-distribution instruction generations. Action QFormer reduces broad upstream representation rewriting while preserving targeted, constructive action-supervised adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Better VLA performance requires not just stronger pretrained backbones, but also improved mechanisms for selecting and organizing inherited multimodal information while controlling how action supervision shapes upstream representations.

title: Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence
summary: Rubrics provide structured, fine-grained signals for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs). Yet reliable query-specific rubrics are difficult to construct. Existing approaches often derive supervision from human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources, but provides no explicit check that a plausible rubric is useful. Such a rubric may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward an optional style, or penalize a valid alternative strategy. We introduce Rubrics on Trial, a query-only framework that evolves a rubric set from an empty set without external annotations or model training. It derives supervision solely from synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs and validates each proposed rubric before adding it, screening out non-discriminative, over-specific, and style-only candidate rubrics. Experiments across five preference benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of Rubrics on Trial, which achieves the best average accuracy and leads on six of seven evaluation sets.

AI.tldr: Rubrics on Trial introduces a query-only framework that iteratively builds a high-quality rubric set from scratch, using synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs to validate each candidate rubric — screening out non-discriminative, over-specific, or style-only rubrics — and achieves state-of-the-art performance on preference benchmark suites without any external annotations or model training.
AI.motivation: Existing rubric construction methods rely on human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources but lacks any mechanism to verify whether a generated rubric is actually useful — it may fail to discriminate answer quality, reward superficial stylistic choices, or penalize valid alternative strategies. This motivates a framework that can autonomously validate and filter candidate rubrics.
AI.method: Rubrics on Trial is a query-only framework that evolves a rubric set starting from an empty set. For each candidate rubric, it generates synthetic rubric-conditioned response pairs and applies validation tests to screen for three failure modes: (1) non-discriminative rubrics that fail to separate quality levels, (2) over-specific rubrics that are too narrow, and (3) style-only rubrics that reward superficial attributes rather than substantive quality. Only rubrics passing all tests are added to the active set.
AI.result: Evaluated across five preference benchmark suites, Rubrics on Trial achieves the best average accuracy and leads on six out of seven evaluation sets, demonstrating its effectiveness without requiring any external annotations or model training.
AI.conclusion: A query-only approach that validates candidate rubrics through synthetic response pairs can generate reliable, discriminative rubrics autonomously, matching or exceeding the performance of methods that depend on human annotations or preference data.

title: TIDE: Trustworthy and Interpretable Battery Degradation Estimation with Contextual Learning and Symbolic Distillation
summary: Battery health estimation is fundamental for battery management in battery-powered systems, where inaccurate health states may affect control, maintenance, and service life. It becomes even more critical in intelligent connected systems, where estimation errors can propagate across interconnected devices and downstream decisions. In this paper, we propose TIDE, a trustworthy and interpretable battery degradation estimator for reliable battery health estimation. TIDE jointly considers accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability, which are all essential for practical deployment and downstream decision making. To realize these objectives, TIDE combines battery-domain knowledge with operational measurements in a three-component backbone. A knowledge-guided degradation prior promotes trustworthy estimation, a monotone residual component provides interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and a contextual learning component captures battery-specific operational effects for improved accuracy. The trained backbone is then distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate that provides a concise model-level interpretation of its learned estimation logic. Experiments show that TIDE achieves strong estimation accuracy, improving overall estimation fidelity by an average of 19.7% over representative baselines. Its knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modelling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, supporting trustworthy estimation. Meanwhile, the backbone enables component-level interpretation, while symbolic distillation provides a compact model-level representation of the learned estimation logic. These results support the practical use of TIDE for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

AI.tldr: TIDE is a battery degradation estimator that integrates accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability through a three-component backbone (knowledge-guided prior, monotone residual, contextual learning) and symbolic distillation, achieving 19.7% average fidelity improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Accurate battery health estimation is critical for battery management, especially in intelligent connected systems where estimation errors can propagate across devices and downstream decisions. Existing methods often lack a joint treatment of accuracy, trustworthiness (aging-consistency), and interpretability — all essential for practical deployment.
AI.method: TIDE employs a three-component backbone: (1) a knowledge-guided degradation prior for trustworthy estimation, (2) a monotone residual component for interpretable aging-consistent refinement, and (3) a contextual learning component for battery-specific operational effects. The trained backbone is distilled into a compact symbolic surrogate for model-level interpretability.
AI.result: TIDE improves overall estimation fidelity by 19.7% on average over representative baselines. The knowledge-guided prior and monotone residual modeling substantially reduce aging-consistency violations, and symbolic distillation provides a concise model-level representation of learned estimation logic.
AI.conclusion: TIDE demonstrates that jointly optimizing for accuracy, trustworthiness, and interpretability yields practical benefits for battery health monitoring and decision support in intelligent connected systems.

title: Analytic Abduction: Causal Decomposition and Governed Commitment for Human--AI Coordination
summary: Abductive reasoning operates in two directions. The synthetic mode builds explanations from available hypotheses; the analytic mode, conversely, identifies the latent factors whose interaction accounts for a complex observed state. This paper develops the analytic mode as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive discipline of commitment, in which candidate factors coexist and interact, resolving into committed conclusions only when explicit governance conditions are met. The formal core is the $κ$-$τ$ apparatus: $κ$ encodes the epistemic interaction among hypotheses, and $τ$ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to the decision's stakes. The central contribution is the causal cluster, a structured object recording which latent factors participate in a decomposition, with what weights and interaction structure, together with a two-level architecture (intra-cluster $κ^*$, inter-cluster $κ^{**}$) that guards against causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis, the framework's contribution to human-AI reasoning is the legibility of suspended decomposition as a shared coordination object, providing structural resistance to premature convergence. In practice, the decision-maker is handed not a single imposed answer but the competing explanatory scenarios, weighted by plausibility and paired with the evidence that would resolve between them, so that sound action is possible even before the ambiguity is resolved.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes the analytic mode of abductive reasoning as a non-greedy, risk-sensitive framework using a κ-τ apparatus: κ encodes epistemic interaction among hypotheses, τ sets a commitment threshold calibrated to decision stakes. The central construct is the causal cluster, governed by a two-level architecture (intra- and inter-cluster κ) to prevent causal misattribution. Demonstrated in epidemiology and cyber threat analysis, the framework outputs competing explanatory scenarios with plausibility weights and resolving evidence, enabling sound action under ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Existing abductive reasoning approaches tend toward greedy, premature convergence to a single explanation, ignoring latent factor interactions and decision stakes. The authors seek to develop the under-explored analytic mode of abduction — identifying latent factors from complex observations — as a disciplined, risk-sensitive process that preserves ambiguity until governance conditions warrant commitment.
AI.method: The core formalism is the κ-τ apparatus: κ encodes epistemic interaction (dependencies, conflicts, synergies) among hypotheses, while τ sets a context-sensitive commitment threshold. The key structural innovation is the causal cluster, which records participating latent factors with their weights and interaction structure. A two-level architecture applies intra-cluster (κ*) and inter-cluster (κ**) interaction encoding to guard against causal misattribution. The framework produces suspended decomposition as a legible, shared coordination object, presenting competing scenarios weighted by plausibility alongside discriminating evidence.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated in two domains: epidemiological crisis decomposition and adversarial cyber threat analysis. In both, it successfully maintains multiple competing explanatory clusters, weights them by plausibility, and identifies the evidence that would discriminate among them — enabling decision-makers to act soundly before ambiguity is fully resolved.
AI.conclusion: The analytic mode of abduction, when disciplined by the κ-τ apparatus and causal cluster architecture, provides structural resistance to premature convergence. For human-AI reasoning, the key contribution is legible suspended decomposition: decision-makers receive not a single answer but competing explanatory scenarios with resolution pathways, making sound action possible under unresolved ambiguity.

title: Trajectory-Aware Flow Matching for Topology Optimisation
summary: Topology optimisation (TO) often requires repeated finite element analysis and sensitivity-based material updates, which can be costly when multiple candidate designs are needed under varying physical and design conditions. Generative TO offers a route to rapid design exploration, but existing models may rely on adversarial training, long reverse-diffusion sampling, or external guidance to maintain structural feasibility and physical consistency. This study develops a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework for conditional topology generation. Linear FMTO is first formulated as an endpoint-based baseline by interpolating between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology. To introduce mechanically meaningful intermediate states, a trajectory-aware FMTO formulation is proposed, where volume-fraction-indexed BESO states are used to construct the probability path and target velocity field. This incorporates physics-guided optimisation history into generative flow learning without adding inference-time optimisation. A path--velocity mismatch analysis explains why moderate trajectory weighting can improve generation stability, whereas excessive guidance may over-constrain the learned transport. Numerical examples show that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, topology fidelity, and substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO achieves the best overall performance with a moderate trajectory weight. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and three-dimensional topology generation further demonstrate the influence of path design and the applicability of the proposed framework beyond two-dimensional problems.

AI.tldr: A flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework is proposed for rapid conditional topology generation. A linear endpoint-based baseline is extended with a trajectory-aware formulation that uses BESO optimization history as physics-guided intermediate states, improving generation stability and performance with fewer sampling steps than diffusion-based methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional topology optimisation (TO) is computationally expensive when exploring multiple candidate designs under varying conditions. Existing generative TO models suffer from limitations including adversarial training instability, slow reverse-diffusion sampling, or reliance on external guidance for structural feasibility. There is a need for an efficient generative framework that incorporates physics-guided optimization history directly into the learning process without requiring additional inference-time optimization.
AI.method: The authors develop a flow matching-based topology optimisation (FMTO) framework with two formulations: (1) Linear FMTO — an endpoint-based baseline that interpolates between a Gaussian source field and the BESO reference topology; (2) Trajectory-aware FMTO — a formulation where volume-fraction-indexed BESO intermediate states construct the probability path and target velocity field, embedding physics-guided optimization history into generative flow learning. A path-velocity mismatch analysis is introduced to explain how moderate trajectory weighting improves stability while excessive guidance over-constrains the learned transport.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate that FMTO generates diverse topology candidates with improved compliance-related performance, volume-fraction satisfaction, and topology fidelity while requiring substantially fewer sampling steps than a diffusion-based baseline. Under limited training data, trajectory-aware FMTO with moderate trajectory weight achieves the best overall performance. Studies on trajectory-anchor density and 3D topology generation further validate the influence of path design and the framework's applicability beyond 2D problems.
AI.conclusion: The trajectory-aware FMTO framework effectively incorporates physics-guided BESO optimization history into flow matching, enabling efficient and high-quality conditional topology generation. The path-velocity mismatch analysis provides theoretical insight into trajectory weighting, and the method generalizes to both 2D and 3D problems, offering a practical alternative to diffusion-based generative TO approaches.

title: Grokipedia vs Wikipedia: An LLM-Based Audit of Political Neutrality along Ideologies
summary: Online encyclopedias shape political opinion and, through it, democratic discourse. In late 2025, Grokipedia was released, an encyclopedia written entirely by the LLM Grok. One motivation behind the project was to provide an unbiased alternative to Wikipedia, which has faced accusations of "left-wing" and "liberal" bias. But does an encyclopedia written by an LLM deliver greater neutrality, or does it simply embed a different ideology? We conduct a large-scale political bias study on Grokipedia and Wikipedia, analysing 1,394 article pairs describing members of government for neutrality along nine expert-coded ideology dimensions employing four LLM judges, Grok, Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. As the LLMs could themselves be biased, we also investigate patterns in their judgments. We find all LLM-judges, including Grok, to rate Grokipedia less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias are rated as portraying politicians favourably overall, but towards different ideological groups. Grokipedia particularly favours economically right-wing politicians and penalises socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia is rated as favourably biased towards the latter.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study comparing political bias in Grokipedia (LLM-written) and Wikipedia across 1,394 politician articles using four LLM judges finds that all judges, including Grok itself, rate Grokipedia as less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias exhibit favorable bias but toward different ideological groups: Grokipedia favors economically right-wing politicians and penalizes socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia shows the opposite pattern.
AI.motivation: Grokipedia was launched in late 2025 as an LLM-generated encyclopedia intended to provide an unbiased alternative to Wikipedia, which has been criticized for left-wing/liberal bias. The study investigates whether LLM-authored encyclopedias achieve greater neutrality or merely embed a different ideological slant, addressing the broader question of how AI-generated content shapes political opinion and democratic discourse.
AI.method: The authors conducted a large-scale bias analysis on 1,394 matched article pairs about government members from both Grokipedia and Wikipedia. Each article was evaluated along nine expert-coded ideology dimensions by four LLM judges — Grok, Claude, Mistral, and DeepSeek. To account for potential judge bias, the study also examined patterns and disagreements in the LLMs' judgments.
AI.result: All four LLM judges, including Grok (which wrote Grokipedia), consistently rated Grokipedia as less neutral than Wikipedia. Both encyclopedias portrayed politicians favorably overall, but diverged along ideological lines: Grokipedia exhibited favorable bias toward economically right-wing politicians and penalized socially liberal ones, while Wikipedia showed favorable bias toward socially liberal politicians.
AI.conclusion: LLM-generated encyclopedias do not resolve the problem of political bias; rather, they introduce a different ideological slant. Grokipedia's claim to neutrality is not supported by the evidence, as it embeds its own systematic political preferences distinct from Wikipedia's.

title: Scalable Training of Continuous-Time Spiking Neural Networks with Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization
summary: Continuous-time spiking neural networks (SNNs) provide an event-driven framework for temporal computation, computational neuroscience, and neuromorphic hardware.
