However, training deep continuous-time SNNs is severely constrained by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which evaluates and retains candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. Here we introduce a memory-efficient training framework based on differentiable spike-time discretization (DSTD) for leaky integrate-and-fire neurons with general membrane and synaptic time constants. DSTD maps irregular presynaptic spikes onto differentiable weighted events at fixed time points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with $M$ fixed time intervals while accurately approximating continuous-time membrane-potential dynamics. This reduces candidate-related activation memory from $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}N_{\mathrm{in}})$ to $O(N_{\mathrm{out}}M)$ in the case of time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, where $N_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{out}}$ denote the numbers of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons, respectively. We further introduce synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization that organizes layer-wise firing windows, mitigates dead-neuron failures, and enables pipeline-like processing. In dense LIF layers, DSTD reduced peak memory consumption by up to approximately 100-fold and training time by up to approximately 20-fold compared with exact spike-time computation. Together, these methods allowed us to train 9-layer convolutional SNNs on CIFAR-10 and 20-layer convolutional SNNs on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: DSTD replaces exact, memory-intensive spike-time computation in continuous-time SNN training with a differentiable discretization onto M fixed time intervals, reducing activation memory from O(N_out·N_in) to O(N_out·M). Combined with synfire-chain temporal regularization, this enables up to ~100× memory reduction and ~20× speedup, allowing training of deep convolutional SNNs (9-layer on CIFAR-10, 20-layer on Fashion-MNIST) on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Training deep continuous-time SNNs is bottlenecked by the memory required for exact spike-time computation, which must evaluate and store candidate firing times over intervals determined by presynaptic spike ordering. This O(N_out·N_in) memory scaling makes training deep networks prohibitive, especially under TTFS coding. The authors seek to decouple memory cost from the number of presynaptic neurons while preserving accurate membrane dynamics.
AI.method: (1) Differentiable Spike-Time Discretization (DSTD): maps irregular presynaptic spike times onto differentiable weighted events at M fixed temporal grid points, replacing the input-dependent candidate dimension with a fixed discretization. This approximates continuous-time LIF membrane potential dynamics while reducing candidate memory. (2) Synfire-chain-inspired temporal regularization: organizes layer-wise firing windows into sequential, pipeline-like processing to mitigate dead-neuron failures and improve training stability.
AI.result: DSTD reduced peak memory by up to ~100× and training time by up to ~20× compared to exact spike-time computation in dense LIF layers. The combined approach enabled training a 9-layer convolutional SNN on CIFAR-10 and a 20-layer convolutional SNN on Fashion-MNIST on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: DSTD with temporal regularization makes training deep continuous-time SNNs feasible on resource-limited hardware by breaking the memory bottleneck of exact spike-time computation, without sacrificing the differentiable approximation of membrane dynamics.

title: TopoAgent: A Self-Evolving Topological Agent for Multimodal Scientific Reasoning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in general tasks, rigorous scientific reasoning remains challenging due to the limitations of monolithic, linear planning. Such sequential designs often suffer from visual-semantic misalignment, long-context hallucinations, and brittle execution under fixed task granularity. We propose TopoAgent, a self-evolving topological framework that replaces linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution. TopoAgent first employs a front-end decomposer to fracture complex queries into visually-grounded atoms. These atoms are organized into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) based on their dependencies, enabling strict context isolation to shield the reasoning engine from irrelevant historical noise. Furthermore, we introduce adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically splits bottleneck nodes into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime when tool capability boundaries are exceeded. Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks demonstrate that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, providing a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning.

AI.tldr: TopoAgent replaces linear planning in MLLMs with a self-evolving Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) that decomposes complex scientific queries into isolated atomic units, dynamically splitting bottleneck atoms at runtime to surpass tool limits, achieving state-of-the-art results across math, physics, and chemistry benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs rely on monolithic, linear planning for scientific reasoning, which causes three critical failure modes: (1) visual-semantic misalignment between modalities, (2) hallucinations from long-context dependencies, and (3) brittle execution when task granularity is fixed and mismatched with tool capabilities. A new paradigm is needed that provides structured isolation and adaptive granularity.
AI.method: TopoAgent introduces a topological reasoning framework with three key components: (1) a front-end decomposer that fractures complex queries into visually-grounded atomic units; (2) a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) organizing these atoms by dependency, enforcing strict context isolation so each reasoning step is shielded from irrelevant historical noise; and (3) adaptive atomic fission, which dynamically detects bottleneck nodes that exceed tool capability boundaries and recursively splits them into finer-grained sub-atoms at runtime.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across mathematics, physics, and chemistry benchmarks show that TopoAgent significantly outperforms state-of-the-art linear agent frameworks, demonstrating superior robustness, noise resistance, and self-correction in autonomous scientific reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: TopoAgent establishes a robust, noise-resistant, and self-correcting paradigm for autonomous scientific reasoning by replacing linear trajectories with dynamic, state-isolated graph evolution, effectively overcoming the core limitations of monolithic planning in MLLMs.

title: Linear representations of grammaticality in neural language models
summary: Whether neural language models (NLMs) possess the ability to distinguish strings on the basis of their grammaticality remains a debated topic in the computational linguistics literature. Existing evidence has largely relied on probability-based measures, testing whether models assign higher probabilities to grammatical than ungrammatical strings. However, probability comparisons have been criticized as a measure for grammatical knowledge based on the assumption that grammaticality is inherently entangled with likelihood. Model-assigned probability is a function of many related sentence properties, such as lexical frequency, plausibility, and world knowledge. In this work, we move beyond probability-based evaluations and investigate whether grammaticality is encoded in the internal representations of NLMs. Using mass-mean probing, we test whether grammatical and ungrammatical sentences are systematically separated in representational space. We further examine the extent to which these representations are independent of sentence properties that are correlated with grammaticality, as well as their generalization across grammatical phenomena and languages. Our results provide evidence that grammaticality is robustly encoded in sentence representations of a wide range of pretrained NLMs, yielding clear representational separation on the dimension of grammaticality that cannot be fully explained by alternative sentence-level factors. Moreover, this encoding generalizes across a broad range of grammatical phenomena and to some degree, across languages, suggesting that grammaticality constitutes a coherent representational dimension in contemporary NLMs. These findings contribute new evidence to debates about the nature of syntactic knowledge in language models and offer a complementary framework for evaluating grammatical competence that is not dependent on string probabilities alone.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether grammaticality is encoded in the internal representations of neural language models (NLMs) using mass-mean probing, finding robust representational separation between grammatical and ungrammatical sentences that generalizes across phenomena and languages, independent of probability-based measures.
AI.motivation: Prior work on grammatical knowledge in NLMs relied on probability-based measures (comparing likelihoods of grammatical vs. ungrammatical strings), which are confounded by lexical frequency, plausibility, and world knowledge. The authors argue that grammaticality may be encoded in representations rather than reflected in output probabilities alone, motivating a shift to representation-level analysis.
AI.method: The authors employ mass-mean probing, a technique that tests whether grammatical and ungrammatical sentences form separable clusters in the representational space of NLMs. They further control for correlated sentence-level properties (e.g., plausibility, frequency) and test generalization across different grammatical phenomena and multiple languages.
AI.result: Grammaticality is robustly encoded in sentence representations across a wide range of pretrained NLMs, showing clear representational separation that cannot be fully explained by alternative sentence-level factors. This encoding generalizes broadly across grammatical phenomena and partially across languages, suggesting grammaticality forms a coherent representational dimension.
AI.conclusion: Grammaticality constitutes a coherent, systematic representational dimension in NLMs. The findings offer a complementary framework for evaluating grammatical competence beyond string probabilities alone, contributing new evidence to debates about the nature of syntactic knowledge in language models.

title: Grad2Fair: A Gradient-driven Approach for Graph Fairness without Demographics
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) frequently encounter group fairness issues, often yielding biased predictions against specific demographic groups defined by sensitive attributes such as gender or race. While this challenge has motivated extensive research, most existing solutions rely on the strong assumption that demographics are fully available. To bypass this strict requirement, a few recent studies have attempted to use predicted demographics as proxies to enforce fairness constraints. However, predicted demographics may be inaccurate, resulting in the failure to improve fairness. In this work, we investigate the problem of graph fairness without demographic information and avoid the utilization of predicted demographics. Motivated by our observation that the gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, we first propose GradDist, a gradient-based metric that quantifies bias by measuring the distance between local modes within these distributions. To mitigate this bias, we propose Gradient-to-Fairness (Grad2Fair), a gradient-guided approach for group fairness without demographics. Due to the potential demographics in gradients, Grad2Fair directly leverages gradients to debias and eliminates demographic prediction, thereby enabling stable fairness performance. Experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Grad2Fair, as evidenced by superior performance over baselines in most cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZzoomD/Grad2Fair.

AI.tldr: Grad2Fair proposes a gradient-based approach for achieving group fairness in GNNs without requiring demographic labels, using gradient distribution patterns as implicit proxies for bias and directly debiasing through gradient manipulation.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN fairness methods assume full availability of sensitive demographic attributes (gender, race). Recent work attempts using predicted demographics as proxies, but prediction inaccuracies undermine fairness improvements. The authors observe that gradient distributions of misclassified nodes implicitly encode demographic information, motivating a demographic-free debiasing approach.
AI.method: (1) GradDist: a gradient-based metric quantifying bias by measuring distance between local modes in gradient distributions of misclassified nodes. (2) Grad2Fair: a gradient-guided debiasing framework that directly uses gradients to mitigate group unfairness without requiring demographic prediction, exploiting the implicit demographic signals in gradient distributions for stable fairness performance.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple real-world datasets show Grad2Fair achieves superior fairness performance over baseline methods in most cases, demonstrating the effectiveness of gradient-guided debiasing without demographic information.
AI.conclusion: Gradients of misclassified nodes carry implicit demographic signals. Directly leveraging these gradients for debiasing (rather than predicting demographics) enables stable and effective group fairness in GNNs without requiring sensitive attribute labels. Code is publicly available.

title: SmartRAG: Native Graph-Based RAG for Mobile Device
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) as personal assistants on mobile devices demands privacy, low latency, and offline availability, yet the computational cost of giant models clashes with strict edge-hardware budgets. We argue that this tension cannot be resolved by model compression alone; it requires decomposing on-device intelligence into complementary functional roles. We present SmartRAG, a fully on-device framework that organizes an intelligent assistant around four coordinated modules -- Perception, Memory, Focus, and Thinking. At the core of SmartRAG is EvoNER, a continually learnable named-entity recognizer that incrementally expands its label inventory through teacher-distilled updates, enabling the system to absorb previously unseen entity types without retraining the backbone LLM. Extracted knowledge is stored in MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph, and retrieved at query time through a hybrid pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search. The on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value semantic operations -- labeling, planning, and answer synthesis -- keeping inference costs bounded. Experiments on four QA benchmarks (TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MultiHopQA) show that SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone achieves multi-hop reasoning performance competitive with models up to 18$\times$ larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency envelopes.

AI.tldr: SmartRAG is a fully on-device framework that decomposes mobile LLM assistants into four modules (Perception, Memory, Focus, Thinking), using a continually learnable NER (EvoNER) and a provenance-preserving knowledge graph (MRGraph) to achieve competitive multi-hop QA performance with a quantized 1.7B model on commodity smartphones.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs as personal assistants on mobile devices requires privacy, low latency, and offline availability, but the computational demands of large models conflict with edge-hardware constraints. The authors argue that model compression alone is insufficient and that on-device intelligence must instead be decomposed into complementary functional roles.
AI.method: SmartRAG comprises four coordinated modules: (1) Perception, featuring EvoNER, a continually learnable NER that expands its label set via teacher-distilled updates without retraining the backbone LLM; (2) Memory, using MRGraph, a three-layer provenance-preserving knowledge graph for storing extracted knowledge; (3) Focus, a hybrid retrieval pipeline combining graph traversal, lexical matching, and dense semantic search; and (4) Thinking, where the on-device LLM is invoked only for high-value operations (labeling, planning, answer synthesis) to keep inference costs bounded.
AI.result: On four QA benchmarks — TriviaQA, Natural Questions, HotpotQA, and MultiHopQA — SmartRAG with a quantized 1.7B-parameter backbone matched the multi-hop reasoning performance of models up to 18× larger, while running entirely on commodity smartphones within practical memory and latency limits.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing on-device intelligence into specialized, coordinated modules (rather than relying solely on model compression) enables effective personal assistant capabilities on mobile hardware, achieving competitive QA performance at a fraction of the model size.

title: T^2MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence
summary: Transformer reasoning is limited by autoregressive decoding, which repeat edly compresses rich hidden computation through token space and makes it difficult for intermediate reasoning states to persist across time. We in troduce Transformers with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence (T2MLR), a transformers-based latent reasoning architecture that fuses a cached middle layer representation from the previous token directly into an earlier layer of the current token position, enabling abstract intermediate computation to persist across decoding steps with little inference overhead. Across natural-language pretraining and multi-hop reasoning finetuning, T2MLR consistently outperforms data- and parameter-matched Transformer base lines. Moreover, applying recurrence to only a localized middle-layer block (as little as 20% of the network) often outperforms full-layer recurrence. Im portantly, T2MLR does not require pretraining from scratch: retrofitting the recurrent pathway into an existing pretrained 1.7B Transformer and briefly finetuning substantially improves math reasoning, lowering the barrier to practical adoption. These results suggest that effective latent reasoning in Transformers does not require looping over all layers as in previous works, but can instead emerge more strongly from targeted middle-layer recurrence.

AI.tldr: T2MLR introduces targeted middle-layer recurrence in Transformers, caching a middle-layer representation from the previous token and fusing it into an earlier layer of the current token. This enables persistent intermediate reasoning across decoding steps with minimal overhead, outperforming baselines on reasoning tasks, and can be retrofitted into existing pretrained models with brief finetuning.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive decoding in Transformers compresses rich hidden computation through the token bottleneck at each step, preventing intermediate reasoning states from persisting across time. Prior latent reasoning approaches (e.g., looping over all layers) are costly. The authors seek a more efficient mechanism for sustained abstract computation across decoding steps.
AI.method: T2MLR caches the representation from a middle layer at the previous token position and fuses it into an earlier layer at the current token position via a recurrent pathway. Crucially, recurrence is applied only to a localized middle-layer block (e.g., 20% of the network) rather than all layers. The architecture can be retrofitted into existing pretrained Transformers and requires only brief finetuning, avoiding pretraining from scratch.
AI.result: T2MLR consistently outperforms data- and parameter-matched Transformer baselines on natural-language pretraining and multi-hop reasoning finetuning. Localized middle-layer recurrence often surpasses full-layer recurrence. Retrofitting a 1.7B pretrained Transformer with the recurrent pathway and briefly finetuning substantially improves math reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: Effective latent reasoning in Transformers does not require looping over all layers. Targeted middle-layer recurrence is sufficient and often superior, offering a practical, low-overhead path to improved reasoning that can be retrofitted into existing large pretrained models.

title: MESHA: Mechanism-Enforced Sequential Halving for Strategic Linear Bandits
summary:
We design and analyze \underline{M}echanism-\underline{E}nforced \underline{S}equential \underline{HA}lving (MESHA), an algorithm for Best Arm Identification (BAI) in strategic linear bandits. In this setting, each arm may strategically misreport its feature vector to maximize the probability of being identified as the best arm, when rewards are generated from the arms' true but unobservable features. The design of MESHA applies the naïve uniform sampling rule and an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC): the former reduces the impact of arms' strategic behaviours and the latter eliminates arms whose reported features severely deviate from the ground truth. Considering an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium, we prove that any arm would attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize its identified probability and derive an upper bound on the failure probability of MESHA within a fixed budget $T$. We also show that state-of-the-art linear BAI algorithms with $G$-optimal design would fail in such strategic environment, as the optimal design (OD)-based sampling rule based on strategically reported features may {\it starve} the optimal arm of any sampling budget. Finally, extensive numerical experiments indicate that MESHA
  outperforms baselines that rely on OD-based sampling rules as well as the feature-agnostic baselines, corroborating the efficacy of MESHA.

AI.tldr: MESHA is a best arm identification algorithm for strategic linear bandits that combines uniform sampling with an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition to counter strategic misreporting of features by arms, provably bounding failure probability and outperforming G-optimal design baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard linear BAI algorithms using G-optimal design fail in strategic settings because arms can misreport their feature vectors to manipulate selection. The optimal design-based sampling rule may "starve" the true optimal arm of any sampling budget, leading to incorrect identification.
AI.method: MESHA employs two key mechanisms: (1) naive uniform sampling to reduce the leverage of strategic misreporting, and (2) an epoch-wise Grim Trigger Condition (GTC) that eliminates arms whose reported features deviate significantly from the ground truth. The algorithm is analyzed under an arbitrary Nash Equilibrium.
AI.result: The authors prove that under Nash Equilibrium, arms will attempt to pass the GTC check to maximize identification probability. They derive an upper bound on MESHA's failure probability within a fixed budget T. They also formally demonstrate that G-optimal design-based BAI algorithms fail in this strategic environment.
AI.conclusion: MESHA outperforms both OD-based sampling rule baselines and feature-agnostic baselines in extensive numerical experiments, validating the efficacy of the proposed approach for best arm identification under strategic behavior.

title: Mask-Aware Policy Gradients for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning has proven effective for improving reasoning in large language models, but extending it to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) remains challenging due to the intractability of the log-likelihood estimation. Existing approaches approximate this log-likelihood by modeling only the token predictions, ignoring the order in which positions are unmasked during generation. We observe that MDLM generation involves two decisions at each step: what tokens to place at each masked position and which positions to remask. We formalize this as a two-stage action MDP, showing that the policy gradient naturally decomposes into a token term and a masking term. Combining optimization of both terms leads to state-of-the-art outcomes on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, with scores of 87.1% on GSM8K and 53.4% on MBPP.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage action MDP formulation for reinforcement learning on Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs), decomposing the policy gradient into token and masking terms. Optimizing both jointly yields SOTA results on math reasoning (87.1% GSM8K) and coding (53.4% MBPP).
AI.motivation: RL has improved reasoning in autoregressive LLMs, but extending it to MDLMs is challenging because the log-likelihood of the generative process is intractable. Existing methods approximate this by modeling only token predictions while ignoring the unmasking order, leaving a crucial optimization signal unused.
AI.method: The authors formalize MDLM generation as a two-stage action Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each step involves: (1) selecting tokens for masked positions, and (2) choosing which positions to remask. This yields a policy gradient that naturally decomposes into a token term and a masking term, enabling joint optimization of both decisions via RL.
AI.result: The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance: 87.1% on GSM8K (mathematical reasoning) and 53.4% on MBPP (coding), demonstrating the benefit of optimizing both the token and masking decisions jointly.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage action MDP framework effectively enables RL for MDLMs by capturing both what to place and where to remask. Joint optimization of both terms yields significant improvements over prior methods that only model token predictions.

title: Counterfactuals for Feature-Weighted Clustering
summary: Counterfactual explanations provide local, interpretable insight by identifying changes to an input that would alter its assigned outcome. Although well established in supervised learning, their extension to clustering is less direct, since cluster assignments are unlabeled and governed by the geometry of the partition. This paper introduces VoICE, a Voronoi-Induced Counterfactual Explainability framework for feature-weighted $k$-means clustering. Rather than treating cluster change as a crossing of a single pairwise centroid boundary, VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, incorporating feature weights directly into both the clustering geometry and the counterfactual objective to yield least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints. Target regions are further intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted towards their centroids, limiting extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. VoICE consistently produces valid target-cluster membership, across several benchmark datasets, where the leading pairwise baseline does not.

AI.tldr: VoICE generates counterfactual explanations for feature-weighted k-means clustering by projecting instances onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, yielding least-cost, parsimonious, and valid explanations under actionability constraints.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual explanations are well established in supervised learning but poorly adapted to clustering, where assignments are unlabeled and geometry-driven. Existing pairwise-boundary approaches fail to reliably produce valid target-cluster membership, motivating a geometry-aware method that respects the full partition structure.
AI.method: VoICE formulates counterfactual generation as projection onto the full weighted Voronoi region of a target cluster, embedding feature weights into both the distance metric and the counterfactual objective. Target regions are intersected with data-derived bounds and homothetically contracted toward centroids to reduce extrapolation and boundary sensitivity. The framework produces least-cost and parsimonious explanations under actionability constraints.
AI.result: VoICE consistently achieves valid target-cluster membership across multiple benchmark datasets, whereas the leading pairwise baseline method does not.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating the full weighted Voronoi geometry into counterfactual search yields reliable, cost-effective explanations for feature-weighted k-means clustering, overcoming the validity failures of pairwise-boundary approaches.

title: Stop Thinking, Start Looking: Efficient Post-Training for Multimodal Document Question Answering via Reasoning-Free Alignment
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026, Workshop on Efficient Multimodal Question Answering (EMM-QA)
summary: Efficient multimodal document question answering with explicit visual grounding, locating the precise document region that supports each answer remains an open challenge. Current approaches bifurcate into Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which requires large annotated datasets and reaches optimization plateaus, and reasoning-centric Reinforcement Learning (RL), which depends on verbose intermediate traces that inflate inference token cost without clear benefit. We introduce Perception-RFT, a training framework that applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to directly align visual features with structured grounding outputs. To rigorously evaluate the necessity of reasoning, we construct a reasoning variant under identical reward settings. We find that reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies at the 4B parameter scale, reducing per-query inference token length by more than 60%, while reasoning-enabled RL underperforms perception-only training. Through a fine-grained analysis of Qwen3-VL-4B optimization dynamics, we confirm that SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability established in text-domain post-training extend to multimodal, and identify a previously uncharacterized Grounding Divergence: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision on two out of distribution (OOD) benchmarks (4,828 samples) under joint RL optimization. We further show that an early SFT$\rightarrow$RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.

AI.tldr: Perception-RFT introduces GRPO-based RL for multimodal document QA that directly aligns visual features with grounding outputs, bypassing reasoning tokens. At 4B scale, reasoning-trained models suppress traces and converge to perception-only policies, reducing inference tokens by 60%+. The paper identifies "Grounding Divergence" — a trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision under joint RL — and shows early SFT→RL transition saves 65% training data.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal document QA approaches face a dichotomy: SFT requires large annotated datasets and plateaus, while reasoning-centric RL inflates inference token costs with intermediate traces that provide no clear benefit. The authors aim to determine whether explicit reasoning traces are necessary for visual grounding and to characterize optimization dynamics in multimodal post-training.
AI.method: Perception-RFT applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) directly to multimodal document QA, bypassing intermediate reasoning tokens to align visual features with structured grounding outputs. A reasoning-enabled variant is constructed under identical reward settings for controlled comparison. Fine-grained optimization analysis is conducted on Qwen3-VL-4B, with evaluation across two OOD benchmarks (4,828 samples).
AI.result: Reasoning-enabled models suppress their reasoning traces during training, converging to direct perception-based policies. Perception-only RL outperforms reasoning-enabled RL, reducing per-query inference tokens by >60%. SFT saturation and cold-start RL instability extend from text to multimodal domains. A new phenomenon, Grounding Divergence, is identified: a selective trade-off between semantic robustness and geometric precision under joint RL optimization. Early SFT→RL transition achieves comparable precision with 65% less training data.
AI.conclusion: Explicit reasoning traces are unnecessary and even detrimental for multimodal document visual grounding at the 4B parameter scale. GRPO-based perception-only RL is more efficient and effective. The discovery of Grounding Divergence reveals fundamental tensions in joint optimization of semantic and geometric objectives, and the early transition strategy offers practical data efficiency gains.

title: Expanding the Lexicon of Ge'ez Based African Languages: A Comparative Study of Amharic and Tigrinya
summary: Multilingual pre-trained language models (PLMs) exhibit degraded performance on low-resource, non-Latin-script languages, driven by high out-of-vocabulary (OOV) rates and excessive subword fragmentation that result from Latin-script-centric tokenizer training. We introduce VEXMLM, a vocabulary-extended variant of XLM-R targeting the two highest-resource Ge'ez-script languages, Amharic and Tigrinya, and further evaluated on 17 additional low-resource African languages (19 total). We train a language-specific SentencePiece tokenizer on curated Amharic and Tigrinya monolingual corpora, extend XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords derived from this tokenizer, and initialize their embeddings by averaging the embeddings of their constituent subwords under XLM-R's original tokenizer. VEXMLM is trained in two stages: (1) continued masked language modeling over the extended vocabulary on the curated corpora, and (2) supervised fine-tuning on question answering (QA), named entity recognition (NER), and sentiment analysis (SA). On Amharic/Tigrinya QA, VEXMLM achieves 87.0 EM /90.0 F1, versus 66.0 EM/78.0 F1 for XLM-R and 74.0 EM/ 78.0 F1 for Glot500. On SA, VEXMLM reaches 80.0\% accuracy versus 77.0\% (XLM-R) and 46.0\% (Glot500). On NER, VEXMLM raises OOV-token entity accuracy from 81.4\% to 94.3\%, averaged over 11 of the 19 evaluated languages for which OOV analysis was possible. Our contributions are: (i) a vocabulary-extension and embedding-initialization procedure tailored to Ge'ez script; (ii) a two-stage training strategy under which vocabulary and continued-pretraining gains on Amharic/Tigrinya transfer to 17 typologically related, unaugmented African languages; and (iii) an evaluation spanning both intrinsic tokenization metrics (vocabulary coverage, fertility, OOV rate) and extrinsic task performance across all 19 languages.

AI.tldr: VEXMLM extends XLM-R's vocabulary with Ge'ez-script subwords to improve performance on Amharic, Tigrinya, and 17 other low-resource African languages, achieving substantial gains in QA, NER, and sentiment analysis by reducing OOV rates and subword fragmentation.
AI.motivation: Multilingual PLMs like XLM-R suffer degraded performance on low-resource, non-Latin-script languages due to Latin-script-centric tokenizer training, causing high OOV rates and excessive subword fragmentation. This is especially acute for Ge'ez-script languages such as Amharic and Tigrinya.
AI.method: (1) Train a language-specific SentencePiece tokenizer on curated Amharic/Tigrinya corpora; (2) Extend XLM-R's vocabulary with 30,000 Ge'ez-script subwords; (3) Initialize new embeddings by averaging constituent subword embeddings from XLM-R's original tokenizer; (4) Continue MLM pre-training with the extended vocabulary; (5) Supervised fine-tuning on QA, NER, and SA tasks.
AI.result: On Amharic/Tigrinya QA: 87.0 EM/90.0 F1 (vs. XLM-R 66.0/78.0 and Glot500 74.0/78.0). On SA: 80.0% accuracy (vs. XLM-R 77.0% and Glot500 46.0%). On NER: OOV-token entity accuracy improved from 81.4% to 94.3% averaged over 11 languages. Gains transfer to 17 additional unaugmented African languages.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary extension with script-specific subwords plus embedding initialization via constituent averaging, combined with continued MLM pre-training, effectively mitigates OOV and fragmentation issues for low-resource non-Latin-script languages, with benefits transferring to typologically related languages not seen during vocabulary augmentation.

title: What's in a Smoothness Constant? Tighter Rates for Local SGD with Bounded Second-order Heterogeneity
summary: Local SGD, also known as Federated Averaging, is a widely used distributed optimization algorithm. Although Local SGD often outperforms alternatives such as Mini-batch SGD in practice, theory still only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Recent work by [Patel et al., 2025] shows that a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption captures the efficiency of Local SGD for strongly convex objectives, and conjectures that the same principle extends to the general convex setting. In this paper, we prove this conjecture by establishing an improved convergence guarantee for Local SGD on general convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity. We also improve the best-known lower bounds for Local SGD in this setting, showing that our upper bounds are nearly tight. Together, these results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD. As a further application of our techniques, we provide a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement, showing how second-order heterogeneity captures the impact of rare high-curvature clients.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a conjecture by Patel et al. (2025) that bounded second-order heterogeneity explains the efficiency of Local SGD for general convex objectives, establishes matching lower bounds, and extends the analysis to serial SGD with replacement.
AI.motivation: Local SGD (Federated Averaging) empirically outperforms mini-batch SGD, but existing theory only partially explains when and why local updates help under realistic data heterogeneity. Prior work established results for strongly convex objectives under bounded second-order heterogeneity and conjectured the same principle holds for general convex settings — this paper aims to prove that conjecture.
AI.method: The authors derive improved convergence upper bounds for Local SGD on general convex objectives under a bounded second-order heterogeneity assumption (Hessian dissimilarity). They also construct worst-case problem instances to establish lower bounds, demonstrating near-tightness. The techniques are further applied to analyze serial SGD with replacement, capturing the effect of rare high-curvature clients.
AI.result: The paper proves the conjecture: under bounded second-order heterogeneity, Local SGD achieves provably faster convergence for general convex objectives. The derived upper bounds are shown to be nearly tight via improved lower bounds. Additionally, a lower bound for serial SGD with replacement is established, showing how second-order heterogeneity quantifies the impact of rare high-curvature clients.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a sharper, more fine-grained convergence theory for Local SGD, demonstrating that bounded second-order heterogeneity is the key structural condition that captures when and why local updates are beneficial — extending this understanding from strongly convex to general convex objectives.

title: InCarEmo: A Multimodal Dataset for In-Cabin Emotion Recognition and Driver State Monitoring
summary: Understanding driver emotion and state is critical for the next generation of intelligent in-cabin systems that ensure safety and enhance human-vehicle interaction. However, existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing are largely limited to visual modalities and rarely include conversational information, making it difficult to capture the linguistic and interactive cues underlying driver emotion. To address these gaps, we introduce InCarEmo, a multimodal dataset for in-cabin emotion recognition and driver state monitoring. InCarEmo integrates RGB and infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text collected from scripted in-cabin scenarios designed to simulate realistic driver behaviors, covering diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts. The dataset supports three primary tasks: 1) multimodal emotion recognition, 2) fatigue detection, and 3) distraction monitoring. In addition to the original Chinese data, we construct an auxiliary English benchmark to support preliminary cross-lingual evaluation. We provide a unified benchmark with extensive baseline results across unimodal and multimodal methods, including analyses under modality-missing and noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of multimodal fusion and reveal remaining challenges under real-world noise and low-light conditions. By releasing InCarEmo, we aim to establish a comprehensive foundation for robust, interpretable, and human-centric in-cabin affective understanding, promoting safer and more empathetic driver-vehicle interaction.

AI.tldr: InCarEmo is a multimodal in-cabin dataset integrating RGB/IR video, audio, and dialogue text for driver emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring, with benchmarks for both Chinese and English cross-lingual evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing public datasets for in-cabin affective computing rely predominantly on visual modalities and lack conversational/linguistic data, which are essential for capturing the full spectrum of driver emotional and cognitive states. This gap hinders the development of robust multimodal systems for intelligent in-cabin safety and interaction.
AI.method: The authors construct InCarEmo by collecting scripted in-cabin scenarios under diverse lighting conditions and driving contexts, recording synchronized RGB video, infrared video, in-cabin audio, and dialogue text. They define three primary tasks — multimodal emotion recognition, fatigue detection, and distraction monitoring — and establish a unified benchmark with extensive unimodal and multimodal baselines, including modality-missing and noise-robustness analyses. An auxiliary English-translated benchmark is also created for cross-lingual preliminary evaluation.
AI.result: Multimodal fusion consistently outperforms unimodal approaches across all three tasks. However, performance degrades under real-world noise and low-light conditions, highlighting unresolved robustness challenges. The cross-lingual benchmark provides initial comparative insights between Chinese and English settings.
AI.conclusion: InCarEmo fills a critical gap in multimodal in-cabin affective computing by providing a linguistically and visually rich dataset. It establishes a foundation for robust, interpretable, human-centric driver monitoring systems, though significant challenges remain in real-world noise resilience and low-light performance.

title: In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs
summary: A tokenizer fixed at the start of pre-training allocates vocabulary in proportion to the pre-training corpus, reflecting the deployment priorities at that time. When those priorities shift, languages added later are split into many more tokens per word, which can raise latency, compute, and energy consumption for users of those languages. Cloud models can afford a broad vocabulary because the embedding and LM-head matrices are a small fraction of their parameters. On a compact model those matrices are a material share of per-token decode bandwidth, so on-device models ship small vocabularies and accept fragmentation outside a fixed language set. We present tokenizer expansion, an in-place recipe for upgrading a pre-trained model's tokenizer when the model producer controls its design. We continue the existing tokenizer's BPE merges on a multilingual corpus, so most source tokens carry over unchanged as single tokens and every new token has an exact decomposition into source tokens. We copy the carried-over embedding rows unchanged and initialize new rows as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings. A two-stage adaptation, embedding-only training then full-model continued pre-training, recovers source-checkpoint quality. We apply the recipe to a continued pre-trained checkpoint of LFM2-8B-A1B, an 8B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model, to help produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K tokenizer. The expanded tokenizer encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in roughly $2.4\times$ and $2.6\times$ fewer tokens than the source (up to $4.0\times$ on Thai). Combining these reductions with the measured per-token cost of the larger vocabulary, we estimate a $2.2$-$3.7\times$ per-character decode speedup for these languages across our reference devices. We release the model weights and the expanded tokenizer, and report the negative findings that shaped the recipe.

AI.tldr: A method to expand a pre-trained model's tokenizer in-place, continuing BPE merges on a multilingual corpus so that existing tokens carry over unchanged and new tokens are initialized from source sub-token embeddings. Applied to an 8B MoE model, it achieves 2.4–4.0× token reduction for under-represented languages, yielding an estimated 2.2–3.7× per-character decode speedup on-device.
AI.motivation: On-device compact models ship with small vocabularies optimized for a fixed set of languages at pre-training time. When deployment priorities shift to new languages, those languages suffer from severe token fragmentation (many tokens per word), increasing latency, compute, and energy consumption. Cloud models can afford large vocabularies, but on-device models cannot due to the material share of embedding/LM-head matrices in per-token decode bandwidth. The paper addresses the need to upgrade a tokenizer post-hoc without retraining from scratch.
AI.method: Tokenizer expansion: (1) Continue the existing BPE merge table on a multilingual corpus, preserving all original merges so source tokens remain single tokens and every new token has an exact decomposition into source tokens. (2) Copy carried-over embedding rows unchanged; initialize new rows as the mean of their source sub-token embeddings. (3) Two-stage adaptation: embedding-only training (freezing all other parameters) followed by full-model continued pre-training to recover source-checkpoint quality. Applied to LFM2-8B-A1B to produce LFM2.5-8B-A1B with a 128K vocabulary.
AI.result: The expanded 128K tokenizer encodes Hindi and Vietnamese in roughly 2.4× and 2.6× fewer tokens than the source tokenizer, and up to 4.0× fewer on Thai. Combined with measured per-token cost of the larger vocabulary, this translates to an estimated 2.2–3.7× per-character decode speedup across reference devices. The two-stage adaptation recovers source-checkpoint quality.
AI.conclusion: Tokenizer expansion is a practical, in-place recipe for upgrading a pre-trained model's tokenizer to support new languages efficiently, without full retraining. The method preserves existing token mappings, minimizes disruption to learned representations, and delivers substantial efficiency gains for under-represented languages on resource-constrained devices. The authors release model weights and the expanded tokenizer, along with negative findings that informed the recipe design.

title: GAttNHP: Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process for Extrapolation Reasoning in Temporal Knowledge Graphs
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) record how facts evolve over time, but forecasting future events on a TKG remains difficult for three reasons: (i) long-range temporal dependencies are hard to encode; (ii) events on different chains mutually excite or inhibit one another in ways that snapshot-level models cannot express; and (iii) inter-arrival times are heavy-tailed and statistically sparse, so deterministic time predictors are unreliable. We address these three issues with a single framework, the \textbf{Group Attention Neural Hawkes Process (GAttNHP)}, built around three matched components. First, a self-attention encoder casts each subject--relation chain as a continuous-time point process and captures the lingering excitation of distant history. Second, a semantic soft-grouping module turns globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, so chains share excitation patterns through their latent group memberships rather than through exhaustive pairwise computation. Third, a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head replaces mean-based time prediction, providing calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates that remain stable under heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. On six benchmark TKG datasets, GAttNHP improves over state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction, and ablations confirm that its largest gains arise on the long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.

AI.tldr: GAttNHP combines self-attention over continuous-time point processes, a semantic soft-grouping module with Hawkes priors for cross-chain excitation, and Non-Crossing Quantile regression to address long-range dependencies, mutual excitation/inhibition, and heavy-tailed inter-arrival times in TKG forecasting, achieving SOTA on six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Three core challenges in TKG forecasting: (1) difficulty encoding long-range temporal dependencies, (2) snapshot-level models cannot capture mutual excitation/inhibition across different event chains, and (3) heavy-tailed, statistically sparse inter-arrival times make deterministic time predictors unreliable.
AI.method: A unified framework with three matched components: (1) a self-attention encoder that models subject-relation chains as continuous-time point processes to capture lingering excitation from distant history; (2) a semantic soft-grouping module that transforms globally learnable Hawkes priors into an analytical cross-attention mask, enabling chains to share excitation patterns via latent group memberships rather than exhaustive pairwise computation; (3) a Non-Crossing Quantile (NCQ) regression head that produces calibrated, monotonically ordered quantile estimates stable under heavy-tailed distributions.
AI.result: GAttNHP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both entity prediction and time prediction across six benchmark TKG datasets. Ablations show the largest gains occur on long-tail event chains where existing models fail most severely.
AI.conclusion: The GAttNHP framework effectively addresses the three identified challenges in TKG forecasting, with the NCQ regression head and semantic grouping providing particularly critical improvements for long-tail and heavy-tailed scenarios.

title: AI vs Human Expert Reasoning: Assessing Agreements in Building Typology Predictions based on Street View Imagery
summary: This research investigates the potential of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to infer building typologies: Construction, Current Use, and Storeys from Google Street View (GSV) images. Predictions generated by VLMs are compared with inference by human experts (civil engineers and architects) as a source of manually labelled ground-truth data. We evaluate several state-of-the-art VLMs, including GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash. By applying different scaling strategies and prompting techniques, we found that Chain-of-Thought prompts provide an overall more stable model performance. We also investigate the reasoning behind VLMs' building-typology predictions by examining the probabilities of keywords appearing in AI explanations. This enabled us to analyse patterns in these reasonings and identify key themes driving both agreements and disagreements between VLM and expert labels. We find that AI tends to focus on visual indicators, whereas human experts place greater emphasis on broader contextual cues and domain knowledge, in addition to visual cues. Overall, VLM can approximate experts' capability in building-typology classification at scale, with an average accuracy of approximately 70%. The study demonstrates the VLM's potential for AI automation in tasks that require pattern recognition and object identification in an urban context. AI have the potential to serve as complementary and collaborative tools for urban analysis, leveraging their strengths in understanding visual patterns. This study contributes to the exploration of the efficiency and scalability of AI visual prediction and provides insights into the reasoning processes that could support automation processes in urban analysis and prediction.

AI.tldr: VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) can infer building typologies (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) from Google Street View images with ~70% accuracy. Chain-of-Thought prompting yields the most stable performance. AI relies on visual indicators, while human experts incorporate contextual/domain knowledge, suggesting VLMs can serve as complementary tools for urban analysis.
AI.motivation: To assess whether Vision-Language Models can automate building-typology classification at scale from street-level imagery, and to understand how AI reasoning compares with human expert judgment in this domain.
AI.method: Multiple state-of-the-art VLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.0 Flash) were prompted to predict building typologies (Construction, Current Use, Storeys) from GSV images. Various scaling strategies and prompting techniques (including Chain-of-Thought) were tested. Predictions were benchmarked against ground-truth labels from civil engineers and architects. Keyword probability analysis of AI explanations was used to probe reasoning patterns and identify drivers of agreement/disagreement with experts.
AI.result: Chain-of-Thought prompting produced the most stable model performance. Average classification accuracy was approximately 70%. AI predominantly focuses on visual indicators, whereas human experts also leverage broader contextual cues and domain knowledge. Keyword analysis of AI explanations revealed distinct reasoning themes underlying both concordance and discordance with expert labels.
AI.conclusion: VLMs show strong potential as scalable, complementary tools for urban analysis, particularly in pattern recognition and object identification tasks. They can approximate human expert performance in building-typology classification, but their visual-centric reasoning differs from the context-rich judgment of domain experts. The study advances understanding of AI reasoning processes that could underpin automation in urban analysis.

title: Language Identification via Compositional Data Analysis: A Linear-Time Classifier Based on Log-Ratio Geometry
summary:
Language identification is commonly addressed using either neural architectures or statistical n-gram models. Neural approaches typically require substantial computational resources, whereas classical frequency-based methods offer efficient linear-time performance, but rely on distance metrics that are not always appropriate for compositional data.
  This work models character and bigram frequency distributions as compositional vectors constrained to the simplex and mapped via the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation bijectively onto the $(D-1)$-dimensional zero-sum subspace of $\mathbb{R}^D$, where Euclidean distances correspond to Aitchison distances. A pipeline is proposed, combining CLR-transformed unigram and bigram features with Laplace smoothing to address sparsity. The method is evaluated on six languages.
  Experimental results show that the proposed approach achieves robust accuracy across different text lengths, with strong performance for longer sequences. These findings indicate that compositional representations provide a deterministic and computationally efficient alternative for language identification, particularly in settings where interpretability and low resource consumption are essential.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a language identification method that treats character n-gram frequencies as compositional data on the simplex, applying the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation so that Euclidean distance equals Aitchison distance, combined with Laplace smoothing, achieving robust accuracy with low computational cost.
AI.motivation: Neural language identification methods are computationally expensive, while classical n-gram frequency methods use distance metrics (e.g., Euclidean, cosine) that are statistically inappropriate for compositional/proportional data constrained to the simplex. This motivates a principled compositional approach using Aitchison geometry.
AI.method: Character unigram and bigram frequency distributions are modeled as compositional vectors on the simplex. The centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation maps them bijectively to a (D-1)-dimensional zero-sum subspace of ℝ^D, where Euclidean distance equals Aitchison distance — the natural metric for compositional data. Laplace smoothing handles zero-count sparsity. A pipeline combining CLR-transformed features is evaluated for language identification across six languages.
AI.result: The CLR-based compositional approach achieves robust accuracy across varying text lengths, with particularly strong performance on longer sequences, demonstrating competitiveness as a lightweight alternative.
AI.conclusion: Compositional representations with CLR transformation offer a deterministic, computationally efficient, and interpretable alternative for language identification, well-suited to low-resource settings where neural methods are impractical.

title: ChronoQG: Towards a Temporally Expressive and Hop-Bounded Benchmark for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Generation
summary: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) aims to generate natural-language questions from structured graph evidence. Existing KGQG benchmarks, however, are mostly built on static knowledge graphs and do not encode the temporal scopes of graph facts. As a result, they cannot evaluate whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal validity, event ordering, and answer-determining temporal constraints. In this paper, we study temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), where a generated question must be faithful to both the support subgraph and the temporal constraints required to identify the target answer. We propose ChronoQG, the first temporally expressive and hop-bounded benchmark construction framework for TKGQG. ChronoQG integrates a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy, topology-temporal subgraph sampling, and trace-grounded question generation to construct temporally faithful questions. The framework produces four benchmark datasets from heterogeneous temporal knowledge graphs, totaling 16,011 verified questions. We evaluate representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines across diverse TKGQG settings, including temporal-constraint counts, topological templates, and temporal-constraint types. The results show that existing methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types. These findings reveal a clear gap between static KGQG and TKGQG, and establish ChronoQG as a challenging testbed for temporally faithful question generation.

AI.tldr: ChronoQG introduces the first benchmark framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation (TKGQG), producing 16,011 verified questions with rich temporal constraints. Existing LLM-based KGQG methods struggle to preserve temporal constraints, especially in multi-constraint and harder temporal scenarios, revealing a significant gap between static and temporal KGQG.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQG benchmarks rely on static knowledge graphs that lack temporal scopes (e.g., validity periods, event ordering). Consequently, they cannot assess whether generated questions faithfully preserve temporal constraints critical for identifying the correct answer. This motivates the need for a temporally expressive benchmark to evaluate TKGQG.
AI.method: ChronoQG combines three components: (1) a comprehensive temporal-constraint taxonomy covering various temporal reasoning types; (2) topology-temporal subgraph sampling that extracts hop-bounded support subgraphs with temporal annotations; and (3) trace-grounded question generation that produces natural-language questions faithful to both the subgraph structure and temporal constraints. The framework is applied to four heterogeneous TKGs, yielding 16,011 verified question-answer pairs.
AI.result: Evaluation of representative LLM-based KGQG methods and prompting baselines shows that all existing approaches struggle to preserve temporal constraints. Performance degrades notably under multi-constraint settings and harder temporal-constraint types, demonstrating that current methods are insufficient for temporally faithful question generation.
AI.conclusion: There exists a clear and substantial gap between static KGQG and TKGQG. ChronoQG establishes a challenging testbed that exposes the limitations of current methods and calls for new approaches capable of faithfully incorporating temporal constraints into generated questions.

title: Global Index on Responsible AI: 2026 Report
summary: Grounded in human rights-based frameworks such as the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, the Global Index on Responsible AI (GIRAI) examines how countries translate responsible AI commitments into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms. GIRAI 2026 assesses these across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service. A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points on 38 indicators organised across three pillars: government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), civil society engagement (5), enabling conditions (15), and documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. The data covers November 2023 to September 2025. A score of 100 is derived from the indicators to rank all countries. Findings show that while responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government policy or initiative across the 17 AI Policy indicators, this does not often translate into meaningful protection. For instance, Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new cases of indicators with frameworks since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks remain non-binding compared with 42% in the Global North. Government commitment to AI governance also does not extend to their own algorithms: whereas Transparency and Explainability is the strongest performing indicator, with 58% of countries having some framework, only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was also found in 35 countries. These findings show that responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress.

AI.tldr: GIRAI 2026 evaluates 135 countries on responsible AI governance across 38 indicators, finding that while AI policy frameworks are expanding globally, they rarely translate into binding, enforceable protections — particularly in the Global South, where 78% of frameworks remain non-binding. The study also documents unacceptable-risk government AI deployments in 35 countries.
AI.motivation: To assess whether countries' responsible AI commitments — grounded in human rights-based frameworks like the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI — are being translated into enforceable protections, institutional capacity, and redress mechanisms, rather than remaining as non-binding policy statements.
AI.method: A global network of 135 country-level researchers collected and assessed 68,138 data points across 38 indicators organized into three pillars: (1) government AI policy and implementation (17 indicators), (2) civil society engagement (5 indicators), plus enabling conditions (15 indicators), and (3) documented cases of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems. Data spans November 2023 to September 2025. A composite score out of 100 ranks all countries across five dimensions: Inclusion and Diversity, Ethics and Sustainability, Labour and Skills, Trust and Safety, and AI Use in Public Service.
AI.result: Responsible AI governance is expanding, with 126 of 135 countries having at least one government AI policy or initiative. However, this rarely translates into meaningful protection. Global South countries account for 203 of 306 new framework cases since the first edition, yet 78% of their frameworks are non-binding versus 42% in the Global North. Transparency and Explainability is the strongest indicator (58% of countries have some framework), but only 18% require Public Disclosure of Government Algorithms. Credible evidence of government deployment of unacceptable-risk AI systems was found in 35 countries.
AI.conclusion: Responsible AI governance must move beyond framework adoption toward enforceable rights-based protections, adequately resourced oversight institutions, and accessible redress mechanisms to close the gap between commitment and meaningful protection.

title: TikStance: A Multimodal and Hierarchical Dataset for Multi-target Stance Analysis in TikTok Political Conversations
summary: Political discourse has increasingly moved to short-video platforms, yet computational analysis of such content remains constrained by the scarcity of datasets that jointly preserve audiovisual information and hierarchical conversations. Here we present TikStance, a multimodal and context-aware dataset comprising 161 videos and 13,876 comments from TikTok, designed for stance detection in political discussions. The dataset covers three major political figures in the 2024 U.S. election cycle--Donald Trump, Joe Biden, and Kamala Harris--with content collected between September 2023 and January 2025. Each discussion unit links a host video and its metadata to a parent-linked comment tree, enabling stance analysis within both audiovisual and conversational context. Each item was independently labeled by three annotators using a three-class scheme (Favor, Against, None) for video-to-target and comment-to-target stance; items with disagreement were re-annotated, and the final Krippendorff's \(α\) reached 0.743, 0.723, and 0.722 for the Trump, Biden, and Harris subsets, respectively. Descriptive analysis further reveals target-dependent differences in stance distributions and conversational depth, with nested replies accounting for 23.3\% of all comments. By combining multi-target coverage, hierarchical conversations, and reliable multi-level human annotations, TikStance supports research in multimodal stance detection, political communication, computational social science, and context-aware natural language processing.

AI.tldr: TikStance is a multimodal, context-aware dataset of 161 TikTok videos and 13,876 comments for political stance detection, covering Trump, Biden, and Harris during the 2024 U.S. election cycle with hierarchical conversation trees and high inter-annotator agreement (α ≈ 0.72–0.74).
AI.motivation: Political discourse has shifted to short-video platforms like TikTok, but existing datasets lack joint audiovisual information and hierarchical conversation structure, limiting computational analysis of stance in multimodal, context-rich environments.
AI.method: The authors collected 161 TikTok host videos and 13,876 comments (September 2023–January 2025) targeting Trump, Biden, and Harris. Each discussion unit links a host video with metadata to a parent-linked comment tree. Three independent annotators labeled each item with a three-class scheme (Favor, Against, None) for both video-to-target and comment-to-target stance. Disagreements were re-annotated, with final reliability measured via Krippendorff's α.
AI.result: Krippendorff's α reached 0.743 (Trump), 0.723 (Biden), and 0.722 (Harris), indicating substantial inter-annotator agreement. Descriptive analysis revealed target-dependent differences in stance distributions and conversational depth; nested replies constituted 23.3% of all comments.
AI.conclusion: TikStance, with its multi-target coverage, hierarchical conversations, and reliable multi-level human annotations, supports research in multimodal stance detection, political communication, computational social science, and context-aware NLP.

title: Evaluating Epistemic Uncertainty: Beyond OOD Detection and Active Learning
summary: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on tasks such as out-ofdistribution detection and active learning. However, the Bayes-optimal decision strategies for these tasks do not coincide with the scores commonly used to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Building on the epistemic reject-option framework, we evaluate epistemic uncertainty using its ability to identify regret, the reducible error. Formulating selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret, we prove the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of the ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical unification exposes a weakness in recent uncertainty disentanglement literature: we demonstrate that standard correlation metrics between learned components do not necessarily predict their actual operational utility. We instead propose to evaluate the achievable risk, regret, coverage surface of the decomposition as a diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. Benchmarking standard methods on datasets with dense human annotations reveals that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions between methods that are top-ranked on one criterion and bottom-ranked on other.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes evaluating epistemic uncertainty through its ability to identify regret (reducible error) within a selective prediction framework, proving the optimal selector is a thresholded convex combination of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. This theoretical result exposes that standard correlation metrics fail to predict operational utility, and the authors instead advocate evaluating the achievable risk-regret-coverage surface, demonstrating that decision-theoretic rankings often disagree with proxy-task rankings.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of epistemic uncertainty relies on proxy tasks (e.g., OOD detection, active learning) where Bayes-optimal decision strategies do not align with commonly used uncertainty scores. This misalignment means standard metrics like correlation between learned uncertainty components may not reflect their actual downstream utility. The authors aim to bridge the gap between theoretical decision rules and practical evaluation of uncertainty disentanglement.
AI.method: The authors formulate selective prediction as a constrained optimization over coverage, expected risk, and regret. They theoretically prove the optimal selector takes the form of a threshold on a convex combination of ground-truth aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties. Using this insight, they propose evaluating uncertainty decomposition methods by measuring the achievable risk-regret-coverage surface rather than proxy correlation metrics. They benchmark standard disentanglement methods on datasets with dense human annotations to compare decision-theoretic rankings against proxy-task rankings.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis reveals that standard correlation metrics between learned aleatoric and epistemic components do not necessarily predict operational utility. Empirical benchmarking shows that decision-theoretic rankings can disagree substantially with proxy-task rankings, including pairwise rank inversions where methods top-ranked on one criterion are bottom-ranked on another.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating epistemic uncertainty should be grounded in decision theory rather than proxy correlation metrics. The proposed risk-regret-coverage surface provides a more reliable diagnostic for joint disentanglement and utility. The findings caution against relying solely on proxy-task performance for comparing uncertainty quantification methods.

title: Transcoders for Investigating Deception in Language Models
summary: Transcoders have recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability (MI), enabling circuit-level analysis of model behaviour. In this paper, we investigate the use of transcoders to analyse deceptive behaviour in language models, a behaviour that poses a safety and security risk. Using a Qwen3-4B model with pre-trained transcoders, specifically per-layer transcoders (PLTs), we construct attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies, allowing circuit-level analysis of deception. Through feature steering and circuit analysis, we identified a dictionary of deception-related features and show that these features exert a stronger influence on deceptive outputs, as they produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses. These findings suggest that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms and highlight the potential of transcoders for behavioural monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviours in language models.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates using per-layer transcoders (PLTs) on a Qwen3-4B model to construct attribution graphs for circuit-level analysis of deceptive behavior, identifying deception-related features that causally influence deceptive outputs and can shift model responses between deceptive and non-deceptive states.
AI.motivation: Deceptive behavior in language models poses safety and security risks, and there is a need for mechanistic interpretability methods to understand how deception emerges from internal model mechanisms at the circuit level, enabling behavioral monitoring and early vulnerability detection.
AI.method: The authors apply pre-trained per-layer transcoders (PLTs) to a Qwen3-4B model to build attribution graphs that capture feature activations and inter-feature dependencies. They then perform feature steering and circuit analysis to identify a dictionary of deception-related features and test their causal influence on model outputs.
AI.result: A dictionary of deception-related features was identified. These features exert stronger influence on deceptive outputs and produce predictable shifts between deceptive and non-deceptive responses when steered, demonstrating that deception emerges from internal model mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Transcoders are a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of deceptive behavior in LMs. The identified deception features and their causal role suggest that transcoder-based circuit analysis can enable behavioral monitoring and early detection of security vulnerabilities related to malicious behaviors.

title: Beyond the Leaderboard: Design Lessons for Trustworthy Multimodal VQA
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 39th IEEE International Symposium on Computer-Based Medical Systems (IEEE CBMS 2026) as a regular paper
summary: Healthcare multimodal AI must combine visual and textual evidence while remaining reliable and interpretable. Using MediaEval Medico 2025 as a retrospective GI endoscopy case study, we analyze design choices across nine documented systems for question answering and explanation quality. Parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones provides strong challenge performance, but answer-level gains do not consistently translate into faithful and complete clinical reasoning. Methods enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding show more reliable behavior across heterogeneous question types, although the evidence is correlational rather than ablation-based. These results motivate evaluation beyond lexical overlap, standardized evidence-linked explanations, leakage-aware data governance, and lightweight robustness and calibration checks. The findings support trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI based on data fusion, explainability, and resilient evaluation.

AI.tldr: Analysis of nine Medico 2025 GI endoscopy systems reveals that parameter-efficient fine-tuning yields strong QA performance, but answer accuracy does not guarantee faithful clinical reasoning. Structured reasoning and explicit grounding methods show more reliable behavior, motivating evaluation beyond lexical overlap and standardized explainability benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Healthcare multimodal AI systems must be both accurate and interpretable, yet current evaluation paradigms overemphasize answer-level metrics (e.g., lexical overlap) without adequately assessing whether the underlying reasoning is faithful, complete, and clinically grounded.
AI.method: Retrospective case study using the MediaEval Medico 2025 challenge on GI endoscopy. Nine documented multimodal systems are analyzed across design dimensions including parameter-efficient adaptation of pretrained backbones, structured reasoning enforcement, and explicit visual-textual grounding. Evaluation examines both question-answering accuracy and explanation quality.
AI.result: Parameter-efficient adaptation achieves strong challenge performance, but gains at the answer level do not consistently translate into faithful or complete clinical reasoning. Systems enforcing structured reasoning and explicit grounding demonstrate more reliable behavior across heterogeneous question types, though evidence remains correlational rather than causally established through ablation.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy multimodal healthcare AI requires evaluation frameworks that go beyond lexical overlap, incorporating standardized evidence-linked explanations, leakage-aware data governance, and lightweight robustness and calibration checks. These pillars — data fusion, explainability, and resilient evaluation — are essential for clinically deployable systems.

title: Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss for Peak-Critical Time Series Forecasting
summary: In many operational time-series forecasting applications, such as crowd demand forecasting, the risk related to under-prediction is substantially higher than that of over-prediction. Accurate prediction of rare demand spikes plays a critical role in downstream tasks. Yet most time-series forecasters are trained with symmetric objectives (e.g., MSE, MAE) and evaluated primarily on aggregate error, which can mask failures in extreme-values and peak-timing predictions. We introduce Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss (APAL), a simple, model-agnostic objective that (i) penalizes under-predictions more heavily and (ii) increases the training weight of peak regions within each forecast window. We further propose a peak-critical evaluation protocol that complements MAE/MSE with channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%) and peak metrics (precision, recall, F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error). We evaluate APAL on long-horizon multivariate forecasting across five state-of-the-art backbones, with a focus on pedestrian demand forecasting using (i) a production-ready subset of the City of Melbourne pedestrian hourly count dataset and (ii) a beach visitor count dataset. The generality of the loss function for time-series forecasting is tested on additional benchmarks. Across peak-critical datasets and settings, APAL improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while exposing a controllable trade-off with aggregate error, making it a practical solution when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.
