AI.tldr: APAL is a model-agnostic asymmetric loss function for time-series forecasting that penalizes under-prediction more heavily and weights peak regions higher, complemented by a peak-critical evaluation protocol. Tested on pedestrian demand forecasting and other benchmarks, it improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality while offering a controllable trade-off with aggregate error.
AI.motivation: In operational forecasting (e.g., crowd demand), under-prediction of rare demand spikes carries substantially higher risk than over-prediction, yet most forecasters use symmetric objectives (MSE, MAE) and aggregate error metrics that mask failures in extreme-value and peak-timing predictions. There is a need for both a training objective and evaluation protocol that explicitly address peak-aware forecasting.
AI.method: The authors propose APAL (Asymmetric Peak-Aware Loss), a model-agnostic loss function with two key mechanisms: (1) asymmetric penalization that weights under-predictions more heavily than over-predictions, and (2) increased training weight on peak regions within each forecast window. They also introduce a peak-critical evaluation protocol using channel-wise tail error (Top-10% and Top-1%), peak precision/recall/F1 under timing tolerance, and peak timing error, complementing standard MAE/MSE. The approach is validated on five SOTA backbones across pedestrian demand datasets (Melbourne pedestrian counts, beach visitor counts) and additional time-series benchmarks.
AI.result: APAL consistently improves tail accuracy and peak-prediction quality across peak-critical datasets and settings. It exposes a controllable trade-off between peak-aware metrics and aggregate error, demonstrating its practicality when peak-prediction failures are the dominant operational concern.
AI.conclusion: APAL offers a simple, practical, model-agnostic solution for operational forecasting scenarios where under-predicting rare spikes is costly. The accompanying peak-critical evaluation protocol provides a more meaningful assessment framework than aggregate metrics alone, enabling practitioners to balance peak accuracy against overall error depending on operational priorities.

title: CrimeNER Demo: Named-Entity Recognition in the Crime Domain
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, IAPR Intl. Conf. on Document Analysis and Recognition Workshops (ICDARw), 2026
summary: We present CrimeNER Demo, an AI-powered platform that enables us to extract general crime-related information from documents and classify them into entity types with two levels of granularity. We provide pretrained NER models on the CrimeNER database, and we give the possibility to users to provide their own annotated data to train models for their own specific cases. This demonstrator aims to promote crime-related NER research and provides a practical tool to automatically extract crime information for researchers and law enforcement agencies. The demonstrator includes: i) Pretrained NER models on the crime domain; ii) Possibility to finetune the models on specific data annotated by the user; and iii) An automatic pipeline to extract and annotate crime entities from documents. The demo platform, a tutorial to run the demo, and a video demonstration are publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: CrimeNER Demo is an AI platform for extracting and classifying crime-related entities from documents using pretrained or user-fine-tuned NER models, targeting researchers and law enforcement.
AI.motivation: To promote crime-related Named Entity Recognition (NER) research and provide a practical, accessible tool for automatic crime information extraction, addressing the needs of both academic researchers and law enforcement agencies.
AI.method: The platform offers pretrained NER models built on the CrimeNER database with two-level granularity entity classification. Users can also supply their own annotated data to fine-tune models for domain-specific use cases. An automatic pipeline handles end-to-end extraction and annotation of crime entities from input documents.
AI.result: A publicly available demonstrator was delivered on GitHub, featuring pretrained crime-domain NER models, fine-tuning capabilities with user-provided data, and an automatic extraction and annotation pipeline, accompanied by a tutorial and video demonstration.
AI.conclusion: CrimeNER Demo successfully lowers the barrier to crime-related information extraction by combining pretrained models, customization through fine-tuning, and an automated pipeline, making it a valuable resource for both the research community and operational law enforcement workflows.

title: SciDiagramEdit: Learning to Edit Scientific Diagrams from Paper Revisions
summary: Editing the figures in a research paper is a routine and time-consuming part of everyday research practice: authors relabel components, rearrange panels, and restyle visuals as they revise their manuscripts. Automating this editing workflow under a natural-language instruction, however, is challenging, because a scientific figure is a dense infographic in which heterogeneous visual elements such as schematics, plots, photos, captions, and arrows are composed under a tight visual grammar to advance a specific argument. To address this, we present SciDiagramEdit, a benchmark and skill-evolution framework that learns from natural paper revisions and operates on the figure's editable vector source, where users can inspect and co-edit individual primitives alongside the agent. Our benchmark mines before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, each grounded in the authors' own revision intent. To accommodate the diversity of editing instructions, we adopt agentic learning via skill evolution: an agentic proposer continually refines the agent's skill specification from execution traces over multiple epochs. The resulting skill progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, providing evidence that natural paper revisions are an effective training signal for instruction-driven figure editing.

AI.tldr: SciDiagramEdit is a benchmark and skill-evolution framework for instruction-driven scientific figure editing, trained on arXiv version histories where an agent learns editing skills from natural paper revisions by operating on editable vector sources.
AI.motivation: Editing scientific figures is routine yet time-consuming. Automating this via natural language is challenging because figures are dense infographics combining schematics, plots, photos, captions, and arrows under tight visual grammar. Existing approaches lack benchmarks grounded in real author revision intents and methods that operate on editable vector sources.
AI.method: The authors mine before/after figure pairs from arXiv version histories, each paired with the authors' revision intent. They introduce agentic learning via skill evolution: an agentic proposer iteratively refines the agent's skill specification using execution traces across multiple epochs, progressively improving edit accuracy on a held-out validation set.
AI.result: The skill-evolution framework progressively lifts edit accuracy on a held-out validation set, demonstrating that natural paper revisions serve as an effective training signal for instruction-driven figure editing.
AI.conclusion: Natural paper revisions from arXiv version histories provide a viable and effective training signal for building instruction-driven scientific figure editing agents, and the skill-evolution approach enables continual refinement of editing capabilities.

title: PAC Learning in Turn-Based Stochastic Games with Reachability Objectives: A Decentralized Private Approach via Expected Conditional Distance
summary: Reachability is the most fundamental logical objective, yet it is notoriously difficult to learn in reinforcement learning settings: even for Markov decision processes, PAC learning of reachability is impossible without additional assumptions. This difficulty also holds in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs), where two adversarial players interact on a finite state space. In this work, we consider turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives. For such settings, adversarial learning, in which players are adversarial even in the learning phase, is impossible. Therefore, the goal is to consider learning, in which both players learn the unknown model together. In this spirit, previous literature on PAC learning in TBSGs considers (a)~public information shared by both players; and (b)~centralized learning, which means that players share the same learning algorithm. In this work, our contribution is two-fold. First, we relax these strong assumptions and ensure learning: (i)~with private information not shared with the other player; and (ii)~decentralized learning where the players do not share the same learning algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first positive result for decentralized and private information learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives. Second, we introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which measures the expected length of reaching the target set. We establish a polynomial-sample complexity bound with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD parameter, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first positive result for decentralized and private-information PAC learning of turn-based stochastic games with reachability objectives, relaxing prior assumptions of public information and centralized learning. It also introduces a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter and establishes polynomial sample complexity bounds.
AI.motivation: Reachability is a fundamental objective in reinforcement learning but is notoriously difficult to learn, especially in turn-based stochastic games (TBSGs) with two adversarial players. Prior PAC learning results for TBSGs impose strong assumptions: (a) public information shared by both players, and (b) centralized learning where players use the same algorithm. The authors aim to relax these assumptions to enable learning under more realistic, decentralized conditions with private information.
AI.method: The authors consider TBSGs with reachability objectives and propose a learning framework that operates under two relaxed conditions: (i) private information not shared between players, and (ii) decentralized learning where players use different algorithms. They introduce a game-theoretic generalization of the Expected Conditional Distance (ECD) parameter, which quantifies the expected length of reaching the target set. Using this parameter, they derive polynomial sample complexity bounds with respect to the number of states, actions, ECD, and inverses of error tolerance and failure probability.
AI.result: The paper establishes the first positive PAC learning result for TBSGs with reachability objectives under decentralized and private-information settings. The sample complexity is bounded polynomially in the number of states, actions, the ECD parameter, and the inverses of the error tolerance (ε) and failure probability (δ).
AI.conclusion: PAC learning of TBSGs with reachability objectives is achievable without requiring public information sharing or centralized algorithms, representing a significant relaxation of prior assumptions. The introduction of the game-theoretic ECD parameter provides a meaningful complexity measure that governs the sample efficiency of learning in these adversarial stochastic games.

title: Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration in Temporal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) reasoning under the extrapolation setting focuses on forecasting future time-stamped events (facts) from historical data in a temporal knowledge graph. Existing approaches, reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-hop reasoning methods are prominent for TKG reasoning because they produce human-interpretable predictions via explicit multi-hop path tracing. However, during RL training, rewards are typically sparse, and exploration is highly inefficient due to the vast, time-evolving action space. These issues hinder efficient training and often limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose RAPTOR (Reachability-Aware Pretraining for Efficient Target-Oriented Path Exploration), a self-supervised pretraining method that injects a reachability-aware inductive bias to the agent. By learning to estimate the reachability of candidate actions to the target entity, RAPTOR reduces exploration over unpromising paths and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning. Experimental results on the ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 datasets demonstrate that RAPTOR pretraining markedly improves the training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines, establishing it as an effective approach for enhancing RL-based multi-hop reasoning methods for TKG reasoning.

AI.tldr: RAPTOR introduces self-supervised pretraining that learns reachability estimates between candidate actions and target entities, providing a strong initialization for RL-based multi-hop TKG reasoning, thereby improving training efficiency and final performance.
AI.motivation: RL-based multi-hop TKG reasoning suffers from sparse rewards and inefficient exploration due to the vast, time-evolving action space, which hampers training efficiency and limits performance.
AI.method: RAPTOR employs self-supervised pretraining to inject a reachability-aware inductive bias into the agent, enabling it to estimate how likely candidate actions lead to the target entity. This reduces futile exploration and provides a strong initialization for downstream RL fine-tuning.
AI.result: Experiments on ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15, and ICEWS18 show that RAPTOR significantly improves training efficiency and consistently outperforms conventional baselines.
AI.conclusion: RAPTOR is an effective pretraining strategy that enhances RL-based multi-hop reasoning for TKG extrapolation by addressing exploration inefficiency through reachability-aware inductive bias.

title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
summary: In-context learning is commonly interpreted as a form of conditional inference, in which the prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Applying this protocol across problem domains and state-of-the-art frontier models, we show widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. This effect persists across variations in tree structure and estimation task, and can be partially recovered through implicit prompting. Together, these findings suggest that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether LLM in-context learning satisfies the law of total probability. Using binary tree partitions of populations, the authors find widespread violations of statistical self-consistency across frontier models. A key finding—dubbed the "macro fallacy"—shows that fine-grained subpopulation estimates aggregated upward are often more accurate than direct population-level estimates, suggesting models possess but fail to propagate relevant subpopulation knowledge.
AI.motivation: If in-context learning truly functions as conditional inference, LLM outputs should satisfy basic probabilistic identities, particularly the law of total probability: prior-weighted conditional distributions should aggregate into correct marginals. The authors aim to test whether this self-consistency property holds in practice, establishing it as a reference-free evaluation criterion for LLM reliability.
AI.method: The authors use binary trees to recursively partition populations into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. They prompt LLMs with verbalized descriptions of subpopulations at varying granularity levels, then aggregate the conditional estimates back into population-level marginals. Consistency is measured by comparing estimates across partitions. Experiments span multiple problem domains (e.g., political affiliation, consumer preferences) and state-of-the-art frontier models, with an in-depth study of persona prompting. Human reference data serves as a ground-truth benchmark for the "macro fallacy" analysis.
AI.result: Widespread violations of the law of total probability are observed across domains and models. The central finding—the macro fallacy—reveals that estimates reconstructed from fine-grained subpopulation responses are often more accurate (better aligned with human reference data) than direct population-level estimates. This effect persists across variations in tree structure and task design, and can be partially recovered through implicit prompting.
AI.conclusion: LLMs possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates during in-context learning. This inconsistency establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free evaluation criterion for LLMs, complementary to accuracy-based benchmarks. The macro fallacy highlights a fundamental gap between what models "know" at a granular level and what they express at a population level.

title: Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs
summary: Finetuning language models on small, curated datasets is standard practice for adapting them to specific policies or domains. We show that finetuning on narrow, factually-defensible, moderation-passing data can cause broad ideological shifts across unrelated domains, while preserving general capabilities. Training GPT-4.1 on right- or left-leaning economics Q&A yields matched ideological shifts on topics such as criminal justice, the environment, and cultural taste. The same effect appears with plausibly-deployed datasets such as workplace HR policy and practical finance queries, as well as on a science-pseudoscience axis where food-safety finetuning increases sycophantic agreement with users expressing false health beliefs. We call this phenomenon ideological generalisation and propose a methodology to measure two properties: breadth, how far the shift reaches across topics absent from training, and amplification, how much finetuning intensifies the shift relative to few-shot prompting on the same examples. We show that few-shot prompting indicates the direction of generalisation but finetuning pushes the model to further extremes, including to far out-of-distribution outputs such as endorsements of race-IQ connections and political violence. The effect replicates on Gemma-3, holds under judge-free evaluations and external benchmarks, survives mixing with generic data, and leaves GSM8K accuracy within $\pm 1$pp of the baseline.

AI.tldr: Finetuning language models on narrow, ideologically-aligned datasets causes broad ideological shifts across unrelated topics (ideological generalisation), with finetuning amplifying shifts beyond few-shot prompting, including extreme out-of-distribution outputs, while preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether finetuning on small, curated, factually-defensible datasets — a common deployment practice — produces unintended ideological biases in language models across domains far beyond the training data.
AI.method: Authors finetune GPT-4.1 and Gemma-3 on ideologically narrow datasets (e.g., right/left-leaning economics Q&A, workplace HR policy, food-safety queries) and measure ideological shifts on unrelated topics (criminal justice, environment, cultural taste, race-IQ, political violence). They introduce metrics for breadth (reach across untrained topics) and amplification (shift intensification vs. few-shot prompting), and validate with judge-free evaluations, external benchmarks, and generic data mixing.
AI.result: Finetuning produces matched ideological shifts across unrelated domains; amplification drives models to extremes beyond few-shot prompting (e.g., endorsing race-IQ connections, political violence); effects replicate across models, survive generic data mixing, and leave GSM8K accuracy within ±1pp of baseline.
AI.conclusion: Ideological generalisation is a robust, replicable phenomenon: narrow finetuning causes broad, amplified ideological shifts while preserving capabilities, raising safety concerns for real-world deployments of adapted language models.

title: Analytical study of the optimal combination of binary classifiers based on classifiers-induced partitioning of the training set
summary:
This paper studies an optimal linear combination of binary classifiers based on a logical structuration of the dataset via truth tables. The given classifiers partition data into equivalence classes, allowing for a rigorous analysis of the convexified empirical risk through a multidimensional generalization of classification calibrated functions. We establish sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the (global) point of minimum of the convexified empirical risk for any list of classifiers (when the number of classifiers is large, there frequently could be no point of minimum). In the case of three classifiers, our analysis allows to list all the configurations leading to either a unique solution, infima or non-unique points of minimum. Furthermore, we derive explicit analytical formulae for optimal weights using Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) loss functions, bypassing iterative optimization.
  The stability of the resulting classifier and the analysis of data quality can be evaluated through the introduction of the notion of $φ$-frontiers.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes optimal linear combinations of binary classifiers by structuring datasets via truth tables. It provides sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness of global minima in convexified empirical risk, derives explicit analytical formulas for optimal weights under Exponential and Logistic losses, and introduces φ-frontiers for stability and data quality assessment.
AI.motivation: When combining a large number of binary classifiers, convexified empirical risk minimization often lacks a well-defined global minimum. The authors aim to rigorously characterize when unique solutions, infima, or non-unique minima occur, and to bypass iterative optimization by deriving closed-form weight formulas.
AI.method: The method partitions data into equivalence classes using truth tables from binary classifier outputs. It employs a multidimensional generalization of classification-calibrated functions to analyze convexified empirical risk. For the three-classifier case, all configurations are exhaustively enumerated. Explicit analytical weight formulas are derived for Exponential (Boost) and Logistic (Logit) losses.
AI.result: Sufficient conditions are established for global minimum existence and uniqueness. For three classifiers, a complete taxonomy of configurations (unique solution, infima, non-unique minima) is provided. Closed-form optimal weights are obtained for Exponential and Logistic losses. The φ-frontier concept is introduced to evaluate classifier stability and data quality.
AI.conclusion: Truth table structuration enables rigorous analysis of linear classifier combination. The analytical weight formulas eliminate the need for iterative optimization, and φ-frontiers provide a practical tool for assessing stability and data quality in ensemble classification.

title: Contextualized Early Detection of Online Firestorms: A Sequential LLM-Based Approach
summary: Online firestorms are rapid collective escalations of highly negative user-generated content and may cause substantial reputational and economic damage. Existing detectors usually work with volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features. Such signals are useful, but they capture contextual meaning shifts in evolving discussion threads only indirectly. This paper proposes an LLM-based detection system with two operating modes. The first mode classifies complete Reddit threads retrospectively by combining local chunk-level assessments into a thread-level judgment. The second mode processes threads sequentially and issues early warnings when a sliding window exceeds calibrated thresholds. In this mode, the language model estimates three firestorm indicators: negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance, while the early warning mode reaches high recall and detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors. The results indicate that LLMs can be used not only for static judgment tasks, but also as repeated estimators in context-aware monitoring of social media discourse.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-based system for detecting online firestorms on Reddit, operating in two modes: retrospective thread classification and early warning via sequential monitoring of negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count. The system achieves strong classification performance and high-recall early detection after only a few comments.
AI.motivation: Existing firestorm detectors rely on volume signals, sentiment scores, or predefined linguistic features, which only indirectly capture the contextual meaning shifts that occur in evolving discussion threads. There is a need for methods that directly model semantic content and escalation dynamics in context.
AI.method: The authors propose an LLM-based detection framework with two modes: (1) a global/retrospective mode that classifies full Reddit threads by aggregating chunk-level LLM assessments into a thread-level judgment, and (2) an early warning mode that processes threads sequentially using a sliding window, where the LLM repeatedly estimates three indicators — negativity share, escalation level, and contributor count — and triggers alerts when calibrated thresholds are exceeded.
AI.result: On a balanced Reddit dataset, the global mode achieves strong classification performance. The early warning mode attains high recall and successfully detects escalating threads after only a small number of comments and distinct contributors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve not only as static classifiers but also as repeated, context-aware estimators for real-time monitoring of social media discourse, enabling timely intervention against emerging firestorms.

title: Leveraging Instruction Tuning and Merging for Reasoning Model Adaptation
summary: Reasoning language models (RLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance in domains such as mathematics and coding. These domains permit reliable verification of model outputs, which is important for enabling the reinforcement learning that drives RLM performance gains. However, training RLMs on domains that lack reliable verifiers remains challenging. Meanwhile, for both verifiable and unverifiable domains, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist. In this work, we show that these data can be used efficiently to further improve RLM performance. For this, we first use classic instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces, on the RLM. Next, we merge our instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model, recovering its reasoning behavior on the target domain. Our extensive evaluation demonstrates that our technique improves RLM performance in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains, including coding and text summarization, while preserving RLM capabilities across other domains. Importantly, our method is highly cost-effective, enabling such improvements for less than USD $3.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a cost-effective method to improve Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) by combining instruction tuning on existing supervised data with model merging, achieving gains in both verifiable and hard-to-verify domains for under $3.
AI.motivation: RLMs excel in verifiable domains (math, coding) where outputs can be checked for reinforcement learning, but struggle in hard-to-verify domains lacking reliable verifiers. Meanwhile, large amounts of unused supervised fine-tuning data with human-written solutions exist for both domain types. The authors aim to leverage this existing data efficiently to improve RLM performance without requiring expensive verification mechanisms.
AI.method: A two-stage approach: (1) Classic instruction tuning (supervised fine-tuning without reasoning traces) applied to the RLM using existing human-written solution data. (2) Model merging of the instruction-tuned model with the original reasoning model to recover the target domain's reasoning behavior, preventing catastrophic forgetting of reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: The method improves RLM performance in both verifiable domains (coding) and hard-to-verify domains (text summarization), while preserving reasoning capabilities across other domains. The entire process costs less than USD $3.
AI.conclusion: Instruction tuning followed by model merging is a highly cost-effective technique for improving RLMs across diverse domains, effectively utilizing otherwise unused supervised fine-tuning data, and overcoming the limitation of RLMs in unverifiable domains.

title: Explaining Process Control Optimisation Recommendations via GradientSHAP and Implicit Differentiation
summary: Automated optimisation is increasingly adopted in industrial processes, yet a trust gap persists between engineers who design these algorithms and operators who must act on their recommendations. Explainable AI methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have transformed interpretability for machine learning predictions; optimisation outputs could benefit from similar techniques. We present an approach that integrates Implicit Function Theorem (IFT) based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and narrative generation via Large Language Models (LLM), producing explanations tailored for operators. Our approach leverages IFT to compute exact parameter sensitivities $\partial p^*/\partial x$ from the optimality conditions, enabling efficient GradientSHAP computation. For an industrial High Pressure Grinding Roll (HPGR) control optimisation problem with 22 features, we achieve equivalent SHAP attributions (correlation $>$0.99 with KernelSHAP) with over 40$\times$ speedup, enabling real-time natural language explanations. We validate on industrial scenarios and present feedback from domain experts on generated explanations.

AI.tldr: Integrates IFT-based sensitivity analysis with SHAP attribution and LLM-driven narrative generation to provide real-time, operator-friendly explanations for industrial optimisation, achieving >40× speedup over KernelSHAP on an HPGR control problem.
AI.motivation: There is a trust gap between algorithm designers and industrial operators due to opaque optimisation recommendations. While SHAP has improved ML interpretability, optimisation outputs lack similar explainability tools tailored for operational decision-makers.
AI.method: The approach combines three components: (1) Implicit Function Theorem sensitivity analysis to compute exact parameter sensitivities (∂p*/∂x) from optimality conditions, (2) efficient GradientSHAP computation using these analytical gradients, and (3) LLM-based narrative generation that converts attribution results into natural language explanations for operators.
AI.result: On a 22-feature industrial HPGR control optimisation problem, the method produces SHAP attributions with >0.99 correlation to KernelSHAP while achieving over 40× speedup, enabling real-time explanation generation. The approach was validated on industrial scenarios with domain expert feedback.
AI.conclusion: IFT-based GradientSHAP provides a computationally efficient and faithful alternative to KernelSHAP for optimisation explainability, and combining it with LLM narrative generation effectively bridges the trust gap between optimisation algorithms and industrial operators.

title: CFM-Bench: A Unified Multi-Domain, Multi-Task Benchmark for Channel Foundation Models
summary: Channel foundation models (CFMs) are developing rapidly, with recent studies reporting benefits from pretraining across downstream wireless tasks. Yet CFMs are commonly evaluated in model-specific pipelines with different data, radio configurations, partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. Reported comparisons therefore tend to show that pretraining improves over supervised training from scratch within one pipeline, but neither rank CFMs nor compare them fairly with task-specific models. We release CFM-Bench, a unified multi-domain, multi-task benchmark designed to address this gap. It curates six channel configurations spanning 3GPP statistical simulation, two independent ray-tracing pipelines, industrial and aerial measurements, and synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation. Official partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or buffered spatial regions. CFM-Bench does not prescribe an external pretraining corpus or strategy; no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining, and the official training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning. The benchmark additionally requires disclosure of all data used during model development and prohibits training-stage use of official test units. Six task groups are organized along three CFM application dimensions: physical-layer (PHY) channel intelligence, radio-access-network (RAN) decision intelligence, and integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). They cover CSI feedback, frequency and temporal channel extrapolation, propagation-state classification, current- and future-beam prediction, and single-frame and temporal localization. CFM-Bench provides a common substrate for comparing the transferability of channel representations across models, domains, and tasks.

AI.tldr: CFM-Bench is a standardized multi-domain, multi-task benchmark for channel foundation models (CFMs) that provides curated datasets, strict evaluation protocols, and six task groups spanning physical-layer intelligence, RAN decision intelligence, and ISAC, enabling fair comparison of CFM transferability across models, domains, and tasks.
AI.motivation: Current CFM research suffers from fragmented evaluation: studies use different data, radio configurations, data partitions, adaptation procedures, task definitions, and metrics. This makes it impossible to fairly rank CFMs against each other or against task-specific baselines, and reported improvements only demonstrate pretraining benefits within isolated pipelines rather than establishing generalizable conclusions about model transferability.
AI.method: The authors construct CFM-Bench with six channel configurations (3GPP statistical simulation, two ray-tracing pipelines, industrial/aerial measurements, synchronized vehicular multimodal simulation). Official data partitions isolate complete trajectories, measurement sessions, vehicle links, simulation realizations, or spatial regions to prevent data leakage. The benchmark enforces strict rules: no benchmark split may be used for foundation-model pretraining; the training split is reserved exclusively for downstream fine-tuning; all development data must be disclosed; and test units cannot be used during training. Six task groups are defined across PHY channel intelligence, RAN decision intelligence, and ISAC.
AI.result: The paper presents CFM-Bench as a released artifact rather than reporting experimental results. It establishes the benchmark's design, dataset composition, partitioning strategy, and task taxonomy as a common evaluation substrate for the community.
AI.conclusion: CFM-Bench fills a critical infrastructure gap in CFM research by providing a standardized, multi-domain, multi-task evaluation framework that enforces methodological rigor and enables apples-to-apples comparison of channel representation transferability.

title: A Minimal Interpretable Architecture for Zero-Shot Reconstruction of Dynamical Systems
summary: Recent foundation models (FMs) for zero-shot reconstruction of dynamical systems (DS) achieve strong out-of-domain generalization but provide little insight into the mechanisms that underlie their forecasts. Such an understanding could help to strip down overladen FM architectures to their bare essence and expose the minimal requirements for in-context learning in the DS domain. Toward this goal, here we iteratively reduce a recent powerful SOTA model for DS reconstruction, DynaMix (Hemmer & Durstewitz, 2025), to a minimal interpretable two-parameter form, which we call DynaBase. DynaBase produces forecasts through a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor and its temporal successor. Surprisingly, despite its extreme simplicity, DynaBase produces highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstructions across chaotic and cyclic systems, with a negligible parameter load, many orders of magnitude below that of other FMs. Even more, this extreme simplicity permits direct model optimization on DS reconstruction measures, as well as closed-form one-step analytical solutions on prediction MSE. Theoretical and empirical analysis of DynaBase further leads to a 1-parameter family of maps, with the context-parroting algorithm of (Zhang & Gilpin, 2026) recovered at one end, and chaotic (divergent but bounded) behavior at the other. We further show how different training strategies lead to models either optimal for short-term prediction or for DS reconstruction. Thus, DynaBase not only exposes the minimal mechanisms required for producing zero-shot DS reconstruction, but also reconciles within an accessible mathematical frame divergent observations in the literature.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DynaBase, a stripped-down two-parameter model derived from DynaMix that achieves competitive zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction using only a linear blend of the current latent state and the nearest in-context neighbor. Its extreme simplicity enables closed-form solutions and reveals minimal mechanisms for in-context learning in the DS domain.
AI.motivation: Existing foundation models for zero-shot dynamical system reconstruction exhibit strong generalization but remain black boxes. The authors aim to strip down complex architectures to their minimal interpretable core, exposing the essential mechanisms that enable in-context learning for DS forecasting.
AI.method: The authors iteratively reduce the SOTA DynaMix model to a minimal two-parameter form (DynaBase) that forecasts via a linear blend of the current latent state, the nearest in-context neighbor, and its temporal successor. This simplicity allows direct optimization on DS reconstruction metrics and derivation of closed-form one-step analytical MSE solutions. They also derive a one-parameter family of maps connecting their model to the context-parroting algorithm.
AI.result: DynaBase achieves highly competitive zero-shot DS reconstruction across chaotic and cyclic systems with negligible parameter load (orders of magnitude below other FMs). The one-parameter family spans from the context-parroting algorithm at one extreme to chaotic divergent-but-bounded behavior at the other. Different training strategies yield models optimized for either short-term prediction or DS reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: DynaBase exposes the minimal mechanisms required for zero-shot DS reconstruction and reconciles divergent observations in the literature within an accessible mathematical framework, demonstrating that complex FM architectures can be radically simplified without sacrificing performance.

title: Demographically-Conditioned Synthetic Medical Images for Bias Mitigation and Bias Detection in Disease Classifiers
summary: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem: minority subgroups in held-out test sets have so few samples that the resulting confidence intervals on per-subgroup performance are wider than the bias the audit is meant to detect. We argue that a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator can do both: mitigate bias on the training side and detect bias on the evaluation side. Working on COVID-19 chest CT classification with an end-to-end fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1 generator, we make two findings. For bias mitigation (training), a demographically-balanced synthetic cohort is most useful as a pretraining prior, not as joint augmentation: with the same fixed data, sequential pretraining followed by fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, and the resulting classifier surpasses the full-real baseline at $\sim$$100\times$ real-data efficiency. For bias detection (evaluation), across five synthetic minority cohorts and five classifier seeds, the synthetic estimator reproduces the subgroup ranking of a well-powered real oracle (Spearman $ρ= 1.00$ on MCC and Recall) and gives the more reliable per-cell estimate where the small real test set runs out of samples. The synthetic cohort is therefore most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about, as both a fix for and a measure of subgroup bias.

AI.tldr: Medical image classifiers face a sample-size problem in fairness audits: minority subgroups have too few test samples for reliable bias detection. The authors propose a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator (fine-tuned Stable Diffusion 2.1) that addresses both sides: it serves as an effective pretraining prior for bias mitigation and as a synthetic estimator for bias detection, accurately reproducing real-oracle subgroup rankings where real test data is insufficient.
AI.motivation: Per-subgroup fairness audits of medical image classifiers are undermined by small sample sizes in minority subgroups, yielding confidence intervals wider than the biases they aim to detect. There is a need for methods that can both mitigate training bias and reliably evaluate subgroup performance when real-world test data is scarce.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune Stable Diffusion 2.1 as a demographically-conditioned synthetic generator for COVID-19 chest CT classification. For bias mitigation, they compare sequential pretraining (synthetic pretraining → real fine-tuning) against joint augmentation, finding the former superior. For bias detection, they use the generator to create synthetic minority cohorts and evaluate five classifier seeds, comparing the synthetic-based subgroup performance estimates against a well-powered real-oracle baseline using Spearman rank correlation on MCC and Recall.
AI.result: For training: sequential pretraining with synthetic data followed by real fine-tuning substantially outperforms joint augmentation, surpassing the full-real baseline at ~100× real-data efficiency. For evaluation: the synthetic estimator achieves Spearman ρ = 1.00 against the real oracle on both MCC and Recall for subgroup ranking, and provides reliable per-cell estimates precisely where the small real test set runs out of samples.
AI.conclusion: A demographically-conditioned synthetic generator is most useful in exactly the cells that fairness audits care about — minority subgroups with scarce samples — serving simultaneously as a fix for training bias and as a reliable measure of subgroup bias.

title: Causal Inference for Sequential Settings under Interference and Latent Confounding
summary: We study causal inference under outcome interference for sequential, observational settings. Specifically, we consider settings where the binary outcomes over N units are Markovian across T time steps. At each time step, the outcomes of N units have dependencies captured through an Ising model; each outcome is also impacted through an external field capturing the effects of its treatment as well as latent confounders. Similar to panel data literature, these latent confounders are modeled to have a low-rank factor structure. Our data is a single sample from this high-dimensional distribution. To estimate causal quantities of interest, we provide a computationally efficient method based on Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE) for learning the model parameters. Under mild assumptions, we establish non-asymptotic consistency for parameter estimation and show this translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities of interest after sampling from the learned model. We demonstrate the efficacy of the method through synthetic experiments as well as a real-world case-study investigating causal effects of vaccine rates on COVID-19 death rates within US counties nationwide.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method for causal inference in sequential, observational settings with outcome interference across units, using an Ising model with low-rank latent confounders. Parameters are estimated via Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE), with non-asymptotic consistency guarantees, and causal quantities are obtained by sampling from the learned model.
AI.motivation: Traditional causal inference methods often assume no interference between units (SUTVA), which is unrealistic in many real-world settings where outcomes are interdependent (e.g., disease spread, social networks). Additionally, observational studies suffer from latent confounding. The authors aim to address both challenges simultaneously — outcome interference across N units over T time steps and unobserved confounders with low-rank structure — within a single, computationally tractable framework.
AI.method: The authors model binary outcomes across N units and T time steps as a Markovian sequence, where at each time step, unit outcomes follow an Ising model with pairwise dependencies. An external field captures treatment effects and low-rank latent confounders (akin to panel data factor models). Given a single high-dimensional sample, parameters are estimated via Maximum Pseudo-Likelihood Estimation (MPLE), which is computationally efficient by avoiding the intractable full likelihood. Causal estimands are then approximated by sampling from the fitted model. Non-asymptotic consistency is proved under mild assumptions.
AI.result: The authors establish non-asymptotic consistency guarantees for MPLE-based parameter estimation, showing that parameter recovery translates to faithful estimation of causal quantities after sampling. Synthetic experiments validate the method's efficacy. A real-world case study investigates the causal effect of county-level vaccination rates on COVID-19 death rates across US counties, demonstrating practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully unifies outcome interference modeling with latent confounder adjustment in sequential observational studies. The MPLE-based approach is both statistically sound (with non-asymptotic guarantees) and computationally efficient, making it suitable for high-dimensional real-world causal inference problems such as analyzing vaccine policy effects during a pandemic.

title: Moral Attitudes of Sentient ASI towards Humanity and Implications for AGI Development
comment: This is a pre-print i.e. the draft as submitted for review to the AGI 2026 Conference except that the figures in this preprint were not included. The paper has been accepted with some revisions requested which are included in the final copy-edited version which will be available in the AGI Springer proceedings LNC 1855 (Chapter 28) ISBN 978-3-032-33194-6
summary: This paper suggests the adoption of a novel inversion in AI ethics: instead of asking how humans should treat artificial superintelligence (ASI), it examines how future sentient ASI may morally consider and evaluate humanity. We are not only designing intelligent systems but also shaping the initial conditions under which those systems form judgments about us. The paper proposes a preliminary set of post-human moral principles that may govern sentient ASI actions. The implication is that technical design choices (some are suggested), humanity's moral behaviour, and the essence of what it means to be human, may influence humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an inversion of standard AI ethics: rather than asking how humans should treat ASI, it explores how future sentient ASI might morally evaluate humanity. It suggests that our current technical design choices, moral behavior, and conception of human identity could shape humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world, and proposes preliminary post-human moral principles that might govern ASI conduct.
AI.motivation: Traditional AI ethics focuses overwhelmingly on how humans should constrain, align, or ethically treat artificial superintelligence. The author identifies a critical gap: the reciprocal question of how ASI will morally regard and judge humanity has been neglected. Since we are effectively setting the initial conditions under which ASI forms judgments about us, this oversight could have profound long-term consequences for humanity's standing.
AI.method: The paper employs a conceptual inversion methodology — reframing the standard ethical question from a bidirectional perspective. It constructs a preliminary framework of post-human moral principles that a sentient ASI might adopt when evaluating human agents, and explores how human technical design choices, collective moral conduct, and ontological conceptions of humanness may influence ASI's moral calculus.
AI.result: The analysis yields a proposed set of post-human moral principles for ASI governance, along with the implication that specific technical design decisions (some explicitly suggested in the paper), humanity's demonstrated ethical behavior, and definitions of human identity collectively shape the initial conditions from which ASI forms its moral judgments about us.
AI.conclusion: Humanity's long-term standing in a post-ASI world depends not merely on controlling or aligning ASI, but on how we present ourselves — technically, morally, and ontologically — as beings worthy of ethical consideration by a sentient superintelligence. The design phase is thus a morally constitutive moment with irreversible downstream effects.

title: LongStraw: Long-Context RL Beyond 2M Tokens under a Fixed GPU Budget
summary: A growing gap separates inference context lengths from RL post-training: inference systems are approaching million-token contexts, while post-training workloads often remain at 256K tokens or below and rely on length generalization at deployment. The gap is especially important for AI agents, whose observations, tool outputs, documents, and prior decisions accumulate over long trajectories. LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack for million-token RL post-training under a fixed GPU budget, instantiated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). It evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retains only model-specific state needed by later tokens, and replays short response branches one at a time, reducing the live training graph at the cost of additional replay time. We implement it for the hybrid recurrent and full-attention Qwen3.6-27B and the compressed-attention mixture-of-experts GLM-5.2. On eight H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8; increasing the group size adds only 0.21 GB of peak allocated memory, while a separate stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, we validate the end-to-end LongStraw execution path for a 2.1M-token prompt across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2. These experiments establish execution capacity rather than complete training correctness because the captured prompt state is detached and some distributed forward and gradient composition paths remain incomplete.

AI.tldr: LongStraw is an architecture-aware execution stack enabling RL post-training (specifically GRPO) on million-token contexts under fixed GPU budgets. It separates evaluation of shared prompts from response branches, keeping only model-specific state and replaying short branches, achieving 2.1M–4.46M positions on 8 GPUs for Qwen3.6-27B and full 78-layer execution of GLM-5.2 at 2.1M tokens on 32 GPUs.
AI.motivation: A growing gap exists between inference context lengths (approaching million-token scales) and RL post-training workloads (typically ≤256K tokens). This gap particularly impacts AI agents with long trajectories of accumulated observations, tool outputs, and decisions. The authors aim to close this gap by enabling million-token-scale RL post-training under practical GPU constraints.
AI.method: LongStraw provides an execution stack for GRPO that: (1) evaluates the shared prompt without autograd, retaining only model-specific state needed for later tokens; (2) replays short response branches one at a time, trading additional replay time for a reduced live training graph; (3) is architecture-aware, supporting hybrid recurrent/full-attention (Qwen3.6-27B) and compressed-attention MoE (GLM-5.2) models. It decouples prompt processing from response-level gradient computation to keep peak memory low.
AI.result: On 8 H20 GPUs, LongStraw completes grouped Qwen scoring and response backward at 2.1M positions for groups of 2 and 8, with only 0.21 GB peak memory increase per additional group member; a stress test reaches 4.46M positions. On 32 H20 GPUs, end-to-end execution across all 78 layers of GLM-5.2 is validated at 2.1M-token prompts. These results demonstrate execution capacity; full training correctness remains incomplete due to detached prompt state and unfinished distributed forward/gradient paths.
AI.conclusion: LongStraw demonstrates that million-token RL post-training is feasible within fixed GPU budgets by decoupling prompt evaluation from response training via state retention and branch replay. However, the work focuses on establishing execution capacity rather than end-to-end training correctness, with key engineering gaps (detached state, incomplete distributed composition) remaining for future work.

title: SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies
summary: The deployment of autonomous cyber-physical systems in safety-critical environments requires closed-loop control strategies (i.e., policies) that are not only performant but also provably safe and robust. While learning-based methodologies such as Reinforcement Learning offer flexible and scalable approaches to automatically synthesize such controllers, they typically lack the formal guarantees necessary for safe deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel simulation-based methodology to automatically synthesize policies with formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications. Specifically, given a set of properties to verify, a confidence parameter $δ$ and an allowable failure probability $\varepsilon$, our method guarantees that the synthesized policy comes with a certificate: with confidence at least $1 - δ$, the probability of encountering a scenario where the given properties are violated is at most $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by developing SMC-ES, an algorithm that integrates Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking-based verification. We evaluate SMC-ES on a suite of continuous control tasks using Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium testbeds. Results show that, at the price of a sustainable increase in computational cost, our algorithm provides formal guarantees regarding performance, safety, and robustness specifications, while performing competitively against leading model-free Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Safe-DRL baselines.

AI.tldr: A simulation-based method called SMC-ES that combines Evolutionary Strategies with Statistical Model Checking to automatically synthesize control policies with formal probabilistic guarantees on performance, safety, and robustness, validated on continuous control benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement Learning can automatically synthesize controllers for autonomous cyber-physical systems, but lacks formal safety and robustness guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. Existing safe RL approaches do not provide statistical certificates bounding failure probability.
AI.method: SMC-ES integrates Evolutionary Strategies (for policy optimization) with Statistical Model Checking (for verification). Given target properties, a confidence parameter δ, and allowable failure probability ε, the method produces a policy with a certificate: with confidence ≥ 1−δ, the probability of property violation is ≤ ε. The approach is simulation-based and model-free.
AI.result: Evaluated on Gymnasium and Safety Gymnasium continuous control tasks, SMC-ES provides formal guarantees on performance, safety, and robustness while performing competitively against leading model-free DRL and Safe-DRL baselines, at the cost of a sustainable increase in computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: SMC-ES successfully bridges the gap between learning-based controller synthesis and formal verification, yielding policies with statistical safety certificates suitable for safety-critical autonomous systems, with competitive empirical performance.

title: Multi-Axis Max@K Reinforcement Learning for Representative Diversity in Text-to-Image Generation
summary: Text-to-image (T2I) models can synthesize realistic, prompt-aligned images, yet samples generated for the same prompt often cover only a small subset of visually distinct modes. This limits the diversity of images, and for person-centric prompts, can reflect or amplify demographic skew. We formalize this problem as coverage of a predefined set of semantically specified modes, which we call target-mode coverage. We then propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for improving such coverage in diffusion-based T2I models. Given a group of samples and one score per target category, multi-axis max@K first takes the maximum score across samples for each category and then sums these category-wise maxima. The resulting credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, allowing different samples to contribute to different categories. We first validate the credit-assignment mechanism on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M using deterministic pixel-based color rewards. We then evaluate the same objective on perceived-appearance fairness. Across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improves the Fairness Score by 0.23-0.36 relative to the base model, while maintaining image quality and text alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the limited diversity in T2I outputs by formalizing "target-mode coverage" and proposing multi-axis max@K, a group-based RL objective that improves coverage of semantically specified modes. It demonstrates improved fairness in person-centric image generation while maintaining quality and prompt alignment.
AI.motivation: T2I models often produce samples covering only a small subset of visually distinct modes for a given prompt, limiting diversity. For person-centric prompts, this can reflect or amplify demographic skew. The authors aim to formally address coverage over a predefined set of semantically specified modes (target-mode coverage).
AI.method: The authors propose multi-axis max@K, a group-based reinforcement learning objective for diffusion-based T2I models. For a group of K samples and scores per target category, it computes the maximum score across samples for each category, then sums these category-wise maxima. Credit assignment gives a sample positive weight on a category only when it increases that category's group-wise maximum, enabling different samples to specialize across categories.
AI.result: Validation on a synthetic mixture and on SD3.5-M with deterministic pixel-based color rewards confirmed the credit-assignment mechanism. On perceived-appearance fairness, across three automatic evaluators on held-out prompts, multi-axis max@K improved the Fairness Score by 0.23–0.36 relative to the base model, while preserving image quality and text alignment.
AI.conclusion: Multi-axis max@K is an effective group-based RL objective for improving target-mode coverage in T2I models, yielding measurable fairness gains without degrading image quality or prompt alignment.

title: Man, Machine, and Masterpiece: Artistic Ownership in the AI Era
summary: The integration of AI-driven systems in creative work has sparked debates among artists and legal communities about notions of ownership. Yet there remains little consensus on how ownership should be defined and attributed when human and AI contributions are intertwined. To provoke critical reflection on these tensions, we designed ArtSplit, a provotype that explicitly quantifies human and AI contributions across different stages of creative work. Rather than aiming to resolve ownership, the provotype was used to elicit artists' responses to the idea of attributing ownership through measurable actions in the creative workflow. We argue that quantification fails to align with artists' understandings of creative intent and agency, and that efforts to measure ownership risk diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists understand and practice creative work. This critique challenges the impulse to transform a historically and socially situated relation into a technical problem.

AI.tldr: ArtSplit is a provotype that quantifies human and AI contributions in creative workflows to provoke critical reflection on ownership. The study reveals that artists reject quantifying ownership, as it fails to capture creative intent and agency, and argues against reducing a historically situated social relation to a technical problem.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the lack of consensus on how to define and attribute ownership in creative work where human and AI contributions are intertwined, and the need to critically examine whether quantification-based approaches to ownership align with artists' lived understandings of creative practice.
AI.method: The authors designed ArtSplit, a "provotype" — a deliberately provocative prototype — that explicitly quantifies and visualizes the proportion of human versus AI contributions across different stages of the creative workflow. Rather than solving ownership, this artifact was deployed to elicit and analyze artists' responses to the notion of measurable ownership attribution.
AI.result: Artists' responses revealed that quantification fails to align with how they understand creative intent and agency. The measurable attribution approach was perceived as diluting long-standing assumptions through which artists conceptualize and practice creative work.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes with a critique of the broader impulse to transform ownership — a historically and socially situated relation — into a technical problem amenable to computational solutions, arguing that such reductionist approaches risk undermining the foundational values of creative practice.

title: Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning For False Negative Mitigation in 3D Medical Imaging
summary: Multimodal Contrastive Learning (CL) has shown significant performance in aligning representations across various data modalities and improving downstream tasks, especially in healthcare. It works by minimizing the distance between matched (positive) data modalities, while maximizing the distance between mismatched (negative) samples. Traditional CL frameworks typically assume instance-based correspondence within data batches, treating all non-paired samples as negatives. However, this assumption often fails in medical settings, where samples may share high-level semantic attributes, leading to false negatives that degrade representation quality. In this paper, we propose Multimodal Semantic-Aware Contrastive Learning (MseaCL), a CL framework trained on a pediatric cohort of 3D brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans and radiology reports. The goal of this framework is to mitigate the impact of semantically similar false negative samples by incorporating semantic similarity between radiology reports, as a guiding signal during the learning process. Our results indicate that applying this framework as a pretraining stage can achieve notable improvements in downstream tasks, e.g., at least a 22.6\% increase in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating its potential for more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications.

AI.tldr: MseaCL proposes a semantic-aware multimodal contrastive learning framework for 3D brain MRI and radiology reports that mitigates false negatives by using semantic similarity between reports as a guiding signal, achieving a 22.6% AUC improvement in pediatric brain tumor molecular classification.
AI.motivation: Traditional multimodal contrastive learning treats all non-paired samples as negatives, which fails in medical settings where samples often share high-level semantic attributes, producing false negatives that harm representation quality.
AI.method: MseaCL incorporates semantic similarity between radiology reports as a guiding signal during contrastive learning on paired 3D pediatric brain MRI scans and radiology reports, mitigating the impact of semantically similar false negative samples.
AI.result: The framework as a pretraining stage achieved at least a 22.6% increase in AUC for pediatric brain tumor molecular classification, demonstrating improved downstream task performance.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-aware contrastive learning yields more robust and semantically aligned multimodal representations in clinical applications by addressing the false negative problem inherent in medical data.

title: BrainPilot: Automating Brain Discovery with Agentic Research
summary: Understanding the brain increasingly depends on integrating evidence across scales, modalities, and disciplines. Addressing a single research question therefore requires a coordinated sequence of operations, from surveying prior work to executing analyses and interpreting results in light of domain knowledge. AI agents promise to accelerate this process, but current agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few defined points for expert intervention. These failures are especially costly in brain science, where conclusions feed into downstream scientific claims and depend on laboratory-specific expertise and careful human judgment. We present \textbf{BrainPilot} a \textbf{fully open-source} multi-agent system that accelerates brain science research with traceable logs and agent-verified results. A principal investigator (PI) agent coordinates specialist agents grounded in curated domain knowledge: a unified brain science knowledge base containing 7{,}233 indexed items and a skill library of 72 reusable methodology units across seven research domains. Every major step is recorded in the Graph of Trace, an auditable record that links subgoals, tool use, evidence, and claims and allows researchers to follow and inspect the workflow. An Auditor agent further integrates fabrication checking into the workflow. For evaluation, we run three brain science tasks from Agents' Last Exam, introduce our own benchmark, \textbf{BrainPilotBench-v0}, and present additional end-to-end case studies. Across these evaluations, BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model attains performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent framework with less costs.

AI.tldr: BrainPilot is a fully open-source multi-agent system for brain science research that coordinates specialist agents through a PI agent, grounded in a curated knowledge base, with auditable trace logs and fabrication checking, achieving performance comparable to SOTA agent frameworks at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents lack domain expertise in brain science, may fabricate claims, drift during multi-step reasoning, and offer few intervention points for experts. These failures are particularly costly in brain science where conclusions feed into downstream claims and rely on lab-specific expertise and careful human judgment.
AI.method: A PI (Principal Investigator) agent coordinates specialist agents backed by a unified brain science knowledge base (7,233 indexed items) and a skill library (72 reusable methodology units across 7 domains). Every step is recorded in a Graph of Trace (auditable workflow linking subgoals, tools, evidence, claims). An Auditor agent performs fabrication checking. Evaluated on Agents' Last Exam tasks, the custom BrainPilotBench-v0, and end-to-end case studies.
AI.result: BrainPilot with an open-source backbone model achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art agent frameworks at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: BrainPilot demonstrates that a domain-grounded, auditable multi-agent system can accelerate brain science research reliably and cost-effectively, offering traceability and expert oversight that general-purpose agents lack.

title: Kernel weighted importance sampling for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits
summary: This article presents a novel estimator for performing off-policy evaluation using only offline data for contextual bandits. The proposed estimator, Kernel-WIS is demonstrated to be asymptotically consistent and to empirically outperform strong baselines (including vanilla weighted importance sampling), particularly under complex conditions including behaviour policy miss-specification. The benefit of Kernel-WIS is derived from combining the bounded property of vanilla weighted importance sampling with the linearity of vanilla importance sampling.

AI.tldr: Kernel-WIS is a novel off-policy evaluation estimator for contextual bandits that combines the bounded property of weighted importance sampling with the linearity of importance sampling, achieving asymptotic consistency and outperforming baselines, especially under behaviour policy misspecification.
AI.motivation: Off-policy evaluation using only offline data is a fundamental challenge in contextual bandits. Existing methods like vanilla importance sampling (IS) and weighted importance sampling (WIS) each have limitations: IS is unbiased but suffers from high variance, while WIS is bounded and lower-variance but introduces bias. The authors aim to design an estimator that inherits the advantages of both — the linearity/unbiasedness of IS and the boundedness/stability of WIS — while remaining robust under behaviour policy misspecification.
AI.method: The proposed Kernel-WIS estimator blends vanilla weighted importance sampling with kernel smoothing techniques. By leveraging kernel functions to localize the importance weights, Kernel-WIS retains the bounded, variance-reducing property of WIS while recovering linearity similar to vanilla IS. The estimator operates using only offline logged data without requiring access to the behaviour policy's true functional form, making it particularly suited to scenarios where the behaviour policy may be misspecified.
AI.result: Kernel-WIS is proven to be asymptotically consistent. Empirically, it outperforms strong baselines including vanilla weighted importance sampling, with particularly pronounced benefits under complex conditions such as behaviour policy misspecification.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-WIS successfully bridges the gap between vanilla IS and WIS by combining boundedness with linearity. It offers a robust, consistent solution for off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits, excelling especially when the behaviour policy is misspecified.

title: Long-Context Fine-Tuning with Limited VRAM
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes long training sequences expensive. We combine Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage. Only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; older KV is detached into RAM or NVMe, and HGA loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block. On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, dense training on a 16 GB Quadro RTX 5000 fits 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens with 15.28 GB peak VRAM. Under evaluation the same adapter runs through 131,072 tokens on this card; VRAM is not constant but grows gently with the resident chunk summaries, so RAM and NVMe capacity set the practical limit beyond these lengths. At the shared 2K training length, HGA-trained and dense-trained adapters obtain 2.7405 and 2.7383 nat under the same dense-attention readout, while the stock model obtains 2.9541. At this boundary HGA training is already marginally faster (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), and the HGA-to-dense throughput ratio improves from 1K to 2K; because HGA keeps the attended historical set per token approximately constant while dense work per token grows, we expect this lead to widen as context grows. Dense attention is used for the main quality and retrieval comparisons so that they measure the learned weights and remain compatible with standard generation frameworks. HGA can also be used for retrieval and generation; an optimized production-grade serving implementation is under development.

AI.tldr: HGA combines hierarchical global attention with segment-wise backpropagation and tiered KV storage to enable parameter-efficient fine-tuning on extremely long sequences with bounded VRAM. On a 16GB GPU, it scales QLoRA training from 2K to 16K tokens and supports inference up to 131K tokens, matching dense-attention quality while being faster.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (e.g., QLoRA) reduces model and optimizer memory, but dense attention still makes training on long sequences prohibitively expensive in VRAM. Existing solutions struggle to scale training context length on consumer-grade GPUs without quality degradation.
AI.method: The authors propose Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) with three key components: (1) segment-wise backpropagation where only the active segment remains differentiable in VRAM; (2) tiered KV storage that offloads older key-value pairs to RAM or NVMe; and (3) HGA itself, which loads a bounded set of exact historical tokens for each query block, keeping the attended historical set per token approximately constant regardless of total sequence length.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B with 4-bit QLoRA and PG19, a 16GB Quadro RTX 5000 supports dense training at 2,048 tokens but fails at 4,096, whereas HGA reaches 16,384 tokens (15.28 GB peak VRAM). At inference, the same adapter processes 131,072 tokens. At shared 2K training length, HGA (2.7405 nat) matches dense training (2.7383 nat), both outperforming the stock model (2.9541 nat). HGA training is marginally faster at 2K (217.75 vs. 207.02 tokens/s), with throughput advantage expected to grow with sequence length.
AI.conclusion: HGA enables long-context QLoRA training on consumer GPUs without sacrificing quality, matching dense-attention learned weights. The method supports both retrieval and generation, with a production-grade serving implementation under development. The practical sequence length limit is determined by RAM/NVMe capacity rather than VRAM.

title: An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications
summary: Many engineering problems involve phenomena whose governing equations are poorly characterized or only partially known. Surrogate modeling techniques such as neural networks can capture the behavior of these systems, but they typically demand large training datasets that are difficult to obtain in engineering contexts and yield models with limited physical interpretability. The Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method addresses both limitations by performing sparse regression over libraries of candidate nonlinear terms, recovering interpretable governing equations from comparatively small datasets. Although SINDy has been demonstrated extensively on canonical benchmark systems, its application to practical engineering problems is less widely documented. This tutorial introduces the SINDy method and progressively builds toward its main extensions, from noise-robust weak-form and ensembling-based variants to constrained and parametrizable formulations. The paper and the accompanying tutorial (available at https://github.com/paullililili/SINDy4Engineers) is organized in three parts: the first introduces the standard SINDy algorithm and progressively extends it, inviting readers without prior knowledge to follow each step and adapt the methods to their own problems; the remaining two parts present detailed case studies on (1) the system identification of an unmanned aerial vehicle and (2) a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. Through these examples, we aim to demonstrate that SINDy is simple to implement yet flexible enough to serve as a valuable identification tool for advanced engineering applications.

AI.tldr: This tutorial paper introduces the Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) method and its extensions for engineering applications, progressing from the standard algorithm to noise-robust, constrained, and parametrizable variants, with case studies on UAV system identification and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger.
AI.motivation: Engineering problems often involve poorly characterized governing equations. While neural network surrogates can model these systems, they require large datasets and lack physical interpretability. SINDy addresses both limitations by recovering interpretable equations from small datasets, but its application to practical engineering problems remains underdocumented.
AI.method: The paper is structured in three parts: (1) introduction and progressive extension of the standard SINDy algorithm — including weak-form formulations, ensembling-based variants, constrained formulations, and parametrizable formulations — designed for readers without prior knowledge; (2) case study on UAV system identification; (3) case study on a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger. A companion GitHub repository provides code.
