AI.result: The paper demonstrates through detailed case studies that SINDy and its extensions are simple to implement and flexible enough for advanced engineering applications, successfully identifying dynamics for both a UAV and a chaotic thermosyphon heat exchanger.
AI.conclusion: SINDy serves as a valuable, interpretable identification tool for engineering applications, offering a practical alternative to data-hungry black-box surrogates, and is accessible to practitioners through the provided tutorial and code.

title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
summary:
World models are usually evaluated as components of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) systems, while the world models themselves are rarely studied in isolation.
  We examine five representative visual world-model agents in Atari Pong: DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM. After reproducing their training pipelines and matching the reported agent performance, we freeze the learned world models and evaluate them with a closed-loop rollout diagnostic: a policy trained separately from the corresponding MBRL agent interacts with each frozen model, and the generated video trajectories are inspected for visual and dynamical errors. Across all five models, the rollouts contain clear failures, including ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, and invalid ball-paddle interactions.
  Beyond visual trajectories, we further evaluate them with pixel-space zero-shot MBRL, where a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and then evaluated in the real environment. Across all five models, the resulting policies substantially underperform those produced by the corresponding original MBRL training pipelines. The gap is particularly large for DreamerV3, whose mean return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the minimum Pong return of -21.
  We hypothesize that insufficient modeling of task-critical concepts, such as the ball in Pong, may contribute to these failures. We therefore propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied to segmented concept regions. Experiments show that CGSReg improves both closed-loop rollouts and pixel-space zero-shot MBRL in DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER. Its effects vary across the remaining models and evaluation metrics, indicating that CGSReg alone does not address all world-model bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: World models in MBRL agents are rarely evaluated in isolation. The authors evaluate five world models (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) in Atari Pong, finding significant rollout failures (ball disappearance, incorrect motion) and poor zero-shot MBRL performance when policies are trained inside frozen models. They propose CGSReg, a concept-guided pixel reconstruction loss targeting task-critical regions (e.g., the ball), which improves DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER but does not fully close the performance gap.
AI.motivation: World models are typically evaluated only as components of full MBRL systems, obscuring their individual modeling fidelity. The paper aims to isolate and systematically diagnose world model failures, hypothesizing that inadequate modeling of task-critical visual concepts (like the ball in Pong) underlies poor performance.
AI.method: The authors reproduce five visual MBRL agents (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) on Atari Pong, freeze their world models, and evaluate via: (1) closed-loop rollout diagnostics — a separately trained policy interacts with each frozen model and generated video trajectories are inspected for visual/dynamical errors; (2) pixel-space zero-shot MBRL — a new policy is trained entirely inside a frozen world model and tested in the real environment. To address identified failures, they propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), an auxiliary pixel reconstruction loss applied specifically to segmented concept regions (e.g., the ball segmentation mask).
AI.result: All five world models exhibited clear rollout failures (ball disappearance, incorrect ball motion, invalid ball-paddle interactions). In zero-shot MBRL, policies trained inside frozen models substantially underperformed original MBRL pipelines. DreamerV3 suffered the largest drop (mean return from -5.5 to -20.9, near the Pong minimum of -21). CGSReg improved closed-loop rollouts and zero-shot MBRL for DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER, but effects varied across models and metrics, indicating CGSReg alone does not resolve all world-model bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: World models in state-of-the-art MBRL agents contain significant modeling failures when evaluated in isolation, particularly regarding task-critical concepts. The proposed CGSReg offers partial mitigation but not a complete solution, suggesting that future work should develop more comprehensive approaches to improve world-model fidelity beyond concept-level regularization.

title: Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes
summary: This article explores the application of covariate balance diagnostics for detecting the presence of hidden confounding/model miss-specification in studies applying offline reinforcement learning (RL) to deriving optimal treatment recommendations. The results demonstrate that, either there is a high risk of bias within existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations or, existing covariate balance metrics are not sufficient to assess such studies. Regardless, existing offline RL studies cannot be concluded as being statistically robust. The conclusions propose future research directions for obtaining more methodologically robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether covariate balance diagnostics can detect hidden confounding or model misspecification in offline RL for treatment recommendations, finding that existing studies either carry high bias risk or current balance metrics are inadequate — rendering existing offline RL studies statistically non-robust.
AI.motivation: Offline reinforcement learning is increasingly used to derive optimal treatment recommendations from observational data. However, such data are susceptible to hidden confounding and model misspecification, which can bias results. The authors aim to test whether covariate balance diagnostics — commonly used in causal inference — can serve as a reliable detection mechanism for these issues in offline RL settings.
AI.method: The authors apply covariate balance diagnostics (metrics borrowed from the causal inference literature that assess whether treatment groups are comparable on observed covariates) to existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendation. These diagnostics are used to probe for signs of hidden confounding or model misspecification.
AI.result: The analysis reveals a dilemma: either (1) existing offline RL studies for treatment recommendations carry a high risk of hidden confounding bias, or (2) current covariate balance metrics are insufficiently sensitive or appropriate for evaluating offline RL models. In either case, existing studies cannot be deemed statistically robust.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for new methodological research to bridge the gap between causal inference diagnostics and offline RL evaluation, proposing future directions for more robust applications of offline RL to treatment recommendation problems.

title: The Industrialization of Research ; On AI-Driven Science and Its Consequences
summary: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research -- not merely as a more powerful instrument, but as an autonomous participant in the research cycle itself. This transition constitutes, in the most precise sense of the term, the industrialization of research: a shift from a craft model, in which knowledge, method, and judgment are embedded in the researcher, to a pipeline model, in which these steps are decomposed, automated, and supervised. The US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission is the most ambitious current instantiation of this shift, but the fundamental questions it raises extend far beyond any single program. This essay examines seven such questions: the erosion of the intergenerational transmission of scientific competence; the growing opacity of AI-generated theories; the collapse of peer evaluation under a flood of machine-generated output; the unproven capacity of AI for paradigm-shifting discovery; the capture of the scientific agenda by political and industrial actors; the compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines; and the structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These concerns do not constitute an argument against AI-driven science -- whose demonstrated potential is real and significant. They constitute the conditions under which that potential can be responsibly pursued.

AI.tldr: This essay argues that AI-driven science represents an "industrialization of research" — a shift from a craft model to a pipeline model — and examines seven critical concerns that must be addressed to responsibly pursue AI's potential in scientific discovery, using the DOE's Genesis Mission as the primary case study.
AI.motivation: The author identifies that while AI is transforming science from a tool into an autonomous research participant, the fundamental questions raised by this shift — exemplified by the DOE's Genesis Mission — extend beyond any single program and demand systematic examination before the transition becomes irreversible.
AI.method: This is a critical essay employing conceptual analysis. The author frames the AI-driven transformation of science as "industrialization" (craft-to-pipeline shift) and systematically articulates seven distinct concerns: (1) erosion of intergenerational competence transmission, (2) opacity of AI-generated theories, (3) collapse of peer evaluation under machine-generated output volume, (4) unproven capacity for paradigm-shifting discovery, (5) capture of scientific agenda by political/industrial actors, (6) compounding of systematic errors in closed-loop pipelines, and (7) structural bifurcation of the global research community into incommensurable tiers. These are positioned not as arguments against AI-driven science but as conditions for responsible pursuit.
AI.result: The essay does not present empirical results but yields a structured framework of seven concerns that together define the risk landscape of industrialized AI-driven research. The framing positions these concerns as necessary conditions — not obstacles — for responsible development.
AI.conclusion: AI's demonstrated potential in scientific research is real and significant, but its responsible pursuit depends on confronting the seven identified concerns. The industrialization of research is not inherently negative, but the conditions under which it proceeds will determine whether its benefits are realized without catastrophic erosion of scientific integrity, equity, and epistemic capacity.

title: Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches
summary: This paper develops a categorical framework -- Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches (LINCS) -- as the repair of non-compositionality: failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches lifted to the tangent category setting. Machine learning problems are specified as sketches: graphs with commutativity conditions $\mathcal D$, limit cones $\mathcal L$, and colimit cocones $\mathcal K$, generalizing the usual scalarization of loss functions or vector space assumptions. Non-compositionality is defined purely as failure of a universal factorization problem, not as arithmetic error between the desired and actual predictions. Given a learning sketch $\mathbb S=(S,\mathcal D,\mathcal L,\mathcal K)$, whose underlying graph is $S$, and a model $D:J \rightarrow C$, the base defect is the obstruction to factorization $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(D))$. The tangent lift applies the tangent functor $T$ to obtain $TD:J \rightarrow C$, and LINCS is defined as the obstruction $\mbox{Obs}(\mbox{Fact}_{\mathbb S}(TD))$ -- asking whether infinitesimal perturbations preserve the compositionality constraints.The paper also introduces Tangent Learning Sketches, which are sketches equipped with Cockett-Cruttwell tangent structure. The paper defines the INC endofunctor, which iterates the tangent lift, producing a tower $D,TD,T^2D, \cdots$ of factorization problems. ML is thereby formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize ($νT_{\mbox{INC}}$). Using the Aczel--Mendler theorem, we prove existence of a final INC coalgebra whenever $T_{\mbox{INC}}$ admits a set-based class realization that creates its final carrier. A detailed experimental evaluation of LINCS is underway in a number of concrete ML settings, including deep learning, large language models, and reinforcement learning, and is described in companion papers.

AI.tldr: LINCS is a categorical framework that reformulates machine learning as the repair of non-compositionality — failures of diagrams to factor through quotient sketches — lifted to the tangent category setting. It replaces error-based loss with obstruction theory, iterating tangent lifts to form a coalgebraic tower whose fixed point characterizes learning.
AI.motivation: Traditional ML formalizes learning via scalar loss functions and vector space assumptions. This paper seeks a purely structural, categorical alternative where non-compositionality is defined as failure of a universal factorization problem rather than arithmetic error, providing a more general and principled foundation for diverse learning paradigms.
AI.method: The authors define learning sketches as graphs equipped with commutativity conditions, limit cones, and colimit cocones. A model is a diagram D: J→C. The base defect is Obs(Fact_S(D)), the obstruction to factorization. The tangent functor T is applied to obtain TD, and LINCS is the obstruction Obs(Fact_S(TD)). The INC endofunctor iterates tangent lifts, producing a tower D, TD, T²D, … . Using the Aczel–Mendler theorem, existence of a final INC coalgebra is proved when T_INC admits a set-based class realization. Tangent Learning Sketches are introduced, equipped with Cockett–Cruttwell tangent structure.
AI.result: The paper proves existence of a final INC coalgebra (νT_INC) under set-based realizability conditions, establishing that ML can be formulated as the search for a coalgebraic fixed point where successive tangent unfoldings stabilize. Experimental evaluation is deferred to companion papers.
AI.conclusion: LINCS provides a rigorous categorical semantics for machine learning grounded in obstruction theory and tangent categories, replacing error minimization with compositional repair. The coalgebraic fixed point formulation unifies the learning process across diverse settings (deep learning, LLMs, RL), with empirical validation reserved for companion work.

title: MedFailBench: A Clinician-Built Open-Source Benchmark for Medical AI Safety Boundary Inspection
comment: 6 pages; clinician-reviewed synthetic benchmark; no patient data
summary: Most medical AI benchmarks measure whether a model knows the correct answer. MedFailBench asks a different question: which safety boundary failed? We present a clinician-built synthetic benchmark and failure atlas that labels medical AI errors by severity (1--5) and safety gate type (missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, source support gap). The current public release (v0.2.1) contains 44 clinician-reviewed synthetic cases with severity annotations, a live HuggingFace leaderboard preview, a safety gate taxonomy, a clinical severity rubric, and an automated pipeline for archiving model-response screening runs. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included. MedFailBench is released under Apache-2.0 and CC-BY-4.0 and carries the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21205535.

AI.tldr: MedFailBench is a clinician-built benchmark that classifies medical AI errors by severity (1–5) and safety gate failure type, rather than simply measuring accuracy. The v0.2.1 release includes 44 annotated synthetic cases, a safety taxonomy, a leaderboard preview, and an automated evaluation pipeline.
AI.motivation: Existing medical AI benchmarks only assess whether a model produces the correct answer, failing to characterize how and why failures occur. The authors argue that understanding which safety boundaries are breached — such as missed urgent escalations or fabricated evidence — is critical for clinical deployment safety.
AI.method: Clinicians constructed a synthetic benchmark of 44 cases, each annotated with a severity score (1–5) and a safety gate failure label from six categories: missed urgent escalation, unsafe remote dosing, unsafe discharge reassurance, evidence fabrication, unsafe protocol execution, and source support gap. An automated pipeline archives model-response screening runs, with results surfaced via a HuggingFace leaderboard.
AI.result: The v0.2.1 release delivers the benchmark dataset, severity rubric, safety gate taxonomy, leaderboard preview, and screening pipeline. No patient data, clinical validation claims, or model rankings are included in this release.
AI.conclusion: MedFailBench shifts evaluation focus from correctness to failure-mode characterization, offering a structured framework for auditing medical AI safety boundaries. The authors plan further expansion beyond the initial 44-case release.

title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation is an alternative post-training method in reinforcement learning that alleviates the constraints imposed by reward models by providing token-level supervision from a teacher model. Although on-policy distillation has been studied and applied across various settings, its fundamental design remains underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a new distillation reward, termed the delta signal, instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution. The delta signal is defined as the difference between the teacher model and its base model prior to instruction tuning for reasoning capability. It therefore captures the changes induced by reasoning tuning and provides a more direct signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. Using extensive empirical evidence, we show that the delta signal substantially improves on-policy distillation and refer to the new distillation method as On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD$^2$). Experiments across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that OPD$^2$ consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation, enabling reasoning LLMs to achieve strong performance with only a short post-training period. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/opd2

AI.tldr: OPD² introduces the "delta signal" — the difference between a teacher model and its pre-instruction-tuned base model — as a distillation reward for on-policy RL distillation, significantly outperforming conventional on-policy distillation across math, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks with minimal post-training.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation is a useful post-training method that avoids reward model constraints, but its fundamental design is underexplored. The authors aim to improve how reasoning capabilities are transferred from teacher to student by moving beyond naive imitation of the teacher's output distribution.
AI.method: Instead of directly imitating the teacher's output distribution, OPD² uses a "delta signal" as the distillation reward. This signal is computed as the difference between the teacher model (post-instruction-tuning for reasoning) and its base model (pre-tuning). The delta captures only the changes induced by reasoning-specific tuning, providing a cleaner, more direct supervision signal for transferring reasoning capabilities. The method is applied within an on-policy distillation framework.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that OPD² consistently outperforms conventional on-policy distillation across mathematics, science, and code-reasoning benchmarks, enabling strong reasoning performance after only a short post-training period.
AI.conclusion: The delta signal is a simple yet effective innovation for on-policy distillation, isolating reasoning-specific knowledge from the teacher and leading to substantial improvements over standard approaches. OPD² represents an advancement in efficient reasoning transfer for LLMs.

title: RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models
summary: Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are widely used to model dynamical systems in physics, biology, neuroscience, and physiology, but in many applications some equations of the dynamics are unknown and only a subset of the state variables are measured. We propose a hybrid neural--physics framework in which the known components of the ODE are kept explicit and the missing components are represented by a neural network. The proposed method consists of two stages where we alternate between state and parameter estimation and iterate until a predetermined criterion is met. Specifically, in the first step, we treat the model parameters as being known and we infer the latent states from the available measurements using a Rauch--Tung--Striebel (RTS) smoother. In the second stage, we treat the smoothed trajectories as being known and use them to estimate the neural networks' parameters through backpropagation. We evaluate the method on benchmark systems spanning linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. Across these settings, the proposed method learns missing ODE components from incomplete measurements while exploiting and retaining interpretable mechanistic structure and improving latent-state reconstruction and long-horizon prediction.

AI.tldr: A hybrid neural-physics framework that alternates between RTS smoothing for latent state estimation and backpropagation for neural network parameter learning, enabling recovery of missing ODE components from partial state observations while preserving interpretable mechanistic structure.
AI.motivation: In many dynamical system applications, only a subset of state variables are measured and some governing equations are unknown. Existing purely data-driven approaches often sacrifice interpretability and physical structure, while purely mechanistic models cannot account for missing dynamics. There is a need for a method that learns unknown ODE components from incomplete measurements while retaining known mechanistic structure.
AI.method: A two-stage iterative framework: (1) With neural network parameters fixed, a Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother infers latent states from partial measurements; (2) With smoothed trajectories treated as known, backpropagation updates the neural network parameters representing the unknown ODE components. The alternation continues until convergence.
AI.result: The method was evaluated on benchmark systems covering linear, nonlinear, and stiff dynamics under partial state observation. It successfully learned missing ODE components from incomplete measurements, improved latent-state reconstruction, and enhanced long-horizon prediction while retaining interpretable mechanistic structure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid neural-physics framework effectively bridges mechanistic modeling and deep learning, enabling robust learning of unknown dynamics from partial observations without discarding known physical structure.

title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
summary: AI benchmarks increasingly leverage item-level statistical models, particularly item response theory (IRT), to estimate model capabilities, rank systems, select informative examples, and diagnose benchmark quality. However, AI benchmark data often departs from the data regime of human testing, for which standard IRT estimation tools were originally developed: benchmarks typically involve fewer evaluated models, far more items, and capability distributions that may be skewed, clustered, or multimodal. We examine how these regime mismatches challenge the reliability of IRT modeling for AI evaluation. Using item parameters and capability distributions derived from six widely used LLM benchmarks, we simulate response matrices under three common IRT models and compare four estimation tools used in recent benchmark studies: marginal maximum likelihood, Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational inference, and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator. Across 18,000 simulation conditions, we systematically evaluate computational feasibility, scalability, and the reliability of IRT inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item characteristics. Results show that classical estimators can become infeasible in large benchmark settings, whereas scalable estimators can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences with small or nonnormally distributed model sets. This study identifies when latent trait models reliably support or risk distorting AI benchmarking claims, and what sample sizes and diagnostics are needed for trustworthy use.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the reliability of item response theory (IRT) for AI benchmarking when the data regime differs from traditional human testing—fewer models, many more items, and nonnormal capability distributions. Through 18,000 simulations across six LLM benchmarks and four estimation methods, the authors identify when IRT inferences about model rankings, performance predictions, and item characteristics become unreliable.
AI.motivation: AI benchmarks increasingly use IRT for model evaluation, but IRT tools were developed for human testing settings with many examinees, modest item counts, and roughly normal ability distributions. AI benchmarks invert this pattern: few evaluated models, vast item pools, and often skewed or multimodal capability distributions. This regime mismatch raises concerns about whether standard IRT estimators yield trustworthy inferences in AI contexts.
AI.method: The authors use item parameters and capability distributions from six real-world LLM benchmarks to simulate response matrices under three IRT models (1PL/Rasch, 2PL, 3PL). They compare four estimation approaches—marginal maximum likelihood (MML), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), variational inference (VI), and a neural pseudo-Siamese estimator—across 18,000 conditions. Evaluation criteria include computational feasibility, scalability, and reliability of inferences about model rankings, predicted performance, and item parameter recovery.
AI.result: Classical estimators (MML, MCMC) become computationally infeasible in large-scale benchmark settings. Scalable estimators (VI, neural methods) can produce unreliable item-level and ranking inferences when the model sample is small or the capability distribution is nonnormal (skewed, clustered, or multimodal). Specific diagnostics and minimum sample sizes are identified for trustworthy IRT application in AI benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: IRT can support valid AI benchmarking claims only under specific conditions regarding sample size and distributional shape. Researchers should apply appropriate diagnostics and be cautious when using latent trait models with small or nonnormally distributed model sets, lest IRT-based inferences distort rather than clarify benchmarking conclusions.

title: BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong
summary: World-action models (WAMs) are emerging as a promising foundation for embodied control: rather than predicting actions alone, they learn representations that couple action generation with future world prediction. This coupling is often viewed as a source of robustness, interpretability, and safety, as a robot's action can in principle be checked against its imagined future. In this paper, we show that this assumption is fragile. We introduce BadWAM, a unified framework for modeling and evaluating World-Action Drift Attacks: a new class of WAM-specific adversarial attacks that use small visual perturbations to break the alignment between what a WAM imagines and what it executes. BadWAM characterizes this attack surface along two natural criteria: attack strength and stealthiness. When the adversary prioritizes disruption, BadWAM instantiates an action-only adversarial attack, which directly drives the model toward task-failing actions. When the adversary additionally prioritizes stealth, BadWAM instantiates an imagination-preserving adversarial attack, which seeks to induce harmful action shifts while keeping the model's predicted future close to its clean imagination. Together, these two attacks capture a spectrum of WAM-specific failures: from overt action hijacking to stealthier cases where the model appears to imagine a plausible future but executes a desynchronized action. We evaluate BadWAM across different variants of WAMs. Results show that our attacks substantially reduce task success rates under closed-loop execution. For example, our action-only attack reduces the model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success. The results of our imagination-preserving attack further exposes a WAM-specific vulnerability: moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift.

AI.tldr: BadWAM introduces World-Action Drift Attacks, a new class of adversarial attacks that exploit the decoupling between a WAM's imagined future and its executed action using small visual perturbations. The framework spans two attack modes — action-only (maximizing task failure) and imagination-preserving (inducing harmful actions while maintaining plausible future predictions) — revealing fundamental vulnerabilities in WAM-based embodied control.
AI.motivation: World-action models are valued for their coupling of action generation with future prediction, which is presumed to offer robustness, interpretability, and safety. The authors challenge this assumption, demonstrating that the alignment between imagination and execution is fragile and can be exploited by adversaries.
AI.method: The authors propose BadWAM, a unified adversarial attack framework with two instantiations: (1) an action-only adversarial attack that directly optimizes perturbations to drive the model toward task-failing actions, prioritizing disruption; and (2) an imagination-preserving adversarial attack that jointly optimizes for harmful action shifts while regularizing the predicted future to stay close to the clean imagination, prioritizing stealth. The framework is evaluated under closed-loop execution across multiple WAM variants.
AI.result: The action-only attack reduces model performance from 96.5% to 43.1% success rate. The imagination-preserving attack reveals that moderate future-preserving regularization can maintain strong attack performance while reducing future imagination drift, exposing a WAM-specific vulnerability where the model appears to imagine plausibly but executes desynchronized actions.
AI.conclusion: The coupling between action generation and world prediction in WAMs is not inherently robust against adversarial perturbations. BadWAM demonstrates that adversaries can systematically exploit the action-imagination alignment, and that stealthy attacks can preserve plausible future predictions while still causing task failures, highlighting critical safety concerns for WAM-based embodied systems.

title: Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) automation remains challenging in real-world environments, where dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, and evolving interface states can cause autonomous agents to drift from user intent. Recent vision-based multimodal agents improve flexibility by operating directly over screenshots and natural language instructions, but planning and adaptation often remain internal, limiting users' ability to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior. We present Plover, a plan-centric vision-based GUI automation system that externalizes task plans and replanning as persistent, inspectable, and revisable artifacts. Through a planner--executor architecture, Plover supports explicit supervision of evolving execution, localized correction through editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design. We then evaluate Plover through benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow analyses. Our results show that many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized, and that explicit replanning helps make GUI automation more transparent, controllable, and adaptable.

AI.tldr: Plover is a plan-centric GUI automation system that externalizes task plans as inspectable, editable artifacts, enabling users to supervise, correct, and guide autonomous agents through localized interventions and replanning, making GUI automation more transparent and repairable.
AI.motivation: Current vision-based GUI automation agents suffer from opaque internal planning, making it difficult for users to inspect, supervise, or correct system behavior when agents drift from user intent due to dynamic layouts, unexpected dialogs, or evolving interfaces.
AI.method: Plover employs a planner-executor architecture that externalizes task plans as persistent artifacts. The system supports explicit supervision, localized correction via editable plans, natural-language guidance, and screenshot-grounded interventions, while preserving prior progress during repair. A formative study with six participants informed the interaction design, followed by benchmark failure-case repair and scenario-based workflow evaluations.
AI.result: Many autonomous GUI-agent failures are structurally repairable when plans remain visible and interventions are localized. Explicit replanning improves transparency, controllability, and adaptability of GUI automation.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing plans and supporting localized replanning significantly enhances the usability of vision-based GUI automation agents, enabling effective human-in-the-loop supervision and robust failure recovery.

title: Data Driven Block Replacement Scheduling
summary: We develop data-driven algorithms for maintaining $N$ independent identical machines under a \textit{block replacement policy}, in which each machine is replaced upon failure and all machines are jointly replaced at regular intervals of length $k$. The goal is to learn the cost-minimizing interval $k^*$ from operational data when the lifetime distribution is unknown. At each decision epoch, the operator selects $k \in \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}$, observes the resulting failure history (a mixture of complete and right-censored lifetimes) and incurs a per-unit-time cost governed by the renewal function. We formulate this as a stochastic multi-armed bandit and propose Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based lower-confidence-bound algorithms achieving $O(K \log T)$ regret, matching the Lai--Robbins lower bound. Exploiting a nested observation property unique to block replacement, correlated variants attain $O((K-k^*)\log T)$ regret and require only $O(1)$ direct pulls of suboptimal arms $k < k^*$. A complementary Kaplan--Meier renewal algorithm estimates the lifetime distribution nonparametrically from censored data, achieving almost-sure policy consistency and empirically near-zero incremental regret at long horizons. We additionally analyze two average-cost MDPs: a time-elapsed formulation establishing that block replacement is optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution, and an age-vector formulation proving a monotone threshold structure under increasing failure rate distributions and providing a gold-standard cost benchmark. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical ordering and reveal structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.

AI.tldr: This paper develops data-driven bandit algorithms to learn the cost-minimizing block replacement interval from censored operational data, achieving optimal regret bounds, and establishes structural properties of block replacement policies via MDP analysis.
AI.motivation: In industrial maintenance, block replacement policies — where machines are individually replaced on failure and collectively at fixed intervals — require knowing the optimal interval k*. When the lifetime distribution is unknown, operators must learn k* online from censored failure data while minimizing cumulative cost, motivating a bandit-based approach.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a stochastic multi-armed bandit over k ∈ {1,…,K}. Two lower-confidence-bound (LCB) algorithms using Hoeffding and Bernstein bounds achieve O(K log T) regret. Correlated variants exploit a nested observation property unique to block replacement, achieving O((K−k*)log T) regret with O(1) pulls of suboptimal arms k < k*. A Kaplan–Meier renewal algorithm nonparametrically estimates the lifetime distribution from censored data for near-zero incremental regret. Two MDP formulations — time-elapsed and age-vector — establish the optimality of block replacement within its class and a monotone threshold structure under increasing failure rate distributions.
AI.result: The Hoeffding- and Bernstein-based LCB algorithms match the Lai–Robbins lower bound of O(K log T) regret. Correlated variants achieve sharper O((K−k*)log T) regret. The Kaplan–Meier renewal estimator yields almost-sure policy consistency. MDP analysis proves block replacement is optimal within its policy class for any lifetime distribution and reveals a monotone threshold structure under IFR distributions. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical regret ordering and expose structural cost gaps between optimal block and age-dependent replacement.
AI.conclusion: Block replacement intervals can be learned efficiently from censored operational data using bandit algorithms with strong regret guarantees. The nested observation structure enables significant regret reduction, and nonparametric renewal estimation offers a complementary long-horizon approach. The MDP analysis provides theoretical justification for block replacement and benchmarks for future policy comparisons.

title: Mutable Low-Rank Sketches for Retrain-Free Recommendation
summary: A common bottleneck in two-stage recommendation is embedding staleness: when a user rates a new item, their embedding remains fixed until the next retrain cycle. We propose mutable sketches, which store each user's preferences in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree with sum aggregation), fit a low-rank projection once, and recompute embeddings on-the-fly as ratings arrive. We prove that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope (Theorem 1), a guarantee that FunkSVD and eALS lack. On KuaiRec, the mutable sketch achieves 0.810 RMSE at 1.8% data read vs. ALS 0.822 at 100%, with 8x faster per-batch updates. A new user receives personalized recommendations in <1 ms after their first rating, with no model retraining required. A comparison of sampling strategies across density regimes shows that the KP-tree's norm-proportional sampling provides 40-130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density), while uniform sampling suffices on dense matrices.

AI.tldr: To solve embedding staleness in two-stage recommenders, the authors propose mutable sketches using a KP-tree data structure that computes low-rank user embeddings on-the-fly as new ratings arrive, with provably monotonic error reduction. The method matches or exceeds ALS accuracy while reading only 1.8% of data and updating 8x faster per batch, enabling sub-millisecond personalization after a single rating without retraining.
AI.motivation: In two-stage recommendation systems, user embeddings become stale between retraining cycles — when a user provides new ratings, the model cannot incorporate this feedback until the next expensive full retrain. Existing matrix factorization methods (FunkSVD, eALS) lack guarantees on how predictions improve with incremental observations.
AI.method: The authors introduce mutable sketches: each user's preference vector is stored in a KP-tree (a sparse segment tree supporting sum aggregation with norm-proportional sampling). A low-rank projection matrix is fitted once globally. When new ratings arrive, the embedding is recomputed on-the-fly via the KP-tree without retraining. The method provides a theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) that each new observation monotonically tightens the prediction error envelope. Sampling strategies are analyzed across density regimes.
AI.result: On the KuaiRec dataset, mutable sketches achieve 0.810 RMSE while reading only 1.8% of the data, compared to ALS at 0.822 RMSE using 100% of the data. Per-batch updates are 8x faster than ALS. A new user receives personalized recommendations in under 1 ms after their first rating. Norm-proportional sampling via the KP-tree yields 40–130% better item coverage on sparse data (<1% density) versus uniform sampling, while uniform sampling suffices for dense matrices.
AI.conclusion: Mutable sketches offer a practical solution to the embedding staleness problem, providing competitive accuracy with dramatic data efficiency, fast incremental updates, and instant cold-start personalization. The provable monotonic error reduction distinguishes it from prior matrix factorization approaches.

title: Decoding Market Emotion from Blockchain Activity: A Data-Driven Sentiment Classifier
comment: This manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Symposium on Computers and Communications (ISCC 2026)
summary: The growing use of Bitcoin as a decentralized digital asset and investment tool has sparked strong interest in understanding its market behavior. This study presents a new approach to analyze Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain and financial data with social media posts. Unlike models that aim to predict prices, this work focuses on explaining market sentiment using blockchain transactions, historical price data of Bitcoin, and daily Twitter sentiment classifications. The method merges sentiment trends with on-chain and financial metrics, normalized into a dataset for detailed market analysis. Multiple machine learning models were tested using cross-validation, with Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) emerging as the most reliable model for classifying sentiment, achieving an average F1-score of about 0.84. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), a game theory-based method for model interpretability, was used to quantify the contribution of on-chain features to the model's predictions, improving transparency. The results indicate that this data combination yields meaningful predictive signals and insights, supporting data-driven cryptocurrency analysis and future improvements with deep learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Bitcoin market sentiment analysis framework that integrates on-chain data, financial metrics, and Twitter sentiment. Using XGBoost (F1≈0.84) and SHAP for interpretability, it demonstrates that combining these heterogeneous data sources yields meaningful predictive signals for sentiment classification rather than price prediction.
AI.motivation: The growing adoption of Bitcoin as a decentralized digital asset has created demand for understanding its market behavior. Existing work often focuses on price prediction; this study instead aims to explain market sentiment by fusing blockchain transaction data, historical prices, and social media discourse to provide a more holistic, interpretable view of market dynamics.
AI.method: The authors construct a normalized dataset merging three data streams: on-chain metrics (blockchain transactions), financial indicators (historical Bitcoin prices), and daily Twitter sentiment classifications. They evaluate multiple machine learning models via cross-validation, selecting XGBoost (Gradient Boosting) as the best performer for sentiment classification. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is then applied to quantify feature contributions, enhancing model transparency and interpretability.
AI.result: XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of approximately 0.84 for sentiment classification, outperforming other tested models. SHAP analysis revealed that on-chain features contribute meaningfully to the model's predictions, and the combined data sources yield robust predictive signals.
AI.conclusion: The fusion of on-chain, financial, and social media data provides meaningful and interpretable signals for Bitcoin market sentiment analysis. The approach supports data-driven cryptocurrency research and lays groundwork for future improvements using deep learning techniques.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
summary: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

AI.tldr: AutoSynthesis is an end-to-end multi-agent system that automates the entire meta-analysis pipeline — from literature search and screening to effect size computation and heterogeneity analysis — producing results that closely match expert-conducted meta-analyses.
AI.motivation: Quantitative evidence synthesis (meta-analysis) is essential for evidence-based decision-making but remains largely manual, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Automating this process would accelerate knowledge generation across science, medicine, education, and policy.
AI.method: AutoSynthesis uses a multi-agent architecture that takes a natural language research question and sequentially: (1) formulates a search strategy, (2) retrieves scientific literature, (3) screens candidate studies, (4) assesses full-text eligibility, (5) extracts quantitative statistics, (6) computes standardized effect sizes (Hedges' g), (7) performs random-effects meta-analysis, (8) conducts heterogeneity/moderator analysis, and (9) performs risk-of-bias assessment. Output is a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines.
AI.result: In testing, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates closely matched those from expert-conducted meta-analyses, demonstrating strong agreement with manual evidence synthesis.
AI.conclusion: AutoSynthesis demonstrates that automated, end-to-end meta-analysis is feasible and reliable, offering a scalable solution to accelerate quantitative evidence synthesis and support evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.

title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
summary: Poisoning pretraining data can introduce harmful behaviors to LMs that are difficult to detect and mitigate. Prior work on poisoning pretraining data has largely exploited established data sources such as Wikipedia, which do not represent the large scale and heterogeneity typical of pretraining corpora, and has ignored the interaction between poisoned data and data curation pipelines. We demonstrate that poisoning attacks on pretraining data are feasible beyond this limited setting through an existing web-scale content injection mechanism: public discussion interfaces. Additionally, to measure whether malicious content is included after web crawling and data curation, we introduce HalfLife, a novel analysis for estimating adversarial content inclusion in web-crawl based LM training data. We use HalfLife to explore the feasibility of poisoning pretraining corpora at web scale through open discussion interfaces. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of estimating whether poison injections are included in pretraining data, and establishes third-party webpage content as a possible vector for attacking language model pretraining.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the feasibility of poisoning language model pretraining data via web-scale content injection through public discussion interfaces, and introduces HalfLife, a novel analysis method for estimating whether adversarial content survives web crawling and data curation pipelines.
AI.motivation: Prior work on pretraining data poisoning has been limited to controlled datasets like Wikipedia, failing to capture the scale and heterogeneity of real-world pretraining corpora. Moreover, existing studies ignore how data curation pipelines (crawling, filtering, deduplication) interact with poisoned content. The authors aim to demonstrate that real-world poisoning is feasible through existing web mechanisms and that assessing post-curation inclusion is critical.
AI.method: The authors exploit public discussion interfaces (e.g., comment sections, forums) as an injection vector for adversarial content. They introduce HalfLife, an analysis framework that estimates the probability and proportion of injected poison content that survives the web crawling and data curation pipeline to ultimately appear in pretraining corpora. HalfLife models the temporal dynamics of content persistence, crawl frequency, and curation filtering.
AI.result: The analysis shows that poisoning pretraining data at web scale via public discussion interfaces is feasible: a non-trivial fraction of injected content can survive crawling and curation. HalfLife effectively quantifies adversarial inclusion rates and highlights the risk posed by third-party webpage content as a viable attack vector.
AI.conclusion: Third-party webpage content, particularly via public discussion interfaces, constitutes a realistic attack surface for poisoning LM pretraining data. Estimating poison inclusion post-curation (via methods like HalfLife) is essential for understanding and mitigating such threats in web-scale training pipelines.

title: Falsifiable Release Gates for Self-Improving Systems
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Software, gate suite, run artifacts, and TLA+ specification are open source
summary: Safety claims on self-improving agent runtimes are almost always self-graded: a policy file, a guardrail, or a README commitment. We describe falsifiable release gates, and a methodology to build and validate such systems, such that every new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before it ships, and a fixed set of standing invariants is preserved at each gate. The self-enhancement loop is positively Constrained: the entire write surface is policy rules, tightening changes. may auto-apply loosening changes always require a human merge and a proposal autoclosed is one that mispredicts its own effect; We publish the acceptance measured results for all the seven gates, define precisely the scope of each claim (a bounded of the coordination skeleton (not the learned components) and free the runtime, either command line tools and the gate suite, so the results reproduce, and gates can run against other agent frameworks. Reviewers may repeat the single command central non-bypass in seconds.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a methodology for creating falsifiable release gates in self-improving AI agent runtimes. Each new capability must pass machine-verifiable acceptance tests before deployment, with standing invariants preserved at each gate. The method was applied in Antahkarana, an open runtime, across seven gates — from basic observability to a self-governing loop that proposes policy changes. A safety-critical property capability token system, exhaustive model-checking over a million reachable states, and a constrained self-enhancement loop (auto-apply only tightening changes; loosening changes require human merge) ensure safety. All results, tools, and gate suites are released openly for reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Current safety claims on self-improving AI agent runtimes are almost always self-graded — relying on policy files, guardrails, or README commitments — which are non-falsifiable and lack rigorous, machine-verifiable validation. There is a need for a methodology that provides falsifiable, reproducible, and machine-checkable safety guarantees before new capabilities are shipped.
AI.method: The authors propose falsifiable release gates: each new capability must pass a pre-specified, machine-verifiable acceptance suite before shipping, with a fixed set of standing invariants preserved at each gate. The methodology was instantiated in the Antahkarana open runtime across seven sequential gates: (1) basic observability through to (7) a self-governing loop that suggests changes to its own policy. Key technical mechanisms include: (a) no action reaches an effector without a safety-critical property capability token minted by a control ring; (b) exhaustive model-checking over approximately one million recorded reachable states of a bounded model, re-checked against execution traces; (c) a purposely broken model used to verify the checker has teeth (producing the shortest counterexample); (d) a positively constrained self-enhancement loop where the entire write surface is policy rules — tightening changes may auto-apply, loosening changes always require human merge, and proposals that mispredict their own effect are auto-closed. The runtime, CLI tools, gate suite, and acceptance results for all seven gates are published openly for reproducibility.
AI.result: The methodology was applied successfully across all seven gates. The bounded model-checking covered approximately one million reachable states, and the checker was validated by demonstrating it produces the shortest counterexample on a purposely broken model. The self-enhancement loop's constraints (auto-apply tightening, human-merge for loosening, auto-close on misprediction) operated as specified. Acceptance measured results for all seven gates were published, and the entire system is reproducible via a single command, with the non-bypass property verifiable in seconds.
AI.conclusion: Falsifiable release gates with machine-verifiable acceptance suites provide a rigorous, reproducible alternative to self-graded safety claims. The Antahkarana implementation demonstrates that such a methodology can be practically realized — from basic observability through to a constrained self-governing loop. Open-sourcing the runtime, tools, and gate suites allows the approach to be audited, reproduced, and applied to other agent frameworks.
